webTitle: Ukraine war briefing: Pressure stays on Russian economy until war is over, says Bessent

fields.headline: Ukraine war briefing: Pressure stays on Russian economy until war is over, says Bessent
fields.trailText: US treasury secretary speaks with Russian counterpart who is controversially attending G20 talks; India’s Modi says war must end. What we know on day 1,651
fields.bodyText: No economic relief for Russia is ‌possible ‌until its war in Ukraine ‌ends, the US treasury secretary, Scott Bessent, has told a Russian counterpart. Bessent met with Anton Siluanov, the Russian finance minister, at a G20 finance leaders’ meeting in Asheville, North Carolina, where Moscow’s representatives were a surprise and unwelcome presence. A source told Reuters that Bessent said no agreements of any kind were ‌possible ‌until the war ended. The Russian finance minister’s ⁠first in-person G20 appearance since Russia invaded Ukraine has irritated European officials ‌who are working on more sanctions against Russia. Britain on Monday ramped up pressure on ⁠shadow financial systems underpinning Russia’s war economy, doubling penalties for sanctions breaches, the UK treasury said. Fines would increase from 50% of the value of a sanctions breach to 100%, said John ⁠Healey, the UK finance minister. The UK’s National Crime Agency issued a nationwide ‌alert targeting the Kremlin-backed A7 network, which the British government has said was used to route funds and evade restrictions. Four people ⁠were killed and more than a dozen injured in Russian air attacks on the Ukrainian capital of Kyiv and the surrounding region on Tuesday, local authorities said, as a sixth day of strikes began. In Kyiv, three people were killed ⁠and another five wounded, and a fire broke out in a non-residential area. In ‌Boryspil in the wider Kyiv ‌region, one person was killed and another nine, including a child, were injured after missiles and drones ‌damaged an apartment building and a business, said the governor, Tymur Tkachenko. Odesa in Ukraine’s south came under heavy attack on Monday night, including by glide bombs, local officials said. It comes as Kyiv endures hours of daytime air raids and air raid warnings, Dan Sabbagh writes from the Ukrainian capital. Russia fired 800 jet-powered drones into Ukraine in the previous four days. Past versions of the Iranian-style Shahed drones were propeller-driven. In response, Ukrainian engineers are racing to make faster interceptor drones. “Four companies have developed the relevant interceptor drones, and one company has the most successful technology,” said Volodymyr Zelenskyy, Ukraine’s president. Nato ⁠fighter planes were scrambled, Latvia’s military said early on Tuesday, after ⁠a warning ‌of a ‌possible air ‌threat near the town of Ludza, close ‌to the Russian border. Separately, Russia’s north-western Leningrad region issued a drone ⁠threat alert, according to the governor, ‌Alexander Drozdenko. More than a dozen drones heading for Moscow were shot down, claimed the mayor, Sergei Sobyanin, on Tuesday morning. Ukrainian drones also caused damage in the Samara region, home to ⁠a number of major oil refineries about 800km (500 miles) south-east of Moscow, the local governor said. Finland restricted air ‌and maritime traffic close to Russia, armed forces of both countries said, as Russia’s north-western Leningrad region, home to major export ports, came under drone attack. Ukrainian drones have hit another Wildberries warehouse, this time in Ekaterinburg, Russia. The Russian local governor confirmed the strike ‌on Monday, claiming that drones ‌and debris ‌also struck residential buildings. There were no casualties, he said. The suspected Russian “shadow fleet” oil tanker MV Sun was boarded ⁠by the ⁠European Union’s naval mission in the Mediterranean on Sunday, said Kaja Kallas, the EU’s ⁠foreign policy chief. “The oil ‌tanker MV Sun, suspected ‌of sailing under false flag in breach of international maritime law, was boarded on August 30 in the ‌Mediterranean by Operation Eunavfor Med Irini forces for flag verification,” Kallas posted. The war in Ukraine must end for humanity’s sake, India’s prime minister, Narendra Modi, told Vladimir Putin as the two met in Kyrgyzstan. “Every day that the war continues, humanity is, in effect, set back a step, whilst every step towards peace gives all of humanity real hope for peace,” Modi said. “We need to move from endless war to an end to the war, to a cessation of hostilities. And we will need to move precisely in this direction.” Despite international condemnation and sanctions, India, along with China, has remained one of the biggest buyers ‌of Russian oil, which has helped Moscow fund its war against Ukraine. Modi and the Russian president met on the sidelines of ‌the Shanghai Cooperation Organization summit where Putin ⁠and his Chinese counterpart, Xi ⁠Jinping, also met and briefly discussed ⁠the Ukraine war, the Kremlin said. Indonesia said it was investigating claims that several citizens had joined the Russian military to fight in the war in Ukraine. Information from Ukrainian authorities was being checked, the foreign ministry in Jakarta said. It did not say how many Indonesians were under suspicion, but they risk losing their citizenship. “If the involvement of Indonesian citizens in the armed forces of a foreign country is verified, it is an individual act and does not represent the policy or position of the Indonesian government,” the foreign ministry said. Volodymyr Zelenskyy said on Monday that he ⁠held a “detailed ⁠and constructive” call with US envoys ⁠Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner. Both sides were ⁠working to finalise dates for their visit ‌to Ukraine. “I ‌also informed them about the situation on the battlefield, where Russia’s gains have been sparse and at the cost of ‌huge losses, and about the strikes,” Zelenskyy said. “We shall see what the US president’s representatives manage to achieve. September ⁠could bring about a lot of changes. And we, together with our partners, must do ‌everything we can to protect people.” Polish prosecutors are investigating a fire at a drone factory as an act of terrorism arranged by a foreign intelligence service. The fire at the WB Electronics factory in the central city of Skarzysko-Kamienna was started deliberately using a “device containing flammable materials”, a prosecution statement said. Several countries in eastern Europe have said they have been the target of spying and sabotage as part of a “hybrid war” by Russia. Ukraine’s top sanctions official, Vladyslav Vlasiuk, will visit Washington this week to urge members of the US House ⁠of Representatives to approve sweeping ⁠Russia sanctions legislation. It would enable the president to sanction Russian officials and authorise tariffs on China, India and other countries for buying Russian oil and gas. Some US lawmakers and industries are wary, though, that Donald Trump might abuse the powers that the legislation contains. The House has not yet scheduled a vote on the legislation.

webTitle: Kākāpō rising: 90 chicks swell population of the world’s heaviest parrot

fields.headline: Kākāpō rising: 90 chicks swell population of the world’s heaviest parrot
fields.trailText: Critically endangered New Zealand bird enjoys record breeding season triggered by mass fruiting of native tree, pushing its numbers to 325
fields.bodyText: The population of the world’s heaviest parrot, the kākāpō, has surpassed 300 birds for the first time in 75 years, after a record breeding season triggered by the mass fruiting of a native New Zealand tree. Ninety chicks were officially added to the population of the critically endangered birds on 1 September, pushing the total to 325 – a record high since recovery efforts began. “The last time the population is thought to have exceeded 300 birds may have been as long as 75 years ago,” said Deidre Vercoe, the conservation department’s kākāpō recovery operations manager. “We had a four-year gap between breeding seasons, so it’s fantastic to finally see the population increase after all that time.” Kākāpō, the world’s only nocturnal and flightless parrot, were once abundant across New Zealand. But their population plummeted after the introduction of predators such as cats and stoats. By the 1900s, they were nearly extinct. A recovery programme was established in 1995 with a population of just 51 birds and has battled challenges with genetic diversity, infertility and poor chick hatching rates. There are three kākāpō breeding populations, all based on predator-free islands off the South Island. Kākāpō breed only every two to four years when the native rimu trees produce large numbers of berries, so repopulation is slow. This year, after a four-year wait, a bountiful harvest of rimu berries prompted the birds to breed and produce a record number of chicks. “In the early years of recovery, it took 16 years to produce that many chicks,” Vercoe said. Kākāpō are thought to live between 60 and 80 years, can weigh up to 4kg and are famously entertaining. More than 100,000 people tuned in to watch a live stream of a kākāpō sleeping, eating and attending to her nest and chicks during breeding season. The parrots have unusual mating rituals. Male birds gather in a “lek” to produce a distinctive booming sound, emitted from air sacs in their chests while sitting in a dugout bowl in the ground. The deep boom, which can travel up to 5km, sounds similar to a softly plucked cello string. After choosing a partner and mating, females typically lay one to four eggs. The females become solely responsible for their eggs and hatched chicks for roughly six months. At 150 days of age, the chicks are fledged and considered independent enough to be added to the total population. The youngest chick of the 2026 breeding season was female Awarua-A3, who hatched on 30 March. Modelling indicated the next breeding season could occur as soon as 2028, Vercoe said. “So, while we’ll take a moment to stop and reflect on this remarkable year, we’re already looking ahead to 2028 and preparing for what could come next.”

webTitle: Iceland’s close ties with EU mean no vote is not a Brexit-style rejection

fields.headline: Iceland’s close ties with EU mean no vote is not a Brexit-style rejection
fields.trailText: A yes to membership would have given Brussels a boost but Icelanders have not voted to isolate themselves
fields.bodyText: Iceland’s 52.8% to 47.2% vote against reopening EU accession talks is, undeniably, a blow for Brussels. But claiming it as a Brexit-style victory for “national sovereignty” or evidence of broad rejection of the EU misrepresents the reality of the island’s relationship with the bloc. For the EU, Iceland was a dream candidate: small, stable, prosperous and strategically located in an increasingly contested Arctic. Eager as it is to wield more geopolitical clout and revive flagging momentum around enlargement, a vote in favour would have given Brussels a very welcome boost. Instead, Iceland’s rejection handed Eurosceptics another stick with which to beat the bloc. France’s Marine Le Pen said the result showed the appeal of a Europe of “free, sovereign nations” rather than closer integration, while Reform UK’s Nigel Farage congratulated Icelanders on “voting to keep their independence”. But Iceland is a very special case. Its situation bears precious little relation to Brexit or even to a broader EU-critical movement. Icelanders did not vote to isolate themselves from the EU, tear up any treaties or “take back control” – they voted to preserve a close, customised and largely successful relationship. Unlike accession candidates in the western Balkans or eastern Europe, Iceland does not need EU structural funds to build infrastructure or boost living standards. High per capita wealth generally insulates its population from the economic pressures that can make EU membership an attractive financial proposition. As part of the European Economic Area (EEA) and Schengen passport-free travel area, Iceland is already solidly within the European fold. It accepts free movement of goods, capital, services and people. Its markets – financial services, energy, transport – are EU-regulated and its social and environmental standards are those of the EU. That means it adopts roughly 75% of EU law and directives into domestic law and there is no question of changing that. Icelandic citizens already enjoy full EU single-market rights without full EU membership, and that, a narrow majority decided, was, on balance, good enough. Although the official reaction in Brussels was muted, some acknowledged EU dismay. “The EU doesn’t inspire people any more,” said the Belgian Green MEP Saskia Bricmont. The centrist MEP Sandro Gozi, who represents France, called it “a warning Europe should take seriously”, adding that the bloc’s “power of attraction” should not be taken for granted. Opposition to full membership was focused heavily on the country’s fishing industry, which accounts for 15% of its GDP and 40% of export revenues and which the no campaign claimed would inevitably be threatened – as during the 1960s and 70s “cod wars” with the UK – were Iceland to join the EU’s common fisheries policy. The vote also revealed a stark divide between people in the capital, Reykjavík, who largely saw membership as an additional form of security for a geographically isolated country in the age of Trump and Putin, and those on the rest of the island, many of whom are fishers and farmers, who overwhelmingly voted against. But if Iceland’s particular circumstances mean the “no” victory was not an ideological rejection of the EU and all it stands for, it nonetheless holds lessons for Brussels. The first is that existing EEA/EFTA states are harder to persuade to join the EU than countries outside the single market. For non-EEA nations, joining the EU offers transformative individual and economic benefits – unrestricted access to the world’s biggest trading bloc, freedom of movement, huge financial aid. For citizens of EEA states such as Iceland (and, for that matter, Norway), most of those already exist. When the status quo provides 80% of the benefits of membership and poses no threat (real or imagined) to emblematic national industries, the incremental gains of full accession become a hard sell. What should worry the EU more is that despite growing doubts about the US and Nato security umbrella, Icelanders were not won over by the bloc’s protection offer. For all the talk of the bloc “stepping up” as a defensive force, its mutual defence clause, which provides for solidarity if a member state is attacked, did not convince. There is, clearly, work to be done there. But as the EU law professor Alberto Alemanno argues: “Iceland’s referendum result does not reject European integration … It shows that close integration short of membership can be stable, credible and politically attractive.”

webTitle: Madrid residents brace for noise and disruption from new F1 circuit

fields.headline: Madrid residents brace for noise and disruption from new F1 circuit
fields.trailText: City council emphasises economic case for Madring amid local outrage over disruption and environmental impact
fields.bodyText: Opponents of Madrid’s newly constructed Formula One circuit have accused the regional authorities of putting profit before people’s wellbeing after tests for the inaugural Spanish Grand Prix at the track later this month yielded noise levels that were many times the legal decibel limit. The regional government of Madrid and the city council are hoping that the 5.4km-long (3.3 miles) Madring circuit – which has been built in the north-east of the Spanish capital at a cost of €83m (£71m) – will attract visitors, boost the local economy and put the city firmly on the motor racing map. The Madring bills itself as “a perfectly connected circuit: just 20 minutes from the city centre”. But recent track tests using Formula Three cars have worried local people who are taking legal action over the construction of the circuit and the noise it is expected to generate. The Stop F1 Madrid platform, which was formed a year ago, said neighbours had recorded average noise levels of 102.7 decibels during the tests, with peaks of between 107.7 and 109.1 decibels. The maximum noise level permitted in residential areas is 55 decibels. “It’s not just about the dust and the noise,” said Antonio Ibáñez, a spokesperson. He said there had been complaints from people who argued it was impossible for them to work remotely during the tests, adding: “We’ve also spoken to people who have children with autism and they had to get them out of the area because of [all the distress].” One of the group’s biggest worries is the huge numbers of people expected to descend on the area for the grand prix itself, putting an enormous strain on public transport and the local area. “An urban Formula One circuit is just a bad idea,” he said. “It’s a nonsense idea.” Regional and city authorities have sought to reassure residents and are attempting to stress the economic benefits of the track. Borja Carabante, Madrid’s city councillor for urban planning, mobility and the environment, said measures, such as acoustic panels, would be put in place to minimise noise during the grand prix on 11-13 September. He also said that the Formula Three cars used to test the track “make and emit more noise than Formula One cars, so there’ll be less noise on 13 September than there was during the tests”. Carabante said the city council would work to ensure traffic disruption was kept to a minimum. But he called on the people of Madrid to celebrate the arrival of Formula One in the city: “We should be congratulating ourselves that Madrid is hosting such an important and significant event that will put us at the epicentre of great sporting events. It’s amazing news for all the people of Madrid and it’s putting Madrid on the map.” The regional minister for housing, transport, and infrastructure, Jorge Rodrigo, said the event would be of huge economic benefit for Madrid, and well worth one weekend’s disruption. “It’s worth a little bit of sacrifice from all of us … given the profitability of this event for the Madrid region and the city of Madrid, and, above all, given how it’ll position us internationally.” A spokesperson for the Madring said it was taking “all measures within our reach to minimise the disruption caused by the construction work and the event”, adding: “Protecting the wellbeing of local residents and reducing the environmental impact are a priority for the organisers, and we are therefore working continuously with the relevant authorities and various stakeholders to implement mitigation and improvement measures.” But environmental groups have questioned the wisdom of building a grand prix circuit in a city where summer temperatures can exceed 40C (104F). According to Stop F1 Madrid , more than 700 trees have been felled or moved to make way for the track, while María Ángeles Nieto, a spokesperson for the Madrid Environmentalist platform, said a seasonal wetland that was home to amphibian species had been destroyed. “Madrid is a city with significant temperature increases during the summer months – the entire city is a heat island,” said Nieto. “We’ve pointed out that this just exacerbates that heat island effect.” Nieto said was “no justification whatsoever” for a track that would subject residents to “a living hell” for the duration of the grand prix and other possible events there. “The people in charge of the city are prioritising the economic interests of Formula One over the wellbeing of the citizens in such an absolutely absurd and unnecessary way,” she said. • This article was amended on 1 September 2026 to remove a reference to noise levels being almost twice the legal limit. The decibel scale is logarithmic, where an increase of 10 decibels reflects an approximate doubling of loudness.

webTitle: Singapore asks the $70,000 question: who wants to start a family?

fields.headline: Singapore asks the $70,000 question: who wants to start a family?
fields.trailText: Sum of financial support from a baby’s birth until age 17 is the city-state’s offer to address low birthrate and reluctance of couples to have children
fields.bodyText: With leafy cycle paths, rooftop water parks and child-friendly restaurants, Singapore’s east coast is one of the best places in the island city-state to raise a family. Finance worker Lee lives in an apartment here with his wife and two cats, but like an increasing number of Singaporeans they do not intend to have children. They worry about the challenges of bringing them up, and the disruption to their lives. He knows his parents want grandchildren: “They brought it up a couple of times when we were younger, but now they don’t bring it up any more.” The 34-year-old, who requested his last name only be used, says he and his wife feel the same. “We are happy with our lives right now, so adding a kid will kind of complicate that,” including giving up travel and not being able to go out to restaurants. A survey released this month by YouGov has found that many Singaporeans feel the same, with one in four saying they don’t plan to have children. Grappling with a historically low birthrate, the city-state announced sweeping measures to encourage couples to have children, but it is unclear how successful those measures might be. The prime minister, Lawrence Wong, has said the government will provide almost S$70,000 (US$55,048; £40,647) in direct financial support for every child by the time they turn 17. The policy begins at birth with a S$10,000 baby grant, and two separate $5,000 grants for medical and educational expenses. Other provisions include S$2,000 in “child credits” from ages one to 16, lowering government-subsidised preschool fees to S$150 a month, and giving people more parental leave. “Singapore’s future will only be as strong as the families that build it,” Wong said. Singapore’s birthrate for women of reproductive age – known as the total fertility rate – is a record low of 0.87. A rate below the “replacement level” of 2.1 is the norm around the world today, but Singapore is part of a cluster of countries in Asia with the world’s lowest rates, alongside the likes of South Korea and Taiwan. For governments, the demographic trend poses a major economic challenge, leaving a smaller proportion of working adults to support a growing elderly population. Singapore is projected this year to reach a “super-aged” status, which the UN defines as having more than 21% of its population aged 65 and above. The prime minister’s measures have received a mixed reception, with those interested in having children still worried about the expense of raising a family. The cost of living in Singapore is “insanely high” says Iqbar Hisham, 27, who works as a coordinator in the construction industry, but the new policy has given her and her fiance some hope for starting a family in the future. “These supports do encourage me to have children as soon as possible once I’m married,” Hisham says, noting in particular the help for childcare. Social pressure, including a highly competitive education system and demanding workplaces, and the need for childcare support due to both parents working are also playing into a growing reluctance among some Singaporeans to start a family. As an indication of the times, the pressure around academic results has fuelled a huge private tutoring industry as parents try to ensure their children get ahead. Teo You Yenn, a sociologist and author of Unease: Life in Singapore Families, told the Straits Times she was struck during research for her book by how consumed Singaporean parents were with extracurricular study, starting as early as preschool. In his speech, the prime minister acknowledged that many Singaporeans “worry about the future their children will inherit, and whether they are doing enough to help them succeed”. Lee says financial support from the government isn’t everything. “I think there will be a large portion of time that me and my partner will need to take out in order to raise a child correctly,” he says. “That is something that we are not able to provide at the moment.” Planning manager and mother of three Shu Rong Teo, 41, says having children has always been important for her. But having a family and retaining her job at the Singapore Chinese Orchestra was only possible with the support of a domestic helper, and by living with her in-laws. “Our experience is a testament that it takes a village to raise a child – and that family support remains indispensable for working parents navigating the demands of parenthood.” She welcomes the reforms, in particular increased childcare leave, which will allow her to spend more time with her children. “I used to have two days of childcare leave. Outside the two days, I had to take my annual leave to take care of my children, but with the new measures [my husband and I] have 12 days each. “The biggest difference will be having more time.”

webTitle: Tuesday briefing: Scotland has promised on violence against women – can it deliver?

fields.headline: Tuesday briefing: Scotland has promised on violence against women – can it deliver?
fields.trailText: In today’s newsletter: First minister John Swinney has pledged to put an end to violence against women and girls. But can he turn ambitious laws into real change?
fields.bodyText: Good morning. Violence against women and girls, in all its myriad forms – physical and mental, blatant and insidious – is a global challenge. It reaches back through millennia and, lately, it has been turbo-charged by technology, which offers abusers new ways to shame, harass and monitor victims. What would it take to eradicate it? Scotland’s first minister John Swinney wants to find out. Today, he will set out his programme for government (the Holyrood equivalent of the King’s speech), and Swinney surprised many when he pledged to put ending violence against women at the heart of his government’s ambitions for the coming year and beyond. But haven’t we been here before? Scotland has produced a raft of radical strategies, as well as legislation hailed as the international gold standard on domestic violence. So what hasn’t changed? For today’s newsletter, I spoke to equalities campaigner Talat Yaqoob, who co-chaired the Scottish government’s National Advisory Council on Women and Girls after four years until last month. I asked her what government – and societal – action constitutes meaningful change, and what other countries can learn from Scotland. But first, the headlines. Five big stories Nepal-Tibet | Rescue teams are working to reach more than 900 missing hydropower workers, who are thought to be trapped in underground areas in Nepal, after the devastating flash floods. Iran | The new US sanctions campaign is expected to push many Iranians into deeper poverty as food inflation soars. UK | The British Museum privately hosted Palantir founder Peter Thiel in a private viewing of the Bayeux tapestry, the Guardian understands. Slavery | Countries are legally obliged to consider reparations for the transatlantic slave tried, and address the legacy racial discrimination, a UN committee has said. US news | A Las Vegas jury has found former South Side Compton Crips gang leader Duane Keith Davis guilty of the murder of Tupac Shakur, bringing the case to a close nearly 30 years after the famous rapper was gunned down. In depth: Why Scotland’s pioneering laws aren’t enough We’ll find out later today the detail of the measures John Swinney is proposing, but the SNP leader’s preliminary talk has been big: pledging his personal leadership, acknowledging that alongside resources to protect those most at risk of violence right now, his government needs to address underlying economic inequalities – and hinting at the need for focused prevention when he says that lasting change requires all of society to play our part. The context for Swinney’s vow is bleak: a steady increase in misogyny and violence against women and girls across the world. In Scotland, both domestic abuse and sexual crimes are on the rise – crimes recorded by Police Scotland including rape and attempted rape, sexual assault and communicating indecently were up 10% last year and are now at their highest level since 1971. Rape Crisis Scotland has pointed out that these figures reflect a significant rise in historic offences and that, despite the best efforts of Reform in Scotland to link them with immigration, the vast majority are perpetrated by people known to the victim. Moreover, as Yaqoob tells me, technological advances have “enabled an entirely new field of violence against women and girls – deepfakes, ‘revenge porn’, online coercion and control of women through things like GPS tracking” – while the now-quotidian misogyny of the manosphere is saturating playgrounds and classrooms. A survey of Scottish secondary school boys last year found a third believed that girls who wear revealing clothing were “asking for trouble”, while a third of female teaching staff, in a separate study, reported sexist abuse from children as young as eight years old. “We also know that when there is recession, when there is poverty, there is a rise of the far right, there’s a rise of anger, and women are often the victims of that anger,” Yaqoob says. The Guardian’s own research last year found that two out of every five people arrested after participating in the 2024 summer riots had been previously reported to the police for domestic abuse. Recession hits funding too: many services are on their knees, according to campaigners, while the post-pandemic court backlog and ongoing crisis in the legal aid system continues to deny victims access to justice. *** Haven’t we been here before? When I returned to Scotland to report for the Guardian just over a decade ago, there was a new female first minister, Nicola Sturgeon, one of three women heading the main political parties at Holyrood, and you could taste the change in the air. This visibility of women in top jobs – necessary, of course, but never sufficient – was accompanied by a raft of ambitious strategies and bills. Equally Safe, launched in 2014, was a plan across central and local governments to act together on tackling gender-based violence. The National Advisory Council on Women and Girls, established by Sturgeon in 2017, brought forward radical proposals to offer two months of paid paternity leave and establish a world-leading process for complainants of sexual violence. In 2018, the Scottish parliament passed legislation to criminalise coercive control for the first time, hailed by international experts at the time as “the gold standard”, and three years later added further powers with domestic abuse prevention orders. There’s been funding for sexual violence prevention programmes in schools and universities, and a national advocacy service to support victims as they navigate the justice system. And, in 2025, a landmark justice reform bill abolished the Scottish verdict of “not proven” – a global legal anomaly thought to be a key factor in the country’s significantly lower convictions rate for rape and sexual assault. These offer a useful case study of what Yaqoob describes as “the implementation gap”. While the 2018 Act was undoubtedly radical, campaigners say it hasn’t achieved its full potential because the institutional change demanded of police and prosecutors – including the training of officers and shifting of mindset over charging decisions – hasn’t happened. Only 4% of domestic abuse crimes were prosecuted under the new legislation last year. Meanwhile, many of the 2021 powers are gathering dust because poor drafting has rendered them too difficult to implement. “There is a theme here,” says Yaqoob. “There’s no shortage of inspiring rhetoric and in some cases good strategy and legislation. What there isn’t is the priority and resources when it leaves the desk of the Scottish government and that means a lack of tangible change in women’s lives.” *** What needs to happen now? Removing this block between declaration and delivery doesn’t have to be onerous, Yaqood argues. Partly it’s about making gender equality a priority across the public sector. “Gender equality is always on the periphery of interventions. Until it’s at the centre, you can have as many big commitments as you want, but it will not make a difference enough to women and girls’ lives”. And placing gender equality at the centre is the beginning of the systemic change demanded of the police and prosecution service, as well as resourcing the tailored, often grassroots, projects that can make a difference in schools and communities – especially those designed by and for men – like the Many Good Men project which takes the conversation into football clubs. “We don’t have to reinvent the wheel,” says Yaqoob. “There are years of well-evidenced practice that we need to scale up.” Credit where it’s due: Police Scotland has done some very decent work in recent years with Don’t Be That Guy – a campaign that has young men talking directly to their peers about problematic behaviour. But the force has struggled to take on misogyny and racism within its own ranks. In recent years in Scotland, the discussion around violence against women has been dominated by arguments around women-only spaces – the UK’s most influential gender critical group, For Women Scotland, is based in Edinburgh – and unfounded claims that Scotland’s asylum population is responsible for an increase in sexual violence. Yaqoob is clear: “Anyone who tries to position themselves as protectors of women and girls, but does not have an agenda that is focused on tackling poverty, putting money back into communities for women and girls, or the need for consent and sexuality education in schools, is selling you a lie.” (For more, that broader agenda of tackling gender inequality in all its forms is the subject of a new book of essays, co-edited by Yaqoob.) *** The solution is global – and also local A global problem demands, in part at least, a global solution. As I’ve written in previous First Editions, change at street levels demands that all of us engage in small acts of solidarity. Yaqoob puts it this way: “Whether you’re calling out misogynistic language in the pub or you’re the leader of a local council allocating resources, there are so many different facets of society where people need to take more responsibility for the space they occupy.” So much of this conversation applies beyond Scotland, but back at Holyrood it’s fair to say that, while there’s a bit of eye-rolling as yet another male politician “discovers” violence against women and some head-scratching over precisely what reforms he intends to unveil, there’s also wary optimism to hear this focus at the beginning of the SNP government’s five year term. As one campaigner told me yesterday: “This is an opportunity to kick the door down for bigger changes”. What else we’ve been enjoying Rebecca Solnit is on form in this column lambasting Donald Trump’s plan to “sell off” chunks of Yosemite national park. “The US is being sold for parts or just handed over to the oligarchy,” she writes. Charlie Lindlar, newsletters team I found Ben Quinn’s acute analysis of what’s gone wrong for Reform this summer a useful primer ahead of their party conference later this week. Libby I loved this perceptive piece from Tanya Aldred on the short shelf life of football shirts. For more from Tanya on the intersection of climate change and sport, sign up to The Hotspot. Charlie The story of how Jackson Pollock’s masterwork Blue Poles became Australia’s most controversial painting takes in Gough Whitlam, the Shah of Iran and Paul Hogan – and Guardian Australia’s political editor, Tom McIlroy, tells it brilliantly in this Full Story podcast. Libby Our Laura Snapes’s music coverage is indispensable, yet not even her Taylor Swift opus can compete with this vital piece against the term “picky bits”. “It’s the Boaty McBoatface of dinner time,” she correctly argues, “exposing our once-repressed nation’s surprisingly twee core and total disregard for shame”. Charlie Sport Football | Argentina’s Lionel Messi announced his retirement from international football, following his father’s death and the World Cup defeat by Spain. Tennis | Carlos Alcaraz beat Roman Safiullin 6-4, 6-4, 6-4 in the first round of the US Open in his first match since April. Football | Bukayo Saka scored the only goal of the game as Arsenal held off a much-improved Aston Villa to make it two wins from two in the Premier League. The front pages “Public control of utilities is key to growth – Burnham”, is the Guardian’s front page today. The Times leads with “Healey: I’ll prove I’m no hypocrite on defence”, the Telegraph writes “SAS chief: Army witch hunts put UK at risk”, and the Mail has “Kemi gets Tories battle ready with ruthless reshuffle”. The i Paper’s splash is “Killer kitchen dust: victims’ loved one to receive higher compensation”, the FT says “Crunch warning for consultants as clients harness AI to cut IT spending”. The Express has “Million OAPs hit with top-rate tax bills”, and the Sun’s headline is “Prem’s £10m crypto cash frozen”. The Mirror leads with “Maxwell to beg Trump for freedom”, and Metro’s front page is “Dad’s gift of life”. Today in Focus War of words: my language lessons in Ukraine For Charlotte Higgins, the Guardian’s chief culture writer, visiting Ukraine and meeting the artists, novelists and poets under fire changed her life. “It was even before I went home that I decided I needed to learn some Ukrainian,” she tells Helen Pidd. She talks about why she was inspired to learn Ukrainian and what it taught her about its people. Cartoon of the day | Ben Jennings The Upside A bit of good news to remind you that the world’s not all bad Rachel Aroesti has always loved podcasts, especially the kind that can be described as ‘Two Men Talking (In Excessive Detail About Their Lives)“. Initially drawn to them for their humour, she began to find them hugely comforting – sometimes falling asleep listening to Adam and Joe’s BBC 6 Music show. But, as her consumption increased, she became aware that she used podcasts as a psychological crutch, to prevent being alone with her thoughts. After a silent, tech-free train ride across the East Anglian countryside, Aroesti felt she was undergoing a mental reboot. Her mind flooded with ideas, plans, insights and reflections at a speed and intensity she had not experienced for years. Nowadays, she savors silence and boredom, and has successfully reduced her listening by at least 80%. “I’ve given my mind permission to wander – both productively and pointlessly – again,” she writes. Sign up here for a weekly roundup of The Upside, sent to you every Sunday Bored at work? And finally, the Guardian’s puzzles are here to keep you entertained throughout the day. Until tomorrow. webTitle: Thai resort prepares to host USS Abraham Lincoln sailors after more than 270 days at sea

fields.headline: Thai resort prepares to host USS Abraham Lincoln sailors after more than 270 days at sea
fields.trailText: Security stepped up in Pattaya before arrival of thousands of sailors and marines whose deployment was extended due to US war in Iran
fields.bodyText: Authorities in the Thai resort city of Pattaya have stepped up security as they prepare to welcome thousands of sailors and marines from the USS Abraham Lincoln who have spent more than 270 consecutive days at sea. “About 600 officials will provide security and other necessary assistance,” the provincial governor, Narit Niramaiwong, told AFP. The nuclear-powered aircraft carrier sailed past Singapore over the weekend on its way back to the US after a lengthy deployment in the Middle East as part of the US war against Iran. It left California in November 2025 for duty in the South China Sea and was rerouted to the Middle East before the US-Israeli attacks on Iran that began six months ago. Reports of deteriorating living conditions and poor mental health onboard, including attempted suicides, have made headlines in the US and provoked criticism of Donald Trump’s war against Iran. Pattaya’s mayor, Poramase Ngampiches, said the carrier would dock just after midnight on Wednesday (about 5pm GMT on Tuesday) at Laem Chabang port. About 40 buses have been laid on to transport the sailors to Pattaya and back in staggered groups before the carrier departs on Sunday. After meeting US officials on Monday, Poramase said service members would be banned from certain recreational activities such as parasailing and cannabis use. Medical cannabis was legalised in Thailand in 2022 and dispensaries have become common in Thai cities. Once a sleepy fishing village, Pattaya was transformed by the Vietnam war in the 1960s, when US soldiers on leave began coming for rest and recreation. The city has since become hugely popular with foreign tourists, known for its beaches and a nightlife scene that has long drawn scrutiny over sex tourism. Poramase told AFP there had been a recent crackdown on sex workers but denied this was linked to the US arrivals. Government officials are warning local businesses not to overcharge US sailors, and Poramase said there would be a greater police presence in popular areas along Pattaya beach and Walking Street. The city’s police chief, Anek Srathongyoo, said law enforcements agencies had been ordered to step up security measures to prevent undesirable situations. He said that if any US service members broke Thai law, they would be prosecuted accordingly. Local business owners feeling the tourism slump from the Iran war are eager for the new arrivals. A banner hung over a local bar near a beach read: “Welcome all US military personnel. Thank you for your service.” Bualuang Ponok, a bar employee, said she had seen US service members during past visits but she did not expect many from this crew. “They said 5,000 people will come here but how many will reach us?” she said. Earlier in August, the usually Asia-based USS George Washington relieved the long-deployed Lincoln in the Middle East. The Lincoln, one of the US navy’s largest warships, was part of American efforts in the Iran war, which flared back up over the weekend for the first time in a month. The deployment included a record-setting uninterrupted time at sea of more than 270 days. Trump downplayed concerns over conditions onboard and said the deployment was “not nearly long enough”. Thai officials have said the Lincoln will return to the US after its port call in Thailand. Associated Press and Agence France-Press contributed reporting

webTitle: Echoes of cold war as US accused of meddling in another Brazilian election

fields.headline: Echoes of cold war as US accused of meddling in another Brazilian election
fields.trailText: Claims that Trump and Rubio are trying to influence result have parallels with CIA intervention 64 years ago
fields.bodyText: The year was 1962 and the Kennedy administration was desperate to swing Brazil’s congressional elections against its leftwing president, João Goulart, as a way of countering the supposed communist threat sweeping a region the US considered its back yard. Historians say that in the lead-up to the vote, the CIA and the Department of State secretly channelled millions of dollars to opposition candidates and a group tasked with spreading rightwing propaganda and stirring up unrest. “There was a very heavy-handed intervention here by the US government,” said Chico Rubens Paiva, a political activist whose congressman grandfather Rubens Paiva investigated Washington’s meddling during a 1963 parliamentary inquiry into the conspiracy. More than six decades later, Paiva, whose grandfather was murdered by the US-backed dictatorship that seized power in 1964, is among those who fear history is repeating itself on the eve of Brazil’s 2026 presidential election. October’s vote will pit the leftwing incumbent, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, against the far-right senator Flávio Bolsonaro, son of the former president Jair Bolsonaro, a Donald Trump ally who is serving a 27-year sentence for plotting a military coup. Polls suggest a tight race and Trump and his secretary of state, Marco Rubio, have been accused of trying to tip the scales in Bolsonaro’s favour by launching an overt campaign of economic and diplomatic pressure against Lula. The US measures include imposing 25% tariffs on most Brazilian imports and designating Brazil’s biggest crime groups – Rio’s Red Command and São Paulo’s First Command of the Capital – as foreign terrorist organisations. Brazilian officials suspect this is partly designed to boost Bolsonaro by making Lula look soft on crime. In July, Lula said two Trump officials had been denied entry visas because they planned “to meddle in Brazil’s elections”. Brazilian officials believe the pair, who reportedly planned to meet Flávio Bolsonaro, intended to sow doubt about the reliability of Brazil’s internationally respected voting system – something the Bolsonaros have sought to do repeatedly. Soon after, the visa of Brazil’s ambassador to Washington was revoked. Celso Rocha de Barros, a political scientist and podcast pundit, voiced bewilderment that US interference – which he considered the election’s most urgent theme – was not getting more coverage in mainstream media. “The greatest superpower in human history is explicitly backing a candidate in our election and is strangling the Brazilian economy in order to help him [win],” Barros claimed. “We cannot pretend that this isn’t happening and treat this like a normal election … the Brazilian economy is under attack.” Trump’s tactics have echoes of Washington’s cold war-era attempt to manipulate Brazilian politics in the lead-up to the 1964 coup, which ushered in two decades of authoritarian rule in which hundreds of people were killed or disappeared. Back then, the CIA helped finance the Brazilian Institute for Democratic Action, which, according to the historians Lilia Schwarcz and Heloisa Starling, illegally poured money into the campaigns of hundreds of lawmakers and eight gubernatorial candidates. “The objective was strategic: to create a strong opposition in congress, block government initiatives and prepare the way for a coup d’état,” Schwarcz and Starling argued in their book Brazil: A Biography. Another US-funded group, the Research and Social Studies Institute, was used to disrupt Goulart’s government by bankrolling anti-communist propaganda and anti-government protests. James N Green, a Brown University historian who has written a book about the period, said: “The intention [was] getting rid of Goulart [and] opening the door to the military coming to power.” Green sees parallels between Trump’s use of tariffs to sabotage Lula’s campaign and how in the early 60s Washington sought to enfeeble Goulart’s government by funding his opponents and cutting off loans. Then, as now, the US government was “bent on doing everything possible to weaken the government” in Brazil. But Barros sees one key difference between the two US gambits. “[The 1962 campaign] was done covertly, precisely because the CIA knew there would be real public anger in Brazil if people knew the US was bankrolling candidates. So they did it secretly,” he said. “Today, this is being done openly – and on an incomparably larger scale.” The Department of State rejected claims the US was seeking to meddle in Brazil’s election. “Any insinuation of a ‘ploy’ to undermine a democratic nation’s election is a baseless lie,” an official said in a statement. “We respect the Brazilian people and whatever government that they choose freely through free and fair elections in Brazil. We’ve respected and dealt with governments from both sides of the spectrum in Brazil, and had very successful relationships with them.” Last year Trump was accused of meddling in the politics of neighbouring Argentina after he threw his weight behind its rightwing president, Javier Milei, on the eve of crucial midterm elections. Milei recently attended Flávio Bolsonaro’s campaign launch in Brazil, using his speech to lambaste Lula as a “thief”. Green believes two strategic objectives lie behind the Brazilian pressure campaign being waged by Trump and by Rubio, the son of Cuban immigrants, who has made toppling Cuba’s communist government a personal project. Firstly, it is designed to weaken and delegitimise Lula’s government, making it harder for Brazil, Latin America’s largest democracy, to challenge the US economic asphyxiation campaign against Cuba. Secondly, it is about “neutralising” leftwing forces in Latin America more generally and boosting the right in the hope of helping to elect even more Trump-aligned leaders. Since 2023, a succession of radical rightwing populists have won power in Argentina and Chile, Costa Rica and Colombia. In reference to Trump’s tangerine complexion, this has been nicknamed Latin America’s “orange wave”. Paiva, 38, believes US interference is intended to have a similar effect to the abduction of Venezuela’s dictator, Nicolás Maduro – strengthening “American dominance” in a region it considers a US sphere of influence. Maduro’s removal in January allowed the US to impose a pliant successor, his vice-president, Delcy Rodríguez, who has started opening up the South American country to US oil and mining firms. Paiva believes Bolsonaro’s election will “serve the same purpose: putting people into power who will serve their interests”. He fears that as election day draws near, US social media companies could enter the fray, potentially giving Bolsonaro another lift. “Any kind of change to the algorithm has a brutal impact in the way information reaches people,” warned Paiva, who is running for a seat in congress in the election for the centre-left Brazilian Socialist party. He highlighted “the scary lurch the Silicon Valley bros” had taken into Trump’s camp during his second term. Barros is convinced the US aims to help elect Flávio Bolsonaro, “because Flávio will give them everything they want”, he said. “Flávio will make a rare earths deal no other president would. Flávio will let American big techs do whatever they like in Brazil. Flávio will reduce economic relations with China as much as he can.” He noted that Bolsonaro supporters attended rallies carrying US flags. Barros believes the campaign’s real driving force is not Trump but Rubio, who hopes to bolster a possible 2028 presidential run by showing voters he has “delivered the whole of Latin America to American interests”. “The fact is, this is an election between Lula and Marco Rubio,” Barros said.

webTitle: Norway’s new king swears oath of allegiance with daughter at his side

fields.headline: Norway’s new king swears oath of allegiance with daughter at his side
fields.trailText: Haakon VIII promises to uphold 1814 constitution but his queen misses ceremony because of post-surgery ‘complications’
fields.bodyText: King Haakon VIII swore an oath of allegiance before Norway’s parliament on Tuesday in the first major stage in the passing of the crown since the death of his father after 35 years on the throne. Wearing a ceremonial uniform, Haakon, who became king when Harald V died on Friday, promised to uphold Norway’s 1814 constitution with his 22-year-old daughter, Crown Princess Ingrid Alexandra, by his side. “I promise and swear that I will govern the kingdom of Norway in accordance with its constitution and laws, so help me God, the almighty and omniscient,” the 53-year-old king pledged to cabinet ministers and MPs in the main chamber of the 169-seat parliament. Haakon’s wife, Mette-Marit, 53, was unable to attend the 17-minute ceremony because of complications after a lung transplant in June. Her doctors said such complications were not uncommon. Are Holm, a pulmonologist at Oslo university hospital, said the queen had had “complications on some occasions with the operation, including today. As a result, she must be put under observation throughout the day today.” Harald, whose funeral will be held in Oslo on 9 September, with heads of state from around the world invited to attend, was widely appreciated in Norway for his warmth, unassuming lifestyle and dedication to preserving national unity. Tens ⁠of thousands of Norwegians have flocked to the royal palace to lay flowers, drawings, candles and flags. A poll for the public broadcaster NRK found the monarchy’s popularity had risen over the past few months. The first survey since Harald’s death at the age of 89 found that about 72% of Norwegians supported the monarchy, compared with 54% in May. In February, while the royal family was mired in a succession of scandals, support for the institution fell to 60%. Mette-Marit has faced strong criticism for her association with Jeffrey Epstein, while her son from a previous relationship, Marius Borg Høiby, is appealing against a four-year sentence for two rape convictions. Responding to Haakon’s oath, Masud Gharahkhani, the parliament’s president, who arrived in Norway as a child refugee from Iran, said Harald had personified “the values that underpin our liberal democracy”, including compassion. There will be no formal coronation of the new king and queen because Norway abolished the ceremony more than a century ago but Haakon may, like his father and grandfather, choose to have his accession consecrated at Trondheim’s Nidaros Cathedral. Harald, who will be buried in the royal mausoleum at the Akershus Fortress in Oslo, died while being treated in hospital for haemolytic anaemia, a condition caused by an abnormally rapid destruction of red blood cells.

webTitle: Russia kills at least 12 on sixth night of drone attacks on Kyiv

fields.headline: Russia kills at least 12 on sixth night of drone attacks on Kyiv
fields.trailText: Zelenskyy says Moscow is capitalising on shortage of US-made Patriot interceptors to lower morale in capital
fields.bodyText: At least 12 people have been killed in and around Kyiv overnight as Ukraine’s capital endured a sixth consecutive night of Russian drone and missile attacks aimed at shattering infrastructure and lowering the morale of the city. Eight of the dead were reported killed in Kyiv, including seven at a railway depot on the city’s left bank, and four were killed in Boryspil, to the east of the city, in a wave of strikes at about 2.30am after hours of air alerts. A further four people were killed in other parts of Ukraine, regional officials said, in 28 waves of attacks that included a strike on a border crossing point with Romania on the Danube at Orlivka. Volodymyr Zelenskyy, Ukraine’s president, said “a significant number of jet-powered drones and ballistic missiles were used in the attack” and that Russia was taking advantage of a shortage of US-made Patriot interceptors. In a morning post on social media, Zelenskyy said: “Russia always plans its strikes specifically to cause as much destruction to people’s lives as possible, and it succeeds only when air defence capabilities are insufficient.” Kyiv and the surrounding towns and villages have come under sustained attack in the past few days. Thirty-eight people were killed after a Russian drone struck an ammunition store in Myla, 15 miles west of Kyiv, on Thursday, the hit causing hours of secondary explosions and damaging nearby homes. Ukraine’s air force said Russia had attacked 28 locations, focusing on the cities of Kyiv and Odesa and their surroundings. Air defences shot down five Iskander ballistic missiles, two Banderol and five Kalibr cruise missiles and 187 out of 218 drones. Officials no longer reveal the total numbers of missiles fired. Oleksandr Pertsovskyi, the chief executive of Ukrainian Railways, said six of the seven people killed in and around the depot were employees of the network. Another rail worker was hospitalised, he added. Kyiv has been chronically short of air defence systems since the supply of Patriot interceptors dried up. The Patriots are the only weapon that can effectively stop high-speed Russian ballistic missiles, made at the rate of about 60 a month. Lockheed Martin, the US company that makes the most capable Pac-3 interceptors, produces about 600 a year, but US military supplies have been depleted during the US war with Iran. Ukraine is trying to secure a stockpile of about 300 for the winter, paid for by European allies, in a supply deal agreed with the US. Moscow appears to be trying to take advantage of an absence of air defence capability before winter, in an escalation of a conflict nearly deadlocked on the frontline. Ukraine has been responding by attacking oil refineries, warehouses and other military facilities deep inside Russia, aiming to hurt the country’s economy. Ukraine’s GUR military intelligence said it had attacked an oil refinery at the Baltic port of Ust-Luga, about 550 miles (885km) from its border. Russian officials said a civilian was killed in the border Belgorod region in an attack. Russia captured 35 square miles (56 sq km) of Ukraine’s territory during August, analysis by the AFP news agency concluded. It was Moscow’s largest advance since February but still much lower than the 150 square mile a month average of 2025. There remains little serious diplomatic effort to end the war, although on Monday India’s prime minister, Narendra Modi, urged Vladimir Putin to end the war in public remarks at a bilateral meeting in Bishkek, Kyrgyzstan. “Every day that the war continues, humanity is, in effect, set back a step, while every step towards peace gives all of humanity real hope for peace. We need to move from endless war to an end to the war,” Modi ⁠said. Putin appeared impatient, tapping his feet as he listened. “Thank you very much, prime minister. We are moving forward along this path,” he replied.

webTitle: Edouard Balladur obituary

fields.headline: Edouard Balladur obituary
fields.trailText: French prime minister beaten to the presidency by his former ally Jacques Chirac at the 1995 election
fields.bodyText: For many months before the 1995 French presidential election, Édouard Balladur, the incumbent prime minister, seemed certain of victory. Opinion polls consistently gave him a lead over his conservative rival Jacques Chirac, and the main leftwing candidate. But, as other politicians have discovered, polls can be misleading and voters change their minds. When the ballot papers were counted it was Chirac who won and succeeded François Mitterrand as president. The defeat of Balladur, who has died aged 97, was due partly to his lack of appeal to young voters, a consequence of his public image which, somewhat unfairly, was that of an aloof aristocrat. When he first became a minister, the satirical weekly newspaper Le Canard Enchaîné dubbed him “his courteous self-importance” and Le Monde’s cartoonist Plantu depicted him as a bewigged 18th-century nobleman being carried around in a sedan chair. His manner and style – three-piece English tailored suits, dislike (figuratively and literally) of getting his hands dirty and obvious distaste for close personal contact – did not play well in the context of a presidential contest. There was nothing aristocratic in Balladur’s background, however, about which he maintained a certain mystery. He was born in Smyrna, now Izmir, in Turkey, the youngest of the six children of Pierre Balladur, the manager of a local branch of an Ottoman bank, and Émilie (nee Latour). His parents became naturalised French citizens in 1932 and the family moved to France when Édouard was six, settling in Marseille, where he went to school at the Lycée Thiers. Balladur began studies in law at Aix-Marseille University, then continued them at the Institute of Political Sciences (Sciences-Po) in Paris, living for a while in the Roman Catholic hostel where years earlier Mitterrand had resided. A bout of tuberculosis temporarily interrupted his studies; once cured he completed his military service in Algeria, which was then a French colony, two years before the war of independence, when tensions were high. On his return to Paris, he was accepted into the École Nationale d’Administration (ENA), then the nursery of France’s political, business and technocratic elite. He began his career with the Conseil d’État and the former state broadcasting organisation ORTF but caught the eye of Georges Pompidou, Charles de Gaulle’s prime minister, and became his adviser in 1964. This gave him a ringside seat during the student riots and civil unrest of 1968, and the negotiations that eventually got the country back to work after a national strike. In 1969, Pompidou succeeded De Gaulle at the Élysée, and Balladur went with him, becoming secretary general of the presidency. After Pompidou’s death in 1974, a leading industrialist took Balladur under his wing, and he ran two subsidiaries of a major company, making useful contacts in business. For many years he enjoyed a plum sinecure as president of the company operating the Mont Blanc tunnel. In 1980, he returned to politics. Chirac, who had walked out of his job as President Valéry Giscard d’Estaing’s prime minister in 1976 to found the conservative RPR party and pursue his own presidential ambitions, sacked two of his closest advisers and invited Balladur to replace them. Chirac’s first presidential bid the following year failed (though it sank Giscard), but five years later the conservative right recaptured the Assemblée Nationale, and Chirac was appointed prime minister after negotiations with the socialist Mitterrand in which Balladur played a key role. In this, the first “cohabitation” (in which the president and the government are of different political families), Balladur was appointed minister of finance, economy and privatisation. He was a powerful minister, but was in office for only two years. In 1988, Chirac made a second presidential bid and lost again. The re-elected Mitterrand called a general election, and the Socialists were able to form a minority government. Balladur returned to the world of business, where he now cut a more substantial figure after his experience in government, and set about establishing networks of friends and contacts. It was clear that the Socialist-led government was heading for defeat in the 1993 general election. Chirac, as the leader of the right, was the obvious choice as prime minister after a conservative victory. But he had been so bruised by his experience as prime minister under Mitterrand’s presidency during the first cohabitation that he was not eager to repeat the experience. Balladur emerged as the clear favourite for the role, acceptable to both Mitterrand and the right. It was evident at the time that Chirac saw Balladur as a proxy for himself. One of his closest allies even suggested Balladur might make weekly visits to Chirac in the Paris city hall, where he reigned as mayor, to brief him on government business. But Balladur established himself as his own man. The second cohabitation, unlike the first, was a courteous affair. The public took to the new prime minister, and seemed to appreciate the absence of confrontation between Mitterrand and Balladur. Balladur had never been one of the barons of Gaullism or Chirac’s version of neo-Gaullism, and his instincts appeared to favour Christian democracy on the German model more than the national populism of the likes of Charles Pasqua or Philippe Séguin. There was no shortage of crises – over reform of immigration laws, a strike at Air France that saw clashes between workers and police, the minimum wage for young school leavers, funding for church schools and the plight of French fishermen. Abroad, there were some serious questions over France’s role in the genocide in Rwanda. But Balladur avoided taking on protesters, preferring discreet withdrawal when it appeared there was strong opposition. He was credited with a success in the talks on the General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade (Gatt) in 1993. It rapidly emerged that, far from being a surrogate for Chirac, Balladur was a man with views and, more importantly, ambitions of his own. Month after month, polls showed strong public support for him. Relations with Chirac and his allies deteriorated in spite of occasional public and unconvincing displays of unity. It is not clear when he decided to stand for the presidency, but he formally declared his intention in early 1995. Much of the centre-right and two significant RPR figures – Pasqua and the future president Nicolas Sarkozy – rallied to him. But Chirac had found an issue on which to campaign: the “social fracture” in French society. In the slightly improbable role of the outsider castigating the technocratic elites, Chirac struck a chord, particularly with the young. Balladur’s efforts to reach out to the people, including climbing on tables at public meetings, to much general derision, were less successful. His opinion-poll lead melted, and in the first round of voting Lionel Jospin, the socialist candidate, came top with 23% of the vote, followed by Chirac with a little under 21% and Balladur at 18.5%. Chirac won the run-off. The new president was not the man to forgive what he regarded as treason, and in the new government there was no place for Balladur, who, however, retained political ambitions. When it became clear that Jean Tiberi, Chirac’s successor as mayor of Paris, was tainted beyond political redemption by scandal, Balladur, after some hesitation, declared his candidacy. If he had hoped for help from Chirac, he was disappointed. Tiberi and Balladur split the centre right vote, allowing Bertrand Delanoé to become in 2001 the first leftwing mayor of the city since the Paris Commune 130 years earlier. Balladur continued to serve as an MP until 2007. In later years, questions began to be asked about the financing of his 1995 presidential campaign. The allegations centred on the sale of submarines to Pakistan and possible bribes, commissions and kickbacks. In 2002, a bomb in Karachi killed 14 people, 11 of them French employees of the national shipbuilders. Al-Qaida was initially suspected, but later it was suggested that on taking office Chirac had stopped the payment of kickbacks to middlemen and the bombing had been an act of revenge or intimidation. There were reports that some of the money had found its way into Balladur’s campaign funds. Certainly, claims that the huge sums of cash in large-denomination notes paid into campaign accounts were the product of the sale of T-shirts did not convince everyone. Several members of his entourage were investigated and charged by magistrates looking into alleged misappropriation of public funds in what became known as the “Karachi affair”. In 2017, Balladur himself was charged with funnelling kickbacks on state arms deals with Pakistan and Saudi Arabia, alongside the former defence minister François Léotard. In 2021, the court of justice of the Republic ruled that there was no evidence that Balladur had personally ordered payments linked to the contract, nor sufficient proof to establish the origins of his campaign financing, and he was acquitted of all charges. Léotard was found guilty, and given a suspended prison sentence and a fine. Balladur’s wife, Marie-Josèphe (nee Delacour), whom he married in 1957, died last year. They had four sons, Pierre, Jerome, Henry and Romain. • Édouard Balladur, politician, born 2 May 1929; died 31 August 2026 • Stephen Jessel died in 2025

webTitle: Russia targets Ukraine’s rail network as war enters deadly new phase

fields.headline: Russia targets Ukraine’s rail network as war enters deadly new phase
fields.trailText: Six employees killed on Tuesday after Moscow escalates attacks on infrastructure and Ukrainian capital
fields.bodyText: Russia has opened a deadly new phase in its war against Ukraine by deliberately targeting the country’s railway network, with six employees killed on Tuesday in the latest strikes on Kyiv. Ukraine’s state-owned railway company, Ukrzaliznytsia, said its workers died when a ballistic missile plunged into a locomotive depot. The Russians hit other railway facilities, it added, during a massive bombardment of Kyiv and the Kyiv region. At least 12 people died, with a dozen wounded, including three children. “An unbearably difficult night for the entire railway family. Railway staff have been working at the scene since early this morning. The attack has caused significant damage. Rescue workers are still putting out a number of fires,” said Ukrzaliznytsia’s chair, Oleksandr Pertsovsky. The grim strike took place as Russia escalated its attacks on the Ukrainian capital. It has carried out continuous raids for six days, beginning last week, in an attempt to disrupt daily life and demoralise the city’s inhabitants. The onslaught took place hours before Ukrainian children began a new school year. Since Russia’s full-scale invasion, 58 railway staff have been killed and at least 318 injured. One wounded railway employee, Volodymyr, was taken to hospital on Tuesday, with people urged to donate blood if they were B positive – his group. “Our colleagues are by his side,” Ukrzaliznytsia said, adding it would support victims’ families. Ukraine’s railway network is Europe’s third largest, with 15,000 miles (24,000km) of track. It has been a lifeline for the country’s wartime civilians, transporting four million people and an estimated 120,000 pets. It has brought world leaders to Kyiv, including Joe Biden and Andy Burnham, who arrived last week on an overnight service from Poland. Serhii Leshchenko, a member of Ukrzaliznytsia’s supervisory board, described the railway as the “backbone of Ukraine’s economy”. It was the main logistical supplier for the country’s army and industry, and every week transported 600,000 people, he told the Guardian. With 170,000 workers, it was also Ukraine’s biggest company. For these reasons Russia was trying to destroy railways, he added. In the first year of the war it attacked bridges, which could be easily replaced. Next, it targeted rails and electricity substations. Ukraine then switched to using diesel engines. This year, Russia started “direct attacks on civilian locomotives”, he said – an insidious tactic, at a time when Ukraine is short of air defences. Several drivers have been killed and locomotives targeted inside depots. Leshchenko said that if a Shahed drone came within 50km of a train, it had to be evacuated, and could only continue once the threat has passed. So far this year Russia has hit the network more than 1,500 times – a higher figure than in the whole of 2025. Overall, 249 carriages and 492 locomotives have been damaged. Once known for their punctuality, trains now suffer regular delays, sometimes lasting as long as 12 to 15 hours. Amid air raid sirens, passengers are forced to disembark and take cover, including during winter. Writing on Facebook, the Ukrainian journalist Tetiana Zaiets described how she hid in April when Russian drones flew overhead. “It was hell. The train stopped at night somewhere in central Ukraine. I don’t even know the name of the town. Half asleep, I just heard the conductor say ‘evacuation’. We took only our personal belongings and valuables with us. It was raining outside. Thank you to the conductors for handing out blankets,” she posted. She added: “That’s how we held out for two hours. While kamikaze drones were buzzing overhead, we crawled under a goods wagon. The last carriage in the train was full of children. They were being taken back from hospital. They were crying in their sleep. I thought I’d ended up in some sort of horror film. But no, this is our life.” Since the incident, Zaiets said she was too frightened to travel by train. “Until the war is over, I won’t be using it,” she said, stressing she respected Ukraine’s “courageous” railway workers. Last week, an enemy drone hit a train in the Odesa region with 600 people on board, including 15 children. “The train was stopped, we were kicked out. We heard explosions, everything was burning. It was scary,” one passenger, Andriy, told the website Suspline. Another passenger, Eva, said she was evacuated twice, and “dropped off in a field”. “We sat there and heard something flying. Then we saw a drone very close by.” She managed to collect her belongings and was eventually picked up by a bus, she said. Leshchenko admitted the Russian strikes were hurting Ukraine’s economy and had slowed the export of grain from its under-fire Black Sea ports. He said Kyiv needed air defences from western partners, so it could protects its trains from marauding missiles and drones. “If the whole country is under attack, they will attack railways for sure,” he said. Up until this year more than 90% of Ukrainian trains arrived on time. This was in part down to the fact engines never go especially fast, rolling at 55mph. Carriages are clean and comfortable: the best way of getting around a vast country. Stewards look after night train customers and bring them morning tea in filigree holders. There is a trolley on day trains, and patchy wifi. On international services, border guards scrutinise male passengers, while dogs roam up and down corridors. Since the invasion, men between 18 and 60 have been forbidden from leaving the country, with some exemptions. On trains from Kyiv to Przemyśl, a railway hub in eastern Poland, most travellers are women. Since 2022 about six million people have departed abroad, many exiting by train. In recent days Russia has launched over 1,500 drones at Ukraine, 800 of them jet-fuel models, which are harder to shoot down. In the past, Moscow would send a swarm of drones a couple of times a week, usually at night. Now the attacks continue without a pause, with one or two drones dispatched every hour, paralysing ordinary life. Air raid sirens in Kyiv are non-stop. Pertsovsky, Ukrzaliznytsia’s boss, described the loss of his employees on Tuesday as “terrible”. “We are in touch with their loved ones. Everyone is with them to get through this extremely difficult time. The night is bitter with impossibility,” he wrote.

webTitle: Nepal-Tibet flood deaths pass 1,000 as police ask relatives for DNA to identify victims

fields.headline: Nepal-Tibet flood deaths pass 1,000 as police ask relatives for DNA to identify victims
fields.trailText: Relatives of missing tourists asked for blood samples and photos, as efforts continue to rescue trapped hydropower workers
fields.bodyText: Nepali rescuers have built temporary bridges to reach remote areas and dug through the ruins of hydropower projects in the Himalayas to rescue hundreds of trapped workers, as the death toll passed 1,000 nearly ⁠a week after devastating floods left a trail of destruction across the country’s towns and valleys. About 600 people remain stuck in several devastated hydropower stations that have become the focus of rescue efforts. The prime ⁠minister, Balendra Shah, said more than 11,000 people had been rescued across the affected region, and power and communication lines had been restored in some areas. “Thousands of citizens have lost their homes, families, loved ones and property,” Shah said. Six days after the catastrophe struck the Himalayan border region, 4,400 people were still missing in Nepal and Tibet. Police in Kathmandu have urged relatives of missing tourists to provide DNA samples to assist identification efforts. In a statement posted to social media, Nepal police on Monday asked relatives of those missing to “provide a fresh blood sample for DNA profiling and two passport-sized photographs” to the pathology laboratory at the Nepal police hospital in Kathmandu, or the nearest district police office. Among Nepal’s list of the missing are 592 foreigners, including tourists who had come for mountain trekking and Hindu pilgrims seeking spiritual peace at Tibet’s sacred Mount Kailash, from countries such as India, the US, UK, Australia and Canada. Relatives abroad have been requested to undergo DNA profiling at an authorised laboratory and to “send a soft copy of the DNA profile to Nepal police’s official email address”. In some of Nepal’s flood-affected areas, hundreds of unidentified bodies have already been buried because they are decomposing and there is no room left in hospitals or morgues. At the police hospital in Kathmandu on Tuesday, more than 100 people were waiting to have their blood sampled. Among them was Prakaiti Jurnj. Her mother was still missing, but the family had been able to identify her father’s body from a photograph on the wall outside the teaching hospital, where images of the deceased have been posted in an effort to identify the victims. “Both my father and mother, they were in the village in Nukawot. They were both swept away by the flood,” she said. “We haven’t heard from them since Wednesday. We found my father’s body; my brother saw the photo on the wall.” She was waiting for her two other siblings, who live in the UK, to arrive on Tuesday so they could all try to get up to the village. She said she wanted to contact her grandmother or sister-in-law, who she thinks both survived the flood because their house is further up the mountain. Their village was still in a blackout, and making contact was impossible. “I can’t go there; the situation is very bad,” she said. “I can’t go up there alone. I am not sure if we’ll be able to get them.” The disaster was triggered by a glacier collapse that sent a deluge of ice, rock and mud through Nepal’s border region with China, posing a massive challenge for the country’s six-month-old government. The region is vulnerable to flooding and landslides, and extreme weather events such as intense monsoons and melting glaciers have become more common because of warming due to human-caused climate change. In a late-night social media post, Shah said aid worth more than $42m had poured into the country, but that Nepalis were reeling. “The government understands the immense pain they are enduring. The path ahead is to ‌support them through this suffering and help ‌them return to normal life through rehabilitation,” the prime minister said. Shah also said that 279 workers had so far been rescued from hydropower projects, where authorities estimated close to 1,000 people had been trapped. Days after the disaster, hope was rapidly diminishing that any of those trapped in a series of tunnels could be alive. Pictures and videos shared by rescue teams showed earth-moving equipment digging and shovelling mud and rocks under lights in the dark of the night. Soldiers used torchlight in a big pit they had created to look for space to get into one tunnel. Chinese state media coverage has focused largely on the official response, highlighting the deployment of firefighters, the People’s Liberation Army and instructions from top leaders. Little is known about victims on the Chinese side. The flood was “caused by glacier instability under the long-term effects of global warming”, China’s state broadcaster said on Monday. Shah said the catastrophic event signalled the growing risks that the Himalayan region faces. “The region must therefore remain vigilant. The time has come for us to strongly raise before the international community the disasters we are experiencing as a consequence of climate change,” he wrote in his post.

webTitle: Peekaboo island: the floating forest confounding nature watchers in western Canada

fields.headline: Peekaboo island: the floating forest confounding nature watchers in western Canada
