fields.headline: Trump ally defends Venezuela oil deal amid ‘gunpoint diplomacy’ criticism
fields.trailText: Energy secretary Chris Wright denies US seeks to ‘take’ country’s oil, saying deal is transformation of relations
fields.bodyText: The US energy secretary, Chris Wright, has denied Washington is seeking to commandeer huge quantities of Venezuelan oil, amid growing criticism of Donald Trump’s energy deal with the country’s interim leaders. “Absolutely not,” Wright replied when asked by a CNBC journalist if the US was engaged in a “heavy-handed” attempt to “take” Venezuelan oil in violation of the South American country’s constitution. Wright landed in Venezuela’s capital, Caracas, on Tuesday night, four days after Trump announced what he called “the biggest oil deal in world history”. “I think we are seeing an absolutely historic transformation of both Venezuela and the relations between Venezuela and the US,” Wright said of the deal, which Trump has claimed will give the US control of 65bn barrels of Venezuelan oil. “This is President Trump’s grand plan to replace conflict with commerce,” Wright said. The White House says the deal will help secure US “energy dominance for the next century” as well as “purging foreign malign influence from our back yard” by excluding China and Russia from oilfields in the country with the world’s largest proven oil reserves. But there has been criticism from across the political spectrum. The Wall Street Journal’s editorial board said Trump’s deal with Venezuela’s unelected interim president, Delcy Rodríguez, “looks less like a normal commercial transaction than it does the famous scene of US businessmen meeting with the Cuban strongman in The Godfather Part II”. “The US government is essentially getting in bed with a foreign dictator and her favored capitalist,” the newspaper complained, in reference to Alejandro Betancourt, the Venezuelan tycoon at the centre of the deal. The economist Francisco Rodríguez told Democracy Now: “It’s clear that this is not a deal that any Venezuelan government would have entered into unless this country had been subject to an invasion, and unless its authorities had been held at gunpoint. So I think we’ve replaced gunboat diplomacy now for gunpoint diplomacy.” Delcy Rodríguez was installed as interim president on 5 January, two days after the president, Nicolás Maduro, was abducted by US special forces during a predawn raid on Caracas. Trump warned Rodríguez, who was Maduro’s vice-president, she would face an even worse fate if she did not toe the US line. Since Maduro’s capture, Rodríguez has made a series of once unthinkable concessions to US officials who their nominally socialist political movement, Chavismo, had spent years denouncing as predatory imperialists bent on stealing Venezuela’s natural resources. On Saturday, Rodríguez claimed the oil deal had “endless” benefits and would help produce more than $209bn in revenues that could be used to improve healthcare and education. “We are thinking of Venezuela’s future,” she said during a televised broadcast to the nation. The deal has dealt a body blow to Venezuela’s political opposition, who fear Trump is unlikely to push for a democratic transition or fresh presidential elections given his lucrative arrangement with Rodríguez. “This is a game between the Trump administration and Delcy and her people,” one opposition figure lamented after the deal was unveiled. Speaking at a signing ceremony in the Miraflores presidential palace in Caracas on Wednesday, Rodríguez thanked the Trump administration for its part in what she called a “win-win deal”. She said: “I have faith in the future of Venezuela. What we are doing today represents the future and the hope of the people of Venezuela.”

webTitle: ‘How do I not crumble?’ Loved ones of Australians missing in Nepal-Tibet floods fear others are turning away

fields.headline: ‘How do I not crumble?’ Loved ones of Australians missing in Nepal-Tibet floods fear others are turning away
fields.trailText: In Sydney, Akash and his younger brother are just trying to keep going while their parents remain among the more than 4,000 missing people
fields.bodyText: Akash Venkatraman’s parents wished him a happy 22nd birthday before they left for Nepal on a spiritual pilgrimage. Three days later, a glacial collapse sent a torrent of mud, water and debris through the Nepal-Tibet border, bursting the banks of the Trishuli River, and sweeping away homes, bridges and roads. He hasn’t heard from them since. Venkatraman Balakrishnan, 52, and Chitra Venkatraman, 46, are among 38 Australians who have been reported missing after the deadly flash floods and landslides on Wednesday last week. The couple and their family friends – Sreedharan Iyer, 52, Lakshmi Iyer, 50, and their sons Rishab Iyer, 23, and Rudhra Iyer, 20 – had been taking part in a pilgrimage to the sacred site of Mount Kailash. They were staying in riverside accommodation in Syabrubesi with other members of the Himalayan Glacier Adventures tour group the morning the flood came in. In the days since losing contact, Akash has cried – as a psychology student, he knows not to repress his emotions – but he has also tried to keep going. His parents would have wanted him and his 17-year-old brother who is studying for HSC to maintain normalcy, but it is difficult, he says. “What if I graduate and they’re not there? What if I get my first job and they’re not there?” Akash says. “Because everything you do, you do to make them proud.” Sign up for the Breaking News Australia email ‘That’s my biggest worry’ Akash’s uncle has now travelled to Nepal to search for clues while he and his brother try to help from home. Their family has received an outpouring of support from the community, but as the days pass, Akash worries that Australians’ attention is falling away and that “efforts to find my parents and everyone else with them will also reduce”. “The worst thing that could happen is that they hang on for seven or 10 days and no help comes – that’s my biggest worry,” he says. “Us losing attention could create that situation.” As of Thursday, Nepal’s National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Agency reported 1,204 confirmed deaths and 4,216 missing persons (including 583 foreigners). Police in Kathmandu have urged relatives of missing tourists to provide DNA samples to assist with identification efforts. Though five Australians previously believed to have gone missing in Nepal have now been confirmed safe, the government still holds “grave concerns” for those still unaccounted for. In Kathmandu, the anxiety is palpable. The wall of missing loved ones at the teaching hospital has quadrupled in size. Other hospitals around the city, like the trauma centre, are also filling up. ‘I can’t’ On Wednesday, Uttam Tamang, 25, was standing outside the National Trauma Centre in Kathmandu, clutching his heart. “We are searching for my brother,” Tamang says. His brother, 25, was an electrician working at a hydro plant in the upper Ruswian region – the army has not been able to get in there yet. Now, Tamang spends his days going from hospital to hospital. “I just,” he touches his chest. “I can’t,” he says. Sita Thapa Magar is standing outside at the teaching hospital – her younger brother, Anil Thapa Magar, is also missing in a hydroplant tunnel in the upper region. And they, like many other families, are also doing the daily rounds of hospitals. She says there has not been enough information from the army about why they haven’t been able to search the tunnels yet. “Every day we are looking for information from the government,” Thapa Magar says through a translator. “But we are not getting much information about the missing. “So we have to come here every day; we give his details. It’s been a week, and still, there is not much information.” ‘Still just a crumb’ As the morgues in Kathmandu fill up, a temporary burial site has been set up on the outskirts of the city. While golfers strode around the course next to the forest on Tuesday, police officials laid 85 people from up the valley to rest. It is one of many temporary burial sites around the country. DNA samples and photographs are being collected so families can later reclaim their loved ones’ remains. In Sydney, Sarada Viswanathan, the partner of Rishab Iyer and a longtime friend of his family, is taking matters into her own hands. The 23-year-old medicine student has set up a search HQ from her Sydney home, where family and friends come together to look for signs of their loved ones. They have been monitoring official Nepali websites and calling embassies and nearby hospitals and camps. Every day, they are tracking down the social media accounts of rescued people to ask whether they recognise any of their family members and have liaised with a Jeep vendor company in Nepal so they can track the cars their relatives were driving. “It’s still just a crumb, and we’re trying to follow that trail, but we need a lot more crumbs and a lot more help to get us there,” Sarada says. Akash and Sarada are calling on the Australian government to increase its military and humanitarian support in Nepal, with their petition receiving more than 12,000 signatures. On Thursday, the foreign affairs minister, Penny Wong, announced the government would send a team of specialist drone operators to Nepal and pledged a further $3m in aid, bringing Australia’s total aid package to $11m. The Gyirong Port area, where the Iyer family and Akash’s parents were last believed to have been heading towards, was finally opened on Wednesday. Chinese state media reported the road was open from the Tibetan border and rescue equipment could be brought in. Sarada’s relatives who are in Nepal have been barred from entering the area by the army, so she is hoping Australia’s official on-foot rescue teams will be able to reach Rishab and his loved ones. “I can feel his energy. Even when I’m sitting here, I can feel him next to me, and I can feel that he’s still here, and he’s trying his very best,” Sarada says. “I know that they’re very strong people, they have a very strong will, and I know that they wouldn’t give up. So I’m not going to give up on them either.” Akash could also travel to Nepal to join his uncle in the search effort, but for now he is committed to securing a future for him and his brother. “The next few days is about ensuring that if the worst case happens, how do I not crumble with it?” he says. “Because the worst-case possibility is that I’d have to take care of the family … and take responsibility for our lives.”

webTitle: Iran accuses US of ‘war crime’ after missile blast kills four people at wedding

fields.headline: Iran accuses US of ‘war crime’ after missile blast kills four people at wedding
fields.trailText: Blast also injures 68 guests at the wedding in southern Iran, prompting fears of escalation in hostilities
fields.bodyText: Iran has accused the US of a war crime after a missile blast killed at least four people and injured 68 who were attending a wedding at a private home in a coastal city of southern Iran, as the fresh exchange of strikes prompted fears of a wider renewal of hostilities. Iranian media said that the wedding ceremony was being held in a home in the city of Kuhestak, Hormozgan province, late on Tuesday when a US missile struck, with shrapnel and debris from the strike killing and injuring people. Among the dead was a four-year-old child, Amir-Ali Karimi, and a 16-year-old, Mohammad Mollahi. “It’s a terrible thing. I’m extremely worried and upset about what happened – really upset,” Ali Mollahi, the father of the bride, told Mehr News. A video of the aftermath shows colourful wedding streamers and decorations strewn across the ground, and shoes abandoned in the rush to escape the attack. “You wicked people have attacked people’s homes and turned their wedding ceremony into a funeral,” said a man filming the aftermath of the strike, shared by Fars news agency. The deputy of the provincial government, Ahmad Nafisi, said first responders had headed immediately to the scene and transferred the wounded to the hospitals. Iran’s foreign ministry spokesperson called the US attack a “war crime” and said Iran “will respond to these savage crimes with firmness”. The chief Iranian negotiator, Mohammad Baqer Ghalibaf, said the attack had killed families with children, and called the US the “great Satan”. “If a power acts like Satan, picks targets like Satan and kills like Satan, it’s Satan. Shields a junior Satan that does the same? It’s THE Great Satan,” Ghalibaf said in a post on X. The US attacks followed strikes on Sunday, ending a month-long uneasy truce between the US and Iran, and appeared to signal a resumption of another cycle of escalation. US Central Command (Centcom) said the overnight strikes focused on Iranian military targets, including air defence sites, radars and maritime assets. Iran responded by launching drones and missiles on US bases across the Middle East, including in Bahrain, Kuwait and the UAE. Iran’s military spokesperson, Lt Col Ebrahim Zolfaghari, vowed “heavier, broader, and more crushing and devastating” retaliation. Videos of the aftermath of the strike show a caved-in roof, blown-out windows and ground riddled with debris, as well as walls pockmarked with what appeared to be holes from shrapnel. Footage from a nearby hospital showed women in wedding attire watching as injured children were being treated. “When we arrived there, an explosion occurred. It was very intense. Bricks, stones and cement hit me in the face and head, and many others were injured,” a child who was injured at the wedding told the state-affiliated Fars news agency. A woman with her hands decorated in henna for the nuptials posted a video on Instagram after the attack, saying “my hands and feet are still shaking”. A spokesperson for Centcom, Tim Hawkins, said the US was aware of reports of civilian casualties, but the “US military never targets civilians, unlike the [Iranian Revolutionary Guards Corps]”. In February, a strike on an elementary school killed at least 156 people, including more than 120 schoolchildren. Independent investigations concluded that the US likely carried out the strike with the assistance of AI, though the US government said the incident remained under investigation. Pictures of shrapnel collected at the site of Tuesday’s attack were published on Iranian state media, and appeared to show the internal components of US munitions. Trevor Ball, an independent weapons analyst, identified some of the remnants as belonging to the Standoff Land Attack Missile-Expanded Response (Slam-Er) missile, which is made by the US weapons company Boeing. The Slam-Er is a 1,500-pound, GPS-guided missile touted by Boeing to be “extremely accurate”. It was unclear if the home where the wedding was being held was struck directly, or if a missile hit close to the home and debris from the strike hit the home and its occupants. CCTV footage captured at least six strikes in the area within a minute. A separate strike appeared to hit a communications tower about 150 metres away from the home. Authorities said that several “telecommunications and internet towers and sites were also seriously damaged in the latest strikes”. The US has been targeting communications and radar infrastructure along Iran’s coast to try to stop its blockade on the strait of Hormuz, a chokepoint which prior to the US-Iran war was a transit point for at least 20% of the world’s oil supply. Iran has virtually closed the strait since the start of the Iran war, frustrating the US president, Donald Trump, who is facing a midterm election with expensive gas prices and knock-on inflation across the board. In recent weeks, the US has focused on trying to degrade Iran’s capacity to strike ships transiting the strait to reopen the waterway for traffic.

webTitle: Russian airspace becoming unsafe for commercial airlines, Zelenskyy says

fields.headline: Russian airspace becoming unsafe for commercial airlines, Zelenskyy says
fields.trailText: Ukraine president says aviation industry needs to take account of growing number of Ukrainian drones in Russia
fields.bodyText: Volodymyr Zelenskyy has declared that Russia’s airspace is becoming unsafe for commercial airlines, as Vladimir Putin promised to increase strikes against Ukraine’s energy facilities in the run-up to winter. The Ukrainian president said there was no intention to directly threaten civilian flights, but the growing number of attack drones being flown into Russia by Ukraine would have to be “taken into account” by the aviation industry. “We want to warn every airline that uses Russian airspace, every insurer, and everyone who still uses Russia’s key airports: Russian airspace is becoming completely unsafe,” Zelenskyy said in a statement. Ukraine’s foreign secretary, Andrii Sybiha, said Kyiv had notified the International Civil Aviation Organization that “Russian airspace is not safe for civilian aviation” because of increased military activity. A rapid escalation of Ukrainian military capability in the past few months has allowed Ukraine’s forces to strike at targets around Moscow, St Petersburg and other locations deep inside Russia. Reliable figures for the number of drone flights are hard to obtain but Ukraine is already capable of launching a few hundred a day, and military sources say the country is chasing a target of 1,000 drones in an effort to hurt Russia’s economy. Justin Bronk, an aviation analyst at the Royal United Services Institute thinktank, said he believed Ukraine could force “periodic closures of Russian airports on a semi-regular basis” by relying on an element of surprise. It could do so by flying small waves of drones at short notice, though trying to close an airport permanently would be difficult, he said, because a sustained attack would become predictable and easier for air-defence systems to halt. Ukraine’s commercial airspace has been closed since the beginning of the full-scale invasion in February 2022 because Russia has been able to strike targets throughout the country, making airports unsafe for civilians. This year, Ukraine began bombing oil refineries and warehouses near Moscow and St Petersburg, as well as hitting military and industrial sites at ranges in excess of 2,000km (1,250 miles) from its border. Concerns linger about the safety of civilian aviation in the war zone. A Malaysian Airlines plane flying over eastern Ukraine in July 2014 was shot down by Russian separatists operating a surface-to-air missile launcher. All 298 people onboard were killed. Putin described Zelenskyy’s remarks as “state terrorism”, saying: “Negotiations are not conducted with terrorists.” Giving one of his most detailed updates on the war, the Russian leader told a news conference that Moscow was preparing to increase its bombing of Ukrainian energy facilities this winter, aiming to knock out heating and electricity supplies. “The Russian armed forces have been ordered to prepare and carry out mass strikes on Ukraine’s energy facilities. They are striking us, and they will get a response,” Putin told reporters after a two-day summit in Kyrgyzstan. “I’m not saying we’ll collapse the economy there, but it’s a serious challenge for them.” Asked whether Russia would strike British military facilities in the UK that produced weapons for Ukraine, Putin sidestepped the question, saying: “That’s a military secret.” Russia earlier accused the UK of “escalation” and threatened “consequences” after reports that British-made drones were used by Ukraine in long-range strikes deep inside its territory. Putin sought to stress that Russian forces retained the initiative on the battlefield in Ukraine, despite Moscow’s slowing progress. He appeared to push back against western intelligence reports suggesting he was being given an overly optimistic picture of the war, saying he relied on numerous sources of information that together provided him with an “objective assessment” of the battlefield. Russia’s sluggish advance on the battlefield has fuelled speculation that the Kremlin could resort to another round of mobilisation, the first since Putin called up about 300,000 reservists in September 2022. Zelenskyy and western officials have said Moscow could be preparing such a move, though its diplomats do not consider it a certainty. Putin dismissed the prospect as “nonsense”. Also on Wednesday, the European Commission president, Ursula von der Leyen, said a drone attack on Leipzig airport marked a new escalation by Russia, and that it fitted a broader pattern of “repeated incursions in our airspace, drones that paralyse our airports, interference with our critical infrastructure”. The German government said on Tuesday that Russia was responsible for a drone laden with explosives which was discovered at Leipzig airport last month near a Ukrainian plane used to transport weapons. Von der Leyen said: “Europeans are faced with the hard truth that this is the new normal. We have to step up, and that means being ready to respond to Russia’s recklessness faster and better.” The Nato secretary general, Mark Rutte, told reporters Russia had grown “increasingly reckless” and there had been an increase “in malign activities targeting our territory directly”. The EU is drawing up further sanctions against Russia targeting about 1,600 companies and individuals. Poland’s foreign minister, Radek Sikorski, said the bloc should pass these sanctions in response to the Leipzig attack and others. “Hybrid war is not just nuisance on the internet,” he said, speaking on the sidelines of a meeting with his European counterparts. “Hybrid war means assassination squads, it means arsonists, it means blowing up moving trains, like in Poland, it means breaches of airspace with drones and cruise missiles. We need to convince Putin that such actions are not for free.” The EU foreign policy chief, Kaja Kallas, said the Leipzig attacks had the “hallmarks of state-sponsored terrorism”, adding that Brussels had summoned Russia’s ambassador to the bloc.

webTitle: After the flood: human suffering on an unfathomable scale in Nepal’s worst-hit districts

fields.headline: After the flood: human suffering on an unfathomable scale in Nepal’s worst-hit districts
fields.trailText: Thousands remain missing and aid is hampered by treacherous conditions in communities almost wiped out of existence
fields.bodyText: Searching for the body of his wife in the mud, Dil Bahadur Shrestha lamented that he did not even have a shovel left. For now, he has been using his hands to try to find her as he picks through the ruins of his house. On Wednesday morning last week, Jamuna Shrestha, his wife of 50 years, had been at home in Betrawati on the banks of Nepal’s Trishuli River, feeding her beloved chickens and goats. As deadly flash floods coursed down the river valley, Jamuna was last seen going back into her house, trying to usher her chickens to safety, while others fled uphill. Now that house stands like a muddy carcass, everything inside it destroyed or washed away by the violent force of the water and debris that killed more than 1,200 people in Nepal and Tibet. Dil Bahadur Shrestha, 70, had been tending to his rice fields and feeding his cows on the opposite bank when he felt the ground tremble and saw a black wave, hundreds of metres high, coming down the valley. He ran to safety in the forest, but not before watching two bridges get swept away behind him. “When it hit, everything was destroyed within two minutes,” he said. Dil Bahadur Shrestha, who is searching for his wife of 50 years, Jamuna. He knows in his heart that his wife is gone, but like thousands caught up in the disaster, her body has yet to be found and she is counted among the missing. More than 5,000 people are reported missing in Nepal and a further 546 in the Tibet region of China. Rescue workers have still not reached Dil Bahadur Shrestha’s home, so he returned to try to retrieve her body himself. “Maybe she thought the flood wouldn’t reach inside the house,” he said, wiping away tears. The couple had already rebuilt their home once after an earthquake in 2015 that killed about 9,000 people. As he spoke, his frail body collapsed to the barren, muddy ground where his neighbour’s house once stood. “Even now, I cannot believe that she is gone,” he said. “I cannot forget her. That’s why I keep walking around looking for her. I still feel as if she might be walking around somewhere here. I keep getting this feeling that she might still be here, looking after the chickens and the goats.” A Rasuwa district sign in the flood debris in Betrawati. The scale of the tragedy in Betrawati is unfathomable. It was 8.37am when a melting glacier high up in the Himalayas on the border between Nepal and Tibet crashed into the valley below, setting off deadly flash floods down Nepal’s Bhotekoshi and Trishuli rivers. By 8.50am, with only a few minutes’ warning, the settlement of Betrawati was engulfed. This once-thriving market town was submerged in mud so thick that only the top two floors of a six-storey building are visible. Most houses were washed away entirely or flipped on their sides by the sheer force of the floods. School buses lie overturned. A grocery shop was swept 200 metres from its original location and lies in ruins. The river itself has diverted to a new path that cuts through where the highway once was. An overturned school bus hit by the flood water. Fragments of the lives of the thousands who lived here lie scattered in the debris: kettles, teddy bears, a record-keeping book, saucepans, medicine packets, a pair of glasses. At least 250 people are missing, Dil Bahadur Shrestha’s brother and sister-in-law among them. As Dil Bahadur Shrestha surveyed the ruins of his life, search and rescue teams stood on the opposite bank, looking for the dead. By the end of the day, they had pulled 24 bodies from a single house. A helicopter thundered overhead, white body bags swinging underneath. “I feel there could still be hundreds of bodies here,” said Dil Bahadur Shrestha. “So many people were swept away all at once, carried off by the raging water.” His voice broke: “Now I’m alone. I am completely alone.” Santamaya Lawat tries to retrieve some of her belongings. A few metres away, Santamaya Lawat, 57, stood shaking a thick cake of dirt from the few clothes and blankets she had been able to retrieve from her brother’s home, now only partly standing, with a gaping hole in the side. Her own house, built just 10 months ago with her life’s savings, was still so filled with mud she had not yet been able to get inside. Five members of her family are gone. Santamaya Lawat has lost five members of her family as well as her home and her brother’s home next door. “My heart broke when I came back,” she said. “This was supposed to be the house I lived in for the rest of my life, but everything is gone. It was like heaven here and now it has been turned into hell.” *** Further up the river, in the district of Rasuwa, on the border with Tibet, the scale of destruction only gets worse. Many of the villages here were swept away entirely and are only accessibly by army helicopter. Some are still so cut-off and the ground conditions so precarious that the fate of hundreds of people remains unknown. On Tuesday, police search and rescue teams confirmed they had finally been able to begin ground operations in the border village of Timure, recovering 90 bodies so far. A week after the disaster, survivors who fled up mountainsides were still being collected by army helicopters and evacuated to the army base in Dhunche, Rasuwa district’s administrative headquarters. The mountain village of Syabru Besi was among those wiped clean away, with even the road to the village gone. According to local government officials, at least 500 people there are missing, a quarter of the population. The village resembles nothing more than a muddy riverbed, just one building left standing. Chhiring Dorje, a 50-year-old farmer, was among those who managed to escape Syabru Besi, but five of his family are missing. “There were 15 or 16 of us from the village who made it safely to the forest,” said Dorje. “We stayed there for two days before the army came in a helicopter. We had nothing to eat. We survived by drinking water from the forest.” He stood tightly holding the hand of his nine-year-old granddaughter, Ritu Tamang, who wore a big pink rucksack as they waited at Dhunche army base for a ride down to Kathmandu. Rescue helicopters thundered in and out every few minutes. She said quietly that there was “nothing left where our house used to be. I used to go to school and was in Grade 1. Now the school is gone. There are no teachers either.” Chhiring Dorje, a 50-year-old farmer, was among those who managed to escape Syabru Besi, but five of his family are missing. Chhiring Doreje’s granddaughter Ritu Tamang – waiting to be taken to Kathmandu. With the highways washed away, the only road from Kathmandu to Rasuwa is a perilous unpaved track of mud and stones, weaving through tiny mountain villages. The journey often takes more than 12 hours. The treacherous conditions have made it difficult for aid to reach the worst-hit areas and hindered the rescue and relief operations. Many aid trucks are now stuck in Dhunche, unable to drive further north. At a small relief camp on the road between Betrawati and Dhunche set up by Nepal’s Dhulikhel hospital, people collected medicine and food supplies. Doctors said dozens of the children here had lost their parents in the floods. More than 200 children from the local Nilakantha school, most aged between five and 11, are also missing, believed to have been washed away as they walked to morning classes. Prakash Nepal, a teacher. Prakash Nepal, a teacher, said the school had received a warning just 10 minutes before the flood waters hit, when the school bus was already picking up students. “Luckily, we immediately contacted the bus driver and the vehicle stopped midway so the students were able to survive,” he said. “The surge of water did reach the vehicle, but thankfully it did not cause much damage.” However, many of the local families had been displaced by the 2015 earthquake and still lived in informal settlements along the riverbank. Most of those children had been walking to school when the flood struck. Prakash Nepal’s eyes welled with tears: “We could not save the students who were still on the road.” Amid the tragedy, there were also small stories of hope. Sitting on the porch of their village home in Lachyang, Ram Krishna Neupane, 69, and his wife, Muiya Neupane, 66, said their only son had been working as a vet in Syabru Besi when the village was hit. For two days afterwards they heard nothing and feared he was dead. Then they received a phone call. “He called up from a hospital in Kathmandu; he had been rescued by the army,” said Ram Krishna Neupane. “He could not speak, he was crying so much and we were crying.” It was, added his wife, “a miracle”.

webTitle: Leipzig airport attack fallout exposes Germany’s deepening divide over Russia

fields.headline: Leipzig airport attack fallout exposes Germany’s deepening divide over Russia
fields.trailText: The government’s tougher stance towards the Kremlin is drawing attacks from both the far right and far left
fields.bodyText: Even before the German government laid the blame this week on Russia for an attempted drone attack at Leipzig airport, the topic of German ties to Moscow was high on the political agenda. But the timing of the unsurprising yet explosive Leipzig announcement – days before a key regional vote – has exposed the extent to which German politics is polarised on the issue. Leading the polls nationally and in the state of Saxony-Anhalt, which votes this weekend, is the far-right Alternative für Deutschland (AfD). The party has repeatedly called for a closer bond with the Kremlin, and crucially, for its cheap oil and gas to flow to Germany once again, despite Moscow’s unrelenting onslaught on Ukraine. Germany is already on tenterhooks. The interior minister, Alexander Dobrindt, had warned that Berlin faced a growing threat of hybrid warfare, and on Wednesday morning, the day after the Leipzig announcement, police were investigating a second sabotage assault on the electricity grid within just 24 hours. An explosion at Augsburg railway station in the early hours of Wednesday morning also initially looked like it might fall into the same category, illustrating the extent to which the country remains nervous and on high ‌alert for attacks on its vital infrastructure. Investigations into all these incidents and others from the near past, many of which are said to be linked, are ongoing, even as authorities warned against drawing premature conclusions. Moscow has denied involvement, and accused Berlin of trying to divert attention from its own domestic problems, including the rise of the far right, and the state’s failure to protect its own infrastructure. The resulting uncertainty, chaos and angst appear to be nothing less than grist to the mill of the AfD. Its foreign policy spokesperson, Markus Frohnmaier, accused the government of sorting acts of sabotage “according to political expediency”. While it had “escalated the situation against Russia within days”, he said, the 2022 attack on the Nord Stream pipeline, for which Ukrainian operatives are suspected of being responsible for sabotaging a key route for Russian gas to Germany, had so far remained without consequence. (Two Ukrainian nationals named by Germany as suspects have been arrested over the attack, with one last year extradited from Italy and the other currently in Croatia.) “This is not a consistent security policy, but rather a double standard in foreign policy,” Frohnmaier claimed, adding he was convinced the government would use the Leipzig incident “as justification for even more support for Ukraine and an even deeper involvement of Germany in this war”. The AfD, which has called for talks with Moscow, ending sanctions against Russia, and slashing support for Ukraine, has urged the government to lay bare its proof of Russia’s involvement, saying so far the evidence is lacking. Wary of escalating a conflict with Moscow, the government of Friedrich Merz waited days before making its painstakingly worded declaration. In a more frank admission than the German government has ever made, foreign minister Johann Wadephul stated: “We are not at war, but we are a daily target of hybrid warfare.” The details released on Wednesday of two Russian suspects identified as having been involved in the Leipzig incident are unlikely to assuage the AfD’s complaints or, it would seem, the far-left party Die Linke. Its leading MP, Dietmar Bartsch, said on Wednesday that the suspicions of Russian involvement did not justify the government’s decision to shut down the Russian consulate in Bonn as well as a sprawling Russian cultural centre in Berlin and would not make Germany safer. On the contrary, they increased the risk of a “major war” drawing closer, he said. With the AfD on around 42% in the eastern state of Saxony-Anhalt and possibly poised to form the first far-right-led administration since the second world war, Merz’s Christlich Demokratische Union (CDU), on around 22%, is under intense pressure. Within Merz’s own party, there have been growing calls for him to toughen his stance against Moscow and pure frustration that it has taken so long. For years, members of his Christian Democrats and his current coalition partner, the Social Democrats, along with generations of diplomats, have remained caught up in, and seduced by, the long-standing romantic notion that Russia could be tamed by trade and energy pipelines, according to the CDU’s Roderich Kiesewetter. The former soldier and the party’s respected foreign policy expert told broadcaster InfoRadio that Germany “must give up its caution with regard to Russian state terrorism on German soil, as well as this romantic notion of Russia as a great cultural nation. Russia cares not a damn about this caution, but rather sees it as an invitation to keep escalating.” He criticised Merz’s recent public reference to Russia as a great cultural nation, “because great cultural nations do not subject their neighbouring states to war, violence and child abductions”. He said it was time for Merz to name the current Russian regime for what it was. Konstantin von Notz, foreign policy expert for the Greens, praised the government’s “significantly clear language” over Moscow’s behaviour, even as he described it as “long overdue”. The extent to which voters in Saxony-Anhalt fear how a further deterioration of relations with Moscow could affect them may yet be felt at the ballot box.

webTitle: Israel ‘seeking Trump’s support for plan to expel Palestinians from Gaza’

fields.headline: Israel ‘seeking Trump’s support for plan to expel Palestinians from Gaza’
fields.trailText: Defence minister says he believes US backing could tip regional balance in favour of forced resettlement
fields.bodyText: Israel’s defence minister has said his country is seeking Donald Trump’s support to approve plans to expel Palestinians from the Gaza Strip in what has widely been condemned as a potential war crime. Israel Katz said there was “no real solution for Gaza in the end without this migration” during a conference hosted by the Israeli news site Ynet and the newspaper Yedioth Ahronoth. He said the Israeli government was “organised and prepared to get them out by sea, by air, by every way possible”. Trump discussed a US takeover of the Gaza Strip in early 2025 that would have involved removing Palestinians from the territory, but has since pulled back from the idea. A 20-point peace plan the White House drew up last year did not call for Palestinians’ deportation, an act that would be widely seen as ethnic cleansing. Katz, however, said on Wednesday that he believed US support could tip regional opinion in favour of the forced resettlement of Palestinians from Gaza. He said Trump’s approval was crucial to convince neighbouring countries to accept Palestinian refugees. “Every country that is willing to take them in wants American backing,” he said. “Trump has not cancelled this at the moment. He has frozen it.” The White House did not immediately respond to a request from the Guardian for comment on whether Trump was continuing to hold discussions on Israel’s proposals to forcibly depopulate the Gaza Strip. Katz pointed in particular to Egypt, which he said had lobbied Washington to oppose the forced removal of the Palestinian population. “It has not been cancelled,” he said. “It is being discussed all the time, including now, and I think there is no other solution in the end that is in everyone’s interest.” The remarks come during a competitive election season in Israel in which the prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, and his rightwing allies have appealed to voters by calling for more aggressive measures against Palestinians. Some have been openly inflammatory and cruel. The far-right national security minister, Itamar Ben-Gvir, posted footage on X from a women’s prison where he said he was responsible for the dire conditions in the facility. When one prisoner told him they were not receiving medical care, showering or receiving clean clothing, Ben-Gvir said: “The good conditions in the prisons are over. This is the current situation, and I am directly responsible for everything. I am pleased with these conditions.” Netanyahu visited an Israeli military post close to the yellow line in the Gaza Strip on Wednesday. Israel has said it would not pull back from that line until Hamas disarmed, despite calls for a phased withdrawal to facilitate a recent ceasefire with the group. “We control the territory and are staying on this line,” Netanyahu said. “We are doing everything to achieve our goal – disarming Hamas and demilitarising Gaza. Gaza will no longer pose a threat to Israel.”

webTitle: Bayeux tapestry loan symbolises ‘entente amicale’ between France and UK, says King Charles

fields.headline: Bayeux tapestry loan symbolises ‘entente amicale’ between France and UK, says King Charles
fields.trailText: Monarch tells Emmanuel Macron at the British Museum in London that the two nations will share a future ‘woven together’ by history and shared values
fields.bodyText: The loan of the Bayeux tapestry was “the best possible symbol” of the “entente amicale” between France and the UK, King Charles said, as he visited the famous embroidered masterpiece at the British Museum in London. Though the tapestry recounts a conflict, “here it is today, nearly 1,000 years later, as a precious symbol of trust, at a time when trust seems sadly to be in short supply between nations,” he said. The “70 metres of memory and artistry” were a reminder “that our two nations have been bound together for almost a millennium”, added Charles, speaking at the new exhibition and accompanied by the French president, Emmanuel Macron, and UK prime minister, Andy Burnham. In a speech partly delivered in French, he said: “We have defended our values together in times of peril; we continue to do so today across the world.” He continued: “May this tapestry – and the treasures that will travel in return – stand as symbols not only of our shared past, but our shared future: a future woven, as it should be, by Britain and France together.” Macron, also speaking in French and English, said that the return of the tapestry “had required a little patience”, since he first spoke of it in 2018. “Since the first British request dates back to 1931, I choose to regard eight years as something of a speed record,” he said. He added that, with the tapestry in Britain, his hopes were that the two countries could “forge a bond as close as the threads of this thousand-year-old embroidery”. The tapestry – the embrroidered record of the Norman conquest – has returned to the UK for the first time in almost 1,000 years, and is on loan until September 2027 as part of a special trilateral agreement between the UK, France and the museum. Charles’s reference to entente amicale followed his use of the phrase to rebrand the famous “entente cordiale” between the two nations in his banquet speech at Windsor Castle when he hosted the Macrons in July last year. During Wednesday’s visit, he expressed his “deepest appreciation” to Macron and the French people “for the trust you have placed in the United Kingdom by agreeing to this unprecedented loan”. He said: “It once depicted warriors crossing the Channel; yet today it forms part of a cultural exchange that will see some of the British Museum’s own precious artefacts travel to France in return, in a spirit of friendship.” Thanking all those who made the loan possible, he added: “Anyone studying the tapestry’s scenes in detail will notice that, even in the 11th century, historic events rarely happened without extensive discussion, careful planning and a great deal of organisation beforehand.” The party, which also included Queen Camilla, France’s first lady, Brigitte Macron, and Burnham’s wife, Marie-France van Heel, stopped at key moments along the 11th-century artwork to hear from curators about historic events such as the coronation of Harold Godwinson and the much-disputed depiction of his death by an arrow to the eye at the Battle of Hastings in 1066. At his first prime minister’s questions earlier on Wednesday, Burnham said: “The loaning of the tapestry is a great example of French-British cooperation, the same cooperation that has helped us reduce summer small boat crossings to a seven-year low.” The Labour leader also said the Bayeux Around Britain programme, which will see the digital exhibition displayed in museums, galleries and castles in all four nations, would “give communities across the UK the opportunity to learn about one of the defining stories of our past”. In exchange, Britain will lend the Sutton Hoo treasures – an assemblage of gold and other historic objects dating from the 7th century AD – and a selection of Lewis ‌chess pieces and other masterpieces owned by the trustees of the British Museum to museums in France.

webTitle: Gun found in French lake is analysed by 2012 Alps killings investigators

fields.headline: Gun found in French lake is analysed by 2012 Alps killings investigators
fields.trailText: British tourists reportedly discovered Luger pistol that is latest in long line of potential leads in mystery of al-Hilli deaths
fields.bodyText: Experts are examining a gun found by tourists to determine whether it might have been used to kill a British family in the French Alps 14 years ago. In what remains an unsolved murder case, Saad al-Hilli, 50, his wife, Ikbal, 47, and her mother, Suhaila al-Allaf, 74, were shot dead on a road near Chevaline, a remote Alpine village near Lake Annecy, in eastern France, in September 2012. The couple’s two young daughters, then four and seven, survived but a passing cyclist, 45-year-old Sylvain Mollier, was also killed. The French prosecutor Marie-Céline Lawrysz confirmed that a pistol, thought to be a Luger, was uncovered on 20 August by two tourists swimming in Lake Annecy. The weapon is currently being analysed by ballistics experts in France in connection with the al-Hilli cold case. During the initial investigation, pieces from the butt of the weapon used in the killings, a vintage Luger P06-29 pistol, were found on the ground near the British-registered BMW estate car that the family had been driving at the time of the attack. The gun was identified as a model used by the Swiss army in the 1930s, but its owner has never been traced. In a statement, Lawrysz said a semi-automatic pistol had been found by the tourists, reported to be British, at a depth of about five feet, a few dozen metres away from the shore of Lake Annecy. She said: “They kept the weapon for 24 hours and conducted online research to identify its type. “They subsequently drew a link between the discovered weapon and the one believed to have been used in the Chevaline [near Annecy] killing on September 5, 2012. “On August 21 2026, they handed the weapon over to gendarmes from the local Saint-Jorioz brigade.” Detectives have so far ruled out the possibility of a contract killing, saying a professional killer would not have used such a vintage weapon as the Luger. The discovery of the pistol is the latest in a long line of leads that investigators have followed in an effort to unravel the mystery that has surrounded the four deaths. Suspects previously arrested in connection with the case include an Iraqi prisoner known as Mr S who was claimed to have said he had been offered “a large sum of money” to kill Iraqis living in the UK. Mr al-Hilli’s brother Zaid was also arrested on suspicion of murder in 2013, but was later told he would face no further action after police found there was insufficient evidence to charge him with a crime. In 2022, another suspect was questioned but released without charge. Two years ago, DNA analysis was ordered by detectives in France’s cold case unit on clothes belonging to the victims, as well as on the pieces of the gun and cigarette butts found at the scene. No arrests were made following the tests. • This article was amended on 3 September 2026. An earlier version said the murders took place near the “remote Alpine village” of Annecy. In fact, the location was near the village of Chevaline, near Lake Annecy.

webTitle: Maltese tycoon found not guilty of involvement in Daphne Caruana Galizia murder

fields.headline: Maltese tycoon found not guilty of involvement in Daphne Caruana Galizia murder
fields.trailText: Yorgen Fenech cleared on both charges he faced over 2017 killing of journalist that prompted global outrage
fields.bodyText: One of Malta’s richest men has been found not guilty of involvement in the murder of the anti-corruption journalist Daphne Caruana Galizia. The verdict, which is expected to be appealed against by the prosecution, came as a blow not only to the victim’s family, but to the politicians and campaigners who regard the case as a landmark action in the fight to protect press freedom in Europe. Nearly nine years after Caruana Galizia’s death in a car bombing in October 2017, a jury of six women and three men found Yorgen Fenech, 44, not guilty of both counts with which he had been charged: complicity in the voluntary homicide of Caruana Galizia, and association with the intention of committing a crime. Delivered at 7.30pm, the verdict was decisive. To gasps from the gallery and cheers from Fenech’s relatives, the forewoman announced jurors had voted to dismiss both counts by an eight-to-one majority. As Caruana Galizia’s family listened in shock, with some relatives in tears, the judge, Edwina Grima, immediately ordered Fenech’s release from custody. If convicted, he would have faced a life sentence. He left court through the front entrance, without responding to requests for comment. “Everybody is much more at risk now, because this signals you can kill journalists with impunity,” Caruana Galizia’s sister, Corinne Vella, said. “We knew an acquittal was a huge possibility. But it’s like when someone dies, it still shocks you.” In a message on Facebook, the journalist’s eldest son decried a “terrible decision by the jurors that our country may never recover from. They had a great responsibility to deliver justice. And washed their hands of it”. The leader of the opposition Nationalist party, Alex Borg, requested the urgent reopening of parliament, which is currently in recess, to discuss the verdict. “We believe journalism is the backbone of a democracy,” said Borg, speaking to a crowd of demonstrators that had assembled on Wednesday night outside parliament. He described the verdict as a black spot on the Labour government, and said the press should be free to do its work “independently and without undue pressure”. Fenech, an influential businessman and property developer whose family owns two Hilton hotels and has a share in a power station in Malta, had been accused by prosecutors of paying €150,000 (£129,000) via a middleman, Melvin Theuma, to have the journalist killed. The murder of Caruana Galizia, who targeted Fenech and leading political figures in her reporting, triggered the most consequential political scandal in Malta’s postwar history, becoming a rallying point for anti-corruption and press freedom activism. The fallout resulted in Joseph Muscat, the then prime minister of the EU’s smallest member state, being forced out of office along with two of his ministers and his chief of staff. While Muscat left office, the party he led remains in power. In a statement, the government noted the verdict and appealed for prudence in public comments at a delicate moment, insisting: “The government remains committed to seeing justice served by its institutions.” The two-month trial laid bare the extent of Fenech’s network of political contacts, and raised questions about attempts to sabotage and interfere with the police investigation. Key witnesses, and the defendant himself, claimed the prime minister’s chief of staff had repeatedly leaked sensitive information to Fenech. Summing up the case against him, prosecutor Anthony Vella said Fenech believed he could “buy justice”, telling the jury: “You are being asked to decide whether a man who had extensive contacts in politics and among the heads of public entities had enough power to pay for Daphne to be killed.” The defence argued that the chain of command went higher, with suggestions from Fenech and his lawyers that the person who had ordered the killing was Muscat’s former chief of staff Keith Schembri. They said police had not done enough to investigate allegations about his involvement. “All roads lead to Keith, and all bridges to Keith were burned,” the defence lawyer Charles Mercieca said in his summing up. In his testimony, Fenech told the jury: “I never ordered Daphne Caruana Galizia’s murder, or anyone else’s. I had no role in her murder.” He said he had merely acted as a messenger between Schembri and Theuma, and that the taxi-driver had blackmailed him. Schembri, who gave evidence at the trial, denied all wrongdoing, saying he had no involvement in leaks and no knowledge of the murder. Fenech’s defence lawyer, Giannella de Marco, said Schembri and others should have been investigated. She said the prosecution’s chief witness had not been believed. “The jurors did not believe Melvin Theuma. It was an eight-one verdict, which means unanimous … don’t you think jurors saw who the real masterminds were?” she said. The vote was effectively unanimous because juries in Malta rarely convict 9-0, as this would allow the public to know for certain which way individual members voted. Repubblika, a Maltese campaign group, called for a “national reckoning” in which the corruption investigated by Caruana Galizia, who was 59 when she died and one of Malta’s best-known journalists, is prosecuted. “Those politically responsible for the culture of impunity of the Muscat years must not be rehabilitated into public life. The state must sincerely accept its responsibility and apologise to Daphne’s family,” a spokesperson said. Occupy Justice, meanwhile, described the verdict as “deeply painful and disappointing”, saying Malta remained “without full accountability for the person or people who ordered her murder”. An independent public inquiry, for which the family fought, concluded in 2021 that the state had to shoulder responsibility for the killing because it “created an atmosphere of impunity, generated from the highest levels”. It made a number of recommendations, many of which have yet to be implemented. In a statement, the Daphne Foundation said: “Nine years after Daphne’s brutal assassination, the institutional failures that enabled her murder remain unaddressed and unreformed. Lasting justice means no person should ever face the same risks again. Our country failed to protect Daphne’s life. It owes it to her to prevent other lives being lost.” Tom Gibson, the deputy advocacy director of the Committee to Protect Journalists, was in the courtroom for the verdict. In a statement, he said: “This is a heartbreaking verdict for the family after years of waiting for justice. We will continue to stand by them while they seek accountability for all of those involved in the murder.”

webTitle: Ukraine war briefing: ‘Shameful’ – Zelenskyy furious after shootout between Kyiv’s spy services

fields.headline: Ukraine war briefing: ‘Shameful’ – Zelenskyy furious after shootout between Kyiv’s spy services
fields.trailText: Only shoot at Russian occupiers, president says, after three officers wounded in clash; Patriots could take years to make, says Rubio. What we know on day 1,653
fields.bodyText: Volodymyr Zelenskyy blasted Ukraine’s SBU and GUR after a shootout in Kyiv between the two intelligence and security services reportedly left three officers injured. The SBU is Ukraine’s internal security service, like MI5 or the FBI. The GUR, or HUR, is its armed forces counterpart and also carries out military activities and special operations. Reports said the gunfight stemmed from the SBU taking into custody a leader of an anti-Kremlin Russian unit that fights for Ukraine under the watch of the GUR. Ukraine’s president called the situation “absolutely shameful” as he called in prosecutors and investigators, as well as firing a senior SBU officer. “Here in Ukraine, shooting is only permissible at Russian occupiers in defence of Ukraine,” Zelenskyy said. “Our state will not perceive any other shootout as something that anyone is allowed to do.” Russian drones hit central Kyiv on Wednesday in a seventh ⁠day of intense strikes on the capital. Explosions were heard again in the early hours of Thursday morning. On Wednesday, 11 people were wounded, and residential and ⁠university buildings damaged. Russia also struck power facilities in the southern Odesa region with missiles and drones, authorities said, knocking out power to more than 350,000 homes. Two people were killed and eight wounded in strikes on the south-eastern city of Dnipro, the regional governor said, where food warehouses and educational buildings were damaged. Norway has seized ⁠a Russian cruise ship over unpaid compensation for the illegal annexation of Crimea. In April ⁠2023 a tribunal in The Hague ordered Russia to pay Naftogaz $4.22bn to compensate for its Crimean assets that were seized when Moscow’s forces invaded. Naftogaz is a Ukrainian state oil and gas firm. Russia has refused to pay the compensation. Naftogaz said the seizure was ordered by the ‌Nord-Troms and Senja district court on 31 August. It said the vessel, the Professor Molchanov, was owned by Russia and used for commercial expedition cruises, including to the Norwegian archipelago Svalbard. Ukraine has urged the UN’s aviation agency, the ICAO, and its member countries ⁠to ban their airlines from Russian airspace, a day after Volodymyr Zelenskyy warned it was “becoming completely unsafe” because of Ukrainian drones. Ukraine wrote to agency seeking “the full prohibition by ICAO member states of civil aircraft operations within the airspace of the Russian Federation”. In response to Ukraine’s warning, the ICAO called on its members to ensure the safety of civilian aircraft. “Long-range weapons systems, unmanned aircraft systems [UAS], global navigation satellite system radio frequency interference, and advanced air defence systems are among the military technologies jeopardising civilian aviation.” It could take Ukraine several years to start building Patriot air defence interceptors and doing so is not an immediate solution for Kyiv, Marco Rubio has said. “I mean, these are highly sophisticated weaponry,” the US secretary of state told Fox News. The US was negotiating with Ukraine over licensed production of Patriot missiles, Rubio said. “That may come to fruition, but it really won’t solve the short-term challenge that they’re pointing to,” he said, adding that “the whole world is asking for more air interceptors” but US needs came first. “It’s become the number one defence need on the planet, not just for Ukraine, but on the planet,” including in the Middle East because of the US-Israeli war against Iran. Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Ukraine’s air raid alerting system would be revised into two tiers – red for missiles, yellow for drones – allowing for more “predictability and a better understanding of how to react”. He added that curfew ⁠hours would be reduced and more above-ground transport options offered to compensate for metro closures. The measures were a response to “Russia’s changing tactics” and “its use of drones to wear down civilian life in our cities and disrupt normal economic activity across our country”, Zelenskyy said. Belgium has continued to block EU attempts to use €200bn in frozen Russian assets for Ukraine’s benefit. Opposition from Belgium has forced EU members to instead give Ukraine a €90bn loan off their own backs – but as that fund runs down, four countries have pushed to reopen the debate on the Russian assets. Belgium’s foreign minister, Maxime Prevot, said the Belgian government’s position remained “unchanged … Using these assets through a process akin to confiscation carries significant risk.” The EU foreign policy chief, Kaja Kallas, said after ministerial talks in Ireland that fresh funds for Ukraine should ultimately come from Russia. “That is why some of the member states were proposing to go back to the discussion of the frozen assets. And we will continue that discussion.” Britain’s sanctions enforcer, the OFSI, has fined Citibank £4.7m (US$6.35m) for failings and errors that led to banned Russians getting access to funds. Most of it happened between February and November 2022, the OFSI said. The CBNA London branch processed 970 payments totalling £19.7m – some for state-owned shipping company PJSC ‌Sovcomflot, as well as Alfa-Bank, PJSC Gazprombank and Credit Bank of Moscow. The agency did not consider there to have been any intent by CBNA London to breach sanctions, and the bank voluntarily disclosed most of the breaches. A Citi spokesperson said it ‌welcomed the conclusion of the ‌case and took sanctions compliance seriously.

webTitle: Thursday briefing: What life is like in a West Bank village under siege from Israeli settlers

fields.headline: Thursday briefing: What life is like in a West Bank village under siege from Israeli settlers
fields.trailText: In today’s newsletter: After a summer of increasing violence and settlement expansion in the West Bank, a Palestinian-American details his experience returning to his besieged village
fields.bodyText: Good morning. In the coming days, Andy Burnham’s new government is expected to announce a ban on trade with Israeli settlements on the West Bank. It’s a move long anticipated by campaigners, and after a summer of escalating violence across the West Bank and the expansion of Israeli settlements that are illegal under international law, the UN was warned last month that the area is “at breaking point”. But this is not just a story about high level diplomacy and global trade. It is a story about people’s homes and gardens – people who simply want to walk around them in peace. One of those people is Loui Abu Ridi, and this morning marks the 26th day that his house in the northern West Bank village of Qusra has been besieged by settlers. First, the headlines. Five big stories UK politics | In his first prime ministers questions, Andy Burnham blames the Conservatives’ legacy for leaving the UK vulnerable to market turmoil. US news | JD Vance has said he is “doing as much of God’s work as possible” and that he is OK “if that leads to the end times”, which he says “are coming”. Tech | The UK government does not know what the country’s datacentres are being used for, despite fears over the growing environmental cost of the AI boom, a freedom of information request has found. Nepal-Tibet | There is a high chance that dozens ⁠of workers may be found alive after a week trapped in an underground chamber at Nepal’s Rasuwagadhi hydropower plant, a ⁠Nepal electricity authority official has said. Defence | A former defence minister has admitted misleading parliament over the existence of crucial medical records relating to nuclear bomb test veterans. In depth: ‘We live hour by hour’ Over the past two years, Loui Abu Ridi and his family have worked hard in their garden, which overlooks the village of Qusra, planting cherry, fig and olive trees, installing solar lights and a path to walk through the saplings. But in recent months, harassment by local settlers has intensified: they smashed windows, ripped out cabling and attacked his brother with rocks. They brought their sheep into Ridi’s yard – the sheep ate the saplings. Then, at the start of August, a group of settlers erected a tent outside his house and encircled two others, trapping the residents and blocking access to food and medical supplies. “When my brother called the police, they sent the military,” Abu Ridi explains, “but instead of helping him, they took selfies with the settlers”. “Now, we live hour by hour,” he tells me. The jeopardy is constant: just before we speak, a group of armed militants was circling his property in an ATV. His 83-year-old mother has run out of medicine, but any supplies must be negotiated via the village mayor and take days to arrive. His neighbour’s children should have gone back to school this week after the summer break. “Those kids, they cannot live their childhood. They cannot even go out in their yard to play.” I don’t speak Arabic, but Ridi speaks fluent English – he’s Palestinian-American, and grew up in Qusra, but left to study in the States, and he now runs a chain of gas stations in Ohio. With the assistance of the US embassy, he returned to the West Bank from midwest America soon after the siege commenced in August to be with his mother, brother and sister. “I was escorted into my house and since then, I have not left.” *** What is the West Bank, and who lives there? It’s nearly 20 years since I last visited the West Bank, and I can still remember the scream of a Palestinian mother as a bulldozer splintered the walls of her two-storey house, smashing bright, woven rugs and framed family photographs into dust and debris. The destruction of Palestinian homes and the expulsion of communities has been continuing for decades on this area of land on the west bank of the river Jordan. Since the Six Day War in 1967, the area, including Gaza, has been under Israeli occupation. The first Israeli settlements were established on the West Bank soon afterwards, backed by politicians across party lines, and have been formally recognised as violating international law ever since, although Israel has long disputed this interpretation. In 2024, the International Court of Justice declared that Israel’s continued occupation of Palestinians land unlawful. The 1995 Oslo peace deal created three administrative areas in the West Bank intended to constitute a future Palestinian state, a prospect consistently undermined by successive Israeli governments and their supporters in the settler movement. That encompasses both hardline right factions who claim historical and religious rights to the West Bank as the ancestral land of the Jewish people and other groups, and politicians on the left, who claim Israel needs to occupy Palestinian land as a security measure. While population counts vary, B’Tselem, the Israeli Information Centre for Human Rights in the Occupied Territories, estimates there are around 700,000 Israelis living illegally in the West Bank, including East Jerusalem, and more than 3.5 million Palestinians who call it home. *** How has the violence escalated? Since the Hamas atrocities of 7 October, when 1,200 predominantly Jewish people were killed and 251 taken hostage, settler expansion and accompanying violence on the West Bank has sharply escalated. According to UN figures, between 7 October 2023 and 21 June 2026, 1,105 Palestinians – at least 242 of them children – were killed in the West Bank. What is happening is ethnic cleansing. B’Tselem keeps a detailed chronology of violence, demolitions and displacement, estimating just under 5,000 people have been expelled since 2023, and over 60 communities have been wiped off the map. They are clear that this is the continuation of a systemic campaign rather than sporadic acts of violence by a handful of rogue extremists. The Israeli state has given settlers guns and uniforms, as part of locally established reserve units, and other equipment they use to terrorise Palestinians, including all-terrain vehicles. The aim is to push Palestinians into disconnected enclaves while establishing infrastructure for settlers to use, B-Tselem said, and supported by much of the Israeli government, including the far-right finance minister Bezalel Smotrich, a settler himself. Indeed, Orit Strook, Israel’s settlement minister, drew heavy criticism from opposition politicians and families of 7 October victims, when she described the period of rapid expansion of Israeli settler control in the West Bank after the attacks as “a time of miracles”. In the past month alone, B’Tselem identified further escalation, with hundreds of settlers targeting larger Palestinians villages, attacking families, setting fire to houses and cars, and taking over farmland. Examples of Israeli aggression towards foreign visitors have gained more international attention: British activist Finn Joughin was abducted by armed settlers, then deported from Israel, and NBC News correspondent Matt Bradley required medical treatment after his crew was attacked by masked settlers. But, as Abu Ridi describes, settlers are largely acting with impunity. B’Tselem believe they are using the window before Israeli government elections in the autumn to “change the reality” on the West Bank. The Israeli government is moving ahead with the E1 project, a plan to build thousands of homes on occupied land between East Jerusalem and the Ma’ale Adumim settlement on the West Bank, which many international critics argue would cut the West Bank in two and make the creation of a future Palestinian state even harder, if not impossible. *** Will the sanctions make a difference? On Tuesday, foreign secretary Ed Miliband told MPs: “This government will not acquiesce in the destruction of the two-state solution. We will act, and I will set out a comprehensive set of measures in the coming weeks.” And, the new prime minister, Andy Burnham, has previously made it known he wishes to take a more “robust” position on Israel than his predecessor Keir Starmer. However, this has not been welcomed by all quarters of his party, with Labour Friends of Israel warning that a ban on trade with settlements could become a de facto boycott of Israel due to the difficulty of separating out settlement goods from those made within the internationally recognised borders of the country. That in turn would cause significant harm to the UK’s Jewish community, the group say. But, a recent Amnesty briefing argues that the government can use the same enforcement framework already in place for trade sanctions following Russia’s invasion of Ukraine, which distinguishes between goods originating in occupied Ukrainian territory and those originating in Russia. And within Israel, security chiefs have demanded the government take action to “eradicate Jewish terrorism” on the West Bank. With Israel more isolated internationally than ever, Abu Ridi has tried to use his dual citizenship to draw attention to what is happening across the West Bank. The US ambassador to Israel, Mike Huckabee – usually no ally to the Palestinian cause – recently described the actions of the settlers besieging Abu Ridi’s home as those of “terrorists”. “I am a Palestinian-American. But I’m not the only one living this life. There are hundreds and thousands of Palestinians in the West Bank, being threatened and beaten by Israeli extremists, and forced out of their houses.” At the end of our call, we speak a little more about his garden. Since the beginning of the siege three weeks ago, the settlers have stopped encouraging their sheep on to his property. “I was just talking with my brother about this,” he says. “We’ve started seeing green leaves, so there’s hope for those trees, if the settlers stay away from my yard.” What else we’ve been enjoying We’ve previously covered how big money is distorting politics on First Edition, so it’s very disappointing that Burnham has backtracked on a £500,000 cap. George Monbiot’s column on this is essential reading. Hettie This NYT report on the runway success of Delhi’s sprawling metro system neatly unpicks how it was built from scratch in one of the world’s most densely populated cities (£). Michael Freelancers are being hired to clean up “AI slop”, neatening and retouching content created by machines. It’s soulless work, Aaron Mok finds in this grimly fascinating piece. Hettie I’ve enjoyed so many of Simon Hattenstone’s recent interviews, and his tete-a-tete with Mr T is no exception. Michael When Stephen Buranyi first told me he was investigating the secretive world of restaurant influencers, I couldn’t wait to read what he found. His long read is well worth your time. Hettie Sport Tennis | Katie Boulter was outclassed 6-1, 6-0 in the second round of the US Open in New York, continuing the British No 1’s poor form. Cricket | Brydon Carse has been left out of England’s squad for the final Test of the summer, against Pakistan at Edgbaston next week, with police still investigating allegations of an assault connected with the late-night incident at a Derby bar last month. Football | Manchester City have equalled the British transfer record with a £125m deal to sign Enzo Fernández from Chelsea. The front pages “PM tries to calm bond markets as sell-off threatens first budget”, is the Guardian’s front page today, while the FT says “Burnham seeks to shield steel and farming from ‘Made in Europe’ push”. The Times’ headline is “‘Vibes’ won’t defend UK, Burnham told by Labour”, the Telegraph writes “Tories will cut benefits to hit 3pc on defence”, and the Mail leads with “Kemi: I’ll slash benefits bill to boost defence”. The i Paper’s front page says “Britain’s royals face Russian cyber threat in ‘grey war’”. The Sun splashes “One in the eye for Andy”, the Mirror has “A right whinger”, and the Express says “Voters would punish you if triple lock goes”. Lastly, Metro has “Sad pathetic creeps.co.uk”. Today in Focus: The Latest Iran retaliates after US strikes reportedly kill wedding guests Iran has accused the US of a ‘war crime’ after a missile blast killed at least four people, including a young child, and injured 68 at a wedding at a private house in southern Iran. A month-long uneasy truce between the US and Iran appears to have collapsed again, after US strikes on Saturday on Larak Island in the Strait of Hormuz. Iran has responded by launching drones and missiles on US bases across the Middle East, including the Gulf States. Lucy Hough speaks to Middle East correspondent Will Christou. Cartoon of the day | Ben Jennings The Upside A bit of good news to remind you that the world’s not all bad For many people of colour, finding a reliable place to take care of your hair can be a battle. New York thinks it has an answer to that problem. As of this month, a new law means every hairdresser studying cosmetology will be specifically trained to work with all hair types. In time, this will make many salons more accommodating to more hair types. “No New Yorker should ever walk into a salon and be turned away or receive substandard care because of their hair texture,” New York state assembly member and bill sponsor Michaelle Solages said. “Now, with the adoption of this legislation, they won’t have to.” Sign up here for a weekly roundup of The Upside, sent to you every Sunday Bored at work? And finally, the Guardian’s puzzles are here to keep you entertained throughout the day. Until tomorrow. Quick crossword Cryptic crossword Wordiply

webTitle: More than 800 students and teachers in Indonesia suffer food poisoning after eating government free meals

fields.headline: More than 800 students and teachers in Indonesia suffer food poisoning after eating government free meals
fields.trailText: Hundreds of students fall ill in three seperate incidents in Java and Sumatra this week as criticism of president’s flagship program grows
fields.bodyText: More than 800 Indonesian students and teachers have fallen ill in separate incidents of food poisoning linked to President Prabowo Subianto’s free-meals program this week, with dozens hospitalised after they with struck with nausea, vomiting and stomach aches. The president’s flagship free-meals program was launched last year to tackle malnutrition, with meals distributed to more than 62 million students and pregnant women across the country. But the multi-billion policy has been plagued by controversy, including recurrent cases of food poisonings, alleged corruption, leadership changes, and complaints it is a major lag on the budget. This week 566 students fell ill after eating the government’s free meals in Sidoarjo, East Java, with 88 of them hospitalised. In Nganjuk, also in East Java, 49 students fell ill on Wednesday after eating a free meal of fried rice, chicken and tofu. Another 237 students and teachers in Agam, West Sumatra, also fell ill after their meals on Wednesday, according to local media reports. Eggs were suspected to be the cause. The regional government in Agam has reportedly suspended distributing the meals, pending an evaluation. The kitchen linked to the Sidoarjo case was also suspended on Wednesday. In the past year many Indonesians have complained about the program, writing on social media about maggots in tempeh, shards of glass in rice, and food trays washed in dirty water. Overall, 37,600 people are believed to have suffered food poisoning linked to the free meals as of 8 Aug., according to Network for Education Watch, a non-governmental watchdog. Charles Honoris, a lawmaker and member of the sole political party outside the governing coalition, described the situation as a “failure of the system”. The National Nutrition Agency has blamed previous cases of food poisoning on improper food storage and late delivery of cooked meals. Prabowo has also played down the scale of the problem, saying that of more than a billion meals served, poisoning cases represented just “0.0017% – quite a proud achievement”. He also said the policy had improved school attendance and achievement. In July, a survey by pollster Saiful Mujani Research and Consulting showed only a third of people were satisfied with the scheme, with the reported cases of poisoning cited as a major reason. Despite the mounting criticism, Prabowo told parliament last month the program would be continued, and promised that improvements would be made. “We start with the most fundamental aspect: nutrition. Our children must not study while hungry. No child can learn effectively if they are hungry,” he said. “We cannot accept a situation where one in four Indonesian children suffers from stunting,” he continued, “We cannot accept that.”

webTitle: Wife of British man at risk of deportation from Sweden calls on Burnham to intervene

fields.headline: Wife of British man at risk of deportation from Sweden calls on Burnham to intervene
fields.trailText: Case is latest in string of post-Brexit deportations from country, which has been criticised for high refusal rate for British people to remain
fields.bodyText: The wife of a British man detained by police in Stockholm on Tuesday ahead of a threatened deportation has pleaded with Andy Burnham to get involved in the Brexit catastrophe unfolding for many British citizens in Sweden. Charles, who does not want to be fully identified, and his Swedish wife, Lily, were summoned to the police station at 10am on Tuesday, where he was told he would be held at a detention centre and deported within the next two weeks. Lily, who is a lawyer, was told to go home and get his passport despite her protests that there was a court process under way appealing the deportation order. “I feel shame,” said Lily, who asked that their family’s surname not be published. “To me, Britain represents freedom for human beings, and then to see this British man in detention just because he wants to be with his wife and live in his house, this is not right. “What kind of country are we living in? Is this civilisation? They don’t care about human rights. This is a European country, but it looks like Sweden is like somewhere like Afghanistan,” she said. Lily met her husband in the UK after starting a law degree in London in 2010. She now works for the local authority in Stockholm and returned to Sweden in 2015, with her soon-to-be husband joining her in 2017, three years before Brexit. A former business consultant, now retired, Charles made an application to remain in the country before the deadline for applications after Brexit. His application was rejected two years later in 2022 and the family have been fighting deportation ever since with “six or seven” appeals, said Lily. “The Migration Agency has hunted us for five years.” During the summer the couple received a text asking them to show up at their local police station on 1 September. “They told us they needed to talk and we should show up at 10am.
