Through her association Fie a Manetta, she teaches women how to navigate Venice by motorboat The idea grew from the awareness that navigation remains a predominantly male environment. “Girls, we need to start recognising each other and giving social value and political weight to our role in this city,” Canino said. Slowly, and often without proclamation, women are entering and inhabiting Venice’s public spaces through practice. Their presence does not simply occupy the water, but begins to redefine it.

webTitle: Broken feet, ripped-out hair and now a death sentence: the fate of twin sisters jailed over Iran protests

fields.headline: Broken feet, ripped-out hair and now a death sentence: the fate of twin sisters jailed over Iran protests
fields.trailText: Taraneh Rahimi was told prison guards would rape her sister, Romina, if she did not sign a confession
fields.bodyText: The twins were 19 and still in high school when they were taken from their beds in the dead of night by masked men later identified as being sent by the Islamic Revolutionary Guards Corps. After four months of desperately seeking news from hospitals and state institutions, their mother, Marzieh Nourmohammadi, finally learned their fate. Taraneh and Romina Rahimi had been seized over their decision to join millions on the streets of Iranian cities during the January protests against the regime. The twins were unrecognisable by the time of their mother’s prison visit in May. The women’s scalps were patchy from being dragged around by their hair, and their faces were bruised, according to their US-based cousin. It is claimed that Taraneh, who dreams of running her own horse stable one day, had been told the prison guards would rape Romina in front of her unless a confession was signed. The visit by their mother to Dowlatabad prison, in Isfahan, the main city in central Iran, was five months ago. It has now emerged from the Iranian courts that Taraneh has been sentenced to death for her participation in the January protests, and that Romina has been given a 25-year prison sentence. Neither of the women have been seen by their family since the sentencing. The difference in the sentences remains a mystery, but the twins’ cousin, Masoud Nourmohammadi, who lives in the US state of Utah, said he struggled to understand anything done by the regime. “They do not follow their own law,” said Nourmohammadi. “There is an 18-day period that lawyers can go and appeal but in a lot of [execution] cases recently that has not happened. They just sentence and take the kids and execute them and hang them. So I mean, nothing, nothing really makes sense.” Nourmohammadi, 43, said he believed Taraneh was sentenced to death by hanging because of her obvious innocence. “You can see her eyes and you know right away that she is a kind person,” he said. “My sense is like they’re looking to put fear within the people, to say: ‘Look, no matter how fine you are, no matter how innocent you are, we can get you, and don’t come to the streets any more.’” Despite the logistical difficulties presented by the war with the US and Israel that began in February, Iran has executed more than 500 people this year, including at least 29 people in connection with the anti-government protests in January. At least 16 women have been among those executed. Hundreds more protesters have either been sentenced to death or are facing charges which could carry the death penalty, including more than 70 in Isfahan. Last month, the UK and 30 other countries signed a joint statement condemning the executions of the January protesters and describing them as an attempt to silence dissent. Nourmohammadi, a healthcare IT specialist who arrived in the US from Iran 22 years ago, is speaking out despite receiving death threats via text messages and social media from people who say they know his home address. His cousins’ case, he said, should instil a determination to end the Islamic regime. The two women joined the protests on 8 and 9 January in Istafan, along with 18 million others. The men who came for them a month later dragged them out with bags over their heads and offered no explanation. “The family didn’t know where they were,” Nourmohammadi said. “They had no idea. They were searching for them everywhere, different courts, hospitals. Then my aunt received a call saying: ‘We have your girls, come to see them at the prison.’” Seeing her daughters was heartbreaking for his aunt, Nourmohammadi said. “She did not recognise her own children: they were beaten up, badly swollen faces, bruises all over their body, broken elbows, knuckles, feet, and they basically had no hair because they would pull their hair and drag them from one cell to another cell. She found out that they had been in solitary confinement.” Marzieh Nourmohammadi, who raised her daughters, now 20, on her own, was not allowed to attend their trial. Their lawyers said Taraneh told the court that any admissions had been secured through torture. No evidence of the sisters’ involvement in violence was provided, it is claimed. They had never been involved in protests before. “My mum lives with me,” he said. “There’s not a single second that I pass her and she’s not crying.”

webTitle: Witkoff and Kushner discussed ‘next steps’ with Putin to end Ukraine war, says US

fields.headline: Witkoff and Kushner discussed ‘next steps’ with Putin to end Ukraine war, says US
fields.trailText: Donald Trump’s business ally and son-in-law now heading from Moscow to Kyiv to meet Zelenskyy
fields.bodyText: Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner are heading to Kyiv for the first time in their roles as Donald Trump’s peace envoys to Ukraine, after talks on Saturday in Moscow. The White House said Witkoff and Kushner had “discussed substantive plans for next steps” towards ending the war between Ukraine and Russia during their meeting on Saturday in Moscow with Vladimir Putin. Those steps would be announced in “coming weeks”, a White House official said in a statement, and the envoys “look forward to equally productive meetings tomorrow [Sunday] in Ukraine”. A Kremlin aide gave no indication ⁠of there being a breakthrough towards a deal to end the war. The aide, Yuri Ushakov, said Witkoff and Kushner “outlined a number of ideas regarding possible avenues for a settlement” in more than three hours of “highly useful” talks. He said Putin had told the pair that Russia was making “real progress” on the battlefield and was confident of ⁠achieving its goals, while stressing the necessity of addressing “all the root causes of the conflict”. These are statements that Moscow has made repeatedly since Putin launched the full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022. Both sides have intensified long-range airstrikes in recent weeks while the front⁠lines remain largely static. Meanwhile, the Ukrainian president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, said Russian attacks on Kyiv and Boryspil international airports – which service the Ukrainian capital – were “clearly” a reaction to the US negotiators flying to Kyiv after the talks in Moscow. Zelenskyy on Saturday said Kyiv had “taken note of this Russian move, and next week we will adjust our operation accordingly regarding Russian airspace, which has become dangerous because of our drones and missiles in the sky. “Of course, there are and will be no threats to diplomacy from our side.” Officials visiting Ukraine have largely done so by train, as Ukrainian airspace has been closed since 2022 due to the war. Russia and Ukraine had vowed not to strike each other’s capitals for three days during the negotiations, as Washington tries to revive US-led talks to end Europe’s worst conflict since the second world war. Donald Trump suggested on Friday he had a new proposal to end the war, without providing any details. Trump made ending the war a priority early in his second term, but little has changed so far. Trump said his son-in-law Kushner and business ally Witkoff were bringing “a proposal to end the war”. “Dear colleagues, I warmly welcome you to Moscow. The situation is, of course, not simple,” Putin told the envoys in a grand Kremlin hall in footage aired by Russian TV. “But before we begin to address it, I would like to ask everyone to convey their best wishes and words of gratitude to US president Mr Trump.” The grinding war, launched by Russia in 2022, has brought increasing civilian deaths and attacks this summer. Putin has repeatedly said Moscow intends to seize the rest of east Ukraine. The war has killed hundreds of thousands and displaced millions. Russian strikes on Ukraine on Saturday had killed at least seven people, including in the Kyiv suburbs, Ukrainian officials said. The Kremlin said it would not strike Kyiv from midnight on Saturday, while the Ukrainian president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, said he would halt strikes on Moscow until Monday. Zelenskyy said he had spoken to the US officials and expected them in Kyiv on Sunday. Large gaps remain between Russia and Ukraine on how to end the war. On Friday, the Kremlin said it was sticking by the position Putin set out two years earlier: that Ukraine should give up four regions claimed by Russia and not join Nato. That position is intolerable to Ukraine. As peace efforts have floundered in recent months, with US attention turned to its war with Iran, the conflict has intensified. Ground troops have been locked in a grinding stalemate along the 775-mile (1,250km) frontline with little advance on either side. Both sides have intensified their aerial attacks in recent weeks, hitting increasingly distant targets. Ukraine has carried out long-range strikes on Russian military facilities, oil refineries and e-commerce warehouses, to try to degrade Russia’s war effort and economy. Its strikes on Russian oil refineries have led to fuel shortages and rising prices at the petrol pumps. On Friday, a Russian drone hit the headquarters of Ukraine’s SBU security service, one of the agencies responsible for carrying out deep-strike operations in Russia. Zelenskyy vowed to retaliate. Russia has also increased its attacks on Kyiv and other cities with waves of bombardments, stretching Ukraine’s air defences. Russia on Friday night struck the Kyiv suburbs, reportedly killing two people in the Bucha district. An attack on the Dnipro region killed five people and wounded five more at a factory, according to the local military administration head, Oleksandr Hanzha. He said those killed were employees working at the factory who were “doing their job when enemy missiles cut off their lives”. A 62-year-old man was injured and several homes and a building were damaged in another attack on the region’s Nikopol district, Hanzha said. Russia also struck a shopping centre in the southern Mykolaiv region with drones overnight, damaging the building and injuring a 72-year-old man and a 17-year-old girl. Emergency services said they were repeatedly forced to withdraw because of the threat of more strikes.

webTitle: Far-right AfD predicted to win big in crucial German state election

fields.headline: Far-right AfD predicted to win big in crucial German state election
fields.trailText: Polling stations open in Saxony-Anhalt with anti-immigration party AfD predicted to gain 41% vote share
fields.bodyText: Polls have opened in the east German state of Saxony-Anhalt, where the populist, far-right, anti-immigration Alternative für Deutschland (AfD) is predicted to emerge on top in an election that could have a groundbreaking effect on Germany’s political landscape. About 1.7 million people are eligible to vote. Polling booths opened at 8am local time and will close at 6pm, when exit polls are expected to deliver an initial indication of whether the AfD has secured enough votes for an absolute majority, enabling it to govern the state. That would mark the first time the party had won a state government, and the first time since the second world war that a rightwing extremist party had gained power at regional state or parliament level in Germany. Final polls before the vote showed the AfD to have about 40-41% of support. The number of undecided voters in advance of the vote was much lower than at previous elections, polling showed. Currently, the small state is governed by the conservative Christian Democratic Union (CDU) of the chancellor, Friedrich Merz, together with two smaller parties. The CDU, on about 23%, under its state prime minister, Sven Schulze, hopes to be able to construct a multiparty coalition to be able to retain power. The CDU and all other mainstream parties have refused to be in coalition with the AfD in a government, in what is referred to as a Brandmauer or firewall. The AfD in Saxony-Anhalt has been classed as “rightwing extremist” by Germany’s domestic intelligence agency. The AfD’s lead candidate is Ulrich Siegmund, 35, a former fragrance salesman with a large following on TikTok who has been celebrated like a pop star. He has insisted he will take power only if the party receives an absolute majority, and would not tolerate a coalition with another party. The Saxony-Anhalt election is the biggest test yet for Merz, who is unpopular, along with his government, after having failed in his promises to reset Germany’s struggling economy and reduce the support for the AfD. Irregular immigration has reduced since he has been in office, but not to the extent that it has appeased the average voter. If the AfD won convincingly, it would put huge pressure on Merz. In national polls, the CDU has also been overtaken by the AfD, which has its eyes on victory at the next federal election in 2029. If the AfD is elected in Saxony-Anhalt, Siegmund has promised to start a remigration and deportation offensive, ban rainbow flags in schools and halt the building of new wind farms. He wants to change the slogan of the state from “Think modern” to “Think German” and to reintroduce the singing of the national anthem in schools. Siegmund has sought to capitalise on a mood of ostalgie – nostalgia for communist East Germany – and to tap into discontent amongst east Germans who view themselves as second-class citizens to people from the west. He turned up to vote on Sunday morning with his wife, riding an East German-era moped in the party colours, which was also a prominent prop during the election campaign in rallies across the state. In a statement in front of the polling station, he voiced his optimism that the party would achieve “45%, and some”. Thousands of opponents of the AfD gathered in the state capital, Magdeburg, on Saturday for a “festival of democracy”. On Saturday evening, a message beamed onto the facade of Magdeburg Cathedral read: “We do not abandon what we love. True love of the homeland is not the AfD.” The bishop of Magdeburg, Gerhard Feige, in an address to a gathering of churchgoers, warned against forces “that want to sow discord, stoke mistrust and fear”. He drew parallels to historical developments, warning that a democracy has the potential to abolish itself. “Not everyone who votes or is elected democratically is a democrat,” he said. The German Economic Institute has warned of the far-reaching consequences for the German economy, in Saxony-Anhalt and beyond, specifically over its immigration policy, which it said would be “calamitous” for the state, which has an ageing, dwindling population and is heavily dependent on foreign workers. Critics have also warned, due to the Kremlin-friendly stance of the party, that an AfD-run state could leak sensitive information to Russia. The AfD has dismissed such claims. It has said it would seek to reform the domestic intelligence service, calling it biased. The latest poll by the public broadcaster ZDF on Thursday put the AfD on a decisive lead of 41%, with the CDU trailing on 23%, the far-left Die Linke on 11.5%, the Social Democrats on 8.5% and the Greens on 6%. Two smaller parties failed to reach the 5% hurdle needed to re-enter parliament. Independent election observers are active at polling booths amid speculation from the AfD that voter fraud has taken place, in particular in postal voting, with specific focus on a retirement home. State authorities have denied the claims.

webTitle: Iran war likely to drag on for another six months, ex-US defense secretary warns

fields.headline: Iran war likely to drag on for another six months, ex-US defense secretary warns
fields.trailText: Leon Panetta tells Guardian US is risking ‘forever war’ and says Pentagon ‘turmoil’ sending message of weakness
fields.bodyText: Donald Trump’s war with Iran is likely to drag on for another six months, Leon Panetta, the former US defense secretary, has warned, as the US president struggles to find his way out of the controversial conflict. Panetta declared in an interview that the war with Iran – launched by Trump over six months ago – risks becoming another “forever war in the Middle East”, with no clear end in sight. “It’s no mystery that the United States and Iran are caught in a terrible stalemate, in which there really are very few options available to bring this war to an end,” said Panetta, who also served as CIA director under Barack Obama, suggesting the conflict is on course to become “another failed war” in the Middle East “like Iraq and Afghanistan”. “I think the likelihood is this war is going to continue for another six months without being resolved,” he added. Panetta spoke to the Guardian days after the US army secretary, Dan Driscoll, abruptly resigned, departing amid the conflict, following reports of tensions with the defense secretary, Pete Hegseth, over a series of firings. US service members “are going to war at a time when there’s tremendous turmoil at the Pentagon, in the command structure, which really creates a sense that there’s nobody in charge”, Panetta, who served as defense secretary from 2011 to 2013, added. “And I just think that, whether it’s Iran, or whether it’s our adversaries, they’re now looking at the United States, and see weakness in terms of our ability to be able to really implement our military capability of defending our country.” He said: “My biggest concern right now is we live in a very dangerous world, with the primary threats coming from China, from Russia, from North Korea, and from terrorism, and yes, from Iran as well. But what I’m concerned about is that we’re sending a message of weakness to our primary adversaries. “And while they continue to meet and support each other in this axis that’s been created, I think they look at the United States as being particularly weak right now, and that’s a horrible message to send at a time when we’re facing those kinds of threats.” In a statement, the Pentagon insisted it was “firing on all cylinders” under Hegseth’s leadership. “The premise that the Department is in disarray is completely baseless and an insult to every dedicated professional and warfighter in this building who comes to work every day to defend this nation,” the chief Pentagon spokesperson, Sean Parnell, said. “This is what reform looks like.” The White House was also contacted for comment. In March, just three weeks after the US and Israel launched their military operation in Iran, Panetta told the Guardian he believed Trump was stuck between a “rock and a hard place” as he weighed whether to expand the war in a bid to eliminate Iran’s leverage over the strait of Hormuz, or “just simply walk away and declare victory”, despite the risk of perceived failure. Earlier this week Panetta said he “absolutely” believed Trump remains in that position. “He’s boxed himself in,” he said. Trump now has three options, according to Panetta. The first would be to walk away and “admit that it’s a failed war”, something Panetta finds it difficult to see Trump doing. The second would be to draw out the current “stalemate, with periodic attacks going back and forth, tit for tat”, and both sides attempting to “avoid the startup of a more dangerous war” while refusing to either negotiate or surrender. That approach, Panetta believes, would produce “what all parties feared”: another protracted war in the Middle East. The third option, he said, would be for the US to take control of the strait of Hormuz, and remove Iran’s “most dangerous leverage point” over the US, “which is the ability … to close and disrupt” the global trade chokepoint. “So the president either steps up and does what’s necessary to open up the strait of Hormuz, or, as I said, he just continues to play … this game of pretending that somehow he’s winning a stalemate when the fact is he’s not,” Panetta said. Asked if he believed the war is “winnable” for the US, Panetta replied: “It’s only winnable if there is a dramatic change in the attitude of the United States that makes clear that the objective, the primary objective by the United States at this point in time, is to reopen the strait of Hormuz.” He also argued that Trump has damaged his credibility by repeatedly erroneously claiming that a deal to end the war is imminent, and that the strait of Hormuz is open. “So the real question is, is he going to make a decision to actually deliver?” Panetta asked. “For a lot of reasons, right now, he’s caught in the worst of every world because not only does he not have credibility, but any threats he makes are totally ignored.” Earlier this week, JD Vance told reporters that he would not describe the current military conflict with Iran as a “war”. And when asked whether he expected the conflict to be over by November’s US midterm elections, the vice-president replied: “I think the reality is I don’t know the answer to that question. You would have to ask the Iranians.” Panetta said he believes many Americans have “lost faith” in Trump’s “ability to handle this war”, pointing to recent polling that he said found that a majority of Americans believe that conflict with Iran was a mistake and are against it. He also said he hopes the Pentagon and Trump’s broader administration learn from what happened with the extremely long deployment of the USS Abraham Lincoln, which arrived in Thailand this week after a record-breaking deployment supporting US operations against Iran that lasted more than 260 days without a port visit, amid reports of deteriorating living conditions and mental health onboard. “Bottom line is, you do not deploy people endlessly into a war zone without making some kind of plans for rotation,” Panetta said. “So it’s not just that the war is going badly – I think there’s also kind of a lack of trust in our military as to whether or not they are properly supporting our men and women who are putting their lives on the line.”

webTitle: Volcanic eruption halts flights at Jakarta and seven other Indonesian airports

fields.headline: Volcanic eruption halts flights at Jakarta and seven other Indonesian airports
fields.trailText: Ash cloud from Anak Krakatau affects hundreds of flights and some school and fishing activities
fields.bodyText: Indonesia halted operations at eight airports on Sunday, including from its main international hub, affecting hundreds of flights as a result of an ash cloud from the Anak Krakatau volcano. Saturday’s eruption, which produced lava and booming sounds that were heard up to 435 miles (700km) away, according to Indonesia’s geology agency, also interrupted some school activities and fishing. Two more eruptions were recorded on Sunday. Ash was detected in the airspace around Soekarno-Hatta international airport near Jakarta, prompting authorities to suspend operations. They announced several extensions of the shutdown, keeping the airport closed to flights until 9.30pm local time on Sunday. The suspension affected hundreds of flights, including international ones, according to the airport operator, Angkasa Pura. Singapore Airlines said it had cancelled flights to and from Jakarta for the rest of Sunday. The Australian flag carrier said there were “disruptions to a number of Qantas services, including cancellations to and from Jakarta today”. “Our meteorologists and operations teams are closely monitoring conditions in and around Jakarta and any impact on our operations,” it said in a statement. “Safety remains our highest priority. We have contacted affected customers and are providing assistance. Services will resume when conditions allow.” Volcanic ash can damage jet engines, baking on to hot internal parts and quickly wearing out turbine blades, as well as clogging fuel and air systems. It can also damage pilots’ windscreens. Ash ‌reached as high as 6,000 metres (20,000ft) ‌on the Java side of the volcano and 15,000 metres on the Sumatra side and some parts of Banten province in Java, the meteorological agency BMKG said. Several schools cancelled activities on Saturday after students and residents suffered eye irritation, and fishers cancelled fishing trips, the local media outlet Kompas reported. The disaster mitigation agency BNPB said it would conduct a weather modification operation, which could include cloud-seeding to promote rain. “If it rains heavily enough, the volcanic ash that has been disrupting our daily lives since yesterday and continuing today will be washed away quickly,” the BNPB chief, Lt Gen Suharyanto, told a press conference. More than 22,000 passengers and 209 flights were affected, the transport ministry said, particularly those bound to and from Singapore. Other affected international routes included Doha, Sydney and Kuala Lumpur. At least 16 domestic flights to Bali were cancelled, local airport authorities said. Anak Krakatau, which means “child of Krakatau”, sits in a strait that separates the islands of Java and Sumatra. The volcano has been sporadically active since it emerged from the sea in the caldera formed after the 1883 eruption of Mount Krakatau. That was one of the deadliest and most destructive volcanic eruptions in human history. About 35,000 people were killed. Port authorities said ships passing through the strait were prohibited from going within a two-mile radius of the volcano and should be vigilant. With Agence France-Presse

webTitle: China prepares £40bn stimulus for financial sector amid fears over sluggish growth

fields.headline: China prepares £40bn stimulus for financial sector amid fears over sluggish growth
fields.trailText: Beijing wants banks and insurers to bolster investment in stock market as it helps to replenish cash reserves
fields.bodyText: China will inject $54bn (£40bn) into its financial sector as Beijing attempts to shore up banks and insurers in the face of faltering economic growth. A host of financial institutions said they were due to receive billions of yuan in capital from state institutions including the ministry of finance and even the company that runs the country’s tobacco monopoly. The stimulus is designed to help China bolster the ability of its financial sector to invest in the stock market and lend to businesses, amid signs that the world’s second largest economy is struggling to escape weak growth. The country’s largest life insurer, China Life Insurance, will get 35bn yuan, while the China Taiping Insurance Group said it would receive 7bn. The People’s Insurance ⁠Company of China said it planned to raise up to 15bn yuan through a private placement of A-shares – stock that specifically allows investors to trade in China-based companies – to the ministry of finance, with the proceeds used to replenish ‌its capital. The initiative could help bolster ‌state insurers that have been directed by Beijing to support the stock market with medium- and long-term funds, while positioning them to help regulators ‌manage smaller, higher-risk insurance companies. The insurance sector has been struggling with eroding profitability owing to persistently low interest rates, with numerous small and mid-sized insurers reporting deteriorating solvency ratios, a measure of financial health. “The injection is an important step by the country to enhance the financial sector’s ability to serve the real economy and promote the high-quality ‌development of the financial and insurance industries,” China Life said, adding that it would strengthen the group’s ability to withstand risk. Separately, three state lenders on Sunday also announced they will receive a combined 290bn yuan in capital injections. The plan was first announced at an annual parliamentary meeting in March this year, extending a financing tool that had helped bolster some other big state banks last year. The Agricultural Bank of China and the Industrial and Commercial Bank of China, two of the country’s largest state banks, said ⁠they planned to raise up to 160bn yuan and 100bn yuan respectively through private A-share placements to the finance ministry, China National Tobacco Corp and its subsidiaries. The two lenders said the proceeds would be used entirely to replenish cash reserves, helping them sustain credit expansion, as Beijing leans ‌on state banks to support growth despite weak demand for loans.

webTitle: Top marks for the Bayeux tapestry | Brief letters

fields.headline: Top marks for the Bayeux tapestry
fields.trailText: Brief letters: Rate that art | Panic buying | Rich pickings | JD Vance’s antichrist | Autumn’s arrival
fields.bodyText: A five-star review of the Bayeux tapestry (The Bayeux tapestry: a stupefying, thrilling, horrifying masterpiece that shakes the earth, 3 September). Even creatives from nearly a thousand years ago are subject to the modern media’s determination to rate art. Still, they will be pleased to have impressed the Guardian. Andrew Vincent Westmancote, Worcestershire • While I understand Angela Eagle’s advice to “store … a bit of food that can keep you going for a while” (Report, 3 September), I fear that this will lead to the kind of panic buying that we had during Covid, when those who can, financially and physically, will stagger out of supermarkets laden with supplies, while those of us less fortunate will find shelves stripped bare. Perhaps we need to bring back rationing? Jean Austin Crawley, West Sussex • “Do the rich behave worse than the rest of us?” asks your report (Rich people more likely to steal children’s sweets, finds Ig Nobel prize-winning study, 3 September). How do you think they got rich? John Roberts London • Interested to hear that JD Vance would not be shocked “if the antichrist was walking among us” (Report, 2 September). Has he tried looking in the Oval Office? Chris Ainsworth Rawtenstall, Lancashire • Sure signs our summer of sunshine is over today (Letters, 31 August): raincoats, calendars and diaries for 2027 on sale, charity Christmas catalogues in the post and a shop-window display of Halloween pumpkins. Valerie Gidlow Faversham, Kent • Have an opinion on anything you’ve read in the Guardian today? Please email us your letter and it will be considered for publication in our letters section.

webTitle: Energy secretary says US might not reach nuclear agreement with Iran

fields.headline: Energy secretary says US might not reach nuclear agreement with Iran
fields.trailText: Chris Wright tells ABC there ‘may not’ be an agreement that would prevent Iran from having nuclear weapons
fields.bodyText: US energy secretary Chris Wright said on Sunday morning that the US may not be able to reach a nuclear agreement with Iran that would prevent the country from having nuclear weapons. Asked on ABC on Sunday morning about any sign of such a deal, as negotiations appear stalled and the US-Israel war on Iran continues, Wright said: “There may not be a nuclear agreement.” He talked about options for ending the “existential threat” of a nuclear armed Iran coming about by further US military action to knock out the country’s capacity to manufacture and deploy such missiles, saying: “It may be simply [a case of] destroying their capabilities to do it” or else “an agreement may await the next administration in Iran”. He later said on CBS that the US was not shutting down diplomatic outreach and was “always open for a deal”. Wright told that network’s Face the Nation show that the “biggest role” of the US military in the Gulf region currently was to stop Iranian energy exports. “We are strangling their economy to try to bring either a change in policy from the existing regime or a new regime,” he said. In an earlier interview with CNN on Sunday, Wright declined to declare the strait of Hormuz safe for oil tankers – unless they are being escorted by the US navy – and stopped short of saying whether the navy would need to remain in the Gulf region “indefinitely” in order to keep the vital energy passageway operating, as the conflict drags on. This came despite Donald Trump’s repeated claims that ships can safely navigate the narrow marine waterway, and the US president’s insistence last week that the US controls the strait, while floating the idea that it be named after him – statements that were followed by further strikes from both sides in the area. Wright, appearing for an interview on CNN’s State of the Union show on Sunday as well as ABC and CBS, was asked whether he could “unequivocally” assure safety to merchant ships transiting the strait. The question came after a New York Times report found that August was the deadliest month for merchant vessels in the area since March. “We’re working cooperatively with fleets that do want to transit. Some ships aren’t transiting, and, of course, that’s their choice. But the United States is working with teams from all the nations in the Gulf to get transits and to continue to ramp them up,” Wright said. “But you’re not saying that it’s currently safe?” host CNN Dana Bash asked, to which Wright replied: “We’re getting a lot of ships through, but, of course, it requires the US military to do that. We are not [at] pre-conflict levels, if that’s what you’re asking.” Bash then asked: “If a country or a company wants to send its tanker through the strait of Hormuz, can they do so safely?” “Well, if they want to work with the United States navy, I think they can,” Wright said. Bash then asked whether the US navy would remain in the region “indefinitely” and whether its presence in the strait was becoming “the new normal”. Wright responded: “Well, it is today, but I think, as you look forward, other nations will come and work with us in this endeavor. Certainly, trade for the world is important. It shouldn’t be just the United States’s responsibility.” “But until Iran changes their position or changes their government, we’ll have to deal with them. But, slowly, their capabilities are being degraded and ours are being enhanced,” he added. Nuclear and diplomatic talks between the United States and Iran appear to have stalled after a June interim agreement to end military operations collapsed without producing a lasting settlement on peace or the future of what remains of Iran’s nuclear program after US strikes last summer caused huge damage. Wright was also asked by CNN if he would say the US is still at war. “We’re still in a conflict, for sure,” he said. On Thursday, the US vice-president JD Vance said at a White House press briefing: “I wouldn’t call it a war,” instead referring to a military conflict. Trump then defended Vance, saying: “A lot of people do not call it a war, I would call it a military conflict, because it’s small potatoes for us … it’s not a big thing.” The Republican US senator John Kennedy of Louisiana was asked on Sunday by NBC if the war would be over by November. “Probably not,” he said. The conflict passed the six-month mark in late August. The former defense secretary Leon Panetta warned in an interview with the Guardian this weekend that it could last a lot longer.

webTitle: US envoys Kushner and Witkoff visit Kyiv for first time after Putin talks

fields.headline: US envoys Kushner and Witkoff visit Kyiv for first time after Putin talks
fields.trailText: Witkoff says he hopes trilateral talks involving the US, Ukraine and Europe will be announced ‘in short order’
fields.bodyText: The US negotiators Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff travelled to Ukraine for the first time on Sunday for talks with Volodymyr Zelenskyy in an attempt to end the war with Russia. The Ukrainian president announced plans to widen peace discussions to include European countries in the near future, saying he wanted to do “everything to ensure that trilateral meetings take place” with Ukraine, the US and Europe. Witkoff said he was hopeful such meetings would be announced “in short order”. The British, French and German national security advisers briefly joined Sunday’s talks. Witkoff said the talks with Zelenskyy had been “very constructive and substantive”. Kushner said the conflict between Russia and Ukraine was “a long, hard and emotional war”. There were otherwise few details from the highly anticipated talks between Washington and Kyiv, which came a day after the US envoys met Russia’s president, Vladimir Putin, in Moscow. Kushner and Witkoff were forced to arrive in Kyiv by train after Russia bombed the city’s two main airports on Friday. Both countries pledged to refrain from attacking each other’s capitals over the weekend to ensure the US envoys’ safe passage. Zelenskyy joked that the delegation should come more often to “protect our citizens who are in the capital”. But the president’s mood was generally sombre. He said Ukraine was “really counting on a winter package” from the US and Europe to enable it to withstand another war-torn winter. “We specifically discussed this with Steve and Jared, as well as with our European partners: air defence, energy support, and as you know we are counting on the serious use of LNG, American LNG,” he said, referring to liquefied natural gas. Zelenskyy greeted the US envoys earlier in the day in Sophia Square, in front of Kyiv’s historic cathedral. The cathedral is a few hundred metres away from the headquarters of Ukraine’s SBU intelligence agency, which was hit by a Russian drone on Friday afternoon, marking an escalation in a conflict that has dragged on for more than four and a half years. Kushner said his team was in almost daily contact with Ukrainian officials. “Just because we haven’t travelled out, it doesn’t mean we haven’t … been communicating,” he said. Expectations going into the talks were low. US-backed mediation has stalled over the past few months as Washington has been focused on the war with Iran. Many Ukrainians are also sceptical that Trump is committed to a peace agreement that is acceptable to Kyiv. “People don’t trust the Russians and people don’t trust Trump personally,” said Artem Bronzhukov, a political analyst. Talks between Russia and Ukraine on ending the war have focused on a 20-point peace plan put forward by Washington and Kyiv in December. But the two sides have failed to reach common ground on several sticking points, including control of territory in east Ukraine. “People mostly understand that if you step back from the Donbas, the next day or the next week, Putin will push for another condition,” Bronzhukov said. A White House official said on Saturday that the talks with Moscow “discussed substantive plans for next steps” for ending the war and that an announcement would follow in the coming weeks. The senior Kremlin aide Yuri Ushakov described the talks as “extremely frank” and said there was an acknowledgement of the need to address “the root causes of the conflict”. Kyiv and the surrounding areas have been hit by a barrage of daily drone strikes for more than a week, the most sustained attack on Ukraine’s capital in months. The capital is now enjoying a reprieve from strikes and air raid alerts that had become a daily occurrence, but other parts of the country are still being hit. Ukrainian authorities reported on Sunday that at least eight people were killed and 69 injured across Ukraine in the past day. Ukraine is facing a critical shortage of US-made Patriot interceptor missiles that can shoot down incoming threats. Many of the recent Russian strikes have been by new-model jet-powered drones that can reach speeds of 250mph, making them hard to intercept. Many Ukrainians are worried about the war dragging on into a fifth year and are anxious about the winter ahead. This week, Zelenskyy’s defence technology adviser, Serhii Beskrestnov, told the Guardian that the government should consider evacuating elderly people from Kyiv as Putin had ordered the Russian military to “prepare and carry out mass strikes” on Ukraine’s energy facilities. Russia and Ukraine have increased their use of long-range missiles in recent weeks in an effort to sap morale in each other’s countries. Additional reporting by Illia Dyadik

webTitle: Ukraine war briefing: US envoys leave Kyiv without breakthrough on ending war

fields.headline: Ukraine war briefing: US envoys leave Kyiv without breakthrough on ending war
fields.trailText: Zelenskyy says after talks with Witkoff and Kushner that Kyiv seeking ‘serious volumes’ of US support for winter defences. What we know on day 1,657
fields.bodyText: US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner have held “encouraging” talks with Volodymyr Zelenskyy in Kyiv in their first official visit to Ukraine but made no breakthrough towards ending the war with Russia. The envoys’ trip followed talks with Vladimir Putin in Moscow on Saturday which a Kremlin aide said were “highly useful” while also giving no indication of a breakthrough. Zelenskyy said at a news conference that his talks with the envoys on Sunday covered air defence needs – including Patriot systems – and a “winter package” of support covering both air defence and energy infrastructure before the colder months. He said Kyiv was seeking “serious volumes” of American support on that front, with backing from European partners as well. It appeared the war would continue into winter, he also said. Zelenskyy said Russia had intensified strikes on Ukrainian cities before Russia’s State Duma election later this month, calling the attacks deliberate “terror” against civilians. Ukraine was working with 67 domestic companies developing systems to shoot down Russia’s jet-powered drones at scale. He said the sides agreed to hold a follow-up meeting involving Ukraine, the US and Europe, with a location still to be set. The US envoys brought new and “more effective” proposals to Ukraine on ending the war with Russia, according to one senior Ukrainian presidential official. “It’s not the same as it was before. This one now is more effective,” the unnamed offical told Agence France-Presse after the talks with Zelenskyy. “They’re still talking. This is actually the most important part. There are three of them now.” Ukraine’s rail operator announced the envoys’ departure from Kyiv early on Monday. Witkoff said earlier that both sides would need to compromise, adding: “We think we have the ingredients to get to that place … and we look forward to continuing this as long as it takes.” Kushner said: “Hopefully this trip has come out with some new ways to advance forward. I think we’ve learned a lot from the trip.” In Moscow the US envoys had “discussed substantive plans which will be announced in the coming weeks”, a White House official said. The Kremlin said the Americans had “put forward a number of ideas on possible routes to a settlement”, without elaborating. Witkoff said he was hopeful a new round of US-mediated Ukraine-Russia talks would be announced “in short order”. Putin has repeatedly said Moscow intends to seize the rest of eastern Ukraine while Zelenskyy insists Russia should not be rewarded for its aggression. A girl ⁠was killed and three ⁠other people ⁠were wounded in a Ukraine ⁠drone attack on the Russia-held Black ⁠Sea port city ‌of Sevastopol ‌late on ‌Sunday, the city’s Moscow-appointed governor, Mikhail Razvozhayev, said on Telegram. Russian forces ⁠struck a ‌Ukrainian ‌cargo vessel in ‌the Black Sea which was carrying military equipment supplied to ⁠the Ukrainian army by western countries, Russian news ‌agencies reported the defence ministry as saying on Sunday. Kyiv’s forces struck the Ryazan oil refinery – about 480km (300 miles) inside Russia – causing a fire, Ukraine said on Sunday. Russia’s foreign minister said Germany’s accusation that Moscow was involved in a ⁠drone incident near a Ukrainian cargo plane at Germany’s Leipzig airport were, “by and large, the ⁠start of a real war”, state news agency Tass ‌reported. “He is, in effect, declaring war on us,” Sergei Lavrov said of the German chancellor, Friedrich Merz. Berlin has ordered a series of measures in response to the attack attempt.

tags.description: A summary of the most significant developments in the Ukraine-Russia conflict

webTitle: Far-right AfD wins key German state election but falls just short of majority

fields.headline: Far-right AfD wins key German state election but falls just short of majority
fields.trailText: Alternative für Deutschland surges to victory in Saxony-Anhalt as Friedrich Merz’s CDU slumps to disastrous result
fields.bodyText: The populist, far-right, anti-immigration Alternative für Deutschland (AfD) has surged to a resounding victory in a crucial state election in Germany, but fell just short of winning a majority in its quest to form the country’s first far-right state government since the second world war. The party of Germany’s unpopular chancellor Friedrich Merz, the Christian Democrats (CDU), slumped to a disastrous result in the eastern state of Saxony-Anhalt. AfD’s candidate for governor, Ulrich Siegmund, said “we have written history” and the party had a clear mandate to govern. He told public broadcaster ARD that voters had sent a signal that “things cannot carry on like this”. “A very good campaigner for us in this election campaign was Friedrich Merz,” Siegmund said. AfD was seeking an absolute majority in the state legislature to govern alone and overcome the so-called firewall of mainstream parties’ refusal to work with the party. AfD in Saxony-Anhalt has been classed as “rightwing extremist” by Germany’s domestic intelligence agency. Final results showed AfD falling three seats short, with 39 lawmakers in an 83-member parliament. Siegmund, 35, said it would not engage in “games” such as a minority government. But it was not evident how its divided opponents could assemble any stable government without it. AfD won 43.8% of the vote, more than double its showing five years ago in the region of 2.1 million people west of Berlin. That was far ahead of Merz’s CDU , which polled 17.2% – losing about half its support – and won 15 seats. The centre-left Social Democrats polled 9.3%, the Greens 8.9% and the Left party 8.6%, winning eight seats apiece. The BSW party, which has said it would not elect either Siegmund or incumbent Sven Schulze as governor but criticises the “firewall” against AfD, took 5.3% and five seats. Participation in the election was at a record high of 76.5%. Addressing jubilant supporters after ⁠exit polls had been published, Siegmund said his party was ready to ⁠reach out to ‌all powers ‌that ‌strove for political change. “We extend a hand to all ‌democratic forces that wish to pursue better policies,” he said, adding that themes such as migration and domestic security were not up for debate. The CDU described its result as “bitter” but said it would not back down from its refusal to rule together with AfD, which the far-right party has also ruled out. Franziska Hoppermann, general secretary of the CDU, called it a “defeat overall” for the Christian Democrats. “And it is also a defeat for all those who have borne responsibility in the democracy in Saxony-Anhalt over the past 35 years,” she added, in reference to the difficult post-communist era. She ruled out any discussion over Merz’s future, which analysts have suggested will increasingly become a topic of debate after his party’s defeat. In one recent poll, only 9% of voters in Saxony-Anhalt said they were satisfied with Merz’s politics. Alice Weidel, AfD’s co-leader, said the result gave her party a “clear government mandate” and that it would “talk to all the parties” to work out a strategy as to how AfD could rule. About 1.7 million people were eligible to vote in the east-central state. Final polls had shown AfD to have about 40-41% of support, and the party appears to have almost doubled its 2021 result of 23.7%. The number of undecided voters in advance of the vote was much lower than at previous elections, polling showed. The small state has been governed since 2002 by Merz’s conservative CDU, together with two smaller parties. The Saxony-Anhalt election had been seen as the biggest test yet for Merz, who is very unpopular, along with his government, a coalition with the SPD. Merz has thus far failed in his promises to reset Germany’s struggling economy or stop the rise of the AfD, which has been making regular and steady gains since it entered parliament in 2017 and is now the Bundestag’s leading opposition party. Irregular immigration has reduced since Merz has been in office, but not to an extent that has appeased the average voter. In national polls, the CDU has also been overtaken by the AfD, which has its eyes on victory at the next federal elections in 2029 or 2033. If the AfD manages to form a government in Saxony-Anhalt, Siegmund has promised to immediately start a remigration and deportation offensive, ban rainbow flags in schools and halt the building of new windfarms. He wants to change the slogan of the state from “Think Modern” to “Think German”, and to reintroduce the singing of the German national anthem in schools. Siegmund also sought in the campaign to capitalise on a mood of “ostalgie”, or nostalgia for communist East Germany, and to tap into discontent among east Germans. He has made repeated references to a rise in foreigner-related crime, even as the crime rate has fallen dramatically. AfD is pro-Kremlin, urging a stop to support for Ukraine and pushing for Ukrainians to no longer receive refugee status. Siegmund turned up to vote on Sunday morning with his wife, riding an East German-era moped in the party colours, which was also a prominent prop during the election campaign in rallies across the state. In a statement in front of the polling station, he voiced his optimism that the party would achieve “45%, and some”, and saying he wanted to “build bridges”. Tensions before the election were high, with a considerable police presence and a number of demonstrations taking place across the state. Thousands of opponents of the AfD gathered in the state capital, Magdeburg, on Saturday, for a “festival of democracy”. On Saturday evening, a message beamed on to the facade of Magdeburg Cathedral read: “We do not abandon what we love. True love of the homeland is not the AfD.” The bishop of Magdeburg, Gerhard Feige, in an address to a gathering of churchgoers, warned against forces “that want to sow discord, stoke mistrust and fear”. He drew parallels with history, warning that a democracy has the potential to abolish itself. “Not everyone who votes or is elected democratically is a democrat,” he said. The German Economic Institute has warned of the far-reaching consequences for the German economy, in Saxony-Anhalt and beyond. It said the AfD’s immigration policy would be “calamitous” for the state, which has an ageing, dwindling population and is heavily dependent on foreign workers. Critics have also warned that an AfD-run state, due to the Kremlin-friendly stance of the party, could leak sensitive information to Russia. The AfD has dismissed such claims. It has said it would seek to reform the domestic intelligence service, calling it biased.

webTitle: UN expert Francesca Albanese calls for ‘true paradigm shift’ as Miliband resets policy on Israel

fields.headline: UN expert Francesca Albanese calls for ‘true paradigm shift’ as Miliband resets policy on Israel
fields.trailText: Exclusive: UN special rapporteur on occupied territories says ban on goods from settlements ‘important’ but must go further if it is to amount to more than a ‘press release’
fields.bodyText: The UK’s planned ban on trade with unlawful Israeli settlements is a welcome, if overdue, first step and must be judged according to its practical impact, a UN expert has told the Guardian. The UK foreign secretary, Ed Miliband, has vowed to act more decisively against Israeli settlements, as well as continued restrictions of aid into Gaza, prompting the US ambassador to Israel, Mike Huckabee, to claim on Saturday that Downing Street was motivated by “Jew hatred”. Miliband said what he had been told about restriction on aid into Gaza had reinforced the need for more decisive action. But Huckabee, writing on X in support of the Israeli foreign ministry’s own criticisms, said: “The Brits have lost it. The Jew hate of their government knows no boundaries and knows no facts.” Huckabee did not mention in his statement that Miliband is himself Jewish. The Israeli foreign ministry had said: “Had the foreign secretary been interested in facts rather than stories, he would have known that there are no restrictions whatsoever on bringing medicines into the Gaza Strip, and that no medicine is being blocked.” Palestinian groups in the UK are holding judgment until they see the fine detail of Miliband’s policy, due to be announced on Tuesday, but are expecting the most significant shift since a previous foreign secretary, David Lammy, withdrew most arms export licences in September 2024. Speaking to the Guardian, Francesca Albanese, the UN’s special rapporteur on the occupied territories, said a “ban on settlement goods was a change in UK government stance and absolutely important”. She added she would “not join those dismissing it as theatre before the details had been announced”. She said a settlement trade ban would have to be part of “a true paradigm shift to Israel-Palestine that ultimately seeks to implement the international court of justice advisory opinion in 2024”, which stated that Israel’s presence in the occupied territories was “unlawful in its entirety”. The opinion, she added, said that “all states carry an obligation – not a preference of an obligation – not to recognise the situation as legal, and not render aid and assistance in maintaining it”. Albanese also said the trade ban could not be narrowly confined to goods – such as agricultural products and cosmetics – since “they are a fraction of what sustains the occupation, and a fraction that Israel can absorb without difficulty”. The package should also aim to include trade in services, she said, progressively suspending British intelligence cooperation, all arms licensing and the unexamined flights out of RAF Akrotiri in Cyprus. Albanese warned that if the steps were not taken or were “completely off the table”, the changes would “over time come to be seen as not amounting to a reckoning, but a press release”. She said that a state banning “dates from Ma’ale Adumim [a city in the West Bank]” while “continuing to licence the equipment used to enforce the checkpoints around it” had not “changed its relationship with the occupation … It has rearranged its communication strategy.” Albanese added that, “because the 2024 ICJ advisory opinion declares the entire Israeli presence in the occupied territories as unlawful, third states’ obligations ‘not to render aid or assistance’ extends to everything that sustains that unlawful presence as a whole.” Albanese said the UK needed to end any ambiguity around the tender for the E1 settlement that will sever East Jerusalem from the rest of the West Bank and cut the territory in two, adding: “Since bids close a week before Israel’s elections on 27 October, there is nothing that London can realistically do in September that can change that calendar.” But she warned the government could not let the tenders simply pass, pointing out that Israel’s finance minister, Bezalel Smotrich, had already said E1 was designed to “bury the idea of a Palestinian state”. “There is a difference between the tenders closing and the settlement getting built and financed,” she added. “Construction on this scale needs finance, insurance and construction firms, and since E1 amounts to annexation and not just settlement expansion, sanctions or similar have to be threatened against those firms that seek to cooperate with the building of E1.” Albanese also called on the UK government to join South Africa before the ICJ, and also support Nicaragua on Monday when the ICJ hears preliminary oral objections from Germany over claims filed by the Central American country that Berlin’s continued arms sales to Israel makes it complicit in genocide. She said: “Britain is not a party to that case. It can still choose which side of the argument it stands on: whether it treats participation in international accountability mechanisms as a threat to an alliance, or recognises that an alliance built on anything other than principle and the rule of law is not an alliance at all. It is an arrangement of convenience, honoured only until convenience changes.” Finally she urged the UK to issue guidance to UK-based firms not to overcomply with sanctions imposed by the US on the international criminal court prosecutor, the deputy prosecutors, eight judges and an increasing number of others, including herself and Palestinian human rights groups that have cooperated with the court. “This has frozen bank accounts, everywhere, for people doing nothing other than their judicial function or providing evidence lawfully requested by an international court,” she said.

webTitle: Ukraine seeks to seize water company owned by billionaire family of British theatre mogul

fields.headline: Ukraine seeks to seize water company owned by billionaire family of British theatre mogul
fields.trailText: Dispute centres on stake held by Patarkatsishvili family in bottled water firm it jointly owns with Russian oligarch
fields.bodyText: A British theatre impresario and her billionaire family are embroiled in a bitter dispute with Ukrainian authorities seeking to seize a water company they jointly own with a Russian oligarch. The row centres on a 34% stake held in the producer of Ukraine’s biggest bottled water brands by the Patarkatsishvili family, including Liana Patarkatsishvili, who recently worked on an immersive show with Toby Jones and Meera Syal. The corporate holdings of IDS Ukraine were frozen by the Ukrainian authorities in 2022 owing to the 49% stake that is also held in the company by Russian investors, including Mikhail Fridman, the founder of the Russian Alfa Group conglomerate. He is under western sanctions for his support for Vladimir Putin’s regime. Ukraine’s asset recovery and management agency (Arma) has been tasked with instructing independent management to take over the running of the company whose other minority shareholders include the Georgian government. The Ukrainian agency’s head, Yaroslava Maksymenko, said they had repeatedly run into legal and bureaucratic obstacles owing, in part, to the shareholders’ resistance to give up control of their assets. The agency further claims to have been the subject of a cyber-attack during one attempt to find an independent manager for the company although there is no evidence as to who was responsible and the Patarkatsishvili family is not suspected. However, Maksymenko claimed New World Value Fund Limited, the vehicle for the Patarkatsishvili’s investment in IDS Ukraine, had pursued an unfounded claim of unlawful conduct by Arma’s officials which she said was “misinformation”. An investigation by the National Anti-Corruption Bureau of Ukraine into the claims of unlawful conduct continues. Maksymenko said her agency had concerns over potential money laundering and value extraction from IDS Ukraine if it remained under the current management although there have not been any official findings of such criminality. There are separate proceedings in the Ukrainian anti-corruption high court in which the shareholders are fighting attempts to nationalise part or all of the ownership of IDS Ukraine, which is seen by some in government as a key strategic asset at a time of war. A spokesperson for the Patarkatsishvili family said they had been committed supporters of Ukraine since Russia launched its full-scale invasion of the country in February 2022, adding that the family were being unfairly targeted and would seek justice in the international courts if necessary. They said: “The Patarkatsishvili family strongly believes that an asset should not be taken away from non-sanctioned shareholders against whom there are no allegations or concerns, and is defending this position through all relevant proceedings before the Ukrainian courts and authorities. “If the Patarkatsishvili family is unable to obtain justice through the Ukrainian courts, and the asset is ultimately taken away through the Arma process, it will, of course, have no choice but to seek justice before the international courts, as it has consistently done in the past.” The family’s shareholding in IDS Ukraine was inherited in 2008 by Liana, her sister, Iya, and mother, Inna, after the death of Badri Patarkatsishvili, a businessman who made his fortune during the breakup of the Soviet Union. Patarkatsishvili fled to the UK in 2007 but died in 2008 of a heart attack at the age of 52 with an estimated fortune of £6bn. Iya Patarkatsishvili and her husband made headlines last year for being granted a refund after buying a £32m London mansion that was said to be infested with moths. Last summer, Liana Patarkatsishvili staged a large-scale immersive theatre production called Storehouse about “misinformation” through her production company Sage & Jester, starring the actors Toby Jones and Meera Syal. A spokesperson for IDS Ukraine said: “Throughout its operations, the IDS Ukraine Group of companies has operated and continues to operate in accordance with the requirements of Ukrainian law, including tax and financial legislation. “No competent state authority of Ukraine, including the state tax service of Ukraine, has established any facts of money laundering, unlawful withdrawal of funds or any other financial activity of this nature on the part of IDS Ukraine. “We are not aware of any investigations or other current inquires of Ukrainian authorities into the operations of IDS Ukraine with respect to any such allegations. “IDS Ukraine has also not ceased operations for a single day since the beginning of Russia’s full-scale invasion. The group continued production and supplied Ukrainian consumers with drinking water even amid continuous missile and drone attacks.” The spokesperson added: “We are aware of statements by the asset recovery and management agency implying but not saying it directly that [a cyber-attack] is somehow connected with the IDS Ukraine Group of companies. However, this information is simply false and in reality completely irrelevant.”

webTitle: Monday briefing: ​How much longer can Nigel Farage survive amid ongoing scandals?

fields.headline: Monday briefing: ​How much longer can Nigel Farage survive amid ongoing scandals?
fields.trailText: In today’s newsletter: ​At Reform’s conference​ the faithful remained defiantly upbeat, even ​through fresh allegations and overnight suspensions,​ with Farage’s grip on the party suddenly looking far less secure
fields.bodyText: Hello. There’ll be a tetchy postmortem taking place at Reform HQ this morning. Its party conference appears to have been a disaster, as scandal once more dogs Nigel Farage and his coterie. Instead of policy announcements and set-piece speeches generating attention, all eyes remain on that footage: in which senior Reform figures – Farage included – appear to play fast and loose (again) with legal process and parliamentary procedure. Two big names have already been suspended, raising further credibility questions for the party and Farage himself – claiming plausible deniability is tricky when you’re caught on camera. But what was the mood among the party faithful in Birmingham? And, as the slew of allegations continue, do Reform voters – or its leadership – even care? For today’s First Edition, Guardian political editor Pippa Crerar, who was at party conference, walked me through the significance of this latest scandal. That’s after a roundup of this weekend’s other big stories. Weekend roundup Germany | The populist, far-right, anti-immigration Alternative für Deutschland (AfD) has surged to a resounding victory in a crucial state election in Germany, but fell just short of winning a majority in its quest to form the country’s first far-right state government since the second world war. Ukraine | US peace envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner headed to Kyiv following talks on Saturday in Moscow. The White House said they “plans for next steps” towards ending the war. US-Israel war on Iran | The US military said Saturday it struck three Iranian oil tankers after US navy warships came under missile attack, further escalating tensions in the region. UK news | Dozens of people dressed in black and wearing balaclavas blocked the road at the port of Dover, chanting “England til I die,” and forcing closures in both directions on Saturday. On Sunday, hundreds of far-right activists descended on Portsmouth, where a small boat with 140 asylum seekers on board was intercepted. Brexit | Travellers to the EU could face renewed border queues as flexibility measures for the bloc’s entry-exit system officially come to an end – although sources have indicated that biometric checks won’t be enforced by some member states. In depth: ‘It definitely felt like the leadership was shaken’ What a difference a year makes. Just 12 months ago, Reform was riding high in the polls – hovering at 30%, sometimes above – and pitching itself as a government waiting in the wings as Starmer’s beleaguered premiership faltered further. After last year’s jaunt (also in Birmingham), Reform basked in a post-conference glow. There was consensus among politicos that an “atmosphere of jubilation” had prevailed. Unions panicked about Labour support leaking to Reform. Big name defections were in the offing. The nation’s bout of Farage-fever appeared to be incurable. This year, Reform needed a repeat performance. After an injurious summer for Reform in which scandal has proved impossible to shake, Farage’s approval ratings had plummeted. Andy Burnham’s arrival in Downing Street had offered Labour a (modest) bounce and knocked Reform from the polling top spot. Farage’s party felt desperately in need of a reset. It wasn’t to be. Reform activists and bigwigs instead ventured home from Birmingham yesterday after another damaging few days, with focus firmly on Farage’s “damaged leadership” and a party “in crisis”. It didn’t start well. On the eve of conference kick-off, footage was released of an undercover sting. Members of Reform’s top team were filmed by reporters appearing to plot ways to avoid strict electoral laws on foreign donations. Dan Jukes, a senior aide to Farage, and James Orr, Reform’s head of policy, apparently plotted routes to circumvent electoral law to secure foreign party donations worth hundreds of thousands of pounds. Jukes appeared to suggest this could be done by channelling American cash through a British citizen. The footage also showed polling costing £30,000 was commissioned by Reform and paid for by a reporter posing as a wealthy American. The polling was beneficial to Reform, and widely publicised on newspaper front pages, but the party failed to disclose their role in its production, or the fact it was paid for by a US donor. “The reality is we could easily get away with it”, Orr told the undercover reporters. Meanwhile, the footage also shows Farage referring to the polling as “bang for your buck,” and thanking the fake donors after they explain their plot to covertly provide funding to the party – which would break the law on party donations. The story has dominated ever since, despite Reform’s best efforts. The police and Electoral Commission are both investigating. *** Vibe in the room Pippa was at the Reform conference, where she found its supporters to be unfazed and fiercely loyal. “The mood in the conference zone was actually very buoyant,” she tells me. “It’s important that we distinguish between how Reform activists and the party itself feel about allegations of financial wrongdoing, and the wider public.” Inside the conference hall and at fringe events, Pippa heard similar refrains repeatedly: that Reform is the “victim of a hoax” and “an establishment plot”; and that these stories are “skewed by the left-wing media.” If anything, Pippa found, among Reform’s base these allegations “are making them even more committed to Farage and the Reform cause”, as has been the case with Trump supporters. The mood is different at the top. A defiant “I have done nothing wrong” tone had certainly been struck by Farage et al in recent months, which was echoed again during his keynote conference speech on Saturday. But while Farage may have trotted out his beloved blame “the establishment” defence, beneath the rhetoric, Pippa has seen positions start to shift among Reform’s upper echelons. Yesterday, Farage admitted the row “looks bad”. “It is becoming quite clear to the party leadership that the wider public aren’t happy, and it’s causing Reform problems,” says Pippa. *** Who got the chop? At 2:30am on Friday morning, both Orr and Jukes were swiftly removed from their positions. These weren’t low-ranking, incidental officials: both had been critical to Farage’s political project. Jukes’s departure in particular is a massive blow to Farage. The pair are said to have something of a father-son relationship, having worked together since Jukes was a fledgling Ukip press officer. “For maybe 15 years, Jukes has been by Farage’s side as a media spokesperson and his closest aide,” says Pippa. “He has been intricately involved in every step of Reform’s development.” Orr, meanwhile, is a Cambridge academic close to far-right politicians like Viktor Orbán, and shares many hard-right views, among them being totally opposed to abortion rights. He became Reform’s head of policy in February after much criticism was raised last year at Reform’s lacklustre platform. “Orr provided Reform with a deeply ideological intellectual heft,” says Pippa. When she arrived in Birmingham on Thursday, Reform chiefs were “boasting about how thorough and comprehensive” their policy platform had become during Orr’s tenure. Pippa spoke to Farage on Thursday and he appeared “characteristically bullish” about the allegations. By the end of the weekend, “it definitely felt like the leadership was shaken.” It’s why Jukes and Orr had to go – losing them both will cause Farage pain, but “Farage was very quickly working to shore up his own position.” *** Had no choice Polling doesn’t show Reform is on the brink of annihilation. Far from it: despite a summer of scandal it remains a serious electoral force, roughly equal to the Tories. Still, it’s a steep decline from where the party sat just months ago often close to 10 points clear of any rival. And while Reform loyalists might show little concern as sleaze oozes from the party, Farage isn’t content with being leader of the third or even second party: he wants a route to power. Unlike US president, Donald Trump, who won by appealing to his Maga base, to win the keys to 10 Downing Street, Farage will need to secure support from beyond his devotees. “These ‘Reform-curious’ voters saw the party as a potential home while there was widespread dissatisfaction with Labour and the Tories,” says Pippa. Burnham’s arrival, Badenoch 2.0, and a stream of Reform scandals has – temporarily, at least – offered Labour and the Tories some reprieve. “Without these voters, it’s not just that Farage can’t win a majority. It’s a case of Reform not even being the biggest party and therefore able to negotiate a way into government.” Give away too much ground, however, and Farage risks alienating his most loyal supporters, with Rupert Lowe and Restore circling. A fine balancing act now faces Farage’s team. “He needs to give a nod to the membership that Reform hasn’t done anything wrong,” says Pippa, “while making sure that they appear to be taking these allegations seriously.” It’s a difficult bind for Farage, who also has his own alleged indiscretions to grapple with. “As things stand it’s not looking great for Farage,” says Pippa. “There is speculation as to whether he’ll even stick it out. He says he will, but we know his family are reluctant, and we know he’s under intense pressure.” It’s far from guaranteed, she says, that he’ll be at Reform’s helm come the next election. That’s not to say he should be counted out yet. Farage is a political cockroach, or as Pippa puts it slightly more flatteringly, “he has spent a career defying political gravity.” The week to come Monday | Jon Healey will deliver his first major speech as chancellor outlining the government’s plan for economic growth. Thursday | New York fashion week, the first of the world’s biggest fashion events, kicks off – with Paris, Milan and London fashion weeks to follow. Friday | The second reading of the assisted dying bill will take place in the House of Commons. What else we’ve been enjoying Teachers undoubtedly have it hard these days – so Nell Frizzells’ surprising, beautifully nostalgic piece, on becoming a teacher in her 40s, felt like a tonic. Poppy People travel from all over the world to stand on the “skim of destiny” and take part in the World Stone Skimming Championship, I enjoyed Patrick Greenfield’s entertaining roundup of the tournament. Katy Vans, newsletter team I enjoyed Polly Hudson’s column on how to cut endless natter short – and will be using Forbes’s very good three phrases in future to do just that. Poppy Sport Football | Mikel Arteta warned that Arsenal are capable of hitting even greater heights after the champions sent a statement to their title rivals by fighting back from a goal down to beat Chelsea. Formula One | Kimi Antonelli won the Italian Grand Prix for Mercedes at Monza, coming back from 19th on the grid to take his first win at his home race. Tennis | Reigning champion Carlos Alcaraz beat Tommy Paul 6-4, 6-3, 6-4 to move into the last eight at Flushing Meadows. The front pages “Families scramble to secure Send plans ahead of ministers’ reforms”, is the Guardian’s front page today. The i Paper leads with “Blunkett’s plea to Burnham: Find the money to fund end-of-life care”, the Telegraph writes “Scrap the triple-lock, businesses tell Healey”, the Times says “Just 1% of asylum pleas are genuine, says insider”, and the Mail has “Labour ‘chickens out’ on curbing migrant rights”. The FT says “Europe is losing battle to halt Russia’s ‘hybrid’ war, defence officials warn”, and the Express has “‘Weak’ Britain a prime target for Russian sabotage attacks”. Metro’s front page is “I was Reform attack victim” and the Mirror has “A&E heroes under attack”. Today in Focus Why Meta started losing in court For years, the investigative journalist Katy McQue has been reporting on the potential harms Meta’s platforms pose to children. Yet, as she explains to Annie Kelly, despite the mountain of evidence compiled by journalists, prosecutors, bereaved families and others, it has been nearly impossible to bring Meta and other social media companies to court. Finally, in 2026, something seems to have changed. Cartoon of the day | Tom Gauld The Upside A bit of good news to remind you that the world’s not all bad Andrea Malone’s 94‑year‑old mother drove to buy a vacuum cleaner she had seen on sale, only to find her local store had sold out. Staff told her the nearest available one was an hour away, a trip she couldn’t manage. As she stood there disappointed, a stranger in the queue offered to drive to the other store, collect the vacuum, deliver it to her home and even assemble it. The woman followed through the next day, and the two later met for coffee. Only afterwards did Andrea’s mother discover her helper was renowned Australian basketballer Michele Timms. This unexpected kindness shows that generosity and community spirit still thrive, even among celebrities. Sign up here for a weekly roundup of The Upside, sent to you every Sunday Bored at work? And finally, the Guardian’s puzzles are here to keep you entertained throughout the day. Until tomorrow. Quick crossword Cryptic crossword Wordiply

webTitle: Weather tracker: Typhoon Saudel causes mass evacuations in south-east China

fields.headline: Weather tracker: Typhoon Saudel causes mass evacuations in south-east China
fields.trailText: Torrential rain causes widespread damage; while north-west South Africa hit by thunderstorms and central-southern US faces oppressive heat
fields.bodyText: Typhoon Saudel brought days of torrential rain to Zhejiang, Jiangxi, Fujian and Guangdong provinces in south-east China last week. The city of Putian, in Fujian province, recorded 416.5mm of rain in a 24-hour period between Thursday and Friday, with surrounding villages recording more than 500mm in the same period. In Fujian, authorities estimate that almost 600,000 people were evacuated from high-risk, flood-prone areas. A further 128,000 people in 53 counties were also affected across Jiangxi, with emergency evacuations affecting 9,000 people. Flooding, landslips and infrastructure damage were reported widely in the region. More than 2,500 teachers and students were trapped in a school compound in the Zhejiang city of Wenzhou on Wednesday after extreme rainfall caused flash floods in low-lying areas. At least 1,260 people reportedly had to be rescued in Putian after a river embankment collapsed on Thursday, flattening 100 homes. On Saturday, a landslip in a village of Suichuan county, in Jiangxi province, killed three people and nine others remaining missing. This is the seventh typhoon to affect China this year, and Saudel arrived shortly after Typhoon Narra dumped heavy rain on Guangdong, Hainan and Guangxi late last month. The South African Weather Service implemented several thunderstorm warnings late last week, covering a large swathe of the northern and western provinces. Disruptive rainfall, damaging winds, excessive lightning and hail were all reported, with rainfall totals expected to have reached at least 75-100mm for parts of the Northern Cape and North West provinces over the weekend. In Johannesburg, eight families were evacuated from an apartment building after strong winds tore off a significant part of its roof. Oppressive heat in the US affected states across the central-southern plains and the Mississippi valley this weekend, with maximum temperatures easily reaching the high 30s celsius (high 90s fahrenheit). However, with high humidities, the heat indices in this region have been closer to 40-43C (105–110F). The unrelenting temperatures will continue across the midwest and southern US this week, with maximum temperatures continuing to reach the high 30s.
