webTitle: Houthis seize key Yemeni port of Mocha in drive to take control of Red Sea coast

fields.headline: Houthis seize key Yemeni port of Mocha in drive to take control of Red Sea coast
fields.trailText: Iran and its proxies move closer to full control of two shipping chokepoints as regional conflict widens
fields.bodyText: Houthi forces in Yemen are making a concerted drive to take over the country’s Red Sea coast fully, claiming control of the key port of Mocha in the most serious wave of fighting with the Saudi-backed government in years, bringing the Iran-aligned group closer to full control of a key shipping route. Seizure of the coast and some of the islands in the sea would be a strategic disaster for Saudi Arabia and the US, taking Iran and its proxies closer to full control of two choke points for western shipping on opposite sides of the Arabian peninsula: the Bab al-Mandab at the southern end of the Red Sea and the strait of Hormuz in the Gulf. Observers have said a reduction in hostilities – the most intense since the UN-sponsored ceasefire of April 2022 put an end to major military exchanges – now seems unlikely in what is seen as an attempt by the Houthis to open a second front in the Iran-US war, alongside the battle for control of Hormuz. Baraa Shiban, the Royal United Services Institute’s (Rusi) Yemen specialist, a London-based security thinktank, said the situation in the country was spiralling out of control, adding that the UN-recognised Yemeni government was opening new fronts against the Houthis in the hope of putting more pressure on their forces than they could withstand. But in the past 48 hours the Houthis had major advances south, down Yemen’s west coast, taking them closer to the high ground overlooking the narrow Bab al-Mandab strait. The fighting has also raised questions about whether Saudi Arabia, which on Thursday launched as many as 40 airstrikes on Houthi targets, will activate the Mecca defence agreement and ask its co-signatories, Pakistan and Turkey, to send forces. The pact is designed to be defensive in nature and believed unlikely to apply to Saudi military activities in Yemen. By taking control of more of the Red Sea coast south of the port of Hodeidah, the Houthis’ aim is to use a new lever to put pressure on Saudi Arabia and the US to agree a deal that lifts the US blockade on Iranian oil tankers in the Gulf. Donald Trump on Wednesday acknowledged he did not expect the war with Iran to end before the US midterm elections at the start of November. The latest phase in the escalation began when Houthis attacked energy installations and southern cities in Saudi Arabia using drones and ballistic missiles. In response, the kingdom’s military forces launched at least 15 strikes between 3 and 7 September. The conflict data monitor Acled estimated there were 276 fatalities over the five-day period alone. The fighting has continued, with the Houthis claiming control of Mocha in Taiz province, as well as the inland city of Hays and the Khalid ibn al-Walid camp, the largest military base in the region. One Houthi-linked estimate suggested its forces had gained control of more than 2,320 sq miles (6,000 sq km) of land. The commander of the Yemeni government forces, Maj Gen Tareq Saleh, admitted he had organised a strategic retreat south of Mocha in order to regroup in a secure location. “The armed forces in the western coast paid a heavy price – martyrs and wounded – over the past days as they confronted the Houthi attack planned by Iran, and supported by it,” he said. Analysts claimed that the effectiveness of Yemen’s government forces was weakened by internal divisions, as well as external pressure from Saudi Arabia. The latter, meanwhile, continues to take advantage of its air superiority to attack Houthi positions, though government sources acknowledged Houthi ground advances along the coast and their missile strikes on the strategic Red Sea islands of Zuqar and Hanish. The clashes have raged across Yemen, including Ad Dali, al-Bayda, Marib, Shabwah, al-Jawf, Hodeidah, and Taiz. In the initial days of the renewed conflict the Houthis were forced back in some areas as battles on multiple fronts overstretched their resources and fighter numbers. The Houthis will be hoping political divisions inside the Yemeni government, reflected in a lack of an integrated military, will slowly give them the upper hand. The United Arab Emirates, previously a powerful player in southern Yemen where it backed the separatist forces of the Southern Transitional Council, withdrew its financial and military support at the turn of the year. The southern forces have refused to fight outside their own region. “A reduction in hostilities anytime soon seems unlikely, as both sides continue to escalate with the goal of inflicting enough damage to the other side to force a compromise,” said Sherwan Hindreen Ali, a Yemen analyst for Acled. “In terms of military capability, both sides are more equal compared to the immediate period prior to the 2022 ceasefire when the Houthis had the upper hand.” He added: “Fighting will remain focused on the fronts of the Red Sea coast in Hodeidah and Taiz, where both the Houthis and the Saudi Arabia-Yemen government have a vested interest in claiming the whole territory to deprive the other side of effective control of the strait of Bab al-Mandab.” The head of the Houthis’ national delegating negotiating team, Muhammad Abdul Salam, insisted non-Saudi commercial shipping would not be attacked. The fighting has contributed to the price of oil rising above $100 a barrel after weeks when it was trading closer to $80. The escalation to this week’s all-out violence has been a slow process. It began after a senior delegation of the Houthi group, which has long been in a complex alliance with Iran, flew to Tehran for the funeral of the Iranian supreme leader Ali Khamenei in July, returning in an Iranian plane that the Saudis refused to land in rebel-controlled Sana’a. The Saudis instead bombed the runway, leading the Houthis to announce a Red Sea naval blockade of Saudi Arabia in what the Yemeni group described as a blockade for a blockade. The 20 July announcement of the blockade was followed by a strike on Saudi Arabia’s Jazan refinery on 25 July and on a tanker off Yanbu on 24 August. Saudi Arabia has become reliant on the Red Sea route for trade after Iran throttled shipping through the strait of Hormuz as a result of US-Israeli attacks.

webTitle: Fascism on the rise in the UK, Anglican bishop says

fields.headline: Fascism on the rise in the UK, Anglican bishop says
fields.trailText: Arun Arora, bishop of Kirkstall in Leeds, condemns ‘twisted theology’ of groups who demonstrated at south coast ports at weekend
fields.bodyText: Fascism is on the rise in the UK, a Church of England bishop has warned, condemning the “twisted theology” of the self-described “Christian patriots” who demonstrated at ports on the south coast last weekend. The masked, black-clad, anti-migrant agitators – led by Daniel “Danny Tommo” Thomas, a former bodyguard of the far-right influencer Tommy Robinson – were heard chanting: “Christ is King.” Arun Arora, the bishop of Kirkstall in Leeds, said the incidents in Dover and Portsmouth were part of an increasingly worrying and disturbing rise in attempts “to tear the social fabric of our country” this year. Arora said the disorder that followed the “evil” killing of Henry Nowak in Southampton earlier this year, the subsequent racist firebombings in Belfast, anti-migration protests in Thetford, Norfolk, and a recent incident in Lancashire – in which the BBC reported that a six-year-old boy had a racial slur scrawled on his forehead – were “the first steps on the journey to open fascist nationalism that takes pride in conflict, hostility and division”. Arora added: “The biggest threat to England’s fabric today is to be found in the tidal wave of nationalism that threatens to destroy the foundations of community, to devastate social cohesion and threaten any sense of unity within this United Kingdom. “What we have seen on our streets in Southampton, in Belfast, in Thetford, in Portsmouth, in Dover is the playing out of a new machtpolitik – the ideology that argues that might is right – that threatens not only those of us who are likely to be targeted or attacked but threatens our way of life as a country. “This goes beyond the racism that many of us grew up with in the 1970s. Rather it is a return to the 1930s, where those dressed in blackshirts gathered on the streets under the banner of fascism.” Arora said the church had to challenge the “sinful idolatory” and “twisted theology” of so-called Christian nationalists, saying they were using the cross of Christ as a fashion accessory, with no understanding of Jesus’s message of love. He added: “We need to be consistent and unequivocal in our theology that there is no national flag that sits atop the cross …. Fascism is on the rise.” Arora made the speech at a Lambeth Palace event this week, hosted with his co-lead bishop for racial justice, Rosemarie Mallett, and the archbishops of Canterbury and York, to celebrate the the contribution of the C of E’s diverse clergy, ordinands and lay ministers. Asked about how people from ethnic minority backgrounds in the UK were feeling increasingly threatened and the misuse of Christian symbols, the archbishop of Canterbury, Sarah Mullally, said: “I think we’re all becoming aware that we have created a society where people feel that it is acceptable to intimidate others. “I think there is an increasing responsibility on Christian leaders to speak up and not be silent, because silence itself encourages a society in which people think it’s alright to intimidate in this way.” The event came five years after the publication of From Lament to Action, a landmark report to address institutional racism in the church. Referring to a recent incident in which a vicar, Rev Canon Dr Richard Frith, was surrounded by anti-immigration protesters inside Doncaster Minster after claims church bells drowned out their rally, Mallett told the Lambeth Palace event that “conflict is being brought directly into our sacred spaces”. She added: “In the same week that hundreds of masked vigilantes marched on Dover and Portsmouth, and a vicar has been surrounded by anti-immigration protesters at Doncaster Minster, it is clear racial justice is more needed than ever. “Fear of the stranger is being performed as a public spectacle. The church can tell the truth about history, protect the dignity of radicalised people, and offer a theological vision of belonging that lives out Jesus’s call to welcome the stranger.”

webTitle: Malta warned of corruption crisis after ‘utter disbelief’ over Daphne Caruana Galizia verdict

fields.headline: Malta warned of corruption crisis after ‘utter disbelief’ over Daphne Caruana Galizia verdict
fields.trailText: Labour peer tells Council of Europe inquiry failure to implement legal protections still putting journalists at risk
fields.bodyText: Malta is vulnerable to “repeated instances of high-level corruption” unless it strengthens the rule of law and protections for journalists, the Labour peer Shami Chakrabarti said at the opening of an inquiry into judicial failures following the death of Daphne Caruana Galizia. Chakrabarti, a member of the House of Lords and former director of the human rights group Liberty, has been named special rapporteur for a Council of Europe investigation into the fallout from the assassination of the anti-corruption journalist, who died in a car bombing in October 2017. Malta is in turmoil after the acquittal of a wealthy and politically influential businessman, Yorgen Fenech, of any involvement in Caruana Galizia’s murder. Fenech denies paying a middleman €150,000 to have her killed. At the inquiry’s first hearing, on Wednesday, Chakrabarti said the verdict had “staggered many throughout Maltese society and beyond. “It’s now almost nine years since the assassination that struck at the very heart of Maltese public life but a mastermind has not yet been held accountable,” she added. The first witnesses on Wednesday were the journalist’s eldest son, Matthew Caruana Galizia, and her sister Corinne Vella, who questioned the verdict, which dismissed both charges against Fenech by an 8-1 majority. Matthew Caruana Galizia told members of the council’s committee on legal affairs and human rights: “The Maltese public have seen all of the evidence against the accused, and the vast majority were convinced of his complicity in the murder. And this is why there is this atmosphere of utter disbelief at how the jury could have reached such a decision.” Malta’s state prosecutor is understood to be preparing an appeal, with the aim of securing a retrial. The Council of Europe, founded in 1949 after the second world war, created the European convention on human rights. It is led by an assembly drawn from members of the parliaments of its 46 member states. During the hearing, representatives expressed shock and concern about the verdict, calling for the European parliament and the European Commission to intervene. Iulian Bulai, a Romanian centre-right politician, suggested the EU could withhold funds from Malta. The procedure, known as the rule of law conditionality mechanism, was first used in 2022, against Hungary. “If there is such huge problem in matter of rule of law and a function of the Maltese institutions, the EU should apply a similar procedure on increasing pressure for reform,” said Bulai. He said the procedure had “functioned in other cases … So why shouldn’t it function in Malta’s case?” Malta, the EU’s smallest member state, with a population of 600,000, is a net recipient of EU money. Analysis suggests that since joining the block 22 years ago, the island has received €2.4bn more in subsidies than it has paid in. Chakrabarti said she would look at why Malta had failed to implement many of the recommendations from a public inquiry held after the murder. “The targeted assassination of a journalist in the middle of investigating high-level corruption sent a chill down the spine of everyone who cares about democratic values,” she said. “Many claim that the legal and policy changes needed to protect journalists to combat corruption and ensure the independent functioning of justice have not been carried out. “I’m extremely concerned by the apparent absence of reforms in critical areas which make Malta vulnerable to repeated instances of high-level corruption and limit the press freedom which should hold it in check.” The public inquiry found although there had been no evidence that the Maltese state had a direct role in the murder, the state bore responsibility for creating a climate of impunity. It recommended Italian-style anti-mafia laws, and making the hindrance of police investigations and abuse of office a crime for public officials. These measures have yet to be implemented. Chakrabarti compared the Caruana Galizia case to miscarriages of justice in the UK, where officials had been involved in coverups, citing the mismanagement of Grenfell Tower, the Post Office scandal and the Hillsborough football stadium disaster. She said her inquiry, titled Justice delayed: the unfinished implementation of the Daphne Caruana Galizia case, was likely to conclude in a year. Vella said fear that serious crimes could go unpunished had increased since the verdict. “Before the verdict was given, we lived in a country where a journalist was killed, but there was a chance of ending impunity. That disappeared as soon as the verdict was out.” She said journalists who had continued to investigate corruption allegations involving former members of Malta’s government “felt uneasy walking to their own cars following that verdict”.

webTitle: Secret systems used by Israel in mass killings of Gaza civilians revealed in new film

fields.headline: Secret systems used by Israel in mass killings of Gaza civilians revealed in new film
fields.trailText: Testimony from Israeli military insiders involved in surveillance and remote killings features in documentary produced by the Guardian
fields.bodyText: Testimony from 24 Israeli military insiders on the secret systems used in the war on Gaza has been revealed in a new documentary film about the mass killing of Palestinian civilians. NAZA, a film from the Oscar-winning Israeli directors Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor, was shown at the Venice international film festival on Thursday as the only documentary competing for its prestigious Golden Lion award. The film’s title comes from an Israeli military acronym used euphemistically to refer to civilians expected to be killed in a military attack. Produced by the Guardian, it features extensive testimony from Israeli intelligence officers and soldiers involved in the surveillance and remote killing of Palestinian civilians. Interviews were filmed at night on rooftops in Tel Aviv, on the condition of anonymity because of the risks involved in speaking publicly about Israel’s war activities. The appearance and voices of participants in the film were digitally altered to disguise their identities. The interviewees detail the secret methods used by the Israeli military in Gaza, including AI-based systems built to identify large numbers of potential low-ranking Hamas targets, who were then bombed in their homes at night, in the knowledge attacks would also kill their families. The Israeli military hacked into phones to identify the location of such targets, and covertly listened into conversations with their wives and children moments before they were all killed. The film also features first-person accounts about the destruction of neighbourhoods where the Israeli military estimated that up to 25% of residents were still sheltering in their homes, the systematic burning of civilian homes, and the killing of civilians at a food distribution site. Abraham said at a press conference in Venice on Thursday: “We just told these officers: ‘Please describe to us what you did. How do these systems work? Sketch it out for us.’ Sometimes, in just asking the questions, you get the answers. “Some of them did not express remorse and some did. Some spoke out of indifference, some out of pride.” Several interviewees worked in a secret intelligence unit that reports directly to the office of Israeli prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu; one said their mission was to “thwart peace”. “We made this film out of a sense of obligation to use our position as Israeli film-makers and journalists to examine the systems behind the mass killing of Palestinian civilians for which our country is responsible,” Abraham and Szor said in their directors’ statement. The directors stressed the film’s focus was not on “sporadic war crimes committed by rogue soldiers”. “It is on the orders themselves, the policies, the accepted practices, the language and logic that make those practices possible, and the people who operate within them,” they said. “The system and its cogs.” The documentary was co-produced by James Wilson and executive produced by Jonathan Glazer, the same team behind the Oscar-winning film The Zone of Interest. The film received a nearly 25-minute standing ovation after its screening, according to Variety, which called it a record for length of applause not just at Venice but at any major film festival and reported that Glazer embraced Abraham and Szor as it went on, while some members of the audience held up Palestinian flags. NAZA builds on revelations first published by the Israeli-Palestinian publication +972 Magazine, the Hebrew-language outlet Local Call and the Guardian between 2023 and 2025. It was filmed and produced under tight security because of the risk to confidential journalistic sources, and its contents have remained a closely guarded secret before Thursday’s premiere. Paul Lewis, the Guardian’s head of investigations and an executive producer on the film, described NAZA as the culmination of “years of painstaking work to uncover and verify the systems used by Israeli military intelligence in Gaza”. Abraham said making the documentary had provided space to explore the collective impact of that work. “In this film we’re talking to 24 people. We are looking at systems of mass killing. There is something about cinema that allows you to explore structures and systems and how you put things together.” Before the premiere, Alberto Barbera, the Venice film festival’s artistic director, told journalists NAZA would be “truly groundbreaking”, calling it “a politically disruptive and cinematically extremely interesting work”. “It’s not just any collection of interviews,” Italy’s Cinecittà News quoted Barbera as saying. “It took them three years to convince these Israeli intelligence and military officials to share the work they did when the invasion of Gaza began, and I assure you, their testimonies are shocking.” Israeli attacks in Gaza since 2023 have killed more than 73,000 Palestinians, the majority of them civilians, and injured more than 174,000 others, together representing more than 10% of Gaza’s prewar population. Israeli restrictions on food shipments created a man-made famine last summer, and the Israeli military razed or damaged more than three-quarters of homes, so surviving Palestinians are now crowded into tent camps with little access to clean water or sanitation. Israel launched its war after the 7 October 2023 Hamas-led attacks on Israel, when more than 1,200 people were killed and 251 taken to Gaza by militants. The majority of the dead and hostages were civilians. Abraham and Szor were two of the four co-directors of No Other Land, which won the Oscar for best documentary in 2025. Drawing a connection between the two films, the directors said: “In the film No Other Land, we spent five years, together with [Palestinian co-directors] Basel Adra and Hamdan Ballal, documenting the army destroying Palestinian homes in order to paint a larger picture of a system of occupation and ethnic supremacy aimed at the removal of Palestinians from the West Bank. “In NAZA, we are similarly connecting the dots of a system, gathering the testimonies of two dozen intelligence officers and soldiers and depicting the military systems used to perpetrate what a UN commission and the world’s leading human rights groups have described as a genocide.”

webTitle: Much of Europe already levies a tourist tax – a nice little earner for Italian hotspots

fields.headline: Much of Europe already levies a tourist tax – a nice little earner for Italian hotspots
fields.trailText: While England makes its first foray into unfamiliar territory, it’s proved a boon for Italy’s cash-strapped municipalities
fields.bodyText: A nightly tourist tax may be unfamiliar territory in the UK, but countries in continental Europe have been cashing in on these kinds of levies for decades. Tourists usually need to pay the tax on the day they check out of a hotel or holiday let, and are often surprised by an extra fee on top of their accommodation costs. Among the earliest introductions of a tourist tax was in Austria in 1842, specifically targeting those who stayed in spa and wellness retreats. Similar measures were later implemented in France, Italy, Germany and Switzerland as a way to prevent the inhabitants of towns hosting such high-end resorts from paying for costs incurred by wealthy visitors. Italy’s tourist tax structure has gone through various changes. During Benito Mussolini’s fascist regime, it was broadened to include any town or city classified as a tourist destination. The tax was then completely abolished for the World Cup in 1990 as Italy embraced more visitors, only to be brought back in nationally in 2011, with Rome becoming the first city to reintroduce the levy. Depending on the destination, and sometimes the hotel type, the nightly fee typically ranges from between €1 (£0.86) and €10 per person, although guests of five-star hotels in Milan pay €12. Venice has also had an entrance fee in place since 2024, although that is only targeted at day-trippers. The overnight levy is a serious earner for popular Italian destinations. In 2024, Rome made €222.4m, followed by Milan (€109.3m), Florence (€82.9m) and Venice (€38.9m), according to data from Siope, the finance ministry’s tracker of public money flows. The revenues are supposed to be spent on local services, especially in towns and cities buckling under the pressure of overtourism, or on maintaining monuments. However, the reality is that cash-strapped municipalities use it for other expenses. “All municipalities want the fee because they need the money,” said Gianluca De Gaetano, the manager of the Rome unit for Federalberghi, the hotels’ association. Tourists mostly just absorb the payment, even if begrudgingly. “They tend to complain when they find that the services in a city are not up to par, especially if they’ve already paid a lot for their accommodation,” said De Gaetano.

webTitle: Orthodox church sends medieval prince’s remains to Russian troops in Ukraine

fields.headline: Orthodox church sends medieval prince’s remains to Russian troops in Ukraine
fields.trailText: Part of Dmitry Donskoy’s right hand sent to ‘spiritually strengthen’ soldiers
fields.bodyText: The Russian Orthodox church has sent a fragment of a medieval warrior prince’s remains to troops fighting in Ukraine, saying the relic would “spiritually strengthen” soldiers and help them achieve victory. A reliquary containing part of the right hand of Dmitry Donskoy, the 14th-century prince revered in Russia for his victory over the Mongolian Golden Horde in 1380, has been taken to Russian-occupied eastern Ukraine and is now being transported along the frontline. The Russian Orthodox church said in a statement: “The holy commander is going to where the fate of the fatherland is being decided today, so that he may invisibly take his place in the same battle ranks as our defenders.” The relic was first brought on Tuesday to the Savur-Mohyla war memorial in the Russian-occupied Donetsk region of Ukraine, where senior Orthodox clergy held a prayer service alongside representatives of the Russian military. The Russian-installed Metropolitan Vladimir of Donetsk and Mariupol said its presence would help soldiers and civilians “mobilise their strength” and secure victory over the enemy. The relic’s journey is the latest example of the Russian Orthodox church’s rabid embrace of the Kremlin’s war in Ukraine, which Patriarch Kirill, its leader, has repeatedly portrayed in religious terms. Since Vladimir Putin launched the full-scale invasion in February 2022, the church hierarchy has become deeply embedded in the Russian war effort. Priests have been sent to military units and occupied territories, while churches across Russia have been instructed to recite prayers asking God to grant victory. Donskoy’s relics were first formally uncovered only last month during restoration work at the Cathedral of the Archangel inside the Kremlin, where generations of Russian princes and tsars are buried. Putin, who has grown increasingly close to the Russian Orthodox church over his more than two decades in power, personally attended the ceremony marking the unearthing. Critics have accused the church of breaking with religious protocol by opening Donskoy’s centuries-old tomb. The location of the prince’s burial had long been known, but the church had previously made no attempt to exhume his remains after he was canonised in 1988. Alexander Zanemonets, an Orthodox priest and historian based outside Russia, said the decision to uncover the relics almost four decades after Donskoy’s canonisation appeared driven by the demands of wartime patriotism. He wrote in a piece for the Carnegie thinktank: “By the fifth year of war, the church leadership in Moscow began to wonder what else it could do to show its support for what Russia terms its ‘special military operation’.” Zanemonets said the portrayal of Donskoy as a defender of the homeland fitted neatly with the Kremlin’s insistence that Russia was defending itself rather than conducting a war of aggression against its neighbour. Earlier this year, relics of Alexander Nevsky, another medieval prince and military hero revered by the Russian Orthodox church, were also sent to the front.

webTitle: Francophiles, Norman outfits and broken threads: visitors see Bayeux tapestry in UK for first time

fields.headline: Francophiles, Norman outfits and broken threads: visitors see Bayeux tapestry in UK for first time
fields.trailText: Visitors got a first glimpse of the medieval artefact after it went on display at the British Museum in London
fields.bodyText: On the day Bayeux tapestry tickets were released, Megan Stockwell was at the beach. She was so determined to lock down her spot, that she sat with her toes in the sand for an hour, waiting in the online queue. “The whole ticket buying experience felt like what other people would do to get Taylor Swift tickets. I was like, ‘oh God, am I, like, the geek version of this?’” she recalled. Like any committed Swiftie, Stockwell felt confident the experience would be worth the hassle and cost. As a self-professed Francophile, she was fascinated by how the tapestry, which is temporarily housed at the British Museum until next July, tells the story of the Franco-British relationship through the Norman conquest, culminating in the battle of Hastings. “You just grow up learning so much about it – at primary school, in history studies. You’ve always got some mention of the Bayeux tapestry, the Normans, the fact there’s even three lions on the back of our pound coins comes from Normandy. “We’ve got such a close connection between French and British culture, our language and everything. This sort of feels like a visual representation of that,” she said. Stockwell’s dogged pursuit of tickets, fascination with the Franco-British relationship, and childhood memories of learning about the battle of Hastings, were experiences shared by many of the visitors on the exhibition’s opening day. Cydney, who lives in Texas, also drew inspiration from her experience queueing for concert tickets to secure a coveted opening day spot. She had woken up at 3am local time to join an online queue for an hour and half to secure them when they were released. She anticipated it would be worth it: “It’s going to be life-changing, we’re so excited.” Cydney had studied history for her undergraduate degree. “So I just really am interested to see what a significant artefact would be and to see how this is basically where the history of England and the UK as we know it really all began. Seeing something so old is just incredible and honestly such an honour.” Her feelings were echoed by Adrian Harris, who was so moved to catch the exhibition that he signed up for British Museum membership purposely to gain early access to tickets. He ended up the second person through the doors on Thursday morning, after joining a “really jolly” queue at 9.30am. “It was incredible. It was very, very moving to walk down the steps and to see the length and breadth of it. And I think they’ve done it so well, the British Museum. It was very profound to see it,” he said, adding he had been especially thrilled to spy Westminster Abbey, where he works, on the cloth. He noted that although he was one of the first through the doors, he felt that 40 minutes was a restricted timeframe to see the 68-metre tapestry, though he observed that attendants were diligent in ushering people along. A number of ticket holders for the Bayeux tapestry at a special first viewing last weekend were reportedly turned away after other visitors took too long to view it. The French owners of the tapestry have issued strict orders on when lights must be turned off in order to preserve the work. Richard and Madeleine Abramson, who were in the first group alongside visitors dressed in Norman costumes, agreed that 40 minutes was a short time, but that it was being well policed. “They’re very clear at the beginning there’s a maximum time … they’re very carefully moving you on,” said Madeleine. However, the oversight did not dampen the pair’s enthusiasm. “It was pretty awe-inspiring,” said Richard. “It’s very well presented, it develops like a film. It’s got a story to tell: it starts quietly, then it gets more intrigue and then you get to the action and it builds up to the battle, which is quite violent.” Madeleine felt the tapestry loomed large for many former English schoolchildren. “Of all the history lessons you have, every child remembers 1066,” she said, adding that the fact the tapestry was stitched by female embroiderers also resonated. “[That they] told this whole story is still phenomenal,” she said. Vivien and Karen had travelled from Hampshire to see the tapestry, also buoyed up by memories of their school days. “We learned about it at school. It’s something that’s always been in the back of your mind, then all of a sudden it’s here, so why not?” said Karen. Vivien practises needlework, and was especially excited to witness the craftsmanship up close. “I’ll be looking for the two broken threads,” she said. Denise Davies had bought two tickets for her husband John’s birthday. As a taxi driver who also runs black cab heritage tours of London, he was looking forward to expanding his historical knowledge. At £33 a peak-time ticket, the exhibition’s cost has attracted some criticism – but Denise felt it was worth it. “I could go to Alton Towers and it would cost me an arm and a leg. This is something special. I would have paid whatever it was because we’re never going to see it again … it’s a tick on the bucket list, basically.” • This article was amended on 11 September 2026 to describe the tapestry as being stitched, not woven, by female embroiderers.

webTitle: Secret son revelation ignites bitter succession dispute in Ugandan kingdom

fields.headline: Secret son revelation ignites bitter succession dispute in Ugandan kingdom
fields.trailText: Family of late King Oyo Nyimba Kabamba Iguru Rukidi IV reject committee’s choice of cousin and TV presenter as new monarch
fields.bodyText: A traditional Ugandan kingdom has become engulfed in a bitter succession dispute after the family of a king who recently died rejected the selection of a television news anchor as his successor. King Oyo Nyimba Kabamba Iguru Rukidi IV, who became the world’s youngest reigning monarch when he took the throne in the kingdom of Tooro in 1995 at the age of three, died on 27 August in the US, where he was receiving cancer treatment. On Wednesday, the royal clan’s succession committee announced it had chosen Oyo’s cousin Prince Edward Rukidi Kijanangoma, a news anchor and editor at the public broadcaster UBC, as crown prince. However, at a press conference held later the same day, Oyo’s sister, Princess Ruth Nsemere Komuntale, said that according to her brother’s will, a son whose existence had not been publicly known until his death should succeed him. The kingdom’s ‌spokesperson shared a section of the document, which says: “I hereby declare and direct that if, at the date of my death, I am survived by a son lawfully recognised as my biological son, I appoint him as my heir to the throne of the kingdom of Tooro.” In a statement on Thursday, Oyo’s mother, Queen Mother Best Kemigisa Akiiki, denounced a “self-appointed group of clan members” who had selected a new king despite having had the will read to them hours earlier. She also claimed that the royal family had been put under house arrest. Troops had “removed the royal guards without notice, and ... were deployed around the palace,” she said. “We cannot leave or receive people freely.” Oyo was unmarried and was not known to have any children. The Tooro kingdom’s prime minister, Calvin Armstrong Rwomiire Akiiki, revealed the existence of a son in a social media post on 27 August when announcing Oyo’s death. “His majesty leaves behind a prince as his heir, whose identity will be formally revealed at the appropriate time, in accordance with the traditions and customs of Tooro kingdom,” he said. Another contender had been Prince George Desmond-Kamurasi, who plays for the London amateur football club South East Dons. According to the committee, the goalkeeper had declined the offer of the throne because of his other responsibilities. The Tooro king is selected by a succession committee appointed by the royal clan. A committee member told the local NTV station that a royal child must be officially introduced to elders in order to be considered for leadership. Andrew Mwenda, ⁠a prominent Ugandan journalist and relative of the royal family, wrote on X on Thursday that Oyo’s family had not been able to produce a photo of the purported son, and declined to disclose details about the family of the boy’s mother. He added that, in Tooro, a king’s son could only succeed him if he were born to ‌a queen officially married to the king. The prime minister called for restraint on Thursday. “There will be time to examine the will, to hear those advancing a different position, and to consider our customs, the applicable law and the proper institutions through which succession should be determined,” he said in a social media post. “That process should take place calmly and credibly, not through competing announcements, confrontation, or attempts to establish facts on the ground while our king still awaits burial.” Edward, a popular TV news presenter, is the son of Prince Christopher Paul Kijanangoma and a grandson of the former king George David Rukidi III. Oyo, who was crowned after his father’s death, will be buried on Saturday at the Karambi royal tombs in the kingdom’s capital of Fort Portal in western Uganda. Uganda has several ancient kingdoms that lack formal sovereignty, but whose leaders are revered as symbols of tradition and wield vast social influence. Tooro is one of five that are recognised by the government. Their monarchs have no political authority and are legally barred from engaging in partisan politics. In 1967 Uganda’s then president, Milton Obote, abolished the kingdoms, saying he wanted to unify the country. They were restored by the current president, Yoweri Museveni, in 1993. The Tooro are the latest African royal family to become mired in a succession dispute. King Misuzulu Sinqobile kaZwelithini, the reigning king of the Zulu people in South Africa, waited 15 months for his coronation after the death of his father because of a bitter feud involving accusations of forgery and poisoning. Reuters and the Associated Press contributed reporting

webTitle: Ukraine war briefing: Nato ‘foils Russian undersea cable sabotage drill’

fields.headline: Ukraine war briefing: Nato ‘foils Russian undersea cable sabotage drill’
fields.trailText: Swindon drone factory was target of Russia plot involving British man, court hears; Poland says Ukraine border crossing came under threat. What we know on day 1,661
fields.bodyText: Nato forces chased away Russian ships in Arctic waters that were training to attack undersea cables with a secret sabotage weapon deployed by submersible craft, Reuters has reported, citing western officials. Reuters said its sources declined to detail how the technology works. The confrontation took place near the remote Svalbard archipelago. British and Norwegian officials took their findings to Moscow to show they were aware of the new technology. CIA director John Ratcliffe’s visit to Moscow in August was partly to warn ‌Russia against escalating sabotage operations in Europe, Reuters said, citing two people familiar with the matter. The US has not publicly explained Ratcliffe’s trip. The Norwegian defence minister, Tore Sandvik, told Reuters: “Through our joint operation, we sent a clear message to Russia that they cannot operate covertly … It is in no one’s interest to escalate tensions in the High ‌North.” Britain’s defence ministry pointed to previous statements about attempted covert activities in and near Norwegian and British waters by Russia’s “deep-sea research directorate”, known by the acronym GUGI, which is under international sanctions. The White House did not respond to a comment request, Reuters said, while the CIA declined to comment. The British man Joshua Cammidge, arrested as an alleged Russian agent, was part of a plot to sabotage a drone factory in England, prosecutors said on Thursday in a London court. Cammidge, 31, is charged with engaging in conduct to materially assist a foreign intelligence service in carrying out activities in violation of the National Security Act. He did not enter a plea and was returned to custody until due in court again on 25 September. Cammidge was in contact with a suspected representative of the GRU Volunteer Corps, a group controlled by Russia’s military intelligence agency, the prosecution told Westminster magistrates court. Cammidge allegedly provided information on four drone manufacturing sites in his home town of Swindon. A Ukrainian missile strike caused damage in the south ⁠of the Russian city of Volgograd, officials said on Friday. The Volgograd oil refinery ⁠run by Lukoil, one of Russia’s biggest by processing capacity, is located ‌in the southern part of the city. A ⁠Ukrainian drone attack ⁠caused ⁠a fire at a warehouse of Russian e-commerce ⁠company Ozon ‌in ‌the city of ‌Saratov, the company said on Friday. Russian airstrikes injured eight and caused a ⁠fire in a ⁠nine-storey apartment building in Kyiv on Friday morning, city authorities said. Poland and Ukraine stopped⁠ a threat to one of their border crossings and expect they will ⁠be further targeted, Donald Tusk said on Thursday, as ⁠Russia attacks wartime routes between Ukraine and its neighbouring allies. “Last night, thanks to cooperation between our services and their Ukrainian ‌counterparts, a direct ‌threat to one of the border crossings was averted,” the Polish prime minister said, adding that he had received “a fairly ⁠precise report directly from the CIA regarding possible events in the coming months”. Poland also suspended flights at its Lublin and ⁠Rzeszów airports on Thursday while its air ‌force conducted what were described as preventive operations related to ⁠Russian missile attacks on Ukraine. On Wednesday, drones hit a border crossing between Ukraine and Moldova in the southern region of ⁠Odesa, killing two people. “We expect similar actions targeting border crossings with Ukraine in other countries, including Poland,” Tusk said. Russia did ‌not immediately comment. A Russian strike on a shopping centre in Pavlohrad, central Ukraine, killed at least five people, authorities said on Thursday. Another 76 people were injured including children, and other parts of the city were also attacked. The city lies on a supply route for the Ukrainian ⁠military connecting central Ukraine to eastern frontlines. Two people were killed by a Russian attack in Dnipro on the ‌US-owned Bunge sunflower oil factory, one of Ukraine’s five largest food plants with a processing capacity of 1,600 tonnes of oilseeds per day. Another five people were injured. “This is no coincidence, but part of Moscow’s systematic terror campaign against American businesses and economic interests,” said the Ukrainian foreign minister, Andrii Sybiha. Before Russia started the war, Ukraine was the world’s largest exporter of sunflower ‌oil. Russia has carried out attacks on oilseed refineries and vegetable oil terminals while claiming to be targeting military ports and shipping. Ukraine’s president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, said Russian forces struck the eastern Donetsk region and the Kharkiv ⁠region in the north-east. In the north-eastern city of Sumy, officials said a jet-powered drone tore into a shopping centre – a day after two people were killed and 20 wounded in a similar attack there. Russian officials said Ukrainian drone attacks on the border region of Belgorod killed ‌two people and injured seven. Two Azerbaijani tugboat ⁠crew members ⁠were killed and two others ⁠injured in a Russian attack ‌on ‌civilian shipping ‌in Ukraine’s southern Odesa region, Kyiv’s infrastructure ministry ‌said. Canada offered support on Thursday to boost Ukraine’s air defences and help replenish its drone stocks, as the countries pledged to deepen their alliance during a visit by Zelenskyy. The support includes C$350m (US$253m) provided through a programme known as Jumpstart run in conjunction with the US. Carney said Ottawa was also offering C$450m in loan guarantees to enhance the Ukrainian energy supply; meanwhile Canada was racing to increase its drone arsenal, from which 30% of Canadian production would go to Ukraine. Russia is illegally trafficking foreigners to fight in Ukraine who quickly become “cannon fodder”, Amnesty International said on Thursday, citing interviews with prisoners of war deceived into signing Russian military contracts. Among the victims were citizens of Brazil, Colombia, Sri Lanka and South Africa lured to Russia through fake job advertisements. “Then it’s coercion. Their passports are taken away. They are made to sign documents they don’t understand,” said Agnes Callamard, Amnesty’s secretary general. “They are given training they don’t understand [and used as] cannon fodder.”

webTitle: Tiananmen Square vigil organisers jailed for seven years in Hong Kong

fields.headline: Tiananmen Square vigil organisers jailed for seven years in Hong Kong
fields.trailText: Pro-democracy activists Chow Hang-tung and Lee Cheuk-yan were found guilty of ‘incitement to subversion’ in controversial national security case
fields.bodyText: Two pro-democracy activists who were put on trial for organising an annual Tiananmen Square massacre vigil in Hong Kong have been sentenced to seven years in jail, in one of the city’s most significant national security cases. Chow Hang-tung, 41 and Lee Cheuk-yan, 69, were found guilty in August of incitement to subversion. The court found they had “incited other persons to organise, plan, commit or participate in acts by unlawful means with a view to subverting the state power”. Chow and Lee were leaders of the Hong Kong Alliance, which for decades organised the city’s annual vigil in memory of those killed in the bloody crackdown on pro-democracy protesters in Beijing in 1989. Lee and Chow received prison terms of seven years, and seven years and three months respectively. Albert Ho, a 74-year-old former lawmaker who pleaded guilty in January, received a sentence of five years and two months. Their case represented one of the last high-profile national security trials to be heard in Hong Kong, as the national security law imposed by Beijing in 2020 extinguishes what was once one of the world’s most widely watched pro-democracy struggles. The Alliance disbanded in 2021 following pressure created by the introduction of the national security law. The case had centred on a slogan that was used for decades by the Alliance: “end one-party dictatorship”. The court ruled that the defendants “intended to cause others to lose confidence in the Chinese Communist party by stirring up hostility and causing division”. The defence said that the Alliance was simply exercising its right to freedom of speech. One supporter who attended the sentencing told the Guardian: “A demonstration that lasted for more than 35 years without any problem is suddenly being seen as subversion.” Chow, a UK educated barrister, represented herself in court. She has been in detention since 2021 and while in prison has frequently written letters published on her social media. In August Chow wrote a note to the UK prime minister, Andy Burnham, calling for Britain “to adopt a more robust stance in the face of the growing threat from a totalitarian and aggressive China”. The UK Foreign Office said it condemned the use of the national security law in convicting the two activists. Before sentencing, members of the public queued up for days to secure a seat in the court. Some in the queue had prepared food and umbrellas in preparation to stay overnight. Hong Kong and Macau were once the only places on Chinese soil where it was permitted to hold public vigils to mourn protesters who died on 4 June 1989 in Beijing. Hundreds, possibly thousands, were killed when the People’s Liberation Army put a bloody end to pro-democracy protests. For decades tens of thousands of people would gather in Hong Kong’s Victoria park to take part in a candlelit vigil. In 2020, Beijing’s sweeping national security law in effect banned public commemoration. In recent years, activists who attempted to publicly mark the day said they were frequently followed, searched and detained by plainclothes police. Authorities said the national security law would only affect a small number of people and was needed to return order after a year of often violent anti-government protests in 2019. But critics say it has transformed the city. “It is still surreal to me,” Lee’s wife, Elizabeth Tang, told the Guardian. “Every time the Alliance had an activity, they would get the police permission for every one. “The vigils are what made Hong Kong different,” she said, recalling the public commemoration that are now banned. “It’s very unjust. Complete silence is really very scary.” The case has seen widespread condemnation from foreign governments and human rights groups who criticised the use of the national security law to convict peaceful protesters and ban the vigil.

webTitle: Friday briefing: Would a wealth tax save our public services or be billionaire repellent?

fields.headline: Friday briefing: Would a wealth tax save our public services or be billionaire repellent?
fields.trailText: In today’s newsletter: Some think taxing the super-rich is a moral obligation, others say it drives cash away from the country. The truth may be somewhere in the middle
fields.bodyText: Morning pals, and let’s join in a heartfelt ευχαριστώ (thank you) to hedge fund billionaire Chris Rokos for the estimated £330m he paid to the UK Treasury last year, and sadly won’t be contributing in future as he’s relocating to Greece. The publicity shy tycoon (and former Tory donor) has not made explicit his reasons for leaving the UK: so one can only speculate Rokos may be drawn by the noted health benefits of the Mediterranean diet, or the Greek government’s attractive €100,000 flat tax for overseas investors. Predictably, one man’s decision is now being framed by some as a dire warning to government to halt taxes on wealth in the UK. Conversely, campaigners are arguing ever more stridently for a specific wealth tax. With taxes already at their highest level since the second world war, could this be the goose to lay the cure-all golden egg and fix our crumbling public services? I spoke to our senior economics commentator, Aditya Chakrabortty, whose response might not be what you first expect it to be. And, yes, we get into goose-plucking too. Five big stories UK politics | Ministers are facing a backlash from the hospitality industry after they announced mayors in England would be given sweeping powers to levy taxes on holiday accommodation such as hotels and Airbnbs. Economy | Nervous investors across big economies have been dumping government bonds, driving up the cost of borrowing, as surging oil prices amplified fears about rising inflation. US news | JD Vance made a clear pitch that he should be the heir to Donald Trump, closing out the Republicans’ midterm convention with a blistering speech that featured exaggerated claims of success. Israel | Testimony from 24 Israeli military insiders on the secret systems used in the war on Gaza has been revealed in a new documentary film about the mass killing of Palestinian civilians. UK news | Consumers will pay higher energy bills unless the UK government speeds up work on a vast programme of upgrades to the electricity grid to enable the switch to renewables, the public spending watchdog has warned. In depth: We need to think about what wealth actually means Taxes are at record highs; satisfaction with public services at rock bottom. It’s a dichotomy familiar to us all from our own private focus groups, be that the street WhatsApp community or the bowling club. Alongside this, wealth is rising exponentially while wages are not: from 2000 to 2025, for example, average weekly earning rose just over 100% while property prices went up by about 240%. According to the British Social Attitudes Survey, the segment of the public who say the government should further increase taxes to spend more on health, education and welfare is at its lowest level in over a decade, at 36%. Aditya offers me a quote from Jean-Baptiste Colbert, the minister of finances under King Louis XIV of France: “The art of taxation consists in so plucking the goose as to obtain the largest possible amount of feathers with the smallest possible amount of hissing.” “This has become harder to do as the tax burden has got higher,” Aditya tells me. “And so wealth taxes have really emerged as an attractive option to people in government, and to campaigners, not just here, but around western Europe and in America too.” *** What is a wealth tax and how would it work? Most advocates, when they talk about a wealth tax, mean an annual tax on assets over a certain threshold. The Green party of England and Wales, for example, proposes an annual tax of 1% on assets above £10m and 2% on those above £1bn, estimating it could raise almost £15bn a year. The campaign group Patriotic Millionaires – a bunch of likable sorts including Gary Lineker, Brian Eno and Val McDermid – suggests a 2% annual tax on total net wealth exceeding £10m, projecting revenue of £24bn a year. Oxfam, which is campaigning alongside them, says this rate would affect 20,000 people – about 0.04% of the UK population – and highlights polling carried out this May by YouGov, which found 76% of the public support “this fair wealth tax”. Campaigners present this as a slam dunk – minimal hissing for maximum feather. But dig into that polling a wee bit further and you’ll find the YouGov tracker poll, which instead indicates that Britons, over the past seven years, have a baseline preference for taxing income, rather than assets. It seems that, while the public are attracted to the concept of a wealth tax, they’re pretty selective about how wealth is defined. *** Why not start plucking? Critics of a wealth tax, in the right-of-centre thinktanks and the publications that report on them, argue that taxing the same wealth every year would penalise saving and investment; that a specific wealth tax would require expensive and unwieldy new administrative apparatus to value wealth; that focusing on the super-rich to raise revenue would make the UK a less attractive place for those people to work and invest. Aditya may not share their ideology, but he has his own reasons for being sceptical about current wealth tax campaigning, which he argues “offers apparently easy solutions, which will always affect someone else and never me”. Crucially, he says, if you’re running the government, the money raised by an annual wealth tax doesn’t make much dent in your bills, relatively speaking. The highest estimate is less than a third of the £80bn the UK government is planning to spend on defence annually by the end of the decade. And, once a tax is in place, so the dodges begin. “The one thing that the wealthy have in droves are advisers to show you how to avoid taxes.” “It doesn’t mean you shouldn’t do it,” he adds, “just don’t oversell it as a magic bullet.” *** What’s this about a one-off wealth tax? So with that bubble burst, Aditya points us to what he considers the most substantial piece of work done on wealth taxes in the UK to date. A couple of academics and a tax barrister came together during Covid lockdown, when the rest of us were struggling with the recipe for banana bread, to form the independent Wealth Tax Commission. They propose a one-off wealth tax, arguing that its fairer because it targets people with the most ability to pay, is very difficult to avoid and wouldn’t distort behaviour because it’s one-time only. Accounting for behavioural responses and admin costs, they estimate this would raise a total of £260bn at a rate of 5% over £500,000 per individual, payable at 1% per year over five years. To be clear: this would be paid by individuals whose total wealth after mortgages and other debts, and after splitting the value of shared assets such as a jointly owned family homes, exceeded the tax threshold, and only on the value of wealth above that threshold. For example, a wealth tax levied at 1% above £500,000 would require a couple to have net wealth of more than £1m before any wealth tax would be payable. This is where Aditya gets excited: “£260bn is more than we get from income tax in a year. It would be transformative – you could put it in a sovereign wealth fund and invest in renewables. Or you could put it directly into the NHS and schools.” It would, however, affect a very different tranche of the population – those de facto millionaires with property in desirable parts of Edinburgh or Manchester or London. And that’s where the hissing starts up again. *** Are there other ways to tax wealth? We’ve heard it many times before over other proposed taxes on wealth: Rachel Reeves reversed her plans to end inheritance tax breaks for farmers after lobbyists drove tractors up to the doors of parliament and drowned out speeches with their horns. When Ed Miliband proposed a mansion tax on properties valued over £2m, to raise £1.2bn annually for the NHS, in his 2015 manifesto, he was eviscerated by the rightwing media, party critics and Myleene Klass, who confronted him in a TV debate, arguing the tax wouldn’t just touch the super-rich but would devastate “little grannies” who bought modest London homes that had simply skyrocketed in value over the decades. But times change, don’t they? And Reeves was able to avoid a similar backlash when she introduced a similar council tax surcharge on properties worth £2m or more at the last budget. The Institute for Fiscal Studies has argued consistently that, rather than introduce a new wealth tax, the government should sort out the mess of current capital and property taxes. In May, Wes Streeting received a mixed reception when he proposed equalising capital gains with income tax, as part of his brief tilt at Labour leadership, describing it as a “wealth tax that works”. And of course, HMRC could get better at collecting tax from the super-rich: its own estimates suggest that at least £2.1bn extra could be raised from closing the wealthy tax gap. The trouble with getting more granular on wealth taxation, Aditya says, is that many of the groups affected – whether that’s farmers, lawyers or GPs in partnerships – are also very well-networked and good at making a noise about the specific unfairness of targeting them as opposed to others. Which takes us back to the more subtle point about burden-sharing and democracy that underlies his arguments: by focusing on the billionaires in the corner, we avoid looking at the millionaires in the mirror – and having an honest conversation about what wealth is and how sophisticated those who have it are at lobbying against further taxes on it. An annual wealth tax has so much support right now because “it’s very politically palatable”, Aditya says. “It will poll brilliantly for you, because everyone will say that won’t affect them”. His advice is to pivot, philosophically: “Forget about the wealthy. Think about wealth.” We want to hear from you Remember the Makerfield test? Andy Burnham promised it would be at the heart of his decision-making: whether policy worked for areas, such as his constituency, that feel overlooked by Westminster. Ahead of the Labour party conference I’ll be asking experts which of the prime minister’s decisions have passed or failed that test. Let me know which policies you want me to ask about by hitting reply or emailing first.edition@theguardian.com. What else we’ve been enjoying After reading this ranking of Céline Dion bangers by Alexis Petridis, I’ll be spending my lunchtime listening to It’s All Coming Back to Me Now on repeat (not for the first time, honestly). Michael Segalov, newsletters team You may vaguely know what the BBC charter is, how it defines the broadcaster’s relationship with the government, and even that it’s up for renewal next year. But what’s at stake in this “elaborate multi-year negotiation”? Barbara Speed investigates in this tremendous long read. Charlie Lindlar, newsletters team I really appreciated this heartfelt ode to RuPaul’s Drag Race UK by Alex Needham, after the BBC announced the show was being culled. It’d be much betta’ if the Beeb U-turned. Michael Between searching the app for winter hats for my son and winter knits for myself, I adored Kate Mossman’s report for the New Statesman on Vinted and its role in Britain’s addiction to fast-paced, low-cost online shopping. Charlie Em Hilton makes a powerful case in her column for the new sanctions on illegal Israeli settlements from the UK government, and the need for imminent further action to halt atrocities in the West Bank and Gaza. Michael Sport Football | Matheus Cunha broke the deadlock and Bruno Fernandes and Benjamin Sesko were also on target in Manchester United’s 4-0 win against Sabah in the Champions League. Tennis | Aryna Sabalenka’s grip on the US Open showed no sign of weakening on Thursday night as the two-time defending champion swept past Jessica Pegula 7-5, 6-2 to move one win from a third straight title. Read Peter Bradshaw’s full review. Read Luke Buckmaster’s full review. Music The Tubs: Hard Life | ★★★★☆ Britain’s best indie-rockers hold fast to their defiantly old-school sound, slipping wry sideways looks at despair in among hooky melodies that always sound like a good time. Read Alexis Petridis’s full review. The front pages “‘A hammer blow’”: plan for English tourist tax angers hotel industry”, is the Guardian’s front page today. The Telegraph says “Labour mayors plot 5pc tourist tax”, the Mail runs with “Burnham’s holiday tax to hammer families on UK breaks”, and the Sun’s take is “What the hol, PM?” The Times says “Households face £100 on bills to pay cost of wind”, and the FT leads with “Oil price surge and signs of stubborn inflation reignite global bond sell-off”. The Mirror, on Esther Rantzen, has “It’s too late for me”. Marking the 9/11 anniversary, the i Paper leads with “The day that changed the world”, and Metro says “25 years”. Donald Trump has pledged a payment of $5,000 to every adult American citizen if the Republicans win in the November midterms. When teen drama Two of Us first aired in 1988, the BBC insisted that the single snog be cut before broadcast, after the show had already been pushed into a late-night slot. And, initially, it was.
