webTitle: Emma Bonino, radical Italian politician who stood up to Vatican, dies aged 78

fields.headline: Emma Bonino, radical Italian politician who stood up to Vatican, dies aged 78
fields.trailText: Militant feminist led campaigns to legalise abortion and divorce and went on to become foreign minister
fields.bodyText: Emma Bonino, the radical Italian politician who led campaigns to legalise abortion and divorce against the objections of the Vatican, has died aged 78. “Today we lose not only our leader but also one of the most clear-sighted, courageous and free figures in the political history of our country,” the small party she founded, More Europe, said on Facebook on Friday. Bonino served as a European commissioner and as foreign minister in Italy but was best known as a militant feminist dedicated to political and humanitarian causes. “Her life was a long struggle against everything that denies freedom: against clandestine abortion, world hunger, the stranglehold of party politics, female genital mutilation, punitive justice, genocide, and every form of authoritarianism,” her party said. A former member of Italy’s Radical party, Bonino commanded respect across the political sphere. Italy’s far-right prime minister, Giorgia Meloni, paid tribute to her, saying that although their “backgrounds and perspectives differed, that never prevented me from acknowledging her significance and her role in our nation’s public life”. Even after the Radicals’ political star faded, Bonino remained a key political figure and human rights campaigner active in Italy for more than five decades. With her sharp wit and cutting insights, she appeared frequently on Italian TV. After a cancer diagnosis in 2015, she would appear in public wearing colourful headscarves. Bonino first got involved in Italian politics after she became pregnant aged 26 and had an abortion, even though it was illegal at that time. “I decided that never, never, never again should anyone have to suffer this humiliation,” she said. She went on to hand herself in to the police, turning her private “offence” into a ⁠public act of defiance. The arrest ⁠made headlines, fuelling a campaign that eventually led to the legalisation of abortion in 1978. It also launched Bonino into parliament with the Radical party, a small but relentless force for civil rights. During her 50-year political career, Bonino served as foreign minister, trade minister and EU affairs minister in Italian centre-left governments of the 2000s and 2010s. She remained an outspoken supporter of Europe and the rights of refugees and migrants. “You can look at the fights I have waged with this point of view: I support a democratic liberal order and believe in the centrality of the individual, his rights but also his responsibilities,” she told the Guardian in 2018. Over the years, Bonino cultivated a deep friendship with the late Pope Francis, despite their conflicting views on key ethical issues, including abortion and euthanasia. Bonino said that during their conversations Francis always encouraged her to bring forward her humanitarian battles, defending those most in need. When asked what battles she still needed to fight, Bonino would say: “Many, too many. Human rights, world hunger, free scientific research … Ten lives won’t be enough.” Bonino is survived by her siblings, Domenica and Giovanni, and their children.

webTitle: How a month-long competitive food tour is rewriting the story of Rio’s favelas

fields.headline: How a month-long competitive food tour is rewriting the story of Rio’s favelas
fields.trailText: ‘The doors that aren’t open to us in the rest of the city, we open for ourselves here,’ Maria Cristina de Sales says
fields.bodyText: Even at the age of nine, Maria Cristina de Sales knew exactly when to ask her mother’s colleagues at the slaughterhouse for a piece of the pig they were butchering: when they got close to the pork leg, her favourite part. When she grew up, Sales followed the path of many others from Brazil’s deprived north-east and moved south in search of better work opportunities. She arrived in Rio de Janeiro and, unable to afford a home in tourist-heavy south zone, moved to a favela further north. She crossed the city every day to work as a receptionist and secretary, but only really found her footing 15 years later when she and her husband opened a burger restaurant, inside the favela. “The doors that aren’t open to us in the rest of the city, we open for ourselves here,” said Sales, 39, inside her restaurant in Maré, a favela complex that emerged in the 1940s in a vast mangrove area, settled by workers who could not afford to live in – or had been evicted by the state from – the wealthier parts of the city. What usually dominates the headlines about Maré, a complex of 16 favelas home to 140,000 people, are problems such as poverty, armed drug traffickers and bloody police operations, but Sales’s restaurant has joined an effort to change that perception. From 1 October, local bars and restaurants will take part in a month-long competitive food trail made up entirely of Maré establishments, hoping to attract visitors from across the city who are often afraid to visit a favela. “We face prejudice simply for saying that we live in a favela, but there are a lot of good things here,” she said. Were it not for the surrounding alleys so narrow that sometimes only one person can pass at a time, the tangled web of electrical wires crowding the utility poles and the occasional young man riding a motorcycle with a rifle, Sales’s restaurant could be anywhere else in the city – a family-friendly, air-conditioned burger joint. The superhero-themed decor was a request by Sales’s sons, and includes a life-size Spider-Man. Her entry for the food trail will be, of course, a pork leg, made into burger named Peppa Pig. “It’s a reference to my story: a girl who came from the north-east, went through hell and is now here, proud and still fighting – just like many other people here in Maré,” she added. One sweet-and-slightly-spicy element of the dish – a pineapple jam with chilli and ginger – she learned to make at Casa das Mulheres da Maré, a centre set up by a local NGO, Redes da Maré, to support women and which organises the food trail, called Comida de Favela, or Favela Food. “When we improve the quality of life of a woman in Maré, we’re improving the whole community,” said Mariana Aleixo, 38, the centre’s coordinator, herself a chef who was born and raised in Maré and has worked in the kitchens of Rio’s luxury hotels, including the Copacabana Palace. The food trail is now in its fourth edition – the first was held in 2015 – and is one of four finalists in the Best Culinary Festival in Latin America category at the 2026 World Culinary Awards, which will announce the winners in October. The 16 restaurants – selected from more than 150 applicants, most of them Black-owned – receive management and marketing training and, starting this year, guidance on how to support customers who report sexual harassment. The winners, chosen by customer vote, receive cash prizes. Reflecting the origins of many residents or their ancestors, many of the dishes feature other references to north-eastern cuisine, such as the “North-eastern Explosion”, a pizza topped with cassava cream, coalho cheese – similar to halloumi – and carne de sol, a lightly salted cured beef usually fried in a clarified butter similar to ghee. “Gastronomy is the biggest economic sector in the community,” said Aleixo, noting that of the roughly 3,200 businesses in the area, about 1,200 are restaurants and bars. Aleixo said she had approached sponsors of other food festivals across the city and had never succeeded in securing their support. “I believe it’s because of prejudice against favelas,” she said. Although the aim is for visitors to experience the favela from a “perspective other than violence”, Aleixo acknowledges that some may witness something that the thousands of people who live there have to contend with: the occasional presence of armed drug traffickers. Police generally do not patrol favelas unless carrying out operations. The food trail has no connection to the criminals, who also do not interfere with its activities because they seem to understand that it benefits the community. “Some of the experiences we live through here are very violent, and we want the city to have access to that. Understanding that sense of indignation that residents often have is important so that people can build a different repertoire for thinking about public security in Rio,” she said. “Violence exists here just as it does in other parts of the city, but it does not define Maré entirely,” added Aleixo. Despite the invitation to outsiders – Favela Food’s social media pages often advertise shuttle vans to bring visitors from other parts of the city and take them back again – another aim is to encourage the circulation of people and money between the complex’s own favelas. While Sales’s burger restaurant is in the Parque União favela, the snack bar run by Beatriz Santos Antônio, 39, is in the Nova Holanda favela, a 15-minute walk away. Born in another city in Rio de Janeiro state, Antônio arrived in Maré 16 years ago because she could not afford to live elsewhere. She and her children went through periods of hunger, but neighbours helped them, and she drew on cooking skills learned from her mother to start selling cassava fritters. Her entry for the food trail consists of four elliptical fritters, a classic Brazilian bar snack that Antônio has taken to new heights: crisp on the outside and moist inside, filled with either roast beef or prawns with cream cheese. “I’ve come a long way,” said Antônio, smiling as she wiped away tears and made the final preparations for her first time taking part in Favela Food. “Today, these tears are no longer because of hunger. Today it’s a story of happiness and of being able to encourage other women to start their own businesses too. There is also a lot of happiness in the favela.”

webTitle: They drive toward tornadoes. We went with them to see how their work could save lives

fields.headline: They drive toward tornadoes. We went with them to see how their work could save lives
fields.trailText: Tornadoes kill hundreds each decade in the US. These researchers are investigating why some storms produce twisters – despite the fatal risks
fields.bodyText: On a narrow road in southern Iowa, my phone shrieked. Tornado warning. Take shelter now in a basement or an interior room on the lowest floor of a sturdy building. Again, the alert sounded. Then again. As if shelter were a choice. I peered through a peephole of scratched glass, wedged into the lead storm-chasing truck with tornado researchers Josh Wurman and Karen Kosiba. On either side of us, only fields. No houses. No basements. No sturdy buildings. The dark belly of a storm dragged across a horizon gone an eerie green. For tornado chasers, it was a near perfect sky. My son Cheney, a photojournalist, was somewhere behind us in a rental car alongside two other research vehicles. The convoy was strung out across miles of highway. He had been tracking my location, but now I had lost cell service. I couldn’t reach him. I kept dialing. No answer. When a call finally went through, Cheney told me the wind was driving the rain so hard the road had disappeared. “I’m scared,” he said. Blinded, he had turned one way, then the other. Finally, he stopped. Either direction, he feared, could put him in a tornado’s path. Cheney was no stranger to danger. He has covered Ukraine during wartime, spent a New Year’s Eve alone in a car reporting on Chicago homicides, and crisscrossed the country documenting violent weather, including the devastating 2021 tornado in Mayfield, Kentucky. I hadn’t heard him express fear since childhood. Then he said it again. “I’m scared. I don’t know what to do.” *** About 1,200 tornadoes strike the United States every year. Between 2020 and 2025, they killed roughly 410 people, injured nearly 3,800 and caused about $8.5bn in reported property damage. The tornado map is changing too. A 2024 study found 25% fewer moderate-or-stronger tornadoes in the western US and 12% more in the east, where mobile homes are more prevalent, basements to get to safety are scarcer, and twisters more likely to strike at night. Sometimes the change from ordinary to deadly takes only minutes. Several months earlier, physician Jason Persoff had told me about chasing near Joplin, Missouri, in May 2011. A little after 5pm, he and his partner began looking for hotel rooms, figuring they were done for the day. “Suddenly, it was as if someone vomited on the radar,” Persoff remembered. “It was incredible.” A violent tornado seemed to emerge from the sky almost fully formed. Its sound lodged deep in Persoff’s body. “I felt irrational fear,” he said. “Like a primal warning.” They pulled over to help stranded truckers as police arrived. Persoff told one officer he was a physician. “I hope you don’t work at St John’s,” the officer told him. “That hospital’s been destroyed.” “That’s still one of the most terrifying things I’ve ever heard,” Persoff said. More than 150 people were killed in that tornado. Wurman, whose team I traveled with, is among the researchers trying to understand why some storms produce tornadoes while others do not, and what tornado winds do close to the ground – knowledge that could improve warnings and help engineers design buildings to withstand them. But the systems built to study and forecast tornadoes are under strain. In the first four months of 2025, the National Weather Service lost roughly 13% of its workforce – more than 560 employees – to firings, retirements, resignations and attrition. By the 2026 storm season, the agency was hiring again, but staffing gaps remained, and some stations were unable to maintain the twice-daily weather-balloon launches on which forecasters and researchers rely. Scientists I spoke with said they had lost confidence in forecast guidance. Chris Weiss of Texas Tech, who led a parallel chase team with the National Severe Storms Laboratory, was blunt: “I don’t remember when a suite of models has performed as poorly as this year.” Frustrated by the blurred, distant view from fixed-site radar, Wurman invented the Doppler on Wheels – mobile radar laboratories known as DOWs – three decades ago. Filling one with diesel costs about $1,000, and that is the inexpensive part: the greater investment lies in the trucks, trained graduate students and experienced crews that take years to build. But funding has become more uncertain. By the end of this field season, neither Wurman’s team nor Weiss’s could count on support for the next one. Cessily Skinner, whose family has lost two homes to tornadoes in west-central Georgia, closely monitors every approaching storm. Now the cuts give her another reason to fear: “As someone who lived through a storm with all the data in place,” she said, “it’s terrifying to think, ‘OK, so now we really are guessing.’” *** With Cheney still on the line, a team member plotted his location against the storm. The radar could see what he could not. A tornado we were tracking was east of him and moving east. Cheney should be safe, she said, as long as he stayed put and waited it out. I repeated this to him. As we spoke, the rain loosened. The sky lifted. The road reappeared. Cheney pressed the gas and began closing the distance between us. The second radar truck arrived first. Fifteen long minutes later, Cheney’s rental car came into view. Relief and disappointment arrived together. The convoy was whole again. But the day had yielded none of the data the scientists had come for. Several tornadoes touched down across the region that afternoon. None crossed the roads where our instruments were waiting. The storms left behind a sky ribboned with dark clouds. Some team members stood outside the trucks and applauded its beauty, lifting their phones for photographs. Wurman and Kosiba were not among them. They were already studying the models, deciding where the team should spend the night to be best positioned for morning. *** Tornadoes offer enough spectacle to draw film-makers, thrill-seekers, and carloads of chasers with cameras. But scientists who chase for data need more than drama. They need geometry: an open horizon, a road in and a road out, a storm that forms where the instruments can reach it. Even when everything lines up, a mobile radar crew can spend weeks following one promising storm after another, only to watch each weaken and dissolve before the instruments capture the measurements they came for. Why do they keep doing it? For data analyst Paul Robinson, the pull started with an image on television: Dorothy clutching Toto, calling for Auntie Em as a black twister writhed in the distance. “The Wizard of Oz is still my favorite movie tornado,” he said. “For me, it captures the feeling.” Growing up in West Virginia, he began keeping a notebook, recording the weather whenever it turned severe. But 31 May 1985, turned that interest into purpose. Everyone on this team seems to carry a storm they cannot forget. Robinson’s was not a single tornado but an outbreak: 43 twisters tearing across Ohio, Pennsylvania, New York and Ontario, killing 89 people. “That convinced me that maybe I could do some good by going into tornado research,” Robinson said. Research scientist Trevor White’s defining storm came later, on 24 May 2016, near Dodge City, Kansas. “Every chaser and their mother came out,” he recalled. “We were on it from the time it was a small cumulus cloud. I had never seen a storm that could effortlessly produce tornadoes. I counted three on the ground at the same time.” In two hours, a dozen tornadoes formed beneath the supercell. It was nearly perfect in the way that mattered most: no one died, and the tornadoes remained mostly over open country. But even experienced researchers cannot always remain beyond a tornado’s reach. In 2013, veteran tornado researcher Tim Samaras was killed near El Reno, Oklahoma, along with his son Paul and colleague Carl Young. Samaras was Wurman’s friend. Wurman’s team was tracking the same tornado that day. Asked by a reporter whether the deaths made him reconsider his work, Wurman noted that covering extreme weather “isn’t dangerous statistically”. Samaras, he said, was among the most responsible chasers he knew. Wurman would not speculate about what had gone wrong but said his own team would review its procedures. Wurman and his colleagues then returned to the data, reconstructing the motion of the nearly impossible-to-see subvortex that had overtaken Samaras and his team. He pursues the sky at its most theatrical without surrendering to drama himself. He would rather leave a question open than force an answer the data cannot support. “I wish this research were more of a eureka thing,” Wurman said, “but it’s not. We can’t do laboratory-type experiments. We can’t put 10,000 patients into a study. Meteorology is horrible that way. We’re trying to understand what’s special about the circumstances where tornadoes form and what it looks like when they do. But we can’t control the environment.” “Every time we’re in a disaster area, I carry with me the trauma of people who survive it,” White told me. “I don’t know if we can do anything to ease the impact of that experience, but I’ll never stop searching. The only thing worse than a human tragedy is a human tragedy where you can’t learn anything.” *** A mile outside Good Hope, Illinois, the deployment order came. Our truck slid to a halt on the shoulder of a two-lane road slick with rain. Robinson jumped out to unleash the radar dish. It began sweeping the sky, each rotation shuddering through the vehicle. Back in the driver’s seat, he talked to himself – “c’mon, c’mon” – as he worked the controls to lower a stabilizing pad into the mud, trying to keep the vehicle’s right side from sinking. He kept the left wheels on the pavement, he told me later, in case we needed to move fast toward – or away from – a tornado. In the back, White balanced one keyboard on his lap and kept several others within reach. Four screens glowed in front of him. “Frustrating,” Robinson murmured. “We’re getting data, but I want to see it; I want to see the fury.” The horizon closed around us. From the front passenger seat, I watched a low shelf of black clouds over the cornfields, its ragged underside reaching down in unfinished gestures. The walkie-talkie crackled, then Wurman’s voice came through. “What do you see?” No one answered immediately. White and Robinson studied the screens and conferred quietly in technical shorthand. They were looking for a hook curling in the rain, a couplet tightening in the wind field, some sign that the atmosphere had made up its mind. The clouds kept darkening. The dish kept turning. The truck kept shuddering. Robinson waited through one scan, then another, watching new data appear on the screens over White’s shoulder. Finally he spoke, his voice tight. “It’s falling apart, isn’t it?” After a few more minutes, Wurman confirmed he saw the same. He called out a new waypoint and then we were speeding again down a country road, pursuing the uneasy hope at the center of this work: a storm dangerous enough to teach but merciful enough to spare. *** When things align, the value of a single intercept can endure for years. On 18 May 2013, the team captured data from an EF4 tornado near Rozel, Kansas. It remained on the ground for about 30 minutes, long enough for the researchers to hold position and gather unusually rich measurements. “That gave us a chance to dig in deep,” Kosiba said. “And that data is still being used by engineers today. That’s why you have to keep going out, even with the misses. We’re in it for the long haul.” A 2024 study co-authored by Wurman and Kosiba analyzed mobile-radar wind profiles from 36 tornadoes. Those findings helped shape new national standards for designing buildings to withstand tornado winds, showing the potential impact of readings collected in the path of storms. This is the scale on which science advances: one measurement clarifying another, a dataset enduring long after the tornado itself disappears. Behind every chase is a life forced to accommodate the forecast. We had driven 2,000 miles in three days, from dawn until after dark, crossing and recrossing North Dakota, Minnesota, Wisconsin, Iowa and Illinois. Wurman’s team had gone weeks without the intercept they needed. Weiss’s team had endured an equally disappointing season. “We put in the same effort for fewer results,” Weiss told me. “We have lives and families, and we’re making a lot of sacrifices. So when it doesn’t work out, it eats at you.” White has a soft spot for hummingbirds. He keeps several feeders at home, and goes to great lengths to find someone to refill them when he’s gone. His absence is measured out in sugar water. He carries a small stuffed hummingbird on the road. “I told my wife a week ago we’d be home tomorrow. Instead, we are still out here, and there’s no end in sight,” he said. “But there’s something fundamental about this research that draws me in. The best version of me is the version that does this work.” Before this trip, I had imagined storm chasing as a form of appetite, the desire to see the most violent thing the sky could make. I hadn’t understood its strange rhythm: tedious hours beneath empty skies, then sudden races down country roads, decisions pressed into seconds, and moments of stark fear. The work demands patience when nothing happens and clear judgment when everything happens at once. Inside the truck, it looked less like appetite and more like devotion: painstaking, deliberate, largely invisible. In a culture that rewards quick verdicts and emphatic claims, these scientists let the sky contradict them. They reverse direction and answer to evidence rather than personal conviction. That discipline feels radical. Years from now, the data they gather may become a stronger roof, an earlier warning, hospital walls that hold. The researchers may never know whose lives their persistence reaches. That last night with Wurman’s team, I wrote three lines in my notebook: We went storm chasing. Nothing happened. We learned a lot.

webTitle: Russia targets Kyiv petrol stations for first time with jet-powered drones

fields.headline: Russia targets Kyiv petrol stations for first time with jet-powered drones
fields.trailText: Three facilities in two days struck as bombardment of Ukraine’s capital enters new phase of intensity
fields.bodyText: Petrol stations in Kyiv have been hit by jet-powered drones in a wave of targeted Russian attacks as the bombardment of Ukraine’s capital enters a new phase of intensity. At least two people were killed and 12 injured in strikes on two petrol stations on Friday morning, according to the city’s mayor, Vitali Klitschko. The rush-hour strikes follow a similar attack on a petrol station on Thursday, the first of its kind in the capital. At the Ukrnafta petrol station in the Pochaina neighbourhood in northern Kyiv, bystanders said three people had been injured in Friday’s blast – the manager of a nearby car wash, his wife and the driver of a passing car. The blown-out vehicle was stranded by the side of the road, its windows shattered and seats spattered in blood. Witnesses said they had heard two explosions, and local authorities later said Russia had carried out a double-tap attack on the facility. “This is probably one of the most difficult periods of the war because life is just like on a rollercoaster,” said Anastasiia Demchenko, 30, who works at a delivery company opposite the petrol station. “It feels like life is on the edge.” All three strikes targeted petrol stations operated by Ukrnafta, a state-owned oil and natural gas extraction company. Sergiy Fedorenko, the acting head of Naftogaz, Ukrnafta’s parent company, said: “There is, and can be, no military objective behind such attacks. This is terror directed at the civilian population, at peaceful people.” A list of 18 petrol stations in Kyiv expected to be hit by Russian drones started circulating on Telegram on Wednesday. The three struck so far were on the list. At the other station hit on Friday, in Desnianskyi district, one of the most densely populated parts of the capital, the manager of a nearby car wash said it had been a miracle that no one had died in the blast. Fedir Lesovin said the air-raid siren had given the petrol station workers time to run to a nearby shelter, and that a customer waiting outside his business saw the incoming drone and also ran to safety. Russia has increased its attacks on Ukrainian petrol stations in recent months. Facilities in the east and south of the country have been repeatedly targeted, but this week’s attacks mark the first time that strikes against a vital part of daily life have been brought to the capital. Ukraine has also targeted Russian oil infrastructure. Its special forces said this week that they had struck facilities at the Caspian Sea port of Makhachkala. Kyiv has been pounded by daily drone and missile strikes since late August, at a time when Ukraine is running low on Patriot interceptors. A brief reprieve for the visit of the US envoys Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff over the weekend ended on Monday. The petrol station attacks happened as Volodymyr Zelenskyy was on an overseas trip intended to drum up international support and aid before what is expected to be a difficult winter. On Thursday the Ukrainian president met Canada’s prime minister, Mark Carney, who offered support to help boost Ukraine’s drone stocks. Additional reporting by Illia Dyadik

webTitle: AfD’s new state MPs include ex-Stasi officer, former porn actor, neopagans and neo-Nazis

fields.headline: AfD’s new state MPs include ex-Stasi officer, former porn actor, neopagans and neo-Nazis
fields.trailText: Far-right German party’s newly elected representatives face fresh scrutiny as it tries to form government in Saxony-Anhalt
fields.bodyText: The Alternative für Deutschland is facing scrutiny over the suitability of some of its prospective new MPs – including a former Stasi officer and a former pornography actor – just days after its historic win in the German state of Saxony-Anhalt. Presented by the AfD’s lead candidate, Ulrich Siegmund, for a photocall in the state capital of Magdeburg on Thursday, some of the members-elect were revealed to have a range of questionable backgrounds, including criminal records, Stasi pasts and connections to far-right networks. German media has revealed that among the 39 parliamentarians who will represent constituencies across Saxony-Anhalt in the state parliament, is a man alleged to have participated in pornography films and falsified academic qualifications; a former officer for the East German secret police, the Stasi; and several members under criminal investigation for their involvement in neo-Nazi organisations. Two MPs are facing investigations into allegations they sought to continue the activities of the banned rightwing extremist organisation Artgemeinschaft, a neopagan group that has embraced nationalist and antisemitic ideas. The younger of the two is also alleged to have violated the law in relation to weapons, according to the public prosecutor’s office. Both reject the allegations. The erstwhile pornography actor was convicted for stealing bedding in bulk from a hotel. A court confirmed he had been a pornography actor after he contested a local newspaper’s claims. He was expelled from a university after being found to have falsified his school leaving certificate, Die Zeit reported. The MP says he was readmitted after a legal challenge. An ex-Stasi officer, aged 78, who won a direct mandate in his constituency, has admitted to having worked for the ministry for state security in the communist GDR, focused on East German citizens who wanted to permanently emigrate. His role as an MP-elect has been criticised by campaign groups on behalf of victims of the former East German dictatorship. Also, an investigation by the broadcaster ZDF revealed that some AfD ministers-elect who were also members of the previous parliamentary group, had ties to rightwing extremist groups. This included some having been members of the subsequently outlawed Homeland-Loyal German Youth group, HDJ. At one stage one of them had led the organisation, while an adviser to the AfD’s parliamentary group wrote a biography described as an “homage to national socialism”. Among the prospective MPs are a number with pro-Kremlin links, as well as some who visited members of the Maga movement in Washington. Russian president Vladimir Putin initially said he would not comment on the AfD victory, but speaking to reporters during a visit to India for the BRICS summit later blamed “western globalists”. “I think that everything happening in Europe right now is basically ‌the result of system errors by the so-called West … the western globalists in politics, security, and economics,” Putin said. The AfD has promised to curb migration and restore ties with Moscow. Asked to respond to the questionable biographies, in particular of the two MPs under criminal investigation, Siegmund, a former fragrance salesman who was unanimously re-elected as the AfD’s parliamentary group leader on Thursday, referred to the men in jest as “the bad guys” and said “we will await the results of the investigations and then discuss them”. Siegmund himself triggered fierce criticism during the presentation of his new parliamentary group after linking the production of arms in Germany to the party’s planned deportation offensive. In response to a journalist’s question about the planned opening of an Israeli arms company in the state, Siegmund said: “We do not categorically condemn the production of arms, because we will of course need equivalent resources for the future remigration and deportation offensive. This is also in the interest of internal security, our own instability and national defence.” The statement was seized on by the party’s opponents. Katja Pähle, the chair of the Social Democrats (SPD) parliamentary group in Saxony-Anhalt, said Siegmund had issued a “political threat” by suggesting the use of “violence as a political tool”. “This reveals the ugly face of a political system whose language and ideas are once again reminiscent of totalitarian models,” she said. Whether the AfD, which secured 44% of the seats, forms a state government, which would make it the first far-right party to gain power in Germany since the second world war, will depend on whether it can find other like-minded MPs who might defect, or a single party willing to support the AfD. So far, the mainstream parties have refused to enter a coalition with the AfD, which has just under half of the 83 seats in the state, three short of an absolute majority. Protests against the AfD are planned in more than 20 cities across Germany this weekend in response to the party’s win last Sunday, and ahead of two crucial state elections on 20 September, in Berlin and in Mecklenburg Vorpommen, where the AfD are predicted to do well.

webTitle: The rapid Houthi advance in Yemen: why it matters and what’s at stake

fields.headline: The rapid Houthi advance in Yemen: why it matters and what’s at stake
fields.trailText: The Houthis have wrested control of Yemen’s Red Sea coast from Saudi-backed government, giving Iran and its allies control over a key shipping lane
fields.bodyText: Violence has erupted again in Yemen, where a rapid advance by the Houthis in recent days is threatening another waterway critical to global shipping. More than 1,000 people have been killed or wounded, and tens of thousands displaced by the most significant fighting between the Iran-aligned Houthis and the Saudi-backed Yemeni government forces in years. Though the immediate catalyst for the fighting has been the US-Iran war, it stems from years of conflict in Yemen itself. Who are the warring parties in Yemen’s civil war and who are their backers? The two main parties fighting in Yemen’s civil war are the Yemeni government forces alongside their allies, and the Houthi movement. Yemen’s government controls the north-east of the country, and its southern port. The government is the internationally recognised authority in the country, but is chiefly backed by Saudi Arabia and a coalition of Arab countries which intervened on behalf of the government during Yemen’s civil war. The Saudi-led coalition, in addition to supporting the Yemeni government forces, directly intervenes militarily in the country, mainly through airstrikes. The government’s control of the country is contested by the Houthis, who hold the western part of the country, including its capital, Sana’a. The Shia group is broadly aligned with Iran and comprises part of the “axis of resistance”, a coalition of Iran-aligned armed groups in the Middle East, such as Hezbollah. But while the group is aligned ideologically with Iran, which supplies some arms shipments, the Houthis are considered an independent group with their own policies. A variety of smaller armed groups are also active in the country. What’s been happening in recent days? Last week the Houthis launched a wide-ranging offensive to take parts of the western coast of Yemen and gain a more strategic position over Bab al-Mandab. Fighting then broke out across multiple fronts in Yemen as the Saudi-backed government forces tried to reconsolidate their position, with clashes starting in al-Jawf, al-Baydaa, Taiz and Hodeidah. The Yemeni government forces then released a statement saying they were launching their own campaign to try to retake Sana’a from the Houthis. The Houthis launched missile strikes on Saudi Arabia on Tuesday, injuring 73 people and causing huge fires at Saudi oil installations. Saudi Arabia then launched more than 50 airstrikes on Yemen in a 12-hour period on Wednesday. It was the most significant fighting in the country since the UN-brokered peace plan in 2022. On Thursday and Friday, a rapid Houthi advance southwards along Yemen’s western coast resulted in the capture of the port city of Mocha and then the strategic island of Perim in the the Bab al-Mandab strait. Pending a counter-offensive from government forces, the group is now in a position to control shipping through the strait. How significant is the strait? Bab al-Mandab is a critical waterway for shipping, with about 10% of global maritime trade passing through the strait. It has become more important since the US started its war against Iran and the latter closed the strait of Hormuz. The Red Sea, via Bab al-Mandab, has become a vital lifeline for Saudi Arabia to export its oil. If the Houthis gained full control over the strait, the group would be able to virtually close shipping through the waterway, or charge tolls. It would give Iran and its allies control over two key shipping lanes in the region. How did the war in Yemen begin? The civil war began in 2014 when fighting broke out between the Houthis and the Yemeni army after Houthi supporters were shot at during mass protests against fuel subsidy cuts in the capital, Sana’a. The Houthis promptly seized the capital, and by 2015 had toppled the government. A coalition of mostly Arab countries, led by Saudi Arabia, then intervened on behalf of the ousted government, with a mostly aerial campaign that was widely criticised for its deadly impact on the civilians of Yemen. The Yemeni government declared the southern port city of Aden to be its temporary capital, while the Houthis continued to maintain their control over Sana’a and much of the rest of north-west Yemen. The government-aligned side was made up of several groups that fractured over the course of the war, primarily along the lines of their two chief backers: Saudi Arabia, which backed the Yemeni government itself, and the United Arab Emirates, which mainly supported the Southern Transitional Council (STC) and the Joint Forces. The country also fractured, with al-Qaida seizing territory in east Yemen, and separatist groups, such as the STC, pushing for division of the country. The Saudi-led coalition also brought foreign mercenaries into the conflict. Frontlines hardened and the war entered a deadlock. The Saudi-led coalition’s intervention was becoming increasingly unpopular internationally and had not led to the defeat of the Houthis. Weary of fighting, warring parties agreed to a temporary UN-mediated truce in 2022. The truce was extended twice, and calm largely held across the country until this September. Why did the UN-brokered peace plan break down? The peace plan has been strained since the war in Gaza started on 7 October 2023. Israel launched the war in response to a Hamas-led attack in Israel that killed about 1,200 people. Israel’s war in Gaza, which has killed more than 70,000 Palestinians and earned widespread condemnation for what a UN committee said was genocide, drew the axis of resistance into the fray. The Houthis, in what they said was a move of solidarity with the people of Gaza, began targeting ships in the Red Sea that they said were heading for Israel. The western coast of Yemen occupies a strategic position for global shipping because it overlooks Bab al-Mandab, a strait that links the Red Sea and the Indian Ocean. The Houthi campaign brought about a US military intervention and strained the truce in Yemen. At the same time, its intervention brought the Houthis support regionally and within the territory they hold. With the Houthis’ position strengthened, the group stopped seriously engaging in negotiations, frustrating Saudi Arabia. In July, an Iranian plane landed in Sana’a airport, despite the protests of the Yemeni government, leading Saudi Arabia to strike the airport. The Houthis then declared a naval blockade of Saudi Arabia in the Red Sea, a key route for Saudi oil since Iran closed the strait of Hormuz in March. What has been the humanitarian impact of the war? The war in Yemen, and the Saudi-led coalition aerial campaign in particular, has devastated the country’s population. At least 150,000 people have been killed since 2014 by fighting alone, while hundreds of thousands more have died from related causes, such as hunger and disease. About 4.5 million people have been displaced by fighting and more than 18.2 million are in dire need of humanitarian assistance, according to the UN. The renewed fighting has further exacerbated humanitarian conditions. The World Health Organization said the latest clashes had killed or wounded more than 1,000 people and displaced tens of thousands.

webTitle: Ireland holds its breath as its leftwing president prepares to meet Trump

fields.headline: Ireland holds its breath as its leftwing president prepares to meet Trump
fields.trailText: Many are rooting for vocal critic Catherine Connolly to let rip in Dublin meeting, but others hope she holds back
fields.bodyText: Catherine Connolly, Ireland’s president, once said she abhorred Donald Trump’s policies. In his sole previous comment on Connolly, the US president seemed to think she was a man. Now that they are about to meet, Ireland is holding its breath. Trump is to fly into Dublin on Saturday morning for a two-day visit centred on golf. But before making it to his beloved greens, protocol obliges him to meet a woman who has given every impression of loathing him. A courtesy call to Áras an Uachtaráin, the Irish president’s official residence and workplace in the city’s Phoenix Park, has left the government anxious and the media reaching for popcorn. “What could possibly go wrong?” headlines ask. Many in Ireland are rooting for Connolly to let rip at Trump for his policies and rhetoric on immigrants and the Middle East. Others hope she will stifle any criticisms to avoid provoking a visitor who could upend Ireland’s economy. The taoiseach, Micheál Martin, said he had no concerns “at all” about the encounter, but one senior official said the government was on tenterhooks. “We need to get him [Trump] in the Áras, then out of the Áras. We’ll breathe easier after,” they said. Before winning the Irish presidency – a ceremonial post – last year, Connolly was an independent leftwing member of parliament for Galway who protested against Trump’s 2019 visit and more recently assailed him over his positions and policies on Gaza, Iran and other issues. “If we are going to act as an independent sovereign state, a neutral republic, we must use our voice to speak to power and the abuse of power by president Trump,” she said. Asked in March about the criticism, Trump replied: “He’s lucky I exist.” Trump is now to meet Connolly – and Martin in a separate meeting – before heading to his golf resort in Doonbeg, County Clare, which is hosting the Irish Open. Heavy security around the Phoenix Park and Doonbeg will insulate the US president from protests, including a “No welcome for Trump” demonstration that is expected to draw thousands to central Dublin on Saturday afternoon. Some hope Connolly will speak for them when she meets Trump behind closed doors. “She should speak truth to power,” Rosie O’Donnell, the US comedian who moved to Ireland after Trump won a second term, told the Irish Independent. “I don’t think she should drop what she believes in to be polite to a madman. He is like a mad king that has destroyed the country.” Leftwing parties that supported Connolly’s presidential run urged the former barrister to “find a way” to convey criticism without causing a diplomatic storm. Trump has expressed affection for the emerald isle but also wants American tech and pharmaceutical firms to move jobs and taxes from Ireland to the US, a scenario that could devastate Irish state finances. During her election campaign, Connolly promised to heed constraints of the office, which is largely symbolic and has no responsibility for foreign policy. She also said that if asked, she would meet Trump. “That implies that it’s not to meet him in order to berate him,” said Bobby McDonagh, an former Irish ambassador to the UK and EU. “She’ll have an opportunity to have a chat with President Trump and make some gentle points reflective of Irish values. I expect it to go smoothly.” Connolly could emulate Martin, who discreetly rebutted some of Trump’s opinions during a visit to the White House, said McDonagh. “He had the emotional intelligence and experience to do it in a way that didn’t provoke any reaction.” The six-time major champion golfer Rory McIlroy said he and other competitors at Doonbeg would focus on the game, not politics. “It’s going to be different with him being here but we’re here to play a golf tournament and it’s a good golf course so we’ll keep our heads down and play,” McIlroy said.

webTitle: Lübeck’s sweetest treat deserves a visit | Brief letters

fields.headline: Lübeck’s sweetest treat deserves a visit
fields.trailText: Brief letters: Café Niederegger | Reading’s Bayeux tapestry | Trump’s renaming spree | The Amerigo Round
fields.bodyText: In her piece on Lübeck (‘Fabulous museums and no queues’: five of the best under-the-radar city breaks in Europe, 6 September), Rachel Dixon didn’t mention the German city’s sweetest treat, the Café Niederegger. Many will know the city’s name from Niederegger marzipan as much as Thomas Mann. Their museum on the floor above the cafe includes a lifesize marzipan statue of the writer, whom they claim was also a fan. Elizabeth Card Leeds • It is surprising that Reading Museum has not used the publicity surrounding the arrival of the Bayeux tapestry in the UK to blow its own trumpet more loudly. Its superb copy of the Bayeux tapestry, produced by 35 women in just over a year, finishing in 1886, is free to view. Joyce Quarrie Leytonstone, London • In answer to Marina Hyde’s question of what’s next in Donald Trump’s huge renaming spree (America: the gulf, the lake and now the state – what’s next on Trump’s huge renaming spree?, 8 September), how about The Donald J Trump Mass Extinction, to sit alongside the Ordovician, Devonian, Permian, Triassic and Cretaceous mass extinctions? President Trump deserves to be remembered for his contribution. David Mond Leamington Spa, Warwickshire • To complete the president’s proposed changes, perhaps the Oval Office should be renamed Amerigo Round. Philip Arundel Colwall Green, Herefordshire • Have an opinion on anything you’ve read in the Guardian today? Please email us your letter and it will be considered for publication in our letters section.

webTitle: Enjoy Łódź – but don’t omit its tragic past | Letter

fields.headline: Enjoy Łódź – but don’t omit its tragic past
fields.trailText: Letter: Dr Richard Bradbury responds to a travel article about the Polish city, home to one of the largest Jewish ghettos during Nazi occupation
fields.bodyText: I was shocked to read your travel article detailing the delights of Łódź without a single mention of the city’s past as the site of one of the largest ghettos during the second world war (A city break in Łódź, Poland’s capital of cinema and factories, 5 September). The article says: “I ask Anna how Łódź fared in the second world war. ‘It was not too badly damaged,’ she says. ‘Both the Germans and the Russians wanted the industry intact.’” I wonder how the surviving family members of the perhaps 200,000 people who died after being herded into the ghetto, often to work as slaves for the Nazi war effort, would feel about that. Łódź is indeed a wonderful city, and I have watched its transformation since I worked there in the late 1980s. Your article highlights the many great pleasures of the city today, as I too experienced on my most recent visit in July. But as so many have said in the past, if we ignore history, all too often we repeat it. Dr Richard Bradbury Exton, Devon • Have an opinion on anything you’ve read in the Guardian today? webTitle: UK sanctions on West Bank settlers are the right step | Letters

fields.headline: UK sanctions on West Bank settlers are the right step
fields.trailText: Letters: Readers respond to the move announced by Ed Miliband to impose sanctions on illegal Israeli settlements
fields.bodyText: As a religious Jew, I am disappointed at the reaction of some of our communal leaders and bodies to the sanctions on trade with illegal Israeli settlements (UK accuses Israeli ‘terrorists’ of ethnic cleansing in West Bank with government backing, 8 September). Many Jews in the UK are horrified by the Israeli government’s actions, which include promises from some ministers of burying the idea of a Palestinian state, and turning a blind eye to unchecked settlement expansion and escalating settler violence. While much of the British media may choose to platform one view as being representative of the Jewish reaction to these sanctions, I would point to organisations such as Yachad and Na’amod, which provide an alternative anti‑occupation narrative. It is also frustrating that the opinion of the chief rabbi is upheld by news organisations as though he is the Jewish version of the pope: he isn’t. There are indeed rabbis in the UK who agree with these sanctions, or who have visited the West Bank and seen displays of injustice and violence with their own eyes, and understand that something must be done (Senior UK rabbis come out in support of sanctions on Israeli settlements, 9 September). There is a multiplicity of opinions on this nuanced subject that cannot be boiled down to a statement from one leader. I walk through the world visibly Jewish with a kippah on my head. I will also be attending synagogue over the High Holy Day period. During this period of increased antisemitism, my safety as a Jew and the urgent need for all countries to “call out” Israel are not mutually exclusive. Jewish people are held responsible for the actions of an Israeli government over which they have no control – that’s true. This, as the foreign secretary has stated, is antisemitism and should be tackled. However, above all, I believe that when we Jews see suffering we have an impetus to act, no matter how conflicting it feels: “If not now, when?” Jonathan Tebble Brighton • The government’s announcement of sanctions against settlements in the West Bank could have been better timed. Those of us in Israel who have worked for years to create a just and secure peace for two nations, and in six weeks’ time have a chance to remove a government that persists in settlement expansion and the denial of Palestinian rights, have just been kicked in the nuts. There is nothing more dangerous than an Israeli electorate who feel that the world is against them. The British government, along with other European countries that made similar declarations, may well have handed an election victory to the very forces they are committed to undermine and remove: the likes of Benjamin Netanyahu, Itamar Ben-Gvir and Bezalel Smotrich. It would have been more sensible to make the announcements after 27 October, possibly when the new government had been formed and was available for policy discussion with its international partners. Clear and sincere commitments to peace and security for both countries would be enormously more helpful than declaring sanctions against West Bank settlements before an Israeli election that is critical for the future of a liberal, democratic state of Israel. Robin Newell Kibbutz Sde Nehemia, Israel • A substantial minority of British Jews like myself agree with the UK government’s new use of the term ethnic cleansing to describe how armed settlers in the occupied territories evict Palestinians from their land, with passive and sometimes active support from Israeli institutions. While the UK’s trade ban on goods from the occupied West Bank and new language is unlikely to be a significant catalyst for change, the terminology is now at least accurate. Tolerating settler violence is longstanding Israeli policy, which I’ve seen with my own eyes. Twenty-two years ago I spent some months in a tiny farming village in the West Bank called Yanoun, where neighbouring armed settlers were severely harassing Palestinian villagers. Settlers killed livestock, contaminated wells, walked with guns through the hamlet, drove their cars up and down village roads, and beat villagers. I saw with dismay the indulgent favour of state forces towards these most renegade settlers: how regional police (settlers themselves) laughed contemptuously at villagers’ complaints; and how, when called upon for protection, the Israeli army arrived slowly or not at all, and did nothing. In the last year, I learned that Yanoun’s villagers have left their beautiful village for a second time, perhaps for good? This is how ethnic cleansing works. Dr Vivienne Jackson Walthamstow, London • Have an opinion on anything you’ve read in the Guardian today? Please email us your letter and it will be considered for publication in our letters section.
