webTitle: US to bar some South Africans over claims of anti-white discrimination

fields.headline: US to bar some South Africans over claims of anti-white discrimination
fields.trailText: Announcement of visa restrictions follows Trump’s false claims of ‘white genocide’ taking place in South Africa
fields.bodyText: The US has announced visa restrictions on some South Africans as Donald Trump’s administration continues to claim that South Africa’s government racially discriminates against white minority Afrikaners. The announcement did not specify individuals who were barred from the US. Trump has spent his second term falsely claiming there is a “white genocide” in South Africa and railing against its affirmative action policies. Since the start of last year, the US has cut aid to South Africa, barred it from this year’s G20 summit in Miami and set up a refugee programme for Afrikaners and other South African racial minorities. Meanwhile, the Trump administration has been dismantling refugee and asylum programmes for people fleeing war and persecution. “The South African people are being failed by a government that is destroying its economy through an obsessive pursuit of racial grievance against the Afrikaner minority,” the US secretary of state, Marco Rubio, said in a post on X. “The South African government has consistently failed to adequately address rural crime, violent and dehumanising rhetoric, and race-based discriminatory policies against Afrikaners and other minority populations.” The US visa restrictions would target “foreign nationals who enact or enable policies that promote race-based discrimination, incite violence, or enable land confiscation without compensation in South Africa”, Rubio added. The US ambassador to South Africa, the conservative media activist Leo Brent Bozell III, said on X: “As has been made absolutely clear, the time for endless ‘dialogue’ has run its course … This visa restriction policy is only the first step in a series of escalatory measures that will show America’s firm resolve in this matter.” South Africa’s foreign ministry said in response that its policies were being misrepresented. “The announcement, once again, aligns with the mischaracterisation of South Africa’s domestic policies by fringe groups who wrongly portray themselves as representatives of “minorities” and Afrikaners in general,” the ministry spokesperson Chrispin Phiri said in a statement that was first published in Afrikaans. Phiri added: “It is our sovereign right to put in place laws that address the nation’s concern over centuries of racial injustice … South Africa respects that the United States may hold different views regarding particular measures and their implementation.” Afrikaners, who are descended from Dutch and French settlers, ruled South Africa during apartheid. The regime discriminated against and repressed the country’s black majority, while keeping white people safe and wealthy. Since Nelson Mandela took office as South Africa’s first black president in 1994, South African governments have tried to redress the country’s racial inequality, including through Black economic empowerment policies and buying land to redistribute. These efforts have had limited impact. White South Africans typically have 20 times the wealth of Black people, according to a 2023 article in the Review of Political Economy, an economic journal. Nonetheless, some white South Africans claim they are now the victims of racial discrimination, allegations that US conservatives have long promoted. Rubio’s visa restrictions announcement criticised land expropriation without compensation. South Africa introduced a law last year that allows the government to seize land without paying for it in specific circumstances, including if it is abandoned or only held for speculation. There is no large-scale expropriation of land. Among white South Africans who think they are discriminated against, many cite the far-left opposition leader Julius Malema’s repeated use of apartheid-era chant “Kill the Boer”, Boer being another word for Afrikaner. A video featuring the chant was played by Trump when he met South Africa’s president, Cyril Ramaphosa, in the Oval Office last year. The ruling African National Congress party has disavowed the chant, which South African courts have ruled is not meant literally and is therefore not hate speech.

webTitle: Merz cancels UN visit after AfD election win puts his leadership on the ropes

fields.headline: Merz cancels UN visit after AfD election win puts his leadership on the ropes
fields.trailText: German chancellor gets support from state leaders but further far-right gains this weekend could spell the end
fields.bodyText: Powerful German state leaders from Friedrich Merz’s party have rallied behind him as speculation builds that his days in office may be numbered. The chancellor’s hold on power has looked increasingly shaky since a bombshell regional election result earlier this month in which the far-right Alternative für Deutschland (AfD) party routed his Christian Democratic Union (CDU) party in Saxony-Anhalt. With two more states heading to the polls on Sunday where the AfD is expected to perform well, Merz cancelled a plan to speak at the UN general assembly in New York next week because “his presence is required in Berlin”, a government official said on condition of anonymity. The announcement triggered fresh rumours that the unpopular chancellor could be preparing his own exit or wanted to remain and fight off a potential coup. With Merz on the ropes after just 16 months in office, eight ⁠state premiers from the CDU issued a surprise joint statement backing him. Citing the threat posed by nativist parties across Europe, they wrote: “Now more than ever, Germany’s political landscape needs stability”, ‌pointing to ‌elections in Poland, Italy, Spain, Greece and France next ‌year in which the political establishment faces a far-right challenge. “The path to restoring public trust in Christian Democrats lies in listening and taking political action, not in debates over personnel.” They added that Germany needed “reliability and decisive action” and, as state leaders, “we want to, and will, do our part to achieve this together with the chancellor”. The signatories included leaders who have been mentioned as possible Merz successors, such as North Rhine-Westphalia’s Hendrik Wüst. Markus Söder, the Bavarian premier and an ambitious conservative populist, has also said he was backing Merz. It remains to be seen how long the demonstration of solidarity with Merz will hold, with much depending on the outcome of the weekend elections. Polls indicate voters are very likely to punish the CDU again in the states of Berlin and Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania on the Baltic coast, amid widespread dissatisfaction with Merz’s federal coalition government formed with the Social Democrats. Merz, who is also the CDU’s chair, will convene a meeting of its leadership on Sunday evening to coordinate a response as the results come in, in what senior party members called a pre-emptive “show of unity” behind the chancellor. The anti-immigration, pro-Kremlin AfD’s resounding win in Saxony-Anhalt sent a shockwave through Europe’s largest economy and beyond, although the party fell just short of the absolute majority required to govern alone in the state. It is seeking enough support from other parties’ lawmakers in the state parliament to make its chief candidate, Ulrich Siegmund, the first far-right regional leader in Germany since the Nazi period. Merz took office in May 2025 promising to cut the surging AfD back down to size by reviving the moribund economy and addressing fears around “irregular” migration. Instead, the AfD is now topping the national polls with clear momentum behind it. The party’s co-leader, Alice Weidel, has targeted the CDU for “destruction” and pledged last week in parliament that Merz’s party would “never win another election again”. During the same debate in the Bundestag, a wan and defensive Merz lashed out at Weidel and the AfD’s lawmakers, accusing them of seeking “ethnic cleansing” with their calls for “remigration”, a legally dubious programme of mass deportations. Critics said he failed to outline a clear vision for the remainder of his term. Weidel, whose party drew congratulations from Donald Trump and Elon Musk for its Saxony-Anhalt victory, on Wednesday taunted the state leaders backing Merz. “The CDU is making it clear that it is committed to ‘business as usual’ rather than the positive changes that citizens need,” she posted on Musk’s social media platform X. “The only way to achieve those changes is with the AfD!” The month’s developments have triggered a sense of helplessness and fear among the mainstream democratic parties, with even the opposition Green party calling on the CDU to right the ship before it is too late. “Get your shit together,” said the Greens co-leader Felix Banaszak in Berlin, appealing to Merz and the CDU to end speculation that he called destabilising. Banaszak said that while he was no fan of the centre-right-led government, he warned that calls for a Kanzlertausch, a swap of the chancellor from Merz in favour of another Christian Democrat, could trigger new elections in which the AfD could come out on top. “We live in such dramatic times that this country just can’t afford that right now,” he said. The next general election is due in 2029.

webTitle: Abortion bans make ‘evidence-based medicine’ impossible in some cases, new report says

fields.headline: Abortion bans make ‘evidence-based medicine’ impossible in some cases, new report says
fields.trailText: Some 41 states restrict abortions, a ‘core component’ of maternal fetal practice, high-risk pregnancy non-profit says
fields.bodyText: Maternal fetal specialists should see abortion care as a “core component” of their practice in states where laws restrict abortion, according to a new special statement from the Society for Maternal-Fetal Medicine (SMFM). Some 41 states ban abortion at some point in pregnancy, and these legal restrictions make it difficult or impossible for clinicians to practice “standard-of-care, evidence-based medicine”, the report, released on Tuesday, says. The Dobbs decision made it even more challenging for patients to access abortion care in the US, as more restrictions went into effect in some states. Deaths from ectopic pregnancies nearly doubled between 2020 and 2025, a ProPublica analysis found, and later-abortion providers in haven states report that patients are showing up “later and sicker”. “In some ways, the practice of maternal-fetal medicine is inseparable from family planning and abortion care,” said Justin Lappen, chair of SMFM’s reproductive health committee and a co-author of the statement. In July 2021, Kate Dineen was about 33 weeks pregnant and giddy with excitement. Her husband was finally able to join her for his first ultrasound of their second child, after Covid restrictions were loosened. But then the room went quiet; the silence stretched on as the ultrasound tech lingered over images of the baby’s brain. Soon, after an MRI and consultation with a pediatric neurologist, they learned that their son had suffered a catastrophic stroke in utero, and his chances of surviving even the pregnancy were poor. Dineen remembers asking, “What are my options?” One of the specialists said, “You may still be able to explore termination – if you’re able to travel.” Dineen was stunned. She lived in Massachusetts, where abortions were banned after 24 weeks except in specific cases – and her case didn’t qualify for an exception, she learned. The maternal fetal team at her hospital offered to link her to a later abortion clinic in Washington DC, Dineen said. She and her husband rushed to find childcare for their 18-month-old son and made the long drive to Maryland, where they stayed multiple nights, to receive care. “We’re just so grateful to get the compassionate care that we needed and deserved, and should have been able to get closer to home,” Dineen said. If she’d been able to get the abortion in Massachusetts, it would’ve been much easier to grieve and find closure, she said. “Instead, our lives were turned completely upside down,” she said. “I feel like I barely survived it.” Maternal fetal specialists are at the forefront of many reproductive health decisions – including genetic diagnosis, ultrasound diagnoses and screening for anomalies, and complicated maternal medical conditions. That’s why guidance from professional societies on supporting abortion is key, so providers may expand their roles and “continue to provide as much care as possible” said Lappen. The statement highlights what can be done on the individual level when it comes to caring for patients, and it points to the role that specialists play in “institutional advocacy” to make sure their health systems have plans to support patients ahead of time, he said. “It’s really important for health systems, for hospitals, to be able to create safe systems of care and to understand what the state reproductive health legal landscape looks like,” Lappen said. That way, they can create the most comprehensive and expansive systems to provide care, he argued. It’s imperative to set guidelines now, before emergencies arise, Lappen said. “When someone’s facing a really significant pregnancy complication, where decision-making has to happen in a critically acute or rapid time frame, that’s not the best time to get on the phone with the lawyers.” Providers and health systems should “expand access to abortion care to the legal limit allowed by state law” to provide the most comprehensive care to patients, the statement says. That means understanding the exceptions to those laws and how providers may offer care in those scenarios, which can often be complicated to interpret but are no less important, Lappen said. “The law is intended to be sort of black and white,” said Lappen. “And healthcare and physiology and pregnancy complications live in the shades of gray.” Dineen, who is now an advocate and board member of Reproductive Equity Now, said it’s “really wonderful” for the medical society to highlight the key role that abortion care plays in maternal-fetal medicine. Providers “should be exploiting exceptions to the fullest extent in ban states”, she said. At the same time, she added, “I wouldn’t want this to be interpreted as ‘bans with exceptions work.’” Maternal-fetal specialists can also advocate against abortion bans in order to serve all of their patients, she said. It’s a “misconception” that adding exceptions to abortion bans means that patients who need abortions will be able to access them, Dineen said. “A ban with exceptions often functions just as a ban.” Even though she believes her providers wanted to give her the standard of care, and even though Massachusetts did carve out exceptions, she still had to travel hundreds of miles to get an abortion. In Massachusetts, she said, “we uniquely are able to demonstrate why bans with exceptions don’t result in patients being able to access care.” In 2022, after Dineen and others testified about how restrictions kept them from medically necessary care, Massachusetts legislators expanded the abortion exception to include “grave fetal diagnoses”. It was an improvement, Dineen said, but some patients were still not getting care. Now, Massachusetts is removing the 24-week ban, which means all patients will have access to standard reproductive care. The law “unties the hands of our world-class MFMs and other providers here to ensure that these deeply personal medical decisions are made between the patient and their provider at any point in pregnancy”, Dineen said. Maternal-fetal specialists in Massachusetts played an important role in changing the law, Dineen said. “That has been a real game-changer, having their expertise guiding the discussion again,” she said.

webTitle: European Union invites Canada to become first ever ‘associate member’

fields.headline: European Union invites Canada to become first ever ‘associate member’
fields.trailText: Commission president says EU must ‘urgently reimagine our partnerships’ as she makes unprecedented offer
fields.bodyText: Canada has been invited to become the first “associate member” of the EU by the European Commission president, Ursula von der Leyen. In an unprecedented offer, von der Leyen said on Wednesday that the EU and Canada “see the world with the same eyes” through shared democratic values and common approaches to many big issues, from AI to climate breakdown, the Ukraine war and geopolitics. Speaking in the presence of the Canadian prime minister, Mark Carney, at the European parliament in Strasbourg, she said: “We want to bring the relationship with Canada to the highest level possible. We must urgently reimagine our partnerships. So, I would like to work with you on opening the door for Canada to be the first associate member of the EU.” Carney, who is due to address the parliament on Thursday, has called for a “unique alliance” with the EU as Canada seeks to reduce its heavy dependence on US trade. He later tweeted: “Canada and the EU are natural partners, united by shared values.” The EU and Canada are due to hold a summit in late October to develop the future relationship. Canada and the EU already have a trade deal and numerous bilateral agreements, but have been moving closer since Donald Trump returned to the White House and raised tariffs on both old allies, while repeatedly talking about Canada becoming the 51st US state and lambasting the EU. Von der Leyen said the existing EU-Canada trade deal would be upgraded to an “alliance for the future” to create a “common prosperity and economic security space”. She said the two sides would also create a tech alliance, integrate defence industrial bases and make the Arctic a “flagship joint project”. EU officials are especially interested in Canada’s energy and natural resources. Von der Leyen pitched joint work on energy, critical minerals, batteries, AI, quantum computing, cybersecurity and economic security. The offer of associate membership is certain to raise questions among other EU allies, including the UK, which has long sought a more flexible approach from Brussels. The 27-member EU has never had an associate membership category, although it has close ties with Norway, Iceland and Switzerland, allowing deep economic integration with these countries, who follow many EU rules. It remains to be seen what associate membership means, including for Canada’s relationship with the EU single market. When the UK was negotiating its departure from the bloc and post-Brexit relationship, EU officials repeatedly said there was no status that enabled a foreign country to be half in and half out of the single market. The phrase itself took EU insiders by surprise since von der Leyen had not used the term when she briefed senior EU diplomats ahead of her speech last Friday. One EU diplomat said member states were “generally very supportive of ambition” in the EU-Canada relationship, but had been slightly worried in recent weeks that von der Leyen was overpromising on Canada. “‘Associate membership’ sounds like a nice headline but in reality 10 member states have still not ratified Ceta,” the person said, referring to the EU-Canada trade agreement that was agreed 10 years ago. A second EU diplomat described associate membership as “an empty phrase”. Carney’s approach to dealing with Trump has however attracted widespread praise among MEPs. Last month, Carney announced he was breaking off trade talks with the US, saying Canada would not be subjugated, and then introduced retaliatory tariffs on billions worth of US goods. By contrast, the EU last year accepted 15% tariffs on many European goods while dropping its own duties to avoid a trade war with Trump. Javier Moreno Sánchez, a Spanish socialist MEP, who leads the European parliament’s Canada delegation, said “for sure” the EU had lessons to learn from Carney’s approach, because “Trump respects people who are strong”. He added: “Canadians are the most European people outside Europe and that is the key point for the development of our relationship.” Martin Leng at the Brussels Institute for Geopolitics thinktank said a world in flux was “pushing the EU towards far greater flexibility in its relations with third states”. He said von der Leyen’s speech, with its focus on different sectoral areas of cooperation “points to the ambition and strategic breadth of the associate membership which the parties have in mind but also suggests that, in reality, Canada’s ‘membership’ may consist of ‘plugging in’ to existing programmes and frameworks, such as the European Defence Agency, rather than joining the union in any traditional sense”. Roland Paris, the director of the Graduate School of Public and International Affairs at the University of Ottawa and a foreign affairs adviser to the former Canadian prime minister Justin Trudeau, said the term “associate member” has taken too much focus and “doesn’t really matter” in the long term. “My hunch is that von der Leyen was hoping to rally supporters of much closer cooperation with Canada by using that label. In the end, what I expect is that we’re going to see a collection of agreements rather than membership in any institutional sense,” he said. Carney’s decision to formalise close ties with Europe however prompted outrage from Conservatives at home. Pierre Poilievre, the Tory leader, posted on social media that he feared Canadians “struggling to pay their rent” would have to pay more taxes “to fund the European Union’s heavy bureaucracy”. “The welder from Welland didn’t elect a Eurocrat to regulate our steel. The farmer from Saskatchewan and the fisher from the Atlantic provinces didn’t choose a Brussels food regulator who has never seen our prairies or our coasts,” he wrote. “We will NEVER be the 51st American state. And we will NEVER be the 28th state of the European Union.” Another, Jamil Jivani, posted that Conservatives “will NEVER support Mark Carney’s Liberal plan to have Canada join the hopelessly run, over-regulated, and self-destructive EU”. Paris said no Canadian leaders “would be interested in formal EU membership if it involves subordinating Canadian law and regulatory structures” to Europe. “I don’t think that’s on the table right now. There has long been a bipartisan push in Canada to deepen trade connections between Canada and Europe,” he said. “We’re now seeing now is a logical extension of those trade discussions into other areas.”

webTitle: EU moves closer to social media ban for under 13s

fields.headline: EU moves closer to social media ban for under 13s
fields.trailText: Ursula von der Leyen announces draft law to stop apps ‘depriving children of their childhood’
fields.bodyText: The EU will move forward with plans for an under 13s social media ban, the head of the European Commission has confirmed. Ursula von der Leyen said on Wednesday that social media apps were “depriving children of their childhood” and big tech platforms needed to prove the safety of their products. She promised a draft law for a total ban on social media for under 13s, while children aged 13-15 would be allowed “mini accounts” under parental supervision with time limits on apps. The commission will publish its social media plan on Thursday, which will have to be agreed by the European parliament and 27 EU member states if it is to become law. Von der Leyen also promised that the commission’s Digital Fairness Act, due to be submitted to the European parliament this year, would tackle features such as addictive design, which she said was “harming everyone”. The commission president made the comments in Strasbourg as part of her annual state of the union address. In a wide-ranging speech covering the EU’s place in a turbulent world and plans for continent-wide legislation, she also promised a European heatwave plan and committed to an emergency response mechanism to deal with sudden inflows of migrants in response to events in the Spanish enclave of Ceuta in August. Von der Leyen also made an unprecedented invitation to Canada to become an “associate member” of the EU, and pledged to set out ideas for a European security council involving Canada, Norway, Ukraine and the UK. The former German defence minister said the EU needed its version of Nato’s article 4 – an “emergency security protocol” that means all member states would convene at the request of another in response to a hybrid attack. “Europe needs its own counter-hybrid playbook,” she said. “We urgently need a consensus on how to respond to certain incidents – those which fall below armed aggression but clearly threaten our national security.” Nato’s article 4, which is separate from the collective defence clause, article 5, means members of the alliance can consult when one of them believes their territorial integrity, political independence or security is threatened. European nations have recently faced a series of hostile acts attributed to Russia, including sabotage, incursions by jets into European airspace and a drone attack on Leipzig airport. Warning that Ukraine faced a tough winter, von der Leyen suggested the EU may have reached its limits on economic restrictions against Russia. “What is needed is not necessarily new sanctions, but above all the enforcement of existing sanctions,” she said. After 21 rounds of measures, EU member states have found it increasingly difficult to agree sanctions on the Kremlin’s war machine, wary of the cost to their own economies. Von der Leyen also touched on Europe’s divisions over whether or not to introduce restrictions on trade with Israel and its illegal settlements in the West Bank. The commission has declined to publish a proposal to ban trade with illegal Israeli settlements, though several EU member states and allies including France, Canada and the UK have moved in this direction. “When Europe is divided, it cannot change the course of events,” she said.

webTitle: US opts not to back Saudi Arabia in Yemen after meeting Houthi leaders

fields.headline: US opts not to back Saudi Arabia in Yemen after meeting Houthi leaders
fields.trailText: Iran-backed militants have offered Trump administration assurances over safety of Red Sea shipping
fields.bodyText: Officials from the US met Houthi leaders over the weekend at the country’s embassy in Muscat, Oman, it has been confirmed, leading to the US decision not to intervene to help Saudi Arabia drive back a Houthi advance inside Yemen. The Iran-backed militant group reassured the US that the ceasefire agreement between the two sides struck in 2025 still held and the movement had no intention of attacking US shipping in the Red Sea. Only Saudi-linked shipping was regarded as a target owing to its blockade of Yemen, the Houthis confirmed. The meeting helps to explain Donald Trump’s decision to condemn the Houthi advance down the west coast of Yemen for threatening freedom of navigation through the Bab al-Mandab strait, but so far to reject any military response in support of Riyadh. The US is already embroiled in an expensive and resource sapping conflict with Iran, which backs the Houthis. The US labelled the Houthis as a foreign terrorist entity in March 2025, but in the recent past American officials have met leaders from Hamas, Hezbollah and Iran. The US vice-president, JD Vance, confirmed on Monday that the US was in direct contact with the Houthis. The US refusal to become directly involved has put pressure on Saudi Arabia to reach either a diplomatic solution with the Houthis over the future governance of Yemen, or to try to build a regional alliance with Pakistan and Turkey to force the Houthis back. In a lightning offensive last week, the Houthis seized control of large swathes of western Yemen along the Red Sea coast. A former deputy US ambassador to Yemen, Nabeel Khoury, said a “kind of tacit understanding” had been struck between the Trump administration and the Houthis. Khoury added: “The Houthis are promising the American administration that American and international navigation will not be affected in the Red Sea, but the only danger is to Saudi ships or those carrying Saudi oil.” In an attempt to build popular support against the Houthis in the region, Riyadh made the disputed claim that the Houthis had fired a drone at the holy city of Mecca on Tuesday, but the missile had been destroyed by Saudi defence forces. It said the drone was entering a prohibited airspace close to Mecca’s most holy shrines. The drone was intercepted at about 6.50pm local time on Tuesday, according to coalition spokesperson Maj Gen Turki al-Maliki. Saudi Arabia said any attack on Mecca was a red line and the move was condemned in lengthy statements by the UN-recognised Yemen government based in Aden as well as the 57-country Organisation of Islamic Cooperation. The Pakistani prime minister, Shehbaz Sharif, condemned what he described as a “dastardly and heinous” attempted attack on Mecca. “The people of Pakistan are saddened and perturbed by this outrageous act,” he said in a statement posted on X. The Houthi leadership – followers of a Shia Zaydism that respects the pilgrimage to Mecca – dismissed the claim as the lie of the century, and said such worn-out lies had been used before and fooled no one. The Houthi’s deputy foreign minister, Abdul Wahid abu Ras, said “whoever opened the land of the two holy mosques to debauchery and entertainment parties, and whoever defiled the land of the two holy mosques by the presence of Zionist Jews in it, is the one who targets Mecca, Medina and the Islamic holy sites”. The Houthis countered that they had shot down a Saudi F-15 plane close to Marib, and attacked an Aramco plant in the Red Sea port city of Yanbu. No supporting evidence was provided by the Houthi military spokesperson, but the head of the Houthi negotiating team, Mohammed abdul Salam, said the downing of the plane was a warning to the west not to fall victim to Saudi propaganda. Mohammed al-Farah, a Houthi political bureau member, said: “The truth is that Saudi Arabia is experiencing a real predicament in Yemen. It became embroiled in a war, a siege and an occupation, and then failed to achieve its goals. “Today, it is looking for external solutions, so it is begging the international community, warning the world about Bab al-Mandab and requesting support from Pakistan, Turkey, America, Israel and Egypt. Then it is trying to mobilise Muslims with a false pretext called ‘targeting Mecca’.” Separately, Israeli officials have leaked details of a secret meeting between military commanders from the US, Israel and several Arab states in Germany last week to discuss the war launched by Israel and the US against Iran. The report from the Axios journalist Barak Ravid said the “private retreat” was organised by the head of US Central Command, Adm Brad Cooper. Citing two unnamed Israeli officials, Ravid reported that the meeting was attended by the military chiefs of staff of Israel, Saudi Arabia, the United Arab Emirates, Bahrain, Kuwait, Qatar, Jordan and Egypt. It was the first such gathering since the US and Israel went to war with Iran more than six months ago. Israel, once a target for the Houthis, is offering to intervene in Yemen on Saudi Arabia’s behalf. A meeting of the UN security council on Tuesday condemned any attempt to close the Red Sea, but the meeting was notable for the Russian envoy beginning to edge away from its previous stance that the UN-recognised government based in Aden was the only legitimate government inside the country. In Beijing, the Iranian foreign minister, Abbas Araghchi, on Wednesday met his Chinese counterpart, Wang Yi, in an effort to secure support for its plans for the future administration of the strait of Hormuz. The strait remains closed owing to separate Iranian and US blockades. A Chinese foreign ministry spokesperson said China did not want to see further regional tension spill over into Yemen and the Red Sea. The Chinese called on the US to return to the talks based on the memorandum of understanding agreed between the two sides in June. Beijing, the main importer of Iranian oil, is eager for a settlement and is resisting any suggestion that US secondary sanctions applied to countries trading with Iran should apply to its own country. Oil prices remain well over $100 (£74) a barrel and a key Saudi east-west pipeline remains closed because of a bombing incident.

webTitle: ‘We are prey’: discovery of seven women’s bodies fuels anger over femicide in South Africa

fields.headline: ‘We are prey’: discovery of seven women’s bodies fuels anger over femicide in South Africa
fields.trailText: String of female murder victims found near Johannesburg’s international airport, including five in the past week
fields.bodyText: The discovery of the bodies of eight women around Johannesburg’s international airport, including five in the past week, has prompted an outpouring of fear, grief and anger over a lack of progress in tackling femicide. When Elizabeth “Tsontso” Moselakgomo did not return after going for a run on 9 September, her eight-year-old daughter alerted relatives, who contacted police. The 38-year-old’s body was found on Saturday and identified by relatives on Monday. The news of her disappearance had gone viral. Police said in a statement on Saturday that four women’s bodies had been found since 15 July in Kempton Park, across the highway from OR Tambo international airport. All were half-naked and with visible bruising. On Monday and Tuesday, two more bodies were found in the town of Olifantsfontein about 15 miles north of Kempton Park. On Tuesday, police said another woman’s body had been found 25 miles to the south-east, naked and decomposed. The acting police minister, Firoz Cachalia, said on Wednesday that another woman’s body found in Olifantsfontein on 7 September, was being added to the investigation. “In this country we are prey,” Sakane Mokoena posted on Instagram after confirmation of the death of her friend and fellow runner Moselakgomo. South Africa has one of the highest rates of femicide in the world. Women were killed at a rate of 12.2 per 100,000 people in 2022, nearly six times the global rate, according to the UN Office on Drugs and Crime. For years, women have called on the South African government to take gender-based violence seriously. After hundreds of women protested on the eve of the G20 summit in Johannesburg in November 2025, President Cyril Ramaphosa declared it a national crisis. However, the lack of a concrete plan or action has frustrated campaigners – and women keep being killed. The latest deaths are being investigated by specialist officers, who said on Saturday: “Women in and around Kempton Park are urged not to walk or run alone, particularly in isolated areas. They should avoid secluded spaces, remain vigilant and, where possible, travel or exercise in groups.” South African women responded with anger at the idea that they had to be responsible for their own safety, with many runners noting they already took precautions, such as sharing routes. “We are tired of being told to be vigilant when women are already doing everything possible to stay alive,” said the advocacy group Women For Change. “It should not take a missing woman, a desperate family, runners and communities searching, and a case going viral, before an area is searched with this intensity,” the group said. Detectives said on Saturday that they were examining a serial killer angle. However, on Monday, a police spokesperson, Athlenda Mathe, told reporters: “For now, nothing tells us that we’ve got a serial killer.” Mathe added that a suspect in the killing in July of the first woman, her boyfriend, was in custody. Ramaphosa said on Tuesday that he had directed police authorities to prioritise the ongoing murder investigations. Although the gender of the suspect or suspects in the other killings has not been confirmed, campaigners called on men to take responsibility for violence against women and children. “When some of these things happen in our presence, most of us men tend to look the other way,” said Bafana Khumalo, a co-executive director of Sonke Gender Justice. “You have excuses like ‘No, it’s not my business’. We feel strongly that violence against women is our business. We need, as men, to begin to face each other squarely and hold each other accountable.” The identification of Moselakgomo’s body has triggered an outpouring of grief. Mokoena met her about two years ago, when Moselakgomo joined a running club so she did not have to train alone on Saturdays. “She’s an amazing woman,” said Mokoena. “She always spoke about her daughter. Tsontso always said ‘Bye guys, I have to go, I have to go to my child’. “That’s just an example of how close she was with her baby girl. And she was a really light-spirited, funny and joyful woman, who was kind – very, very kind.” Running clubs around South Africa organised events to remember Moselakgomo and Mokoena said she hoped this would help push the government and police to do more to protect women. She added: “I’m just happy that the world, or at least our country, was standing still for a moment to acknowledge what is happening. Let’s get this out there and figure out exactly what is happening to women.”

webTitle: Sweden voted against more power for the far right – but are centrists listening?

fields.headline: Sweden voted against more power for the far right – but are centrists listening?
fields.trailText: Even as the ‘extremist’ AfD seeks further election gains in Germany, Europe’s leaders can learn from Sweden’s dangerous embrace with far-right ideology
fields.bodyText: Europe’s focus turned nervously to Sweden on Sunday, after an explosive election in Germany just a week earlier placed a far-right party, officially classed as “extremist”, on the brink of power in a German state for the first time since the Nazi era. A party with neo-Nazi roots has been pulling the government’s strings in Sweden for the last four years. Would the country’s general election put the far right formally in government? Or would enough Swedes opt for a gear change, having seen the Sweden Democrats’ hardline (some would say poisonous) agenda in action? Votes were still being counted on Wednesday but it was immediately clear that the far-right Sweden Democrats had suffered a setback; their first loss of support among voters since entering parliament for the first time 16 years ago. The party slipped from being the country’s second biggest party to its third. The centre-left Social Democrats appear poised for a return to power, although it could take months for their leader, Magdalena Andersson, to form a coalition. Strong results for the left and green parties gave her left bloc a wafer-thin, three-seat majority. Is the far right’s regression, however modest, a turning point? Have Swedes reached the limits of a taboo-busting experiment with populist, nationalist rightwing prescriptions? And is there a message for mainstream leaders across Europe, many of whom seem fatalistic about a continent-wide far-right surge? France goes to the polls in April while governments in Italy, Spain and Poland, all face their electorates later next year. The Dutch political scientist Cas Mudde says elections in one country are a poor guide to what will happen in another. Specific local factors in Sweden, including a scandal, may have dented the far right’s support. For Mudde, the scale of the AfD’s win in Saxony Anhalt, however, was “a black day for Europe” – and with far-right ideas gaining ground, he warned mainstream politicians that “today’s key fight is for democracy, rather than for party or power”. This is where Sweden offers a cautionary tale. Its political establishment had “fully normalised” the far-right party, Mudde said. “Its nativism is now shared by all the major parties, albeit in lighter form, from the Moderates on the right to the Social Democrats on the left.” But the decline in the far right’s support, for now, he thinks, “at the very least creates space for mainstream parties to focus on issues other than immigration”. Ann-Cathrine Jungar, a professor of political science at Södertörn University in Stockholm, is very sure that the Sweden Democrats are not on the way out. Electoral rankings go up and down, she said, and the party’s influence will endure. More important now is how the mainstream parties respond. “We focus a lot on the extreme and radical right parties, but the key to their influence is what the other parties do. Why have Sweden’s mainstream parties adopted the far right’s policies? The Social Democrats have co-opted their ideas, even though they are counter to the country’s needs. In Sweden, we need competent, talented people who want to come and live here, we need labour for health and social care. Yet nationalism seems to be the prevailing ideology now.” In a widely read Guardian essay headlined How Sweden lost its soul – and stopped being Sweden, published before the vote, Martin Gelin documented his country’s transformation after 2022. Rightwing parties that year signed a Faustian pact with the Sweden Democrats, buying its support for a minority rightwing government. The deal? The far right party was given a direct hand in shaping policy. “A new Sweden has emerged, cruel and cold for migrants”, wrote Gelin, with xenophobic and ethno-nationalist ideas “now comfortably embedded in the political mainstream”. Most shockingly, Andersson’s Social Democrats, modelling themselves on their hardline Danish counterparts, had bought into the far right’s framings on crime and immigration. Will Sweden’s Social Democrats now learn from their worst performance in more than 100 years, and embrace an agenda that does not involve deporting toddlers to Iran, people with dementia to the UK, or locking up 14-year-olds? Jungar is sceptical. “When it comes to linking crime and immigration, this is the new normal,” she said. “The Social Democrats will not pursue policies that are more liberal.” Yet the political centre in Sweden could articulate a clear alternative to the far right, Mudde says. The Left and the Greens did significantly better among young voters in this week’s election. “This reflects a development we see across Europe, namely that young people prefer outspokenly leftwing parties over centre-left parties.” *** Ghosts of grievance Like Giorgia Meloni’s party, Brothers of Italy, and Marine Le Pen’s National Rally in France, the Sweden Democrats have “deradicalised” in selective ways, to broaden their appeal, Jungar told me. By contrast, what was striking in Germany, was how the AfD doubled its score to 44% of the vote, on what Constanze Stelzenmuller in the FT called “a programme of stunning malevolence”. Two further regional elections this Sunday in Berlin and Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania will be closely watched, including by the AfD’s American boosters such as Elon Musk. Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania has economic and demographic conditions comparable to Saxony Anhalt. For those struggling to understand the appeal of the AfD in eastern Germany, Carolin Würfel’s essay offered an original insight. Born in the former East Germany, Würfel believes that many voters there don’t actually know or care about the AfD’s detailed policies. But the party had tapped into a legacy of grievance about the economic impact of reunification in the 1990s. “Villages and small towns that had been hollowed out, some of them ghostly and depopulated, were suddenly told again: you matter. Everyone else may have left you behind, but I, we, the AfD, care.” The AfD won’t improve life in east Germany, Würfel wrote, “but that was never the point”. As in Sweden, the political centre in Germany is now being warned that time is running out to offer a credible democratic alternative to the far right. As Florian Ranft of the Das Progressive Zentrum thinktank wrote: “Waiting for the AfD to fail is not a strategy.” To receive the complete version of This Is Europe in your inbox every Wednesday, please subscribe here.
