webTitle: Trump threatens to stop trading with EU over ‘laughable’ membership offer to Canada

fields.headline: Trump threatens to stop trading with EU over ‘laughable’ membership offer to Canada
fields.trailText: US president responds as Mark Carney seeks to move closer to Europe and diversify defence ties
fields.bodyText: Donald Trump has threatened the EU with “serious tariffs” and a halt to trade after the bloc proposed making Canada its first ever associate member – an idea he derided as “laughable”. The US president said that if the EU moved forward with the plan, Washington could impose “very serious tariffs or stop trading with Europe”. He added: “If it’s a good intention, that’s fine. If it’s a bad intention, we’ll put very heavy tariffs on Europe.” Canada’s prime minister, Mark Carney, is due to address the European parliament on Thursday, a day after the European Commission president, Ursula von der Leyen, invited his country to become the EU’s first “associate member”. Von der Leyen pitched closer cooperation on tech, defence and energy to Carney, telling the European parliament that, as democracies faced a “fracture in the international rules-based system”, Brussels and Ottawa needed to pull closer together. She said: “This is a partnership not against anyone else, but for our common strength. In short, we want to bring the relationship with Canada to the highest level possible.” In response to Trump’s comments, France’s Europe minister Benjamin Haddad said on Thursday that Washington had no power to veto EU decisions. “It is not up to the United States, or ‌anyone else, to choose the political and geopolitical direction of the Europeans. Once again, we have a relationship ⁠with Canada, and we are fully entitled to seek to deepen it,” Haddad ‌told Public Sénat TV channel. A European Commission spokesperson said: “As our president made clear yesterday, the proposed strengthening of the relationship with Canada is not against anyone else, but for our common strength.” Carney has called for a “unique alliance” with the EU as Canada seeks to reduce its heavy dependence on US trade. After meeting EU leaders in Strasbourg on Wednesday, he described the EU and Canada as “natural partners, united by shared values” and said that both sides were focused on “a deeper partnership that reinforces our mutual sovereignty to create more opportunities and prosperity for our peoples”. An associate membership agreement would have to be approved by the EU’s 27 member states, who generally support closer ties with Canada, but were taken by surprise by the term. Canada and the EU already have a trade deal and numerous bilateral agreements, but have been moving closer since Donald Trump returned to the White House and raised tariffs on both old allies, while repeatedly talking about Canada becoming the 51st US state and lambasting the EU. In a sign that Canada was seeking to further diversify its defence ties ⁠away from ⁠the US, Carney’s office announced on Wednesday that the country had formally applied to join the British-led Joint Expeditionary Force military ⁠coalition. The force is a rapid response ‌military partnership comprising 10 North Atlantic Nato member states including Denmark, the Netherlands, Norway and Sweden. On Wednesday, Carney and the British prime minister, Andy Burnham, held a bilateral meeting at the ground of Everton football club. The leaders, who are both fans of the premiership club, then attended the team’s game against Wolves. The two discussed deepening defence cooperation and the opportunities and ⁠challenges presented by ⁠artificial intelligence. Downing Street said both prime ministers emphasised the importance of building close ties with European partners, particularly on trade and defence. The 27-member EU has never had an associate membership category, although it has close ties with Norway, Iceland and Switzerland, allowing deep economic integration with these countries, who follow many EU rules. However, it remains to be seen what associate membership means, including for Canada’s relationship with the EU single market. Von der Leyen said on Wednesday that it was time to move from cooperation based on trade to a broader “alliance for the future” and bring the relationship with Canada to the highest level possible. “We will work on intelligent manufacturing. We will create a tech alliance. We will integrate defence industrial bases. We will make the Arctic a flagship joint project,” she said. She listed energy, critical minerals, batteries, AI, cyber and economic security as other fields of cooperation. “This is a partnership not against anyone else, but for our common strength,” she said. With Agence France-Presse and Reuters

webTitle: ‘We left everything behind’: 125,000 people displaced as war reignites in Yemen

fields.headline: ‘We left everything behind’: 125,000 people displaced as war reignites in Yemen
fields.trailText: Fierce fighting has forced people to abandon their homes, leaving everything behind to seek shelter in refugee camps
fields.bodyText: Abandoning their homes and cramming into cars, Yemeni families have fled in their thousands from a lightning advance along the Red Sea coastal plains and up the rugged hills towards the mountaintop city of Taiz as the war returned in dramatic form this month. “We fled a large, comfortable home, and here we are struggling to find a plastic sheet and wooden poles,” said one of the displaced, Asma Taleb, a woman in her 50s who fled her home last week with her two sons and five grandchildren. “This war doesn’t differentiate between people. Rich or poor, high class or low class, we all fled our homes on the same day and are all struggling now to find shelter.” The family fled the Maqbanah district in the wide Taiz region and headed toward Al-Shimayateen District, arriving at a camp for displaced families where she has relatives. More than 100,000 people have fled their homes in the last month. “The fighting was fierce in our village, and some of our civilian neighbours were killed or injured, so we fled home and left everything behind,” she told the Guardian. “Amid the fierce battles you forget everything. We left our home belongings, and one neighbour even left his livestock behind.” As soon as Taleb arrived in the camp, she found three or four families living in every tent because newly displaced people were constantly arriving. Left with no other option, she moved in with a relative’s family and three others. “On the first day, we were happy just to reach safety, but then we felt the suffering the next day. Displaced families kept arriving, and there was no space in the camp and not enough tents,” she added. Some humanitarian organisations intervened, providing displaced families with canned food and hygiene kits. Taleb said she had never left her village in her life except for brief emergencies, always returning in a day or two. This is the first time she has been forced to flee long-term, and she feels returning will be difficult. “I dream of returning to my village today, before tomorrow, but it isn’t in my hands. The fighting is still ongoing, and more families are arriving every day.” Renewed fighting in Yemen has displaced at least 125,000 people (about 18,000 households) since the start of September 2026, according to the UN Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (Ocha). The International Organization for Migration said more than 2,000 people fleeing the hostilities have reached Djibouti’s northern shores so far, landing at scattered points along the coast near Obock. Hatem Qasem, a farmer in his 40s from Al-Wazeyah district west of Taiz city, grew up in a village where residents rely on farming and raising livestock. He stated that when battles approached their village, they thought of nothing but their safety. “We are farmers and rarely leave our village except for emergencies, but three days ago, the shelling and clashes were all around us, and we found ourselves in a position where we had to flee,” Qasem told the Guardian. He explained that they sold their livestock at low prices simply to cover the cost of fleeing, as they could not take the livestock with them to an unknown destination. “We took the children and left – around five families in one car. We couldn’t believe we managed to escape the fighting, but praise be to God, we made it,” he added. They arrived in Al-Shimayateen district in Taiz. Although they do not have shelter there, it is a safe area where many displaced families have sought refuge. “I am happy that we are safe now and that no one in the family was killed or injured, but we have started to realise that it will be difficult to stay here for long. We have no work here and no one to help us,” Qasem said. According to Save the Children, at least 19 children were killed and a further 49 injured between 1 August and 9 September, bringing the total number of civilians killed in the escalating violence in Yemen to 117 and of those injured to 206. At least 175 were killed or injured in a single week (3-9 September), including 43 children, the highest weekly child casualty toll in the past 12 months. With fierce fighting ongoing in Qasem’s village, returning home is not an option. To remain displaced, however, he needs a source of income to provide for his family. “We will wait this month out here and see. If the fighting moves away from our village, we will return; if it continues, we will look for another solution.” Qasem’s family of eight lives with three other displaced families in the same house – each family occupying a single room to share the cost of rent. In Al-Safia makeshift camp, displaced people have no work and depend entirely on humanitarian organisations for their basic needs. In 2026, an estimated 22.3 million people in Yemen – more than half the population – require humanitarian assistance and protection services, including 5.2 million displaced people, according to Ocha. Ali Qaid, manager of the executive unit for Internationally Displaced People Camps Management in Taiz governorate, confirmed that some humanitarian organisations have begun providing aid to newly displaced families arriving in areas like Al-Shimayateen. However, he noted that many civilians remain trapped in active combat zones. “Displacement from the western districts of Taiz governorate is still ongoing, and many people are trapped in the middle of the fighting, preventing humanitarian organisations from reaching them with assistance,” he told the Guardian.

webTitle: ‘We live with a big burden’: survivor of abusive Spotlight priest hopes clergyman’s death brings closure

fields.headline: ‘We live with a big burden’: survivor of abusive Spotlight priest hopes clergyman’s death brings closure
fields.trailText: Keith Townsend says he hopes death of Ronald Paquin in prison helps victims and families to ‘keep pressing forward’
fields.bodyText: A survivor of childhood sexual abuse by a defrocked Boston Catholic priest who was portrayed admitting to molesting minors in the Oscar-winning Hollywood film Spotlight says he hopes the clergyman’s recent death in prison helps victims of his crimes and their families “keep pressing forward every single day”. “We live with a big burden in our hearts and on our backs,” Keith Townsend said on Wednesday while reflecting on the criminal charges which he successfully pursued against Ronald Paquin, who was imprisoned in 2019 and died in custody at age 83 on 11 September. “And my hope is that people can find closure and move on.” Those remarks by Townsend, 52, during a telephone interview were a notable reaction to the death of one of the key figures in the clergy sexual abuse and cover-up scandal with the Catholic archdiocese of Boston that – among other consequences – prompted the resignation of the institution’s archbishop, Bernard Law, at the end of 2002, as well as policy reforms across the US church. That same year, Paquin had pleaded guilty to sexually abusing an altar server from 1989 to 1992 while working at St John the Baptist church in the Boston suburb of Haverhill, Massachusetts. He was stripped of his clerical status and imprisoned in Massachusetts for that abuse, which was first publicly exposed in a Pulitzer-winning series of investigative articles by the Boston Globe newspaper’s Spotlight team. Paquin was freed in 2015. And learning of that release motivated Townsend – once a St John altar server, too – to come forward and report being abused himself by Paquin while on camping trips to Kennebunkport, Maine, between 1985 and 1989. As Townsend put it, he was between the ages of eight and 13 when Paquin molested him. Townsend recalled Paquin plying him with drugs and alcohol during the abuse, eventually leading him to battles with substance abuse addiction and incarceration. A Maine grand jury indicted Paquin in 2017 on new charges of gross sexual misconduct in connection with Townsend and another individual. Paquin faced a jury trial in November 2018 which culminated in a guilty verdict against him with regards to Townsend, though he was acquitted of having abused the other individual. Maine judge Wayne Douglas sentenced Paquin in May 2019 to 16 more years in prison. Paquin was in the Mountain View correctional facility in Charleston, Maine, when he died, the state’s department of correction said in a news release. Speaking five days later, Townsend said he first got word of Paquin’s death from his wife, who saw it circulating on the news and social media. He said he understood the many reactions which he subsequently heard or read that took delight in news of Paquin’s death. But Townsend, now a New Hampshire resident, also said he used the occasion to think about the work he did on himself which culminated in his “shaking off” the drug and alcohol addiction which had a grip on him in the wake of Paquin’s abuse. He said he contemplated the family he had built after overcoming “one of the biggest obstacles that could be thrown” at a person. “I get those who think the attitude should be, ‘Fuck him. Fuck what he did to me,’” Townsend said. “But look where I am today.” Townsend said he sought Paquin’s re-imprisonment with the aim of “protecting children … not [from] a man [but] a monster”. “Massachusetts just kind of let him go,” Townsend said. “So I had to dig deep … [because] I didn’t want anybody else to possibly have to go through [his] abuse. Maine thankfully had the balls to take this case, aggressively prosecute it and get a good outcome.” Townsend said he had not yet been able to see Spotlight, which dramatizes the Globe’s uncovering of the clergy sexual abuse scandal that roiled the city’s archdiocese. And therefore Townsend had not viewed the famous scene in the film in which Rachel McAdams, playing reporter Sacha Pfeiffer, confronts an actor portraying Paquin on his home’s front doorstep about allegations of molesting boys at St John the Baptist. “Sure, I fooled around – but I never felt gratified myself,” the actor playing Paquin, Richard O’Rourke, says in response as the journalist scribbles notes in a paper pad while wearing an astonished facial expression. “Right, um, but you admit to molesting boys at St John the Baptist?” McAdams’ Pfeiffer then asks O’Rourke’s Paquin. The latter’s reply: “Yes, yes. But, as I said, I never got any pleasure from it.” Another person closely familiar with Spotlight offered an opinion of that scene’s legacy on Wednesday. Attorney Mitchell Garabedian – who is portrayed in the 2015 movie by Stanley Tucci and has represented numerous victims of sexual abuse by Paquin and other clerics – said that part of Spotlight provided a powerful cue to survivors of clergy molesters that they were not alone. “It gave a sense of, ‘Aha, I’m not the only one,’” in one of Hollywood’s most critically acclaimed films, Garabedian said. ‘“It wasn’t my fault, and I shouldn’t feel guilty.’” Townsend said ultimately he is grateful for anything that raised awareness about Paquin’s atrocities before his push to bring him to justice. “When I lay my head down tonight, I know it saved lives,” getting Paquin imprisoned for his remaining years, Townsend added. “And that’s what matters to me.”

webTitle: Canada’s Carney embraces EU associate membership proposal

fields.headline: Canada’s Carney embraces EU associate membership proposal
fields.trailText: After Trump describes the tie-up as ‘laughable’, PM says majority of Canadians support closer ties with bloc
fields.bodyText: Mark Carney has welcomed the goal of Canada becoming the EU’s first associate member, calling for “deep cooperation” between Europe and his country to secure their sovereignty, after Donald Trump derided the idea as “laughable”. In an address to the European parliament in Strasbourg, the Canadian prime minister said polling showed that an overwhelming majority of Canadians supported much closer ties with Europe. “Canada welcomes this idea,” he said, referring to European Commission president Ursula von der Leyen’s pitch that Canada should become the EU’s first associate member. “Canada and Europe should secure our strategic autonomy through deep cooperation in the full range of strategic capabilities,” Carney said on Thursday, listing sectors including critical minerals, energy security and AI. Von der Leyen had on Wednesday invited Canada to become the EU’s first associate member in a speech in which she declared she wanted to bring the bilateral relationship “to the highest level possible”. A few hours later, Trump threatened “very serious tariffs” on Europe if the plan went ahead. Asked about Trump’s threats, Carney told reporters: “Canadians are united that nobody is going to tell us what language we speak. No one is going to dictate our culture or with whom we can strike agreements internationally.” The EU and Canada, which already have a web of bilateral trade and sectoral agreements, have sought to move closer in recent months in the face of Trump’s trade tariffs and relentless belligerent rhetoric. Carney received a standing ovation from MEPs in Strasbourg, who waited to shake his hand and get a selfie with him. European lawmakers from pro-EU mainstream parties have already praised Carney’s January speech in Davos, in which he called for middle powers to work together to preserve their sovereignty in a world of great power rivalry where the strong accept no constraints. Carney reprised the theme in Strasbourg, saying: “Canada and Europe are each strong. Europe and Canada are stronger together … The objective is not self-sufficiency, it’s collective resilience.” He went on to say: “I am not proposing a third bloc in order to become a great-power rival, only with better manners,” saying an EU-Canada alliance would be a “beacon for other democracies”. In a speech frequently interrupted by rounds of applause, Carney detailed his plans for the future relationship, saying the two sides could cooperate on critical minerals, defence industrial capacity, AI and computing, energy security, space and payments. He also called for “seamless digital trade in non-agricultural goods and a wide range of services”. He proposed a youth exchange programme that would enable young people to work, study and live in both jurisdictions, as well as Canadian membership of the Erasmus+ scheme, the EU’s education, training and sport programme. No country has ever been offered associate membership before, a category that does not exist in the EU’s treaties. The German chancellor, Friedrich Merz, floated the idea of associate membership for Ukraine as an interim step to joining the bloc earlier this year, but the idea was rejected by other member states. EU member states support the idea of closer ties with Canada, but some have reacted coolly to the name “associate membership”. Asked by a Bloomberg reporter about the concept he preferred, Carney said: “The precise nomenclature for Europe is a question for Europe,” adding that leaders and lawmakers involved “take the view [that] what matters is the substance”. He also said Canada was “not in a position, nor seeking to become, a full member of the European Union” and that the Canadian parliament would debate and vote on the future relationship. Speaking before Carney’s address, Trump warned that if the EU moved forward with the plan, Washington could impose “very serious tariffs or stop trading with Europe”. He added: “If it’s a good intention, that’s fine. If it’s a bad intention, we’ll put very heavy tariffs on Europe.” Responding to Trump’s overnight comments, Carney said the deepening of the EU-Canada relationship was “a positive initiative” and “not a reaction to something else”.

webTitle: Iran school bombing: grounds to believe US was behind atrocity, UN finds

fields.headline: Iran school bombing: grounds to believe US was behind atrocity, UN finds
fields.trailText: Fact-finding mission says military strikes on school in Minab and sports facility in ⁠February constitute war ⁠crimes
fields.bodyText: A UN fact-finding mission has determined there are reasonable grounds to believe the US was behind military strikes on a school and a sports facility in Iran in ⁠February that killed 120 children, and that these constituted war ⁠crimes. The school strike, which killed 156 civilians including 120 children, involved a US Tomahawk missile that collapsed the roof of the Shajareh Tayyebeh primary school, which the UN said was “clearly identifiable”, in Minab, Hormozgan province, on 28 February. The Pentagon’s own secretive investigation into the incident is understood to have concluded several months ago. There have been reports that senior US commanders had been warned that targeting data used during the war – including for the Minab strike – was dangerously outdated. The second cited strike, on the same date, targeted a “clearly identifiable sports complex and residential area” in the southern city of Lamerd with a weapon that scattered tungsten pellets. The UN fact-finding team said in a statement: “Following the United States and Israeli attacks on 28 February, the mission found reasonable grounds to believe the United States committed the war crime of launching indiscriminate attacks resulting in the loss of life or injury to civilians or damage to civilian objects.” The mission also found Iranian authorities had committed crimes against humanity during their deadly crackdown on anti-government protests. The findings by the independent international fact-finding mission on Iran, to be submitted to the UN human rights council in Geneva, examined the ⁠US’s conduct during the Iran war that began in February and the Iranian government’s response to nationwide unrest that began in late December. US officials have previously said military ⁠operations are conducted in accordance with the law of armed conflict, while Iran has consistently rejected allegations of systematic rights violations. The UN mission concluded that the strike on Shajareh Tayyebeh primary school constituted an indiscriminate attack causing civilian deaths and damage to ‌civilian infrastructure, amounting to a war crime under international law. According to the report, the US relied on intelligence suggesting a senior Iranian military commander was present at the site but failed to adequately verify the information before launching the strike. Investigators said the failure to update targeting intelligence and confirm the building was a military objective amounted to more than mere negligence. “Rather, the US directed the strikes at the building of the school while being aware of a substantial risk of striking a civilian object and acting recklessly as regards the possibility that this would happen.” In June the US president, Donald Trump, said ‌“nobody” had purposely attacked a girls’ school in Iran in February, citing an investigation into the incident. The Pentagon has since elevated the inquiry, but it has not published any preliminary findings. UN experts said the school was a clearly identifiable civilian object and found no evidence it was being used for military purposes. The experts reached a similar conclusion over the strike on the sports centre in Lamerd. The report said the attack had damaged nearby residential buildings and a school and killed and injured 22 civilians. It concluded that the strike had been indiscriminate and therefore constituted a war crime. US Central Command said in a statement in March that ⁠US forces had not launched any strikes into the city of Lamerd on that day. The UN mission also found that the Iranian authorities had carried out a widespread and systematic attack against civilians during protests that erupted in late December last year, involving unlawful killings, torture, arbitrary detention, enforced disappearances and severe restrictions on freedom of expression. Rights groups say bystanders were among those killed during the biggest crackdown ‌since Shia Muslim clerics took power in the 1979 revolution. Tehran blamed “terrorists and rioters” backed by exiled opponents and the US and Israel. The investigation said it could not independently verify the death toll, but that it believed the number of dead and injured was probably far higher than official figures, which say 3,038 people were killed and 25,000 people injured. The government’s response to the protests, including violence and killings, cutting off the internet and use of the death penalty, marked a significant escalation from previous patterns of suppressing dissent, the report said.

webTitle: Sweden’s PM resigns after centre-left bloc wins slim majority in election

fields.headline: Sweden’s PM resigns after centre-left bloc wins slim majority in election
fields.trailText: Ulf Kristersson has stood down from his post, paving way for Social Democrats leader to form a government
fields.bodyText: Sweden’s centre-right prime minister, Ulf Kristersson, has stood down, clearing the way for Magdalena Andersson, the Social Democrats leader, to attempt to form a government. In a victory speech on Thursday, Andersson said the Swedish people had “voted for a new direction for our country, voted for unity and against division”. She added: “The Swedish people have voted to take Sweden forward and I will realise the new direction that you have voted for.” Among the priorities she named were the climate crisis, schools, healthcare, elderly care and immigration policy. Andersson spoke as the preliminary count for Sunday’s election was finally completed, with 176 seats for the left-leaning opposition parties – a narrow three-seat majority over the right-leaning ruling Tidö coalition supported by the far-right Sweden Democrats (SD). There were 50,359 votes between the two blocs. Earlier on Thursday, Andersson, who was Kristersson’s predecessor as prime minister, sent an invitation to the other left-leaning parties – Left, Centre and Green – for initial coalition talks. Soon after, Kristersson, the Moderates leader, announced his resignation after four years as prime minister. Before the election, some had feared that the vote would mark a turning point for the far right after Kristersson promised key ministerial posts for the SD if his coalition took power. Instead, the SD lost support for the first time in a general election since its foundation, falling from Sweden’s second biggest party to third. In his resignation letter, Kristersson wrote: “Now it is the speaker who will lead the next steps towards forming a new government. In order for that work to begin immediately, I hereby request to be relieved of my duties as prime minister.” The speaker, Andreas Norlén, will now start working on proposals for a new prime minister after talks with representatives of each of the parties. Four celebration cakes decorated with red roses were brought into the Social Democrats’ headquarters amid cheers from inside. The result will be a considerable relief among Social Democrats, who remain Sweden’s biggest party but received record low support. However, the result marks only the beginning for Andersson of what is expected to be weeks of complicated coalition talks. One of the trickiest negotiations is expected to be between the Centre and Left parties. The Centre party has ruled out being in government with the Left, while the Left has demanded a place in government in return for its cooperation. Other difficult areas are expected to be the Left’s support for a billionaire tax, the Green party’s opposition to nuclear energy and differences of opinion on taxation. The Greens, Social Democrats and the Left are all in favour of tax increases, but the Centre party wants to cut taxes. Nooshi Dadgostar, the leader of the Left party, said: “The Swedish people have voted away Tidö and given us a clear mandate for change.” She added: “This is one of the proudest days of my life.” Elisabeth Thand Ringqvist, the Centre party leader, thanked Kristersson for his work as prime minister but said Sweden was now “entering a new political phase”. She added: “The Centre party will be a constructive force for Sweden to have a functioning government, with policies anchored in the middle.” Andersson, who was prime minister between November 2021 and October 2022, is understood to be reaching out to all the opposition parties, with the exception of the SD. The Liberals and the Christian Democrats have ruled out working with the left, but in his resignation letter Kristersson appeared to leave the door open. However, given Swedish tradition, it is extremely unlikely the Moderates and the Social Democrats would form a coalition. Kristersson wrote that the election had left a “complicated situation” for building a government and called for “constructive openness” from all parties to find a way to form a stable government. In the nervous days since the election, the Social Democrats are understood to have been using the time to prepare for coalition negotiations, where they are understood to be seeking broad cooperation with one or multiple parties. Minority-run governments are common within Swedish politics and it is commonplace for governments to form agreements outside of coalitions. In the last government, the SD were not officially in government, but they held considerable sway over the budget and policies. The Social Democrats are understood to be planning to prioritise making changes to the immigration, integration and climate policies of the last government. But with their policies having moved to the right in recent years, particularly on immigration and crime, much of the legacy of the previous government is likely to remain.

webTitle: All smiles in Strasbourg but uncertainty clouds Canada’s EU membership plan

fields.headline: All smiles in Strasbourg but uncertainty clouds Canada’s EU membership plan
fields.trailText: Although Mark Carney welcomed offer to become bloc’s first associate member, no one seems to know what that means
fields.bodyText: Mark Carney received a rapturous reception in the European parliament when he gave his speech on Thursday welcoming a proposal for Canada to become the EU’s first-ever associate member. Politicians queued to shake his hand and take selfies. One described the speech as a historic moment. “Europe has extended a hand, and Canada has taken it,” said the German Green MEP Terry Reintke, who borrowed a Canadian ice hockey shirt for the occasion. One day earlier, in the same debating chamber, the European Commission president, Ursula von der Leyen, issued the unprecedented invitation to Canada – an idea quickly derided by Donald Trump, who threatened Europe with “heavy tariffs” if it became a reality. But the prospect of Canada’s associate membership is uncertain, not least because no one is sure what it means. “I’m not quite sure why she [von der Leyen] used that term because there’s simply no legal definition,” said one senior politician. “This has just raised lots of questions. So people are talking more about what an associate membership means instead of … this unique partnership and alliance for the future that EU-Canada relations should be about.” The German chancellor Friedrich Merz’s spokesperson welcomed the initiative for a close partnership with Canada and said Germany was “open to discussing new models that reflect the special significance of the relationship”, but called for the associate membership label to be “reconsidered”. Merz himself has floated “associate membership” for Ukraine, as a stepping stone to joining the bloc, but this was quickly dismissed by other member states. One EU diplomat said von der Leyen “seemed a bit far out in floating this” and that even before Wednesday’s speech member states had worried that she was overpromising on Canada. A second diplomat said it was “an empty phrase” and it would be up to member states to define the substance. Any new trading and cooperation relationship with a foreign country would need to be approved by the EU’s 27 member states. There is a lot of common ground: both sides want to deepen cooperation on AI, energy security, critical raw materials, quantum computing and work together in the Arctic – Carney noted that Canada shared an Arctic border with Denmark, referring to the maritime border with Greenland. But difficulties went unspoken. Carney described the 2016 EU-Canada comprehensive economic and trade agreement as “one of the world’s most successful trade agreements”, but 10 EU member states have yet to ratify it, including France, Italy and Poland. With all three countries heading into an election year, that looks unlikely to change. While both sides extol the virtues of deeper trade between allies, they are also pursuing policies that appear to contradict that goal. Last year Canada introduced a buy Canadian policy, to ensure Canadian suppliers get priority in public contracts. The EU is debating its own buy European law, known formally as the Industrial Accelerator Act. The IAA, now being debated in the EU, would oblige member states to meet “made in Europe” content requirements when spending public money on green technologies and electric cars. Associate membership also raises questions about integration into the EU’s tightly guarded single market. Carney proposed “seamless digital trade in non-agricultural goods and a wide range of services”. But the EU has long insisted that the four freedoms of its internal market – free movement of goods, services, labour and capital – are one package that cannot be split and require alignment with EU rules. Now the applause has died down, there are plenty of tricky issues to work out, even for the closest of allies.

webTitle: Nato head: Britain must show ‘credible path’ of annual defence budget increases

fields.headline: Nato head: Britain must show ‘credible path’ of annual defence budget increases
fields.trailText: Mark Rutte said Britain will need to steadily increase defence spending to meet Nato target of 3.5% of GDP by 2035
fields.bodyText: Britain needs to show “a credible path” of annual increases in its defence budgets to meet a Nato target of spending nearly £30bn more on the military by the middle of the next decade, the head of the alliance said on Thursday. Mark Rutte, Nato’s secretary general, said that Britain could not wait until just before 2035 to lift defence spending to 3.5% of GDP, in an unusually pointed intervention a day after he met prime minister Andy Burnham. In an interview with the Press Association, he said: “And that is why you need a credible path towards that 3.5%, and yearly increments.” The alliance’s secretary general, a former Dutch prime minister, made similar remarks to the BBC, where he said that the UK understood that the target could not be met “in one go in 2034” and that it would have to be achieved gradually. Earlier on Thursday, Rutte met with Wes Streeting, the defence secretary, and Ed Miliband, the foreign secretary. He saw Burnham on Wednesday, at a business park in Didcot, and also met representatives from the defence industry. Keir Starmer signed the UK up to a Nato-wide target of increasing defence spending to 3.5% of GDP in the summer of 2025, under pressure from the US president, Donald Trump. The figure has since been endorsed by Burnham and his chancellor, former defence secretary John Healey. Current spending plans, covering until 2028/9, show defence spending levelling off at 2.7%, nearly £30bn below the ultimate target, raising the question of how it would be achieved after the next general election. It is unclear if taxes or borrowing would have to rise, or other government spending cuts. Healey resigned as defence minister in June because Starmer would not commit to lifting defence spending to 3% of GDP by 2030. At the time Healey said Labour needed to set “a clear path” to meet the Nato commitment, similar language to that used by Rutte in his interviews. But since then Healey and Burnham have avoided committing to the 3% by the end of the decade. Decisions on future spending are likely to be left to the next government spending review due next year, prompting the Nato leader to engage in public lobbying on his trip to Britain. Rutte said he was certain the Burnham government remained behind the ultimate goal and the need to increase defence spending gradually. “I am absolutely confident that when it comes to the yearly increments, they totally take it and accept it, that they have to be there,” he told the BBC. “There has to be a credible path. What that credible path exactly will be, we will see with the spending review next year,” Rutte added. A day earlier, Rutte gave a speech to at Ditchley Park in Oxfordshire, in which he warned that the 32 country military alliance faced “the most dangerous and complex security environment in a generation” with wars in Ukraine, the Middle East coming at time of rising state competition. Nato needed “more UK and more Europe”, he added, to take up the slack as the US reduces its military commitment to the alliance. Trump has long argued that the UK and Europe should match US levels of defence spending and take the lead in defending the continent from Russia aggression.

webTitle: Trump administration again denies entry visas to Palestinian officials ahead of UN general assembly

fields.headline: Trump administration again denies entry visas to Palestinian officials ahead of UN general assembly
fields.trailText: For the second year in a row, the administration has barred the Palestinian delegation from US travel for the forum
fields.bodyText: The US state department said on Wednesday that it had again denied entry visas to Palestinian officials ahead next week’s United Nations general assembly gathering in New York. The state department said in a statement the Palestinian Authority (PA) and the Palestine Liberation Organization (PLO) had “failed to live up to their commitments”, accusing the groups of “taking actions to internationalize the Israeli-Palestinian Conflict including through the International Criminal Court (ICC) and International Court of Justice (ICJ)” and of “glorifying terrorism” among other allegations. “As a consequence of their failure to reform, contrary to their commitments to the United States, and their ongoing activities that undermine the prospects for peace, the United States will extend sanctions that deny visas to PLO members and PA officials,” the department said. The move marks the second year in a row the Trump administration has barred the Palestinian delegation from traveling to New York to attend the UN general assembly in person. The foreign ministry of the Palestinian Authority denied the allegations made against it in a statement on Thursday, describing the visa sanctions as an “unjustified measure” that “contradicts the efforts being made to restore trust, develop Palestinian-US relations, and prepare the necessary political climate for implementing the two-state solution and achieving peace and stability in the region”. Among the Palestinian officials barred from entering the US is Mahmoud Abbas, the longtime president of the Palestinian Authority, according to reports. The UN general assembly voted on Thursday to allow Abbas to address the gathering via ⁠video, for the second year in a row. This year’s UN general assembly general debate begins on 22 September.

webTitle: Ukraine war briefing: Poland’s Tusk heads to Kyiv after warning of Russian strikes on Ukrainian allies

fields.headline: Ukraine war briefing: Poland’s Tusk heads to Kyiv after warning of Russian strikes on Ukrainian allies
fields.trailText: Donald Tusk says Moscow will not enter peace talks without Ukraine’s ‘total capitulation’ and will try to inflict a ‘tragically critical’ winter. What we know on day 1,668
fields.bodyText: Russia is planning hybrid strikes with drones or rockets on European countries supporting Ukraine, among them Poland according to its prime minister, Donald Tusk. Russia will pretend the attacks are “accidental” in order to “paralyse or at least weaken the motivation of Nato countries” to rush to the defence of the member state coming under attack, Tusk said in a speech to the Polish parliament. “There is a real risk that drones or other types of projectiles will enter the territory of one or several countries on the eastern flank and even cause destruction,” Tusk said, vowing that “if anyone dares to attack us, they will face a resolute response from us and our allies”. Tusk announced he would travel to Ukraine overnight, arriving on Friday, in what might be seen as an act of defiance against Russia after European leaders were in transit during a drone strike on a train near the Polish-Ukrainian border on Sunday. Officials usually keep their travel plans to Ukraine secret for security reasons. In Kyiv, he said he would discuss with Volodymyr Zelenskyy how to defend against the new types of drones, as well as discuss with partners including Slovakia further sanctions against Russia. The Slovak ⁠prime minister, Robert Fico, ‌also said ‌he would be in Kyiv as he claimed Europe is closer ⁠than ever to a large-scale ⁠war erupting ⁠from the war in Ukraine ⁠and politicians must strive for peace. Fico has ‌kept warm relations with Russia while criticising EU and Nato aid to Ukraine, though Slovakia’s arms industry is simultaneously a producer of artillery shells supplied to Kyiv’s forces. On Friday ⁠the European Union will ⁠disburse €3.3bn to ‌Ukraine to buy missiles and drones, Ursula von ⁠der ⁠Leyen, the European Commission president, has announced. Tusk said Russia was not ready for any peace talks “without the total capitulation of Ukraine”. “They are convinced the winter will be tragically critical for Ukraine.” He said last winter Poland stepped in with deliveries when Ukraine’s energy infrastructure came under attack, but if border crossings are destroyed it will be much harder for Warsaw to offer such help this winter. “Russia’s goal is to destroy as much as possible the economy and logistics of Ukraine,” Tusk said, adding that intelligence indicates continuous attacks of “very high frequency and intensity” on six main Ukrainian cities should be expected in the near future. A drone hit a petrol station near Ukraine’s border with Poland on Thursday, Tusk said separately at a press conference in Warsaw. A spokesperson for the Polish military told TVN24 that air defences were activated on Thursday after a jet-powered drone approached Polish airspace before exploding about 4km (2.5 miles) from the Polish border. Poland’s Lublin and Rzeszow ‌airports temporarily suspended operations on Thursday as the air force responded to Russian drone activity, Polish authorities said. Russian missiles and drones injured at least 19 people in Ukraine’s capital and the surrounding region, authorities said on Thursday. Kyiv’s military administration said more than 10 locations were hit, while 33 sites were damaged in the wider region. A 10-year-old girl and a 12-year-old boy were among the injured, the administration said. Ukraine’s air force said it destroyed or suppressed 131 Russian aerial targets during the overnight attack in the Kyiv, Zaporizhzhia and Odesa regions. The attack involved ballistic and cruise missiles as well as drones and decoys. In Odesa, seven people were injured, including two children, according to Ukraine’s state emergency Service. Apartments on the 14th through 16th floors of a residential building were damaged. A private residential building in Odesa was also destroyed and others damaged. Ukrainian forces struck an oil refinery in Yaroslavl and a military airfield in the Rostov region, Zelenskyy said on Thursday. Zelenskyy said Ukraine’s operation against the Yaroslavl oil refinery was conducted jointly by the country’s Security Service, special operations forces, military intelligence and the foreign intelligence service. The security service also struck a military airfield in Rostov, damaging an An-12 aircraft, two An-26s and three helicopters. Reuters said that according to its industry sources, the refinery halted crude processing after the Ukrainian ⁠attack. The local Russian governor confirmed the damage. A Russian drone struck a civilian vessel flying the flag of Tanzania in the Black Sea on Thursday, killing the ship’s captain and injuring three crew members, according to Oleh Kiper, the regional head in Odesa. Russia damaged the Bilhorod-Dnistrovskyi bridge in the Odesa region, ⁠significantly limiting Ukraine’s ability to transport grain to its Danube river ports, Ukrainian state railway ⁠operator Ukrzaliznytsia ⁠said on Thursday. According to Ukrzaliznytsia, about 3,000 grain wagons ‌are bound for the Danube ports. Without the bridge, they would need 26 days to reach the ports. “The situation is very difficult. We are working to restore the Bilhorod-Dnistrovskyi bridge,” a company official said.

webTitle: Russians go to polls against backdrop of Ukraine war and Putin’s tightening grip

fields.headline: Russians go to polls against backdrop of Ukraine war and Putin’s tightening grip
fields.trailText: President’s United Russia party faces no meaningful opposition after liberal anti-war party barred from ballot
fields.bodyText: Russians are going to the polls to elect a new State Duma in a tightly controlled vote stripped of meaningful competition and with little doubt about the result. Vladimir Putin’s United Russia is expected to extend the grip on parliament it has held for 23 years, alongside a handful of nominal opposition parties that reliably vote with the Kremlin on the issues that matter. The three-day vote begins on Friday, with results expected after polls close on Sunday. For all the predictability of the outcome, the first Duma election since the full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022 is taking place against the backdrop of a war that, once distant for many Russians, is increasingly intruding into everyday life. Swarms of Ukrainian drones have struck oil refineries, factories and logistics hubs across Russia over the summer, while polling has pointed to growing anxiety about the course of the fighting and what may still lie ahead. Against that backdrop, the Kremlin has tightened its grip further. Last month, the authorities barred Yabloko, the liberal anti-war party, from the ballot, removing the only political force remaining in Russia that was openly challenging the invasion of Ukraine. That leaves a handful of other parties, from the Communists to the far-right Liberal Democrats, which together form what is known in Russia as the “systemic opposition”: groups permitted to criticise the authorities at the margins, but which fall into line with United Russia on issues that matter to the Kremlin. For years, they have served as a political safety valve, giving voters somewhere to register discontent without posing a serious threat to the ruling party’s dominance. But even by the diminished standards of Russian politics, these parliamentary campaigns have been strikingly lifeless. “In most elections, candidates compete for attention. In Russia this year, many are doing the opposite,” said Farida Rustamova, a political analyst and founder of the independent Vlast newsletter. “No one wants to come into the spotlight or discuss anything sensitive.” Most candidates have barely campaigned at all, she noted. Televised debates have at times taken place in half-empty studios because politicians failed to turn up, producing awkward clips that quickly became memes online. United Russia’s campaign videos have leaned heavily on low-budget AI, with few memorable slogans or promises. None of the parties has dared to address the growing questions surrounding the continuing war that increasingly dominate private conversations. “The Kremlin is deliberately keeping the election low-key, as greater interest would not benefit them. They don’t want to discuss difficult issues and just [want to] get it over with,” said a person close to the Kremlin, speaking on condition of anonymity. By keeping the election subdued, Moscow hoped to depress turnout among disaffected and independent-minded voters while ensuring its own supporters made it to the polls, said Rustamova. Yabloko’s exclusion followed the same logic. Several observers believe that officials had initially expected the party to receive a negligible result, demonstrating how little support remained for an explicitly anti-war platform. But when polling instead suggested growing support for the party, the authorities removed it from the ballot rather than risk an unscripted result. Vladimir Gelman, a professor of Russian politics at the University of Helsinki, said another purpose of the elections was to provide the Kremlin with a continuing source of legitimacy and reinforce the impression that there was broad public consent behind the political system and the war. “Even though these elections are neither free nor fair, they are still the only source of legitimacy,” he said. In a televised address before the vote this week, Putin explicitly linked participation in the election to the war in Ukraine, presenting voting as a demonstration of unity in the face of outside pressure. “Your choice and your will will once again demonstrate that millions of people stand behind our soldiers, that we are a united people bound together by shared values, historical memory and love for our homeland,” Putin said. Putin himself secured another six-year term in the 2024 presidential election, with genuine opposition barred from the ballot, extending his rule until at least 2030. For many Russians, however, the election’s greater significance lies not in the result, but in what follows. With Moscow’s troops making little progress at high cost in Ukraine, rumours of another large-scale mobilisation have spread across the country. The fear is that once the election is safely out of the way and a compliant new Duma is installed, the Kremlin will have greater freedom to pursue unpopular measures it has so far avoided. The anxiety has already prompted some young men to leave the country, hoping to wait out any new mobilisation – scenes that carry echoes of September 2022, when hundreds of thousands of Russians fled after Putin announced the first wartime draft. The person close to the Kremlin said several friends had sent their sons abroad in recent weeks, a sign, he said, that even among those with access to the system, few are certain what will happen after the voting. Putin has sought to calm those fears. In recent weeks, he has twice dismissed suggestions that a new mobilisation is imminent. But those reassurances have not been enough for some men, including Dmitry, who flew to Yerevan, Armenia last week. “I’ll just wait a few weeks after the elections,” he said, adding that he felt the risk of a new mobilisation was too high to ignore. “Let’s see if anything changes after the vote.”

webTitle: Paul Keating says Aukus locking Australia into a US war against China, which it would ‘certainly lose’

fields.headline: Paul Keating says Aukus locking Australia into a US war against China, which it would ‘certainly lose’
fields.trailText: Former prime minister says US would ‘scuttle itself back to San Diego’, leaving Australia to deal with retribution from China
fields.bodyText: Aukus critic Paul Keating has said the submarine deal is locking Australia in to any future US conflict with China – “a war America would certainly lose” – and making Australia a target for retribution. The former prime minister seized on comments reported out of Washington this week from Republican congressman Michael McCaul – a China hawk and co-chair of the Congressional Friends of Australia caucus – who said “Australia is a target” for enemies of the US already. However, McCaul argued that greater integration with the US military would better protect Australia rather than leaving it more vulnerable. McCaul also said it was “logical to assume” US nuclear-powered submarines rotating through Australian bases could also be nuclear armed after 2032, and that Australia’s participation in a US war against China over Taiwan was assumed by the US military establishment. “I don’t think it was even questioned. It’s just obvious,” McCaul said. “Australia, being a Five Eyes [intelligence-sharing network member] and an ally of the United States, would be at odds with China invading Taiwan and threatening the Indo-Pacific.” He said it was “absolutely critical” for Australian to back any US intervention to protect Taiwan. McCaul met with the prime minister, Anthony Albanese, the defence minister, Richard Marles, and the foreign affairs minister, Penny Wong, during a visit to Australia this month. Keating said the US would “certainly lose” in a war with China over Taiwan. “But having lost, [the US would] scuttle itself back to San Diego, leaving Australia vulnerable to China for having participated in a military escapade against it and its military assets.” Keating said Australia’s increasing enmeshment within the US military, especially through Aukus, was seeing Australia’s “sovereignty effectively being shredded”. “Australia is now getting locked in and locked up to the military prerogatives of the United States.” The Guardian revealed last week that the US military, and its corporate interests, control, or have access to, more than 100 military bases across the Australian continent. More than half of the military installations in Australia have some level of US control or access. Intelligence sites such as Pine Gap play a critical role in US warfighting, downlinking masses of surveillance data from satellites, and providing targeting information for US strikes. In parliament this week, Greens senator David Shoebridge seized on McCaul’s further comments that he considered Australia a “beachhead” for the US in its efforts to deter China and maintain peace in the region. “The US spruikers of Aukus have said they want to make Australia the beachhead for US military war against China,” Shoebridge told a press conference at Parliament House. “I want to be clear what happens at a beachhead: people get killed at a beachhead, destruction happens at a beachhead in someone else’s war. “How on Earth does Aukus make us safe, when a foreign military is bringing their nuclear-armed submarines into this country and consciously saying they want our country to be the beachhead in a war with China? It’s time we ended Aukus before we become the US’s beachhead.” Under Pillar One of the proposed Aukus agreement – a multi-decade deal slated to cost Australia $368bn to the mid-2050s – Australia will buy three “in-service” Virginia-class nuclear-powered, conventionally armed submarines from the US, beginning in 2032. From the early 2040s, Australia expects to deploy a new, larger Aukus-class submarine. The new class will be designed in the UK and the first boat built for the Royal Navy. Australia will then build five Aukus submarines - except for their nuclear reactors - in South Australia. America’s Virginia class submarines do not currently carry nuclear weapons but, from 2032, the US navy is planning to equip some of its Virginia boats with nuclear-armed sea-launched cruise missiles. The regular rotation of US nuclear submarines through HMAS Stirling is also part of Aukus cooperation. The US has a policy of “strategic ambiguity” around the deployment of its nuclear arsenal, refusing to confirm or deny the presence of nuclear weapons on platforms around the world. The Treaty of Rarotonga prohibits Australia from “stationing” nuclear weapons on its territory.

webTitle: ‘Run! Get away!’: witnesses recount Israeli ‘double tap’ strike that killed child and medic in Gaza

fields.headline: ‘Run! Get away!’: witnesses recount Israeli ‘double tap’ strike that killed child and medic in Gaza
fields.trailText: When Mohammad Abdul Zinati, 15, rushed to help a man wounded in a bomb attack, he had no time to react before he too was hit
fields.bodyText: Mohammad Abdul Zinati was walking home from school through the rubble of Salah Khalaf Street, in northern Gaza City, when he stopped at a supermarket where a group of classmates and friends had gathered. Shortly before 3:30pm, an explosion tore through the air. Along with several others, Mohammad rushed into the street to see what had happened. When the smoke and dust cleared, they saw a man lying bleeding on the dusty road. He was badly wounded, but still alive. The man was calling for help, and Mohammad ran towards him. He did not hear the shouts of his cousin, who had spotted an approaching Israeli drone. Within seconds, the drone released a glide bomb, designed to allow operators to identify and strike targets with a high degree of accuracy. The munition plunged towards the street, detonating just metres from the teenager. Mohammad did not have time to react before a second blast killed him. The Guardian verified footage of the attack, and spoke to witnesses and weapons experts in an effort to shed light on the latest Israeli strike to kill a child in Gaza. “We heard a loud explosion and tried to make our way to the scene to find out what had happened,” said Tamer Lubbad, a witness who filmed the attack. “We found a man lying on the ground. He was still alive and calling for help.” The man injured in the initial strike was later identified by Gaza’s civil defense as the paramedic Sharif Shadi Labad. The Israeli military said that Labad was targeted because he was a Hamas militant. Several other civilians approached Labad, as he lay injured in the street. Among them was Mohammad Zinati’s cousin, Mohammed Rajeh Zinati, 26. “I ran from the house towards the street to find out what had happened,” he said. “On my way, I saw my cousin coming out of the supermarket. He was running towards the site of the strike. I started shouting at him: ‘Mohammad, stop!’ but he didn’t hear me and kept going. Then I saw a drone in the sky. “I started shouting: ‘Run! Get away!’ At that moment, Mohammad had reached the injured man. As soon as he got there, the drone struck him.” “Mohammad was hit directly in the chest and abdomen and was killed almost instantly. I couldn’t do anything to rescue him,” said Zinati. Video filmed later showed Mohammad’s body lying under a white shroud outside al-Shifa hospital after the attack, as his father bid him an emotional farewell, reciting verses from the Qur’an. People who knew Mohammad said he was a much-loved figure in the neighbourhood. “He was a kind, helpful, polite and respectful boy,” his cousin said. ‘‘He would help elderly to collect water from the water trucks. When he was killed, people from the neighbourhood came out into the street, crying for him.” The IDF has repeatedly rejected allegations that it deliberately targets civilians, saying it assesses and takes into account the risk of civilian harm when carrying out strikes. However, weapons experts who reviewed the video said the teenager’s death may have been avoidable. ‘‘The bomb that is visible before impact is a Mikholit, which is deployed by Israeli unmanned vehicles (UAVs) or drones, said Trevor Ball, a drones expert and weapons technical analyst with Armament Research Services (ARES). ‘‘These UAVs have high-quality cameras that would have been able to see the teenager and the man approaching the body. Some variants of the Mikholit at least are capable of being redirected to a different target/point while in flight.’’ The strike that killed the teenager and the paramedic appears to fit the pattern commonly described as a “double-tap” attack: an initial strike followed by a second on the same location after rescuers or bystanders have arrived to help the wounded. In a statement to the Guardian, the Israeli military said Sharif Shadi Ibrahim Labad was a Hamas terrorist who belonged to the elite Nukhba forces. The IDF stated that Labad had participated in the 7 October attacks in 2023 at the Erez border crossing and was targeted because he was planning new operations. Asked why the second attack went ahead when its target was visibly a minor, the military did not respond, but said it ‘‘is aware of reports indicating that an uninvolved individual was harmed as a result of the strike targeting the terrorist, regrets any harm to uninvolved individuals and makes every effort to minimise such harm”. The Israeli military said the incident was under review. On Tuesday, medical sources in Gaza reported an Israeli strike on al-Bureij refugee camp that killed an adult and a five-year-old child, identified as Udai al-Muridi. A pregnant Palestinian woman died on Saturday from injuries sustained after being shot in the head by Israeli forces south of Khan Younis, according to her family and medical workers. The woman, named as Iman Shalouf, 27, who was nearly eight months pregnant, was sitting inside her family’s tent in the Mawasi area when Israeli gunfire struck her, according to paramedics and witnesses. The Israeli military said it had no information about the killing of the pregnant woman. According to Unicef, several other children have been killed in Israeli attacks on Gaza in recent days, including two sisters aged six and 12, who were killed with their parents in an airstrike on Beit Lahia while they slept, and three other girls aged, three, eight and nine, who were killed by gunfire. According to the territory’s health ministry, 1,369 Palestinians have been killed and 4,627 wounded since the fragile ceasefire took effect on 11 October 2025. Since Israel’s war in Gaza began on 7 October 2023, at least 73,783 Palestinians have been killed and 174,738 wounded, according to health officials. • This article was amended on 23 September 2026 Trevor Ball is a weapons technical analyst with Armament Research Services, not a a conflict researcher and trainer at Bellingcat, as an earlier version said.

webTitle: Friday briefing: After two months as PM, is Andy Burnham passing his own test?

fields.headline: Friday briefing: After two months as PM, is Andy Burnham passing his own test?
fields.trailText: In today’s newsletter: The Labour leader said he would assess his success by how his policies affected his constituency. From the cost of living to immigration, we look at how Makerfield voters feel about their MP’s choices
fields.bodyText: Good morning. Remember the Makerfield test? When Andy Burnham was elected as an MP back in June, he reassured wary voters that the constituency was not a “stepping stone” (to be fair, it was a bit) but a “touchstone”. He meant that the policies his government devised would have to matter on the high streets of Ashton and Hindley Green. “A Makerfield test at the heart of British politics will make sure that the places Westminster has neglected will now get fairness,” he said. As the Commons breaks for the jamboree of high ideas, low gossip and crap karaoke that is party conference season, it’s a good moment to ask how Burnham’s early decisions as prime minister – he’s been at it under two months, right enough – meet that test and what it tells us about his government. I spoke to someone who, since that byelection, has immersed himself in the opinions of Makerfield voters, and those living in constituencies like it, Luke Tryl, UK director of the research agency More in Common. But first the headlines. Five big stories UK news | Shabana Mahmood has described the anti-asylum activist Daniel Thomas as “a far-right and outright racist” who will feel “the full force of the law” if his organisation commits crimes near contested asylum sites such as Piddington. Russia | Russians are going to the polls to elect a new State Duma in a tightly controlled vote stripped of meaningful competition and with little doubt about the result. UK politics | Andy Burnham is under further pressure to take control of ailing Thames Water from a cross-party group of MPs who are calling for ministers to break off talks with the US hedge funds who are effectively running the company. Royal family | The brother of the late Diana, Princess of Wales, has claimed in published extracts of his new memoir that King Charles sounded “giddily elated – like a lottery winner” in a phone call to him immediately after her death. Nature | A diminutive wild cat that inhabits Bolivia’s ⁠cloud forest has been identified as a previously unknown species, marking the first time a new living feline species has been formally named and described in more than a century. In depth: ‘The top thing for people in Makerfield was that life was a struggle’ “Who cares what Makerfield man or woman thinks? I’m a Holborn and St Pancras via Caerphilly gal myself,” you might be muttering into your overnight oats. But here’s why it matters: Makerfield, like dozens of similar post-industrial seats in the north of England, is the sort of seat Labour used to win so easily they could put up a ham sandwich as a candidate. Things have since changed. The area voted to leave by 65% in the Brexit referendum, and in the May council elections, Reform won all eight council wards in the constituency with about 50% of the vote. In his byelection dispatches from Makerfield, Luke Tryl found a pervasive sense of being left behind and forgotten – despite being “at the centre of the universe”, as one constituent put it, for one frantic month of campaigning. According to the voters Tryl spoke to, the Makerfield test should consist of three elements: Burnham showing that he “gets it”; a record of delivery; and a national plan to address the issues that Makerfield residents share with people across the country. So how has Burnham fared on some of the early challenges he’s faced? Cost of living measures “The top thing we heard in Makerfield was a sense that too much of life was a struggle,” Tryl tells me. And More in Common’s polling has found that, so far, Burnham’s early cost of living measures are very popular across the country: 86% of Britons had heard about the bus fare cap, seven in 10 thought it reflected well on the government; about 8 in 10 had heard about the VAT cut on household electricity bills (amounting to an average of about £45 a year per household), and 67% said that it landed well. Voters in Makerfield-like areas are realistic, says Tryl: “They say: ‘£45 is not going to change my life’, but they see it as a statement of intent”. People who are slightly more engaged with politics specifically mention the budget as a test point: earlier this week Burnham warned of “difficult choices” ahead. The cut-through of these measures to voters is striking: “Part of it is just the ubiquity of Andy Burnham,” says Tryl. Most recent More in Common polling shows people are more likely to have seen him on social media than any of the other party leaders. A fifth of Britons (22%) have seen “Cool Dad” Burnham on social media in the past week, compared to 20% for Reform leader Nigel Farage. I’m fascinated to see that for under-25s that rises to 35%, compared with 13% for Green leader Zack Polanski, who is often touted as catnip for younger voters. Immigration More in Common polling in June estimated that 62% of Makerfield residents consider immigration to be a top issue, making it one of the most concerned constituencies in the country about that issue. Here, Burnham gets a mixed review. The idea of taking in refugees through capped, controlled routes is popular in Makerfield, where voters worry over a lack of control. That’s why Tryl argues that one policy that really does pass the Makerfield test is the community sponsorship scheme, part of Shabana Mahmood’s controversial asylum reforms. But while Burnham has won back Labour-Green switchers over the summer, he’s not been so successful with Labour to Reform defectors – and Tryl believes that’s because he has yet to move the dial on migration. Take, for example, the shift in people’s perceptions: 52% of Britons now cite concern that local women and girls would be at risk of sexual violence as the top reason why they’d oppose asylum accommodation in their area (previously, they were more likely to refer to pressure on services). In socially conservative areas such as Makerfield, voters feel this “much more strongly”. “I think this is an achilles heel”, says Tryl. Prisoner release It’s not just constituencies such as Makerfield where voters think the criminal justice system isn’t tough enough: across the country, nearly two-thirds of Britons think prison sentences are too lenient. “The case of Andrew Harper outrages people across the board,” Tryl tells me, “but particularly in somewhere like Makerfield.” So Burnham played a bad hand well, by explaining the competing priorities to the public, and taking time to examine options before finding a partial solution. “Taking the public on that journey – especially in Makerfield where people are very distrustful of politicians – was important,” says Tryl. Climate Burnham, who is now facing intense pressure over whether to approve oil and gasfields in the North Sea, wrote in the Guardian yesterday that the UK must fully commit to reaching net zero by 2050. While Labour-Reform switchers in places like Makerfield are often deeply worried about climate change, there’s also concern that net zero policies will unfairly punish ordinary people. For many, the issue of climate change falls below more pressing daily concerns like the cost of living crisis. In this context, More in Common’s polling suggests the main test for Britain’s energy policies will be whether they can lower household bills. Party donations Tryl’s fieldwork has found that the public aren’t deeply engrossed in the minutiae of donations limits, although they do want the system to be fair. So Burnham’s early failure to support a domestic cap on donations is unlikely to be a decisive factor when constituents in Makerfield next head to the ballot box. But for the recipient of those crypto-millions, the damage has been done: more than one in three voters now name Farage’s “sleaziness and corruption” as a barrier to them voting Reform. Rather than the party’s core voters, who seem unmoved by the continuing financial scandals, it is Labour-Reform switchers in seats such as Makerfield whose faith has been shaken. But Tryl cautions against over-stressing the issue. “At the next election, if the status quo on cost of living, core public services, andimmigration still feels pretty bad, I don’t think donations in themselves will be an issue” he says. We want to hear from you What do you want to know about the US midterms, and how the Guardian plans to report them? I’ll be putting your questions to our Washington bureau in the coming weeks, so send them in by hitting reply or emailing first.edition@theguardian.com What else we’ve been enjoying I loved our pics gallery of eastern Europe’s socialist hotels, which I hadn’t read about until now. Poppy Noor, newsletters team Cracker of a You be the judge this week: Ayaan lent her brother Ahmed some money thinking it was for something important … then he spent it on a holiday. But does it matter what he did with the cash? Charlie Lindlar, newsletters team I found Zoe Williams’s interview with academic/author/policymaker Camilla Cavendish, on all the reasons we’ve stopped having babies, utterly fascinating. Poppy In case you missed it, make sure you read this viral essay from The Cut (£) on friendless husbands and the wives who try desperately to build social lives for them. Charlie The photos in our piece on the Tate’s Edward Enninful-curated show, c, about how the 90s art and fashion changed British culture, are beautiful and nostalgic. Poppy Sport Cricket | England extended their extraordinary hex over Sri Lanka to a 14th game, Tom Banton and Harry Brook leading them to a six-wicket victory with 47 balls to spare in the second T20 international. Football | Two first-half goals inspired Bournemouth, playing in their first European match, to a 2-1 win against Real Sociedad in the Europa League, while Crystal Palace had a comfortable 4-0 win over Lech Poznan. Athletics | Keely Hodgkinson has lifted the lid on how plans to chase the 800m world record this summer were ruined by a freak accident that her team has likened to whiplash. Something for the weekend Our critics’ roundup of the best things to watch, read, play and listen to right now Music Beabadoobee: Pylon | ★★★★☆ The Filipino-British songwriter’s fourth album sprinkles 90s alt fuzz with disarmingly sweet melodies and an impressive host of guests including Paramore’s Hayley Williams and Turnstile’s Brendan Yates. Read Alexis Petridis’s full review. Film Resident Evil (in cinemas now) | ★★★★☆ Weapons director Zach Cregger delivers a seat-edge thriller with a standout lead performance from Austin Abrams as an everyman navigating chaos. Read Jesse Hassenger’s full review. TV 70 Up (ITVX) | ★★★★☆ The landmark documentary series looked like it was done for good – until one participant was diagnosed with terminal cancer. Asif Kapadia takes the helm for its most elegiac, thoughtful outing ever. Read Lucy Mangan’s full review. Games Marvel’s Wolverine | ★★★☆☆ Logan is well realised by Liam McIntyre and some exquisite character art, but there are lapses in narrative and emotional arcs and some of the combat feels like a chore. Read Keith Stuart’s full review. The front pages “UK must fully commit to hitting net zero by 2050, says Burnham”, is the Guardian’s front page today. The Telegraph has “Labour’s tax raid on holiday cottages”, and the FT writes “BoE warns of higher rates ahead to tackle rising inflation”. On Earl Spencer’s claims, the Times leads with “Charles was elated after Diana died, earl claims”, the Mail splashes “Queen offered to restore Diana’s HRH … after she died”, the Mirror says “War of words”, and the Sun asks “Why is he doing this to the King now?”. The i Paper runs with “Palace on the defensive after Earl’s new claims against King”, and the Express has “Charles was ‘emphatic we respect Diana’s memory’”. Lastly, Metro says “A royal crisis? What crisis?”. The Latest Taking on Trump? Canada and EU forge closer ties Canadian prime minister, Mark Carney, has welcomed the EU’s proposal for Canada to become the bloc’s first ‘associate member’, despite threats from Donald Trump over the plan. The US president said Washington could impose ‘very serious tariffs’ or halt trade if the EU went ahead with the plan. But in a defiant speech to the European parliament, Carney called for ‘deep cooperation’ and said polling showed the overwhelming majority of Canadians supported closer ties with Europe. Lucy Hough speaks to Europe correspondent Jon Henley. Cartoon of the day | Ben Jennings The Upside A bit of good news to remind you that the world’s not all bad West Yorkshire’s moors include beautiful pinks and purples; boast rich biodiversity and a variety of flora and fauna, and play an important part in tackling the climate crisis. But, before now, much of the area’s rural beauty might have gone unnoticed by the wider public. But, on Saturday morning, the Bradford Pennine Gateway Trail will open, the first reserve of its kind in West Yorkshire. It will showcase the area’s astonishing landscape, and it is hoped that it inspires people to explore more in the region. Writer Chris Moss described a trip to the area as embodying a “ local, low-carbon, cheap-as-chips tourism before the jet age” kind of throwback vibe, adding that the new route could offer “a model for how we travel in the future” Sign up here for a weekly roundup of The Upside, sent to you every Sunday Bored at work?
