webTitle: ‘My fear was too great’: the Pussy Riot member recruited by Russian spies to inform on fellow activists

fields.headline: ‘My fear was too great’: the Pussy Riot member recruited by Russian spies to inform on fellow activists
fields.trailText: Exclusive: In her first media interview since fleeing Russia, Rita Flores describes her three years of being run by the FSB
fields.bodyText: First came the blackmail and death threats to secure cooperation, then came a series of tasks, each more sinister than the last: to inform on fellow activists, to elicit personal information from protest-minded artists and – eventually – to help with a plot to kidnap and murder a Kremlin enemy. That is how Rita Flores, a 29-year-old Russian artist, activist and former member of the Pussy Riot collective, described her recruitment and three-year handling by officers from Russia’s FSB security service, a cooperation she only broke when she fled the country last month. Flores made details of her collaboration public in a video discussion with her lawyer, Dmitry Zakhvatov, published just days after she left Russia at the end of August. She explained she was coming clean in the hope that others in a similar situation might feel emboldened to break their ties with the FSB. Now, in her first media interview since leaving Russia, she gave further detail on how she was recruited and run by the FSB. “For the first time in years, I feel calm. All this time I was dreaming about getting out and being able to talk about it all,” she said. The Guardian could not corroborate the details of Flores’s account, but there have been numerous cases of the FSB infiltrating opposition groups over the past few years. Flores, also known as Margarita Konovalova, has been associated with Pussy Riot since 2020, when she was detained after a performance near the Kremlin. She had served several short stints in jail and been subjected to surveillance and house searches on numerous occasions, which intensified after the domestic crackdown that followed the full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022. She was recruited after one of these police searches in February 2023, when two men stayed behind and introduced themselves as FSB officers, she said. They threatened to open a criminal case, under wartime censorship laws, over an Instagram post she had made criticising Russian killings in Ukraine. They also suggested they could arrange for her mother to be killed if she did not sign cooperation papers. “I believed them. I believed they could do everything they said they would … My fear was too great. I was so worried for my family and also for myself,” she said. As a reward for signing, she was given a one-off cash payment of 30,000 or 40,000 roubles (£266 or £355), she said. Her first tasks were to gather information about other opposition-minded artists in the same circles as her and report back to the FSB. The two FSB officers who recruited her became her regular handlers, she said, organising frequent meetings and largely sticking to a classic good-cop, bad-cop routine. She saw the senior officer only occasionally, a crude man in his late forties who introduced himself by a series of different names. In the end, Flores began calling him “the Jacket”, based on the shiny black suit he liked to wear. The junior officer, named Ivan, became her primary handler, and he often tried to be friendly and helpful, leaving direct threats to the Jacket. “Whenever I met with Ivan and the Jacket together, Ivan was silent. The Jacket would be rude, threatening; he’d insult me as a woman. He was the devil incarnate. Then just me and Ivan would meet, and Ivan would be nice, friendly,” she recalled. “He liked to say, ‘The FSB will re-educate you, I will re-educate you, you’ll have a nice and calm life, and you’ll love Russia, have children and be an obedient wife,’” she said. Flores said she was not supposed to tell anyone about her recruitment, but immediately told “about 20 people”, putting it down to the fact she is a “massive gossip”. Still, she stopped short of telling the people from the art world she was meant to report on, instead claiming that she initiated conflicts with them on pretexts, designed to push them away from her and prevent them sharing sensitive information. Her two handlers kept up the psychological pressure by repeating their threats, and even the friendlier Ivan on occasion made it clear that the consequences for crossing him would be severe, she claimed. “He tried to befriend me, but he could also be threatening. He’d calmly say, ‘they’ll kill your mother and you won’t be able to prove anything’ or ‘if you go abroad they’ll find you immediately and kill you,’ and then he would giggle, like it was all a joke. The Jacket, on the other hand, never joked. His threats were more direct.” In time, there were fewer targets to inform on, as most of the protest-minded artists left the country. She described life in wartime Moscow as an exercise in cognitive dissonance. “Moscow is booming; restaurants, bars and clubs are opening and there are a huge number of events. But those people who understand things have empty eyes and speak empty words,” she said. Artists who stayed are careful not to produce any work that could be considered even tangentially political, she said. “People who have stayed in Russia have accepted the rules of a game. You go to a gallery and every artwork may as well come with a sign saying ‘we were forbidden from saying anything’ … there are artists who used to make strong statements, and in 2026 they are drawing flowers in a vase.” Last May, Ivan and the Jacket first started asking her questions about Pyotr Verzilov, an activist previously linked to Pussy Riot who now lives in Ukraine and fights with the Ukrainian army against Russia. A longtime irritant to the Russian authorities, in 2018 German doctors said they believed Verzilov had been poisoned in Russia. Flores said her handlers wanted her to get information from Verzilov, including his address in Ukraine. Then, they suggested she use her old friendship with him to arrange a meeting in Serbia. There, he would be kidnapped and killed by a waiting FSB squad, they claimed. Ivan began to pay her 50,000 roubles a month as an additional incentive to help with the Verzilov case. Meanwhile, Flores said, she was plotting a way out. She married her partner last September, which she said was partly a way of worming out of the Serbia task, so she could claim to Ivan that her husband would never let her go on a trip to meet another man. Previously, her handlers had banned her from leaving the country, she claimed, and it was only when she contacted the lawyer, Zakhvatov, that she realised there could be a way for her to leave. The pair began scheming in secret over the details. “They created a reality where she felt like they controlled everything, but actually it is not that hard to leave,” said Zakhvatov. In 2022, fellow Pussy Riot activists Lucy Shtein and Masha Alekhina fled house arrest in Moscow by dressing up as food delivery couriers to evade police and eventually leave Russia. Flores’s escape was less dramatic, but both Zakhvatov and Flores declined to give details, citing the need to protect methods for future cases. After Flores’s escape, Zakhvatov announced a secure line for people in similar positions to contact him if they need help. Flores said she would also like to work to help others, and added that she was certain that recruitments in activist circles are a “mass phenomenon”. She said there was at least one person in her own surroundings who had informed on her before she agreed to cooperate, a fact she discovered when it turned out that the FSB had possession of a sex tape featuring her, covertly filmed by the person. Earlier this year, Poland jailed an exiled Russian activist for seven years, after it emerged he had passed information about fellow exiles to an FSB handler who had recruited him back in Russia. Flores’s video confession at the end of last month was met with praise from some parts of the exiled Russian opposition, who commended her bravery for speaking out and explaining how the FSB operates, but also some scepticism from those who criticised her decision to cooperate for so long. Since then, Flores has been making calls to people she informed on as well as other old friends to explain herself, and said everyone had been supportive in these conversations. “It’s not a big secret that it’s not great to work for the FSB, but fear can change a person,” said Alekhina. “It’s important that she’s now out of the country and that she said what happened to her out loud. Nobody was killed and nobody went to prison [because of her], so that is good news.”

webTitle: Record fuel prices across EU prompt calls for bloc-wide windfall tax on firms

fields.headline: Record fuel prices across EU prompt calls for bloc-wide windfall tax on firms
fields.trailText: German minister says companies are ‘exploiting situation’ in Middle East, as sky-high prices become major domestic issue for leaders
fields.bodyText: European governments have discussed imposing a bloc-wide windfall tax on energy companies, as near-record fuel and gas prices pile pressure on leaders desperate to contain mounting public discontent and the challenge of the far right. With elections due next year in eight EU countries including France, Italy, Spain and Poland, leaders are scrambling to head off the potential fallout from what analysts have warned could be one of the continent’s biggest energy shocks in decades. Germany’s finance minister, Lars Klingbeil, called on ‌the European Commission at a meeting of EU finance ministers in Dublin on Friday to propose possible ways to tax what he described as the excessive profits of oil companies. “Several member states have been calling for models for a long time,” Klingbeil said, demanding proposals by next month. “People can see how oil companies are exploiting the situation, overcharging and significantly increasing their profits.” Oil futures have climbed back above $100 a ⁠barrel, about 50% higher than before the Iran war, as escalating attacks across the Middle East threaten more supply routes. Derivatives markets suggest traders do not ‌expect a near-term drop in ‌prices. Pump prices have already reached all-time highs across Europe. In Germany, diesel prices surged to a record average of €2.45 a litre on Wednesday, while petrol hit a fresh high of €2.31 a litre, according to Europe’s largest motoring association, ADAC. Prices are even higher in the Netherlands, where petrol eclipsed last week’s record high to reach €2.73 a litre on Wednesday, with diesel at an average €2.78 a litre. Prices have risen higher still for petrol in Denmark and for diesel in Finland. Across the EU, petrol prices are 24% higher than a year earlier, while diesel is up 38% and jet fuel costs more than 100% more. Benchmark gas is trading at €81 a megawatt hour, up 150% on a year earlier, with analysts suggesting it could hit €100. The EU’s economic commissioner, Valdis Dombrovskis, has said the commission has no plans “at this stage” for an ⁠EU-wide taxing mechanism, but stressed it was “ready to engage in discussion” and member states were free to impose their own taxes. Sky-high fuel prices are already a major domestic political issue in France and Italy, both of which next year face crunch elections in which voters’ concerns are likely to be dominated by the soaring cost of living, driven largely by high energy prices. In Italy, Giorgia Meloni’s ruling rightwing coalition, trailing rivals in the polls, said this week it would scrap road tax for 14.5m cars and motorbikes from next year at a cost of over €2bn, on top of a cut to diesel duty that has already cost €2.8bn. “We have chosen to redirect a portion of the resources used to address rising fuel prices into a simple, structural measure designed especially for those who use cars and motorcycles every day to work, take their children, or get around,” Meloni said. France’s president, Emmanuel Macron, told ministers he wanted the government’s “full mobilisation” on fuel supply and prices, including efforts to secure supplies internationally by working toward the “peaceful reopening” of the strait of Hormuz. In the latest of a wave of protests, French fishers blocked access to two ports and a fuel depot in southern France on Thursday over soaring diesel prices that this week rose to €2.37 a litre, just below their record of €2.38. The fisheries minister, Catherine Chabaud, said the fishers had agreed after six hours of talks to lift the blockades after a promise that those with cashflow issues would be granted zero-interest ⁠loans and support measures would to be tied ‌to fuel price changes. The prime minister, Sébastien Lecornu, this week extended emergency fuel subsidies until the end of the year for the agriculture, fishing and construction sectors. But the government is reluctant to step in to cut fuel prices for all. “Blanket measures that affect everyone – including those who don’t need them – are a false economy,” the country’s finance minister, Roland Lescure, told journalists earlier in the week. “Why? Because ultimately, we’ll have to fund them.” In August, Spain doubled its diesel tax discount to €0.20 a litre from 1 September after diesel prices jumped by 15.7% in July, while in Germany, the embattled chancellor, Friedrich Merz, announced a fuel tax cut late on Friday. Taxes on petrol and diesel ⁠would be cut by by €0.17 from 1 October until the end of the year, the government said, as well as holding talks with the oil industry with the aim of introducing a cap on fuel prices by 1 January 2027 ‌at the latest. “Anyone who relies on their car every day is reaching breaking point,” Merz said in a statement. “We are ‌showing that we are resilient in the face of the crisis and are helping our citizens,” he added. Merz’s centre-right CDU was this month heavily defeated in state elections in Saxony-Anhalt by the far-right AfD, and two more state elections this weekend are likely to bring further gains for the far-right party, which has campaigned on a platform of a return to the cheap Russian gas imports Europe largely abandoned after Russia’s invasion of Ukraine in 2022.

webTitle: Pact with Saudi Arabia threatens to draw Pakistan into Middle East conflict

fields.headline: Pact with Saudi Arabia threatens to draw Pakistan into Middle East conflict
fields.trailText: Activation of mutual defence agreement by Riyadh as fighting with Houthis escalates would have wide-reaching repercussions for Islamabad
fields.bodyText: As he stood in Riyadh last September, the world looked like a very different place for Pakistan’s most powerful man, Gen Asim Munir. The country’s army chief was there to witness the signing of a historic defence pact with Saudi Arabia, which he had personally orchestrated with the crown prince, Mohammed bin Salman. To Munir, it appeared to be a highly strategic win: Riyadh would provide cash-strapped Pakistan with billions of dollars of life-saving investments and loans. In exchange, Pakistan agreed to train up the Saudi military, and Pakistan’s armed forces would defend Saudi Arabia in the unlikely event of an attack on its territory. Analysts say it was clear that Pakistan presumed US-Iran relations would soon get back on track and the risk of a conflict sweeping across the Middle East and the Gulf was low. But a very different scenario soon unfolded. By February, the Middle East was on fire after the US and Israel began bombing Iran – and Iran began firing missiles at the Gulf states, including Saudi Arabia, in retaliation. It did not take long for the war to reinflame Saudi’s conflict with the Houthis, the Iran-backed rebel group based in Yemen, and for their fragile truce to collapse. Earlier this month the Houthis made unprecedented territorial gains in Yemen and hit Saudi territory with strikes and drones. Saudi Arabia has responded by pounding Yemen with airstrikes. Some believe a return to full-scale war is on the horizon. The pressure is now mounting on Pakistan, and particularly Munir. In August, the defence pact with Saudi Arabia was extended to include Turkey and renamed the Mecca joint defence agreement. The countries agreed that an armed attack on any one of them would be treated as an attack on all three. Ayesha Siddiqa, a defence analyst and senior fellow at King’s College London, said: “I don’t think Asim Munir properly calculated the threats the region was facing – and that Pakistan might need to put its troops on the line quite so soon.” Saudi Arabia has tens of billions of dollars in fighter jets and war machinery, but it does not have any warfare experience to fight the Houthis, who have proved to be tough, resilient fighters. Pakistan’s forces, trained to deal with the constant menace of India, would be highly valuable on the frontline. Analysts say that if Saudi Arabia decided to activate the Mecca pact to fight the Houthis, Pakistan would have no choice but to send in its troops, including thousands who are already deployed in Saudi Arabia for training. As well as being a defence partner, Pakistan is almost totally economically and geopolitically dependent on Saudi Arabia, which has recently given the country a lifesaving $8bn (£6bn) in funds and investments. Last week, Pakistani government ministers and senior military figures gave increasingly bullish statements, confirming their “unconditional” commitment to the pact and saying Islamabad would go to “any extent” to defend Saudi Arabia. But privately, officials in Pakistan are deeply worried about being dragged into the never-ending war unfolding across the Middle East. The country is already economically crippled, in a de facto war with the Taliban in Afghanistan, and facing an uncontrollable surge in militancy in its border areas. To many, an activation of the Mecca pact would be perceived as Islamabad taking a clear stance against Iran. Before the US and Israeli strikes on Iran, Pakistan had good relations with its neighbour – ties that Munir utilised to bring Tehran to the negotiating table in his attempt to secure a lasting ceasefire. But as the war has dragged on, Pakistan has become increasingly infuriated with Iran, while Tehran has little trust left in Islamabad. As Siddiqa emphasised, Pakistan joining the fight against the Houthis “would come with major repercussions”. After Iran, Pakistan is home to the second-largest population of Shia Muslims, who would probably rise up in protest against any involvement in strikes on the Houthis. Iran also maintains good relations with the Taliban in Afghanistan, posing the risk of further provoking one of Pakistan’s biggest security threats and driving militancy and security problems along the Afghanistan-Pakistan border to even deadlier levels. It also risks inflaming the situation in Balochistan, Pakistan’s unstable border region with Iran, which is home to a long-running and uncontrollable insurgency. Raja Nasir Abbas, the opposition leader in Pakistan’s senate, said that only the very few at the top of Pakistan’s military even knew what conditions and agreements had been made in the Mecca pact. With the military as Pakistan’s de facto rulers, the decision to join was not even put before parliament. “It will be a disaster for the country if Pakistan jumps into war,” said Abbas. “We are already facing two lethal insurgencies; our economy is in a shambles and inflation has rocketed. If we take Saudi Arabia’s side in this conflict, the country will face chaos, instability and religious division.” So far, no one has been able to pinpoint what the “red line” would be that would force the pact to be activated. Analysts said Pakistan appeared to be banking on Riyadh’s reluctance to enter into open warfare with Iran by escalating its fight with the Houthis. Turkey has also made it clear it does not want to enter the fray. “Pakistan will do its best not to get involved in any incursion on Yemeni soil,” said Muhammad Amir Rana, the director of the Islamabad-based Pak Institute for Peace Studies. Speaking privately, one senior official said he did not think the Saudi crown prince “wants to activate the pact now”. “If the kingdom plans to send its ground forces, Pakistan would support that,” he said. “But I don’t think Saudi Arabia would start a full-fledged war against the Houthis without American approval and Trump has snubbed them. Right now, the US does not want to open up another front; they prefer talking to Houthis.” He added: “You can’t predict the future though.”

webTitle: ‘It’s almost impossible not to feel inspired’: how the story of Terry Fox fired up Canada’s patriotic spirit again

fields.headline: ‘It’s almost impossible not to feel inspired’: how the story of Terry Fox fired up Canada’s patriotic spirit again
fields.trailText: Canada’s citizens are finding unity again in the story of the man who ran cross-country on one leg to raise awareness for cancer research
fields.bodyText: Rob Stickle was six years old and waiting to see The Empire Strikes Back when a ripple passed through the crowd. His mother hoisted him on to her shoulders to see a man loping down one of Toronto’s busiest streets. “I was a Star Wars fanatic, and I remember saying to mom: ‘He has a robot leg.’” Who Stickle saw that mid-July day in 1980 was the 21-year-old Terry Fox on his journey to run across the entire breadth of Canada. Residents packed the city’s sidewalks for miles to catch a glimpse. By the time Stickle saw him, and after nearly 2,200 exhausting miles, Fox had completed more than half of his “Marathon of Hope” in aid of cancer research. The distinctive style of Fox’s run – a kind of limping hop – was the result of a journey undertaken on a crude and ill-fitting prosthetic leg made of plastic, leather and metal. “I didn’t fully appreciate what was happening at the moment – that we were all part of something much larger,” said Stickle, now an elementary school teacher in Toronto. “But what I’ve learned since – after losing my mom to cancer and becoming a teacher – is that we were seeing someone special. Someone who chose the route that was going to hurt. Someone who did it because he believed that the cause was important.” Fox’s status as a national hero in Canada has never been in dispute, but at a moment when the country’s sovereignty is under attack and people are once again debating what binds the nation together, his story is attracting renewed, and bipartisan, praise. Indeed, for those outside Canada it can be a surprise to discover the degree to which Fox has become less a person than a national symbol: dozens of roads have been named after him, as have 14 schools. A mountain bears his name. Statues of him dot the country. Canada has issued both stamps and coins with his image. Parks Canada designated him a National Historic Person and called Fox “an enduring icon” who “transformed our vocabulary about personal courage”. The annual Terry Fox Run takes place in late September are now held in more than 60 countries and are the world’s largest one-day fundraiser for cancer research. More than C$1bn (US$715m) has been raised in his name. But in 2026 Fox has also become a vector for a renewed sense of Canadian nationalism. The singer Bryan Adams recently joined the prime minister, Mark Carney, to visit a memorial to Fox, in a moment that seemed to signal a confluence of political and cultural powers coalescing around Fox’s legacy. Adams, whose hits include Summer of ‘69 and (Everything I Do) I Do It for You, has penned a new tribute, The Ballad of Terry Fox. And on 19 September the documentary Run Terry Run will premiere at the Toronto film festival. Compiling previously unseen footage from the 1980s to reveal a shy but determined young man whose singular odyssey enthralled the country before breaking its heart, it also upends myths that Fox enjoyed the country’s full support from day one – showing how he struggled through hundreds of early miles with little support or interest. “Watching him run, it’s almost impossible for a Canadian to not feel moved and inspired,” said director Sean Menard. Fox was an avid athlete from British Columbia whose leg was amputated in 1977 after he developed osteosarcoma. “He’s presented as almost a superhero today, but he was just a person who had to watch other kids die in the cancer ward,” said Menard. In 1980, angered by the lack of support for young people suffering from cancer, Fox decided on an ambitious goal: he would run across Canada to raise money for cancer research. On 12 April 1980, after dipping his foot in the Atlantic Ocean in St John’s, Newfoundland, Fox began a journey that, if completed, would span nearly 5,000 miles. Run Terry Run shows a surprisingly lonely and rag-tag trek, aided largely by friends and family. Dangerous roads, fatigue, heat, rain, wind and painful chafing all threaten to derail the effort. “The first reel that I found was a three and a half minute shot of him just running up a hill,” Menard said. “And he’s constantly adjusting the leather strap on his prosthetic leg because it’s not designed for that type of momentum and movement. It’s a walking prosthetic.” But as Fox moved slowly across the country, completing a full marathon each day, word spread. He soon met the prime minister. And by the time he reached Toronto, he received a hero’s welcome. The film also captures a quiet, goofy and shy Fox, who remains singularly focused on his goal and rarely permits himself moments of emotional respite. In one poignant scene he breaks down while telling a crowd about a 10-year-old boy he’d spent the day with who was also battling cancer. As donation money poured in and Fox exceeded his initial C$1m (US$714,775) goal, he resisted any endorsements or the use of his name. After passing through northern Ontario – what his team called “the backbreaker” – Fox felt optimistic that the worst was behind him. But in late August he developed a cough and grew increasingly tired. The team soon learned the cough was due to cancerous tumors in his lungs. On 1 September, Fox was forced to stop outside Thunder Bay, Ontario, after running 3,339 miles over 143 days. The following day, he tearfully announced the Marathon of Hope was suspended. He died the following June. The documentary has the effect of humanizing a man whose identity has become enmeshed with the country’s narratives. “At this particular moment in time in Canada, having these kinds of stories remind us of how great Terry was … and his bringing us together is a good thing,” said Adams, whose song is featured in the documentary and has been met with chants of ‘Terry! Terry!’ at performances in Canada. In it, he sings: Across the asphalt and the gravel Through the heat and rain He carried the nation’s weight for twenty-six miles Then he’d go again “I tried to encapsulate that story in a lyric as best I could,” Adams said. “I’m glad it’s becoming a near-mythological story in Canada. It should be, because it’s an incredible story about a human being fighting. It’s an odyssey. And it deserves to be folklore.” “We like to think of ourselves as selfless. We like to think of ourselves as brave. He even apologized when he had to stop,” said Stickle. “There’s no scandals for him and so it’s easy for people seem him as the emblematic Canadian hero.” But questions over how much to elevate the runner have long dogged Fox’s legacy. Rick Hansen, a friend of Fox who recruited the young man to play wheelchair basketball in Vancouver, said he understands the temptation. “Terry’s story and his legend is basically steeped in our values and our sense of identity as a nation: one in which people deeply care about each other,” he said. “But he also just had an absolute raw sense of purpose and determination to keep going. “The world is changing dramatically and there are perceived threats to Canada. In this sort of environment, we recognize examples of our country’s DNA in Terry’s journey.” Hansen, who completed his own journey of 25,000 miles around the world by wheelchair, recalled Fox first telling him of his cross-country plan while the pair took a rainy drive in Hansen’s Honda Civic. “I told him, ‘You need a team, Terry. Because there will be days when it gets hard when you need the support of more than just yourself.’” Hansen says there were days on his own journey when fatigue would overwhelm him. “But all it took was a little smile on the road or meeting someone who was in a chair and said how much you encouraged them – that kept me going,” he said. “For Terry, when he met young people with cancer, who were struggling, he showed them what hope looked like.” But Hansen cautions against beatifying Fox, even in a moment of renewed Canadian national spirit. “The one thing he would not want us to do is create this legend to such a lofty and disconnected status where we couldn’t see a bit of Terry in all of us,” he said. “Terry was an everyday Canadian. But he showed us what could be done with extraordinary determination and purpose.” • The subheading of this article was amended on 20 September 2026 because an earlier version referred to Terry Fox running to raise awareness for “children’s cancer research”. In fact it was for all cancer research.

webTitle: Denmark and Greenland say US military agreement will not compromise Arctic territory’s sovereignty

fields.headline: Denmark and Greenland say US military agreement will not compromise Arctic territory’s sovereignty
fields.trailText: Statement sought to clarify Trump’s announcement that US will have ‘permanent control’ over Greenland’s security
fields.bodyText: Denmark and Greenland have said any agreement with the US to develop a significant military presence in the strategic Arctic territory will not compromise Greenland’s sovereignty. In a statement on Saturday clarifying an announcement by Donald Trump that an agreement had been reached to give Washington “permanent control” ⁠over Greenland’s security, Denmark and the semi-autonomous territory ⁠expressed hope that a deal would end friction with the US over the issue. Greenland’s prime minister, Jens-Frederik Nielsen, said he was pleased with the proposed deal. “The agreement recognizes the sovereignty and territorial integrity of our kingdom and the right of the Greenlandic people to self-determination,” he said in a post. “Next week could be a good week – for Greenland, ‌Denmark and the United States,” Denmark’s foreign minister, ‌Lars Lokke Rasmussen, said in a statement. “A time of uncertainty will hopefully give way to a binding agreement that strengthens security ‌in the Arctic and the north Atlantic, and thereby our shared security within Nato Europe – while respecting the Danish kingdom’s red lines,” Rasmussen said. The US, Denmark and Greenland said late on Friday they had reached a deal to allow the US to develop a significant military presence on Greenland, while prohibiting US adversaries from building their ⁠own bases on the island. The deal is expected to be signed during the UN general assembly next week. Key details of the agreement have not been made public, including the degree of the US military presence in the self-governing Danish territory and whether any formal power over foreign policy and resources would be ceded to Washington. Trump said on social media that under the deal, “the United States will FOREVER have the complete ability to do what is necessary in Greenland in order to secure and defend the security of Greenland, and the United States of America”. He added that the agreement would give the US “permanent control over security, and all ‌other needs, in Greenland”. The security and mineral resources of the vast northern island have been subject to Washington’s foreign policy and attention since the start of the second Trump administration, with officials citing national security, access to valuable natural resources, including rare earth minerals, and control over emerging Arctic shipping lanes. The island had a significant US military presence in the 1950s, when fears of annihilation in a US-Soviet nuclear exchange required that long-range nuclear bombers and early-warning systems be based on Greenland. The US still maintains a reduced military presence at the Pituffik space base, formerly known as Thule, on the island to monitor for missiles. Mikkel Vedby Rasmussen, a political science professor at the University of Copenhagen, told Reuters that the Denmark-US deal “is probably not the end of President Trump’s ambitions for Greenland and certainly not the end of US strategic interest in the territory and its resources”. Rasmussen added that if Copenhagen cedes any formal power to Washington over Greenland, which it has held for 1,000 years, it would raise questions for Greenlanders of whether “this is the beginning of replacing the colonial relationship with Denmark with a colonial relationship to the United States”. US ambitions for greater sway over the Arctic island have strained relations with Nato. In January, European member nations sent military personnel to Greenland to demonstrate military readiness. Eight European allies issued a joint statement confirming their commitment to Arctic security. Negotiations followed. A Nato spokesperson ‌on Saturday said the alliance welcomed the agreement, which would “help advance security, stability and cooperation in this vital region”. Reuters contributed reporting

webTitle: Caribbean nations draft action plan to push UK to redress reparations over slavery

fields.headline: Caribbean nations draft action plan to push UK to redress reparations over slavery
fields.trailText: Leaders hope UK will agree to targeted discussions around reparatory justice, but could consider legal options if Britain resists
fields.bodyText: Caribbean nations are drawing up a multi-pronged “action plan” with legal options to push the UK into negotiating a decades-long slavery reparations deal, officials at a reparations conference have said. Leaders in the region are hoping the UK would agree to targeted and constructive negotiation talks at upcoming Commonwealth and UN summits, but they are ready to take the matter to international courts if Britain continues to resist diplomatic options. Earlier this month, a spokesperson for Andy Burnham reiterated the British government’s long‑held position that “the UK does not and will not pay reparations”. Ralph Gonsalves, the former prime minister of St Vincent and the Grenadines, said the Caricom Regional Conference on Reparations, which took place this week, hosted by Barbados with the Caricom Reparations Commission (CRC), was key for agreeing a unified strategy to bring Britain to the negotiating table. Gonsalves is now an elder and adviser for the Repair Campaign, a social movement for reparatory justice. He said that slavery happened over centuries and reparations had to be realistic and set over decades. “We need a concrete, multigenerational plan,” he said. On the legal options available to the Caribbean, Gonsalves challenged arguments that Britain did not violate historical laws during transatlantic slavery, adding that the UK’s signature on contemporary UN conventions had established a binding legal obligation for reparative justice. “The fact is that the consequences of slavery fall squarely under the Committee on the Elimination of Racial Discrimination, which obliges states to help address the consequences of native genocide and slavery,” Gonsalves said. In March this year, 123 nations voted for a landmark UN resolution that described chattel slavery as the gravest crime against humanity. The UK was one of several European countries that abstained from voting in the resolution. But, last month, a UN committee on the elimination of racial discrimination said countries were legally obliged to consider reparations for the transatlantic slave trade and take other ⁠measures to address the enduring ⁠legacy of racial discrimination. David Comissiong, the deputy chair of the Barbados National Task Force on Reparations, said the Caribbean nations were considering “several legal strategies”. “You’ve had Jamaica trying to engage with the national legal judicial system of the UK, the privy council – that is one strategy,” he said, adding that going to the international court of justice for an advisory opinion was another option. Prof Sir Hilary Beckles, the chair of the CRC, said reparations was a matter of justice, adding that countries in the region were forced to create viable democracies “out of the mess” of colonialism, which was still having an impact today. “When Jamaica took its petition to the UK, we had to surround that petition with the fact that when Jamaica became independent in 1962, 80% of the black people in Jamaica could not read or write. After 300 years of British colonisation, they moved into independence with 80% illiteracy. How do you build a modern nation, not even a competitive economy, with 80% illiteracy?” Speaking at the conference, Mia Mottley, the prime minister of Barbados, said the Caribbean had “no desire to bankrupt anybody”. “But we have a desire for justice,” she said. Earlier this year, Barbados commissioned a report which showed that Britain stole 25 million years of life and labour through slavery in the country. She added: “The British government took almost 200 years to repay the debt that it incurred when it paid the slave owners £20m.” Mottley pointed to the fact that Germany paid $95bn (£71bn) to the Jewish community because of the horrors of the Holocaust. Mottley said that she did not want “anybody to diminish the fact that in this country here, which I have the honour to lead, that from settlement in 1627, 400 years ago next year, for 211 years, not six, people were treated as chattel”. “If they dared to speak or to do things that were displeasing, their lives and limbs were put at risk. The evidence is clear. What is absent is the will,” she said.

webTitle: Thick smoke seen near Riyadh airport as Houthis claim attack on Saudi capital

fields.headline: Thick smoke seen near Riyadh airport as Houthis claim attack on Saudi capital
fields.trailText: Authorities issued warnings for city in first such alerts for Riyadh since fighting with Iran-backed Houthis escalated in July
fields.bodyText: Yemen’s Houthis said they attacked “sensitive” sites in the Saudi capital with missiles and drones, hours after flames and a large plume of black smoke were seen rising above Riyadh airport on Saturday. The Saudi government sent air raid alerts to citizens by phone overnight warning of aerial attacks, marking the first time the government has issued such alerts for Riyadh since fighting with the Iran-backed Houthis escalated in July. Explosions were heard in Riyadh as firefighters battled to extinguish the flames of a burning fuel tank emblazoned with the logo of the Saudi oil company Aramco near the city’s King Khalid international airport. Residents told Agence France-Presse that hours after the alert, they had heard what sounded like another round of explosions echoing through parts of the Saudi capital. According to tracking website FlightRadar24, there were “major problems” at the airport and it has been listed under its maximum disruption index. “In the direction of the airport, we saw black smoke and fire,” one resident told AFP, speaking on condition of anonymity. The Saudi civil defence force sent air raid alerts overnight on Friday to residents of Riyadh, Jeddah and other cities including Yanbu, a major industrial port which is home to critical oil facilities. The military coalition fighting the Houthis said its air defences had destroyed a missile fired by the Yemeni group toward Riyadh. The all-clear was given shortly afterwards, but residents were encouraged not to gather in crowds. A Houthi military spokesperson, Yahya Saree, said the group had foiled unspecified “criminal attempts” ⁠in the Yemeni capital of Sana’a, blaming Saudi Arabia and vowing a response. The group also said the Saudi air force had conducted hundreds of airstrikes against it in recent days. The UN security council condemned the continued Houthi attacks against Saudi Arabia in a statement on Friday. It said they had included attacks that affected civilian and energy infrastructure and had injured civilians, including women and children. It also condemned the Houthis’ military offensive in Yemen, where nearly 105,000 people have fled their homes, the International Organization for Migration said on Wednesday. The security council’s 15 members called for “practical cooperation” to prevent the Houthis from acquiring arms, military training, financing and other military-related assistance needed to carry out their attacks. They stressed that all countries must enforce the UN arms embargo against the group. The Houthis recently seized control of the strategic Red Sea islands of Greater and Lesser Hanish. Earlier this month, the group captured the port of Mokha and Perim island in the Bab al-Mandab strait, fueling fears the world could face a second oil supply crisis. The fighting between the Houthis and Saudi Arabia has developed as a new theatre of conflict in the wider war that began with US and Israeli strikes against Iran at the end of February. Donald Trump has rebuffed Saudi requests for direct US military intervention against the Houthis. A US state department security alert issued on Saturday for Americans ‌in the Middle East cited Houthi attacks. The state department urged US citizens in the region to “exercise heightened vigilance” and said Americans outside the Middle East “should seriously reconsider travel to and through the region”. Elsewhere in the region, Israel’s military launched airstrikes in several areas of southern Lebanon after it said that two of its soldiers were wounded by a “Hezbollah explosive device”. Associated Press also reported on Saturday that Israeli strikes had killed three men in the Gaza Strip. In Iran, a man accused of spying for Israel was executed in the latest of a recent surge of executions in the country.

webTitle: Future of German chancellor hangs in the balance as two states go to polls

fields.headline: Future of German chancellor hangs in the balance as two states go to polls
fields.trailText: Embattled Friedrich Merz faces nervous wait while far-right Alternative für Deutschland party targets further gains
fields.bodyText: Voters in two German states are going to the polls with the political future of the embattled chancellor, Friedrich Merz, hanging in the balance and an emboldened far right targeting further gains. Coming two weeks after a seismic election in Saxony-Anhalt in which the anti-immigration, pro-Kremlin Alternative für Deutschland (AfD) scored its highest ever result in a regional poll, the nativist party is expected to drain support again from Merz’s conservative Christian Democratic Union (CDU). Just how brutal the outcome is could affect Merz’s ability to hang on as leader after only 16 months in power, possibly setting wheels in motion for his replacement or even snap elections – currently regarded as unlikely but not ruled out. About 2.5 million people are eligible to vote in the capital Berlin and nearly 1.3 million in the Baltic coast state of Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania. Polling booths open at 8am local time on Sunday and will close at 6pm, when Merz and his allies will be watching exit polls on tenterhooks. The luckless chancellor has resisted calls to quit and vowed to fight for a signature package of economic and social welfare changes he argues are crucial to Germany’s future. “We as a government were elected for four years, I was elected for four years,” he told an industry group. “And I want to use these four years to lead the country out of this difficult period.” Merz, whose personal approval ratings have nosedived to 10%, cancelled a plan to speak at the UN general assembly in New York because “his presence is required in Berlin” after the elections, a government official said. His credibility has been tarnished by broken campaign promises to return Europe’s largest economy to growth and cut the AfD, the biggest opposition party in parliament and number one in opinion polls, down to size. The AfD fell just short of an absolute majority in former communist Saxony-Anhalt, which would have allowed it to govern on its own. It is looking for defectors from other parties to make it the first far-right force to run a German state since the Nazi period. However, polls indicate the AfD will fall well short of such a prospect in both of Sunday’s elections, even with its palpable sense of momentum. In Berlin, which is one of Germany’s 16 federal states, the incumbent CDU is vying for first place against the far-left Die Linke, which has called for expropriation of corporate landlords to fight rising housing costs. About 85% of Berlin households rent their homes and advertised rents have nearly doubled since 2014, when the city was still labelled “poor but sexy” by its then mayor, Klaus Wowereit. The AfD is polling strongly in third or fourth place, even in the cosmopolitan capital. The current mayor, Kai Wegner of the CDU, abandoned his re-election bid in July after getting tangled in contradictions explaining a decision to play tennis while large parts of the German capital were hit by an arson-triggered power blackout last winter. Stefan Evers, Berlin’s chief finance official, replaced him as the candidate but has failed to lift the party’s polling scores. In Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania, the situation looks even dicier for Merz, whose weakness regional leaders have blamed for their poor showing. The AfD and the Social Democrats are locked in a neck-and-neck race while the CDU risks its first single-digit result in 75 years. If it crashes out of parliament entirely by falling below the 5% bar to representation, it would be unprecedented in the postwar period and mark a stinging setback for Merz’s quest to stay in office. The AfD’s triumph in Saxony-Anhalt sent shock waves through Germany and beyond and has left Merz’s back to the wall, with speculation rampant he could be replaced by another Christian Democrat as chancellor well before the next general election, due in 2029. Holger Schmieding, the chief economist at Berenberg bank, said he still expected Merz to serve out his full term. “But the risk that the CDU may revolt against him and replace the unpopular chancellor seems to have risen from 20% 10 days ago to roughly 35% now, in my view,” he said in a research note, underlining the impact of a global rise in petrol prices on already angry voters. Although some economic indicators have improved on Merz’s watch, soaring living costs and deindustrialisation in core sectors such as automaking in the face of Chinese competition have taken a heavy toll. Meanwhile a significant reduction in new arrivals at the border has failed to win back AfD voters, who are responding to the party’s strong focus on economic anxiety, fears around crime, and resistance to Merz’s staunch support for Ukraine. The AfD built its victory in Saxony-Anhalt in large part by mobilising non-voters. Its opponents are hoping the spectre of a far-right juggernaut across Germany will get voters to the polls in support of mainstream democratic parties, after tens of thousands joined anti-AfD street protests in the wake of the Saxony-Anhalt rout.

webTitle: Ukraine war briefing: Kyiv denounces Russia’s inclusion of annexed regions in parliamentary elections

fields.headline: Ukraine war briefing: Kyiv denounces Russia’s inclusion of annexed regions in parliamentary elections
fields.trailText: Ukrainian officials call the move illegal while European Commission condemns ‘another blatant violation of international law’ in parliamentary poll. What we know on day 1,670
fields.bodyText: Ukraine has denounced Moscow for having Russia’s parliamentary elections for the first time include residents of regions it illegally annexed from Ukraine during the war. Kyiv officials called the action illegal and a human rights activist described residents there as being coerced to participate in the poll, which is part of Kremlin efforts to cement its gains in Ukraine. The vote across Russia started on Friday and lasts until Sunday but balloting has in fact been under way in the annexed parts of Ukraine and some areas on the Russian side of the border since the end of last month, with Russian officials citing security reasons for the extended period. Russian authorities say the Donetsk, Luhansk, Kherson and Zaporizhzhia territories – annexed by Russia in September 2022 in a move not recognised internationally – have more than 3.5 million voters. Authorities in Kyiv called the voting in those territories illegal and urged foreign governments and international organisations not to recognise the election. They warned Ukrainians that taking part in organising the vote for the State Duma – Russia’s lower house of parliament – could carry criminal liability. Vladimir Putin has emphasised the importance of balloting there in a poll intended to show public support for the war and widely expected to see the ruling pro-Putin United Russia party retain its dominance. The European Commission said the voting in Russian-held regions represented “another blatant violation of international law”. “The European Union does not and will never recognise either the holding of these so-called elections, sham elections, in the temporarily occupied territories of Ukraine or their results,” spokesperson Christian Wigand said. Ukrainian human rights groups called on residents of the Russia-held territories to stay away from the polls and “above all, to protect their lives and health and to look after their own safety”. “Holding Russian elections in the temporarily occupied territories is an attempt to use the electoral process to legitimise the Russian occupation and the attempted annexation of Ukrainian territories,” the coalition of nine groups said in a statement. Violeta Artemchuk, coordinator of the Donbas SOS human rights group that was among those who signed the statement, said members of local election commissions were going house to house – escorted by Russian troops and security agents – to force people to vote. Russian authorities reported attacks ⁠on voting systems and communication lines across the country on Saturday amid the poll. The attacks were ‌continuing, Central Election Commission chair Ella Pamfilova was cited as saying by state media, but all were being successfully repelled. Putin has accused Ukraine of trying to interfere with the vote, without providing evidence, while Kyiv has called the election farcical. The US has approved a potential $2.68bn sale of air defence equipment to Ukraine, after Kyiv made repeated pleas for support to fend off Russian attacks. The state department said in a congressional notification that it made “a determination approving a possible foreign military sale to the government of Ukraine” for buying air defence development upgrades and related equipment and services. The proposed sale is subject to congressional review. Luxembourg’s authorities were investigating drone sightings that forced the temporary suspension of operations at the nation’s main airport overnight, the prime minister said on Saturday. Luc Frieden said Luxembourg was cooperating with Nato allies over the incident, which came amid heightened concerns in Europe over hybrid attacks from Russia. He said the presence of “potentially bigger drones” in the country’s airspace had been observed “over the past few days” but it was too early to say where they had come from. Ukraine and Russian have positions on the Black Sea that are “difficult to reconcile” to end the attacks there, Turkish foreign minister Hakan Fidan has said. Exasperated by the strikes, Turkey sent a proposal to Russia and Ukraine to end attacks on civilian ships, a Turkish diplomat told Agence France-Presse on Thursday. “We received responses from both sides,” Fidan told television’s NTV on Saturday. “We are trying to reach a conclusion. Frankly, both sides have demands and positions that are difficult to reconcile. Our first priority is the extraction of grain from the Black Sea. Countries around the world need it.”
