webTitle: Fears mount that next UN chief will downgrade climate action

fields.headline: Fears mount that next UN chief will downgrade climate action
fields.trailText: Experts say some of António Guterres’s possible successors could be ‘disastrous’ for efforts to tackle crisis
fields.bodyText: Fears are mounting that the next UN secretary general will downgrade the priority of the climate crisis, according to climate and civil society experts. The current secretary general, António Guterres, has been the most forthright on the subject, calling fossil fuel companies “the godfathers of climate chaos” and warning governments they are rushing down a “highway to hell” by failing to cut greenhouse gas emissions. His repeated championing of the urgency of the crisis and willingness to take on vested interests are credited with significant global impacts, forcing governments to confront their policy failures and keeping alive the aims of the 2015 Paris climate agreement, despite the rising tide of populism and disinformation. Guterres must step down at the end of his second five-year term on 31 December and the choice of his successor will be one of the top concerns among the scores of heads of government meeting in New York this week for the UN general assembly. Many of Guterres’s most likely successors have shown less enthusiasm for tackling the climate crisis, despite rising alarm at its impacts, and experts have told the Guardian that some of the candidates could be “disastrous” yet could enjoy the support of influential countries including the US and its allies. Three candidates in particular have raised concerns: the Argentinian diplomat Rafael Grossi, who heads the International Atomic Energy Agency; Macky Sall, the former president of Senegal; and Olara Otunnu, a Ugandan former presidential candidate who has served as UN undersecretary general for children and armed conflict. Numerous insiders and experts told the Guardian that Grossi was “trying to be a friend of Donald Trump” and maintained close links with Argentina’s populist president, Javier Milei, a climate denier. “Grossi is not a climate denier himself, but those links could lead him to downplay climate,” said one close observer, who could not be named. Sall is seen as a potential champion of gas in Africa as a “transitional fuel”, which many African leaders want to exploit. “I wonder how far he would be willing to push [climate action] when it conflicts with African [fossil fuel] energy interests,” said the observer. Otunnu may feel national pressure on the politics of African gas and oil exploration, as Uganda has discovered large oil and gas deposits that it plans to exploit. “He’s a big question mark,” said another expert. “Given the fossil fuel politics of Uganda, would he make climate constraints politically binding when they conflict with development priorities?” Andreas Sieber, the head of political strategy at the campaign group 350.org, said: “The gender gap is impossible to miss: all five women candidates range from credible to genuinely compelling, while the men could be auditioning for a job description from the past century.” Some candidates have a stronger climate record. Carolyn Rodrigues-Birkett of Guyana has pushed strongly for Indigenous rights and social development, particularly on fairer finance. Rebeca Grynspan, an economist from Costa Rica, has linked the climate crisis to debt in the developing world, arguing both crises need to be tackled together. Michelle Bachelet, the former president of Chile, has said governments can no longer treat climate action as a choice but a necessity, but she was reported this week to have dropped out of the race. María Fernanda Espinosa, a former foreign minister of Ecuador, led the country’s negotiating team at several UN climate Cop summits. Ivonne Baki, also known as Ivonne A-Baki, another Ecuadorian former minister, has pioneered several conservation schemes but expressed doubt over the efficacy of emissions reductions, to the consternation of climate campaigners. A spokesperson for Baki told the Guardian: “Ambassador A-Baki’s commitment to climate action is longstanding and unequivocal. What she has questioned is not the need to reduce emissions, but whether climate policy will succeed if it becomes detached from economic realities, development needs and the livelihoods of the people it is intended to protect. Her position is that the world must pursue emissions reductions while dramatically strengthening adaptation, climate finance and protection of the natural systems on which human security depends.” Carlos Lopes, a professor at the Nelson Mandela School of Public Governance at the University of Cape Town, said: “There is a real risk that the next secretary general may be less forceful on climate than Guterres has been, not necessarily because of the individual ultimately selected, but because the political environment has changed considerably: climate diplomacy is facing stronger geopolitical headwinds, the multilateral system is under greater strain, and we are seeing forms of ‘climate hushing’, including among countries that only a few years ago wanted to be seen as leaders.” He added: “A new secretary general may understandably want to establish a distinctive agenda, but climate cannot now be treated as one issue among many competing for attention.” Continuing Guterres’s strong sense of mission on the climate must be the minimum for his successor, experts told the Guardian. “It’s absolutely critical that the climate remains at the heart of what the UN does,” said Cosima Cassel, the climate diplomacy programme lead at the E3G thinktank. The new incumbent must take on fossil fuel interests emboldened by the Trump administration and with profits bolstered by soaring fuel prices. Against a rising tide of climate denialism and misinformation, the UN is also asking governments to regulate AI, a task begun under Guterres but which will fall mainly to the next head, and could be crucial in determining whether AI becomes a vast new source of emissions. Focusing on methane – a greenhouse gas 80 times more powerful than carbon dioxide, which comes from leaky oil and gas operations, waste landfills and agriculture – should be a top priority, said Durwood Zaelke, the president of the Institute for Governance and Sustainable Development. “Cutting methane is the single most important strategy to slow near-term warming,” he said. “If we want to stop the punishing heatwaves, we need to turn off the methane blowtorch.” Countries have few constraints on the gas at present: even basic efforts such as plugging abandoned coalmines are still lacking. Electrification, which will be under the spotlight at the Cop31 summit this November, should also be a key push, aided by concerns over oil dependence raised by the Iran war. And climate finance is still not flowing to poor countries: as the tragedy in Nepal demonstrated, countries stricken by climate disaster are not receiving “loss and damage” money promised for their rescue and rehabilitation. The new UN chief must threaten and cajole rich countries into paying their share, even while the UN faces budget cuts of its own amid the withdrawal of US cash. Claudio Angelo, of the Observatório do Clima network in Brazil, said: “A secretary general can only be as good as the institution they head, and the UN is being hollowed out by the US.” Many prominent figures in climate diplomacy see the UN as an essential linchpin in climate action. Mary Robinson, the former president of Ireland, said: “We are watching the planet’s life support systems collapse around us. This could not be more urgent. The next secretary general doesn’t just need to match the ambitions of previous SGs, they have to make this one of their top priorities and be a beacon for leaders all over the world to phase out fossil fuels.”

webTitle: Top South African police officer charged with raping woman, 18, and grooming 16-year-old girl

fields.headline: Top South African police officer charged with raping woman, 18, and grooming 16-year-old girl
fields.trailText: Arrest of Shadrack Sibiya comes as country reels from cases of femicide and alleged police corruption and criminality
fields.bodyText: One of South Africa’s most senior police officers has been charged with raping an 18-year-old woman and grooming a 16-year-old girl, as the country’s police face allegations of corruption and failing to tackle violence against women and girls. Shadrack Sibiya, who was already suspended from his role as deputy national police commissioner over allegations he interfered with political killings investigations, was arrested on Monday. He is facing charges of rape, people trafficking, promoting the sexual grooming of a child and two counts of grooming a child. Sibiya appeared briefly in a Johannesburg court on Tuesday. He was then taken to prison in the capital, Pretoria, before a bail hearing on 29 September, as prosecutors had argued he was an escape risk. South Africa is reeling after the discovery of nine women’s bodies across Ekurhuleni, the municipality east of Johannesburg, in September. Meanwhile, the Madlanga Commission judicial inquiry has been examining allegations of corruption and criminality within the police for the last year. Puleng Dimpane, the acting national police commissioner, said: “Police officers are entrusted with protecting women and children. They cannot themselves be implicated in conduct that undermines this responsibility. As the country continues to confront the scourge of gender-based violence and femicide, there can be no room for anyone within the police service who is alleged to abuse their position or violate the rights of women and children.” Sibiya is accused of raping an 18-year-old woman at a hotel in May in the Sandton business district of Johannesburg. The alleged rape took place “whilst she was passed out due to intoxication administered by the accused”, according to a copy of the charge sheet. The alleged grooming of the 16-year-old girl took place over WhatsApp between 20 July and 3 August, according to the charge sheet. This allegedly included Sibiya sending the girl naked photos of herself, which she had not sent to him. Sibiya did not enter a plea at the hearing on Tuesday. His lawyer told the court that they needed more time to consult with and get instructions from him, according to News24. Firoz Cachalia, the acting police minister, said: “We strongly condemn the alleged conduct. “Where allegations of sexual offences are made against a member of the service, they must be investigated without fear or favour.” When Sibiya appeared before the Madlanga Commission in February he denied allegations that he had moved 121 political killings investigations from KwaZulu-Natal province to the national head office without explanation. Sibiya also denied that he had received a gift of 20 impalas from Vusimuzi ‘Cat’ Matlala, a businessman who received an allegedly fraudulent 360m rand (£16.7m) police health services contract soon after the alleged gift. Matlala, who has been charged with attempted murder, alongside several other charges including fraud and money laundering, declined to comment on the impalas when he appeared at the Madlanga Commission in August. He said he did not want to incriminate himself as the matter was under investigation.

webTitle: Chagos Islands deal ‘can’t go ahead’ without US support, Streeting says

fields.headline: Chagos Islands deal ‘can’t go ahead’ without US support, Streeting says
fields.trailText: Defence secretary places annual payments to Mauritius on hold as UK government reviews deal over Diego Garcia base
fields.bodyText: Wes Streeting has said annual payments worth at least £120m to Mauritius are on hold as the government reconsiders its deal over the Chagos Islands, after Donald Trump refused to back the agreement. The defence secretary said the payments would not be made “at this stage” and confirmed the deal “can’t go ahead without US support”. Last year, the UK signed a treaty to transfer sovereignty over the Chagos Islands to Mauritius, while retaining control of the joint UK-US military base on Diego Garcia under a 99-year lease. Mauritius was also set to receive £165m for three years and £120m a year from the fourth year. Asked on BBC Radio 4 Today’s programme if the payments would still go ahead, Streeting said: “Not at this stage. We’ve got to get to a point where we can agree a deal … This deal as it is currently constituted can’t go ahead without American support. So we have to get a deal to a place where it commands American support as well as the agreement of the government of Mauritius and our government. “And the reason why that is important is because we are trying to safeguard, not just now but for the longer term, the base at Diego Garcia, and the capability it provides the United Kingdom and the United States for our national and collective security.” Streeting said the payments would be a “price worth paying” if they secured Britain’s long-term ability to operate from Diego Garcia. Trump doubled down on his criticism of the agreement when he met Andy Burnham at the UN general assembly in New York on Tuesday, describing the deal to transfer sovereignty over the Chagos Islands to Mauritius as “terrible”. “I don’t support it,” Trump told reporters after a bilateral meeting with Burnham on the fringes of the general assembly adding: “I think it’s a terrible deal.” After meeting Trump, the prime minister said the government would “work hard” to find a resolution that was acceptable to the different sides. Streeting said Trump’s criticism had not come as a surprise to ministers. “This isn’t news to us,” he said, “President Trump has been clear that he has concerns about the deal as it’s currently constituted. We will work through the detail of the US concerns and seek to reach a point that all of us can sign up to.” The agreement can’t proceed as it is without US support because of the importance of the joint UK-US military base on Diego Garcia, Streeting said. The defence secretary also warned that Britain could not adopt an “ostrich strategy” of sticking its head in the sand and hoping the row over the Chagos Islands would go away, as he warned settling the dispute would involve “painstaking work”. “The strategy is not to wait out President Trump. I think the approach will be to work with President Trump and his administration,” Streeting told Times Radio. “I’m not pretending that’s an easy position and that resolving this is not going to be difficult. It is difficult and necessarily painstaking work, but it is necessary. “And the ostrich strategy of sticking our heads in the sand … , I would caution is not a wise strategy when it concerns one of the most sensitive national security assets we have anywhere in the world,” Streeting added. He also warned ignoring that Mauritius’s claim to sovereignty posed its own risk to the military base’s future. He said the ruling from the international court of justice in 2019 is “advisory now, [but] there is a potential further course of legal action avenue open to the government of Mauritius”.

webTitle: Iran denies dropping preconditions amid ‘very productive’ three-hour UN talks in New York

fields.headline: Iran denies dropping preconditions amid ‘very productive’ three-hour UN talks in New York
fields.trailText: Trump says further talks possible as barrel of Brent crude falls to below $100 for first time in two weeks
fields.bodyText: Iran has pushed back on claims that it dropped former preconditions for reopening the strait of Hormuz in surprise talks held in New York under the mediation of Qatar between Tehran’s foreign minister, Abbas Araghchi, and Donald Trump’s envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner. Trump said the three-hour talks held in a room at the UN headquarters had gone very well and been very productive. He suggested further talks were possible imminently, which led to the price of a barrel of Brent crude to fall to below $100 (£75) for the first time in two weeks. Witkoff said the talks had been “encouraging, constructive and successful”. In his speech to the UN general assembly, Trump said he had a decision to make very soon on whether to “annihilate the Islamic Republic” or help turn it into one of the great countries of the Middle East, the kind of bombastic threat Trump often deploys during talks with Iran. In Tehran, the foreign ministry spokesperson, Esmail Baghaei, confirmed the talks had occurred, but appeared not to confirm any shift in the Iranian negotiating position. He said: “The interaction that took place with the American side was through Qatari mediation. This interaction was aimed at conveying Iran’s conditions, including the end of the war in all its dimensions, the cessation of American aggressive actions, the naval siege, and the economic war, the release of Iranian assets and so on.” Aware of the potential domestic backlash, he added that Iran’s conditions had been conveyed. Iran set seven preconditions before returning to talks, and in a new development over the past 48 hours said the crucial strait of Hormuz could be reopened within seven days if those conditions were met. It is likely that the US and the Gulf states would have to accept a navigational route for shipping in the strait of Hormuz – a key waterway for transporting oil – that requires commercial shipping to enter through a sea lane mainly in Iranian waters and under Iranian rather than Omani control. The fact that the talks lasted three hours suggests some progress was made. The US side is under pressure to leverage down oil prices and increase the availability of refined oil before the midterm elections in November. Latest published figures suggest the number of identifiable tankers making it through the strait is fewer than five a day, but estimates of the US navy are much higher. The blockage in the strait is made worse by the uncertainty surrounding the control by the Houthis’ (the Iranian-backed Yemeni paramilitaries) of a second energy transport chokepoint, the Bab al-Mandab strait that leads from the Red Sea into the Indian Ocean. There is little sign that Trump wants to relaunch a full-scale war with Iran or indeed with the Houthis as Republicans battle to turn the domestic political agenda away from a hugely unpopular war that the Americans think they are losing. Iran is under ever more intense pressure from sanctions, and a US naval blockade is making it nearly impossible for Iran to export oil, depriving the country of badly needed foreign currency. Iran’s civilian aircraft on Wednesday faced a potential worldwide grounding owing to the threat of US secondary sanctions on any entity that engaged with Iran’s civilian fleet. Iranian officials negotiated frantically with neighbouring countries to try to maintain an air bridge, but it appears Oman and Iraq have been forced to close their airspace to Iranian civilian planes. The president of Iran, Masoud Pezeshkian, is due to address the UN general assembly on Wednesday after arriving in New York on a flight from Tehran as talks were under way. Pezeshkian is an advocate of negotiations with the US but has not played a direct role in the talks. He has said the memorandum of understanding (MoU), agreed with the US on 17 June, remained the starting point. Implementation of the MoU fell apart after the two sides accused one another of breaching its terms by trying to take control of the strait. Iran said the MoU clearly left Iran in control of the strait for an interim period before a long-term agreement on its management was reached, including the possibility of Oman and Iran charging fees for navigational services. Pezeshkian is expected to condemn western double standards over what he regards as an illegal US assault on Iran that has left schoolchildren dead and infrastructure ravaged. Europe’s preparedness to call out Russia for its invasion of Ukraine, and its reticence in criticising the attack on Iran, or Israel’s treatment of Palestinians in Gaza, has been a constant theme of Pezeshkian’s remarks. Many of the most powerful speeches on Tuesday at the UN general assembly came from European and Arab politicians who decried the inability of the west to enforce peace. In his farewell speech to the UN, the French president, Emmanuel Macron, criticised the attempt to overthrow the Iranian government by the US and Israel, arguing: “Every time a few states, sometimes even in the name of international order, have tried to replace the people in order to change a regime or a system, they have plunged those states into even greater chaos.” He also said that the west had not imposed a peace in Gaza. “Some boast of a supposed peace. But this peace hasn’t reopened humanitarian routes for a single second. Must we stand by and watch this spectacle that shames us all? Never!” Macron landed himself in hot water with Israel when he suggested Hamas was not present in the West Bank, as opposed to Gaza. Netanyahu’s office responded, using the biblical name for the West Bank: “Hamas terrorists carry out attacks against Jews almost every day. They have murdered countless Israeli civilians in Judea and Samaria.” Jordan’s King Abdullah II attacked the Israeli government for “moving the goalposts”, for continuing attacks and the destruction of civilian infrastructure in Gaza, and for refusing to withdraw from the war-torn Palestinian territory. This has forced the Palestinian population in Gaza into barely one-third of the territory, he said. Observers must no longer treat Israeli policies as “temporary military measures” or a “consequence of war”, he said. “Accountability begins when we call things what they are: an attempt to erase Palestinian life and impose a new territorial reality in Gaza,” he added.

webTitle: Police use teargas on protesters as disabled woman, 87, evicted from Madrid home

fields.headline: Police use teargas on protesters as disabled woman, 87, evicted from Madrid home
fields.trailText: Housing rights campaigners decry landlord’s ‘barbaric behaviour’ after apartment Maricarmen had lived in for 71 years was bought by a developer
fields.bodyText: There were violent scenes in Madrid on Wednesday as riot police fought with protesters trying to prevent the eviction of an 87-year-old disabled woman from her apartment in the Retiro district. Hundreds of protesters had gathered, many of them overnight, in an effort to block the fourth attempt to carry out the eviction. Activists from the Madrid and Barcelona tenants’ union, and celebrities including the actor Carlos Bardem and the singer and actor Ana Belén, joined the protest. Police fired rounds of teargas and made repeated baton charges as they tried to open a path for a judicial committee to carry out the eviction order, which was eventually executed on Wednesday morning. The tenant, known simply by her first name, Maricarmen, is about to turn 88. Demonstrators chanted “Ayuso’s attic for Maricarmen”, a reference to the scandal surrounding the Madrid regional president Isabel Díaz Ayuso’s alleged purchase with public money of a €6.3m residential apartment for her use as a temporary office. Behind the building’s locked door, more protesters occupied the staircase leading to Maricarmen’s flat while neighbours handed out snacks and offered the demonstrators the use of their bathrooms. When a developer bought the building Maricarmen had lived in for 71 years, she was offered the chance to buy her apartment for €247,000 (£212,000), an impossible sum for a pensioner. They then raised her rent from €500 to €1,650 a month, while she receives a state pension of €1,350. An unnamed “prominent” writer offered to pay the €1,150 difference indefinitely but their offer was ignored. In a video recorded by the local tenants’ union before the eviction, a tearful Maricarmen said: “Good morning, everyone, I thank you for the action you are taking, spending the whole night sleeping in the street. Please, keep going, but don’t hurt one another. This has to be peaceful. “I can still hear all your noise. A hug to everyone and to all the people who are supporting me in this cruel struggle against a person who wants to make money but who should not forget that they have parents and that one day they could find themselves in the situation that unfortunately I am in.” The original 1956 contract for the flat was in Maricarmen’s father’s name. When he died, the apartment passed to his wife, and on her death in 2008 it was then sublet to Maricarmen. The landlords, Urbagestión SL, successfully argued in the supreme court that this subletting was invalid and that the contract was no longer valid. Urbagestión SL has been approached for comment. Speaking at the scene, Aldo Reverte, a spokesperson for the Confederation of Tenants’ Unions, said: “Maricarmen’s case is just one more example of what happens when housing is put in the hands of landlords. The difference is that a lot of people have become aware of her situation and the tenants’ union has shown that we can fight this type of barbaric behaviour.” However, for all their efforts, the protesters were unable to stop the eviction. Beatriz Duro, the lawyer representing Maricarmen, said: “The owner isn’t prepared to negotiate or accept any sort of offer. We have asked for a place where we can take Maricarmen’s personal belongings.” So far this year, 4,000 evictions have been carried out in Spain.

webTitle: Delcy Rodríguez poses with Trump in New York as Maduro languishes in jail nearby

fields.headline: Delcy Rodríguez poses with Trump in New York as Maduro languishes in jail nearby
fields.trailText: Venezuela’s interim president hails ‘historic meeting’ and does not say whether she will visit snatched predecessor
fields.bodyText: Venezuela’s interim president, Delcy Rodríguez, has celebrated a “historic” meeting with Donald Trump in New York, posing for a smiley photo with the US president, less than nine months after he ordered the abduction of her boss, Nicolás Maduro. The former foes met at a five-star hotel a few blocks from Trump Tower in Manhattan late on Tuesday on the sidelines of the UN general assembly. The hotel is about 7 miles from the Brooklyn prison where Maduro has been held since he was snatched during a special forces raid on Caracas in January. On the eve of Tuesday’s encounter, an American reporter asked Rodríguez if she would be visiting Maduro, under whom she served as vice-president, during her stay in New York. She did not reply. But she did find time to meet Trump at the luxury Lotte New York Palace hotel, with the get-together seen as a key part of Rodríguez’s push for international legitimacy after years of Venezuela’s diplomatic isolation under Maduro’s dictatorship. On Wednesday she is expected to address the annual UN assembly. “We held a historic meeting with … Donald Trump, with whom we discussed strengthening the bilateral relationship between our countries and advancing a cooperation agenda in strategic areas such as energy, mining, security and other matters of common interest,” Rodríguez wrote on Instagram, in a 133-word statement that made no mention of her incarcerated ally. Oliver Blanco, one of Rodríguez’s top diplomats, claimed the meeting marked “a new stage of dialogue and understanding between both countries” and was “an important step toward new opportunities for our country and our people”. Blanco also posted a cheery photo in which he and Trump smiled and gave the thumbs up to the camera. A White House aide said the meeting was also attended by top US officials including the secretary of state, Marco Rubio, and the deputy chief of staff Stephen Miller. “It was a short meeting but it was an important meeting,” Rubio said on Wednesday, telling reporters it had focused on Venezuela’s economic recovery and political transition. Hours earlier, Rodríguez had sat in the general assembly hall watching Trump celebrate the “massive military operation” during which Maduro – whom he called an “outlaw dictator” and “a real criminal” – was captured. “It was a war … [and] to the victor belong the spoils,” Trump bragged of the recent oil deal between the US and Venezuela, as Rodríguez appeared to wince. Some observers also detected signs of discomfort in the body language captured in the photo of Trump and Rodríguez, who appeared to be clenching her left fist. Some of Rodríguez’s critics in Venezuela called her treatment by Trump an unmitigated humiliation for a socialist party politician who has spent years railing against American imperialism. After Maduro’s capture, Trump warned that Rodríguez would “pay a very big price, probably bigger than Maduro,” if she did not toe the US line. Since then, Rodríguez has made a series of concessions, including ceding control of Venezuela’s oil revenues to Washington and agreeing to a controversial 65bn-barrel oil deal that Trump on Tuesday called “the largest oil deal in history”. One opposition figure denounced the Rodríguez-Trump meeting as an encounter between a “shameless puppet and her unscrupulous puppeteer”. But Rodríguez has succeeded in consolidating power, with Trump seemingly more focused on gaining access to Venezuela’s natural resources than pushing for a fresh presidential election that would move the South American country back towards democracy. Trump has repeatedly praised Rodríguez’s “fantastic” and “terrific” leadership while sidelining her main rival, the opposition leader María Corina Machado. Machado, who left Venezuela late last year to receive her Nobel peace prize in Oslo, has been unable to return and is exiled in Panama. She reportedly made three attempts to return to Venezuela this week but failed. Orlando Pérez, a Latin America expert from the University of North Texas at Dallas, rejected the idea that Rodríguez had been humiliated by her meeting with Trump. “It’s a huge triumph [for her]. She got the photo op she wanted. I frankly don’t think you can overestimate how important the photo op was for her,” said Pérez, who believed the image legitimised Rodríguez’s position as president and signalled that Washington was happy to keep working with her and for other leaders to engage with her. For Trump, meeting Rodríguez was a way to show Maga voters he had “won Venezuela” by commandeering its massive oil reserves with January’s invasion. “So that picture was a win-win for Delcy and for Trump,” Pérez added. Before Tuesday’s tête-à-tête, the presidents of the US and Venezuela had last met in 2015, when Barack Obama and Maduro spoke briefly during a regional summit in Panama. In the decade that followed, Maduro became an international pariah as he led his country into economic chaos and increasingly authoritarian rule, and Venezuela was hit by punishing international sanctions. At the 2015 summit, Obama conceded that the days in which “the US could meddle with impunity” in Latin America were over. But Trump has dramatically different ideas and has been forging ahead with attempts to reassert US dominance in a region it has long considered its back yard. As well as capturing Venezuela’s government and trying to topple Cuba’s communist government by strangling its economy, Trump’s push for hegemony has also seen the US accused of trying to swing Brazil’s presidential election in favour of the far-right candidate Flávio Bolsonaro through diplomatic and economic pressure. Addressing the UN assembly on Tuesday, the Brazilian president, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, hit back at such efforts, without directly citing the US. “We will not allow the enemies of democracy – internal or external – to attack the will of the people. Brazilian democracy belongs to the Brazilians,” said Lula who is facing a tough battle to win re-election in October’s vote. “Brazil doesn’t fit into anyone’s back yard,” added Lula, who also called for elections in Venezuela. He did not meet Rodríguez during her visit to New York but said the “people of Venezuela deserve to decide their own future”.

webTitle: The EU’s Canada offer is more mood than reality but it could hint at a future geometry for the bloc

fields.headline: The EU’s Canada offer is more mood than reality but it could hint at a future geometry for the bloc
fields.trailText: While Brussels and Ottawa desire a deeper partnership born of Trump-era volatility, ​the EU has no legal framework to accommodate it
fields.bodyText: The EU and Canada, Ursula von der Leyen said last week, “see the world with the same eyes”, with shared stances on everything from AI to the climate crisis, the Ukraine war and the unholy chaos unleashed by the current occupant of the White House (OK, she didn’t actually say that last bit. But I like to think she almost certainly thought it.) So, the European Commission president went on, Canada should become “the first associate member of the EU”. In the audience, Mark Carney beamed with delight. The next day, Canada’s prime minister enthusiastically embraced the idea of an “alliance for the future”, to build “collective resilience” through “deep cooperation”. Cue standing ovations, warm handshakes – and a great deal of head-scratching in Brussels and assorted EU capitals. Because “associate membership” of the EU is not, in fact, a thing. Nor, as a Guardian editorial pointed out, is there “any blueprint for what such a thing might involve”. The term was, the editorial argued, “a political hypothesis”, describing “a relationship of intimate strategic alignment with the EU, stopping short of actual membership, in ways that are significant but undefined”. So what exactly are the commission and Canada playing at here, and where might it lead? You can see where they’re coming from. On paper, in a world of unpredictable and increasingly aggressive great powers, it makes perfect sense. For Canada – which already has the Ceta free trade agreement with the EU – the catalyst for even closer cooperation is clearly Donald Trump: incessant tariff threats, an escalating trade war, bullying talk of Canada as the “51st state”, the renaming of Lake Ontario – all have left Ottawa eager to diversify its relations. Aligning with European industrial strategy, working together on defence and AI, and joining EU scientific research and student exchange programmes would offer Canada a reliable counterweight to its all-too-unreliable southern neighbour. (Unsurprisingly, Trump called the tie-up “laughable”, and threatened more tariffs.) For the EU, meanwhile, Canada is a dream partner: a stable, like-minded “middle power” rich in critical minerals, rare earths and – as Carney couldn’t resist noting – good manners. Plus, Canada’s unbridled EU-enthusiasm is a pleasing boost to the bloc’s bruised ego after Iceland’s recent rejection of more EU accession negotiations. There’s only one problem: “associate membership” is not a status in the EU treaties, and creating such a status would mean treaty reform, which member states won’t contemplate. There are things called “association agreements”, such as with Ukraine, Moldova or Georgia, but those are essentially stepping stones to full membership – which Canada can’t aspire to, for the very good reason that it isn’t in Europe. But if “associate member” sounds vaguely familiar, that’s because the EU has been talking about a “second circle” since the days of Jacques Delors: an outer ring of countries bound by shared values, free trade and security cooperation to an inner core of members, but without full voting rights or complete regulatory integration. Emmanuel Macron’s European Political Community is a variation on this theme, and Germany’s chancellor, Friedrich Merz, recently floated “associate member” status for Ukraine. Indeed, non-EU nations in the European Economic Area (EEA) and European Free Trade Association, such as Norway, Iceland or Switzerland, already function as quasi-associate members, enjoying single-market access while being largely “rule-takers”: adopting EU rules without having a vote in Brussels. Writing in the Guardian, Fabian Zuleeg suggested that Canada and Europe actually need more of an “integrated partnership” – a model that leaves single market access to one side, focusing instead on concrete collaboration in areas such as defence, supply chains and EU programmes like Horizon and Erasmus+. Alberto Alemanno, a professor of EU law, noted that a realistic EU-Canada landing zone would have to go further than Ceta and might more resemble the kind of tailored framework of the EU-Swiss relationship. But the real significance of any formal new status, he said, was that it could make the EU “an institutional hub around which other democracies organise strategic autonomy – but without joining the union”. What that might actually look like is anyone’s guess: visa-free work access, shared military procurement, Canadian seats on EU regulatory committees? For the moment, Canada’s hypothetical “associate membership” is more of a mood than a reality: the expressed intent of a democratic bloc and a middle power to deepen ties in the face of mounting global uncertainty. Does it, all the same, hold any hope for Brexit-regretting Britain? As Jill Rutter of the Institute for Government highlighted, the EU’s sudden willingness to display “institutional imagination” at least shows that the bloc is willing to think about adapting when geopolitical pressures demand. But a new deal for Canada won’t automatically fix the UK’s issues. As Joël Reland of UK in a Changing Europe pointed out, the vagueness of the EU offer to Canada might look promising for the UK. But Canada wants “deep cooperation” without touching single-market rules, and the UK’s main problem is that it is now shut out of that same market. Whatever Canada eventually gets, it’s unlikely to work for the UK. *** A miserable time for Merz Friedrich Merz is in trouble. A fortnight after the far-right Alternative für Deutschland (AfD) swept to a crushing victory in one state election in Saxony-Anhalt, the German chancellor’s centre-right CDU failed to clear the 5% threshold needed to enter the state parliament in another, Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania. It fared a little better in Berlin, where it was the incumbent, but was still beaten – by a clear five-point margin – by the far-left Die Linke. And the AfD made headway in the capital, too, surging to a double-digit result. The embattled chancellor has vowed to fight on, but faces an uncomfortable choice: revise the unpopular economic reforms he insists are essential, or risk oblivion defending them. Meanwhile, as long as he refuses to step aside and no one is actively seeking to replace him, a volatile and damaging deadlock will reign in Europe’s biggest economy. After 16 months in office, it is becoming increasingly clear – as a Guardian editorial noted – that Merz is “ill-suited for the job” of defending Germany’s democratic future against the far right. To receive the complete version of This Is Europe in your inbox every Wednesday, please subscribe here.

webTitle: Harvey Weinstein sentenced to 15 years after sexual assault conviction

fields.headline: Harvey Weinstein sentenced to 15 years after sexual assault conviction
fields.trailText: Sentencing comes after years of appeals and retrials in case involving former TV production assistant Miriam Haley
fields.bodyText: Harvey Weinstein was sentenced to 15 years on Wednesday after being convicted of sexually assaulting former TV production assistant Miriam Haley in 2006 at his Manhattan apartment. Haley appeared in court on Wednesday morning and delivered a victim impact statement. In her statement, Haley spoke about the harassment and humiliation she has endured over the past seven years, saying she was publicly smeared by Weinstein, his defense team, and podcasters she suspects were paid to damage her image. Haley added that her experience following the assault has “already been a life sentence” for her, and asked the judge to take all of this into consideration. New York assistant district attorney Nicole Blumberg addressed the court on behalf of the prosecution. She asked the court to sentence Weinstein, 74, to 20 years with five years of post-release supervision, stating he never showed any type of remorse for his crimes. Weinstein said in his statement he has remorse for Haley. “I live with many regrets and sincerely apologize for my actions,” he said. Weinstein’s defense had also argued that their client is too sick to serve a long sentence following a diagnosis of several health conditions including blood cancer and heart disease. The defense asked for a nine-year sentence. Before sentencing, Judge Curtis Farber acknowledged that Weinstein would be remembered not just for producing films, but for being the face of the #MeToo movement. Farber said Weinstein took advantage of Haley’s dreams of working in the film industry. “You had it all,” Farber said. “Your legacy could have been cemented with greatness. But you threw it all away by assaulting Miriam Haley.” The latest sentencing comes after years of appeals and retrials in the closely watched case. Weinstein was sentenced to 23 years in prison in 2020 after a jury convicted him of sexually assaulting Haley and raping aspiring actor Jessica Mann. But in 2024, New York’s highest court overturned the convictions, saying Weinstein’s trial had been prejudiced by the judge allowing woman who alleged they were sexual assault victims of Weinstein to testify, despite not being plaintiffs in the case. Weinstein went on trial again in 2025 and was once more convicted of a criminal sexual act involving Haley. Jurors acquitted Weinstein of a separate sexual assault charge involving former model Kaja Sokola but could not reach a verdict on the rape charge involving Mann. Prosecutors retried the Mann charge earlier this year, but the jury deadlocked in May. The charge was later dropped after Mann said she could not endure another trial. Weinstein is also awaiting resentencing in a separate California rape case. In June, a California appeals court upheld Weinstein’s 2022 rape and sexual assault conviction. He was found guilty of assaulting an Italian model in her hotel room during a film festival. He could serve the California sentence before beginning the sentence imposed in New York. Farber said at Wednesday’s sentencing that California will have the final say on whether Weinstein’s sentences run consecutively or concurrently. The accusations and subsequent charges against Weinstein were one of the biggest factors in launching the #MeToo movement. More than 80 women have come forward with allegations of sexual assault or misconduct against him.

webTitle: Janet Davies obituary

fields.headline: Janet Davies obituary
fields.trailText: Other lives: Dedicated worker for Christian Aid in Merseyside and the north-west
fields.bodyText: My sister, Janet Davies, who has died aged 89, dedicated most of her adult life to international development, ecumenical partnership and social justice. From 1968 to 1986 she worked for Christian Aid in Merseyside and the north-west, and later became regional organiser. Based in Liverpool, and supported by Edward Patey, then dean of the city, Janet used her formidable communicating, networking and nurturing skills to forge grassroots alliances across denominations to deliver and celebrate the practical demonstration of ecumenism that was Christian Aid Week. Her work in the establishment of the Merseyside Churches Ecumenical Council also helped to lay the foundation for the “Better Together” partnership of Bishop David Sheppard and Archbishop Derek Worlock. Born and raised in Formby, Lancashire, to Margot (nee Rose) and Philip Crisall, a civil engineer, Janet went to Streatham House school, Crosby, and later trained and worked as a secretary. Janet was a gifted pianist and choral singer. At the Southport Gramophone Society in 1968, she met and later married Alan Davies, an occupational therapist at Moss Side high security hospital in Maghull, Merseyside. He was a great supporter of her Christian Aid work. His death from cancer 11 years later was a great loss. In her overseas work on behalf of Christian Aid, Janet became transformed by encountering and standing with those in dire poverty. She told of being up to her knees in filth and excrement in the shantytowns of Calcutta (now Kolkata) in 1975, of the horrors of racial segregation in apartheid South Africa in the late 1970s and early 80s, and how deeply this had affected her spiritually. A great motivational speaker, never using notes, Janet was undaunted by addressing an audience of 1,500 at the Royal Liverpool Philharmonic Hall where, in 1985, she publicly received a cheque for Christian Aid’s appeal for the Ethiopian famine, the proceeds of a concert featuring Paul Tortelier playing the Elgar cello concerto. A classic late developer, Janet studied for and gained a certificate in theology from Birmingham University in 1994. Returning from the first of many visits to Lebanon and the occupied Palestinian Territories in 1982, she wrote movingly about her “alternative pilgrimage” in They Came and They Saw: Western Christian Experiences of the Holy Land (2000), edited by Michael Prior, in which she catalogued the need for peace and justice in those tormented lands. Becoming a driving force in Middle East peace advocacy, she led related programmes for USPG (United Society Partners in the Gospel) from the mid-80s to the early 90s and the United Reformed Church (1992-95), and in retirement established Sabeel-Kairos UK (formerly Friends of Sabeel-UK), a charity committed to solidarity with the Palestinian Christian community. She is survived by me, and nine nieces and nephews. Our older brother, Chris, predeceased her.

tags.description: Obituaries pages traditionally describe and celebrate the lives of the great and good, the famous and infamous. There is another type of life that deserves noticing: people less in the public eye, or lives lived beyond formal recognition. To offer a piece to Other Lives, contact us here.

webTitle: Iran’s president hits out at ‘bully’ Trump in UN speech but signals willingness to talk

fields.headline: Iran’s president hits out at ‘bully’ Trump in UN speech but signals willingness to talk
fields.trailText: Masoud Pezeshkian says Tehran is ready for dialogue and diplomacy ‘but without the language of force’
fields.bodyText: Iran’s president, Masoud Pezeshkian, turned the tables on Donald Trump, describing the US as the true bully and terrorist in the Middle East while insisting that Iran had always shown a commitment to the negotiating table. In a defiant speech to the UN general assembly in New York, his first since the US and Israel launched an all-out war on Iran, Pezeshkian repeatedly vowed that Tehran would never bend the knee to the US. But he balanced defiance with a willingness to talk, saying: “It must be understood by President Trump and those who seek to bully us that we are ready for dialogue and diplomacy and negotiations but without the language of force.” On Tuesday, the US president had told the UN he was weighing whether to “annihilate” Iran, but went on to hail renewed talks between Tehran and Washington’s negotiators. A surprise three-hour meeting between Iran’s foreign minister, Abbas Araghchi, and the US special envoy Steve Witkoff on the sidelines of the assembly the same day was regarded as constructive by both sides. It was the first such meeting since June, but did not stop the US delegation from walking out at the start of Pezeshkian’s speech. The Iranian president did not go into any details about the talks, but conveyed the impression that he was focused on winning the support of Iran’s Arab neighbours for the proposals Tehran has drawn up for the future of the strait of Hormuz, the vital waterway that has been intermittently blockaded since the start of the war, causing global energy prices to soar. He made it clear Iran could not tolerate the strait being used to transport arms that could then be used against it, a statement that suggests the Islamic republic will demand the right to inspect ships travelling through the strait in the future. Iran’s goal, he said, was to live independently. Pezeshkian accused Washington of “terrorism” for assassinating the supreme leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei at the start of the war. He held up photographs of the dead leader and more than 150 schoolchildren killed in the opening days of the conflict, before insisting Tehran had never started a war. “We have only defended ourselves. We are not terrorists,” he said. “Our innocent people have been the targets of cowardly attacks and aggressions imposed upon our country.” He said Iran had the right to pursue a peaceful civil nuclear programme and it did not want to build nuclear weapons. He repeatedly argued that the answer to regional security lay in agreement within the region and not with outsiders such as the US. Iran did not see its neighbours as security rivals, he said, but as partners in security. “In today’s world, those that are unable to defend themselves will be trampled upon,” he added. Iran has repeatedly targeted US allies in the region since the start of the war. Insisting Iran was the true victim of terrorism, Pezeshkian questioned why “Israel kills, yet Iran is subject to sanction”. He added: “They kill, we are sanctioned. Iran did not seek special treatment but wanted equal rights.” Pezeshkian’s speech received domestic praise, but the hardline secretary of the supreme national security council, Mohsen Rezaei, refused to describe the talks with the Americans as negotiations. He said: “Mr Araghchi [Iran’s foreign minister] has announced Iran’s conditions, and until Iran’s conditions are implemented, the strait of Hormuz will not be opened nor will there be any negotiation.” He warned Iran’s neighbours implementing a US-induced ban on Iranian travel: “If you stand alongside the United States, we will not stand by and watch.” He cautioned that should Iranian flights face bans through regional cooperation with Washington, “their airports will have no flights either”. Pezeshkian’s attendance at the UN’s signature diplomatic event, in the heart of Manhattan, had been in doubt as it was unclear whether the US would issue a visa. Ultimately, Washington granted the permit but denied visas to several members of Pezeshkian’s entourage. In Tehran, the foreign ministry spokesperson, Esmail Baghaei, confirmed talks had taken place between the two sides but appeared not to confirm any shift in the Iranian negotiating position. He said: “The interaction that took place with the American side was through Qatari mediation. This interaction was aimed at conveying Iran’s conditions, including the end of the war in all its dimensions, the cessation of American aggressive actions, the naval siege, and the economic war, the release of Iranian assets and so on.” Aware of the potential domestic backlash, he added that Iran’s conditions had been conveyed. Iran set seven preconditions before returning to talks, and in a new development over the past 48 hours it said the strait of Hormuz could be reopened within seven days if those conditions were met. It is likely that the US and the Gulf states would have to accept a navigational route for shipping in the strait of Hormuz that requires commercial shipping to enter through a sea lane mainly in Iranian waters and under Iranian rather than Omani control. The fact that the talks lasted three hours suggests some progress was made. The US side is under pressure to leverage down oil prices and increase the availability of refined oil before the midterm elections in November. The latest published figures suggest the number of identifiable tankers making it through the strait is fewer than five a day. The blockage in the strait is made worse by uncertainty surrounding the control by the Houthis – the Iran-backed Yemeni paramilitaries – of a second energy transport choke point, the Bab al-Mandab strait that leads from the Red Sea into the Indian Ocean. There is little sign that Trump wants to relaunch a full-scale war with Iran, or indeed with the Houthis, as Republicans battle to turn the domestic political agenda away from a hugely unpopular conflict that Americans think they are losing. Iran is under ever more intense pressure from sanctions, and a US naval blockade is making it nearly impossible for it to export oil, depriving the country of badly needed foreign currency. Iran’s civilian aircraft on Wednesday faced a potential worldwide grounding owing to the threat of US secondary sanctions on any entity that engaged with Iran’s civilian fleet. Iranian officials negotiated frantically with neighbouring countries to try to maintain an air bridge, but it appears that Oman and Iraq have been forced to close their airspace to Iranian civilian planes.

webTitle: No signs Chagos deal can be adapted to suit Trump, say UK officials

fields.headline: No signs Chagos deal can be adapted to suit Trump, say UK officials
fields.trailText: Agreement with Mauritius over Diego Garcia unlikely to be revived unless president changes his mind, insiders believe
fields.bodyText: The Chagos Islands deal is on hold for as long as Donald Trump objects to it, UK officials believe, with no immediate signs it can be adapted to suit the US president. After Trump savaged the three-way plan as “a terrible deal” during a meeting with Andy Burnham at the UN general assembly, the prime minister said he was “confident” the UK would be able to find a solution to revive the idea. But while efforts are still taking place to do this, there is an acceptance in the government that it is extremely unlikely unless Trump has another change of heart. “Until the president changes his mind there will not be any progress,” one official said. “We are where we are. We were waiting for the president to present a view, which he has.” The UK signed a treaty last year to transfer sovereignty over the Chagos Islands to Mauritius, while retaining control of the joint UK-US military base on Diego Garcia, part of the Indian Ocean archipelago, under a 99-year lease. Mauritius was set to receive £165m for three years and £120m a year from the fourth year. Wes Streeting, the UK defence secretary, said on Wednesday morning that payments worth at least £120m to Mauritius were on hold given the deal could not go ahead without US support. “This deal as it is currently constituted can’t go ahead without American support,” Streeting told BBC Radio 4’s Today’s programme. “So we have to get a deal to a place where it commands American support as well as the agreement of the government of Mauritius and our government.” The US had supported the plan, but Trump changed his mind amid a wider deterioration of relations with Keir Starmer over the lack of UK support for the US attacks on Iran. Speaking after their first in-person meeting at the UN in New York on Tuesday, Trump praised Burnham but gave no ground on his scepticism about the Chagos deal. “I don’t support it. I think it’s terrible,” Trump told reporters. “It was a terrible deal. [Mauritius] all of a sudden say they have ownership. Somebody has ownership that never showed up before, after decades and centuries. I think it’s ridiculous.” Burnham later said he had “inherited the situation” and had told Trump “that we will work to find that resolution between the different sides”. He added: “It was clear that we need to come to that agreement, but I’m confident we can find it working with our US partners.” Given Trump’s objections appear based on the core element of the deal – the transfer of sovereignty to Mauritius – there appears to be no immediate way forward. The UK government has previously made clear that Washington’s approval is a prerequisite for the plan. UK officials stress, however, that while Burnham inherited the impasse from Starmer, there is no intention to deprioritise a plan, begun under Rishi Sunak, that the government says is vital to ensure the future of the strategically vital Diego Garcia base, given Mauritian claims to sovereignty of the archipelago. “It’s not back to the drawing board, as we do need to find a diplomatic solution to this,” another UK official said. “Everyone agrees something has to be done, which is why several prime ministers and even more foreign secretaries have tried to get it over the line.” Streeting stressed the same point to the BBC, saying: “The ostrich strategy of sticking our heads in the sand … I would caution is not a wise strategy when it concerns one of the most sensitive national security assets we have anywhere in the world.”

webTitle: How the ‘poisonous tide’ of disinformation spreads division and despair

fields.headline: How the ‘poisonous tide’ of disinformation spreads division and despair
fields.trailText: Whether produced by Russia, China or far-right influencers, deepfakes and disinfo are being used to spread deceitful narratives
fields.bodyText: Russian disinformation campaigns are varied in their falsehoods and strategies. The narratives range from a deepfake Tom Cruise criticising the Paris Olympics to portraying a recent Russian attack on a train near the Ukraine-Poland border as a false-flag operation. Some efforts are blatant deepfakes, such as stamping the BBC logo on a video wrongly blaming Ukraine for a deadly missile salvo on its own citizens in Kramatorsk four years ago. The tactics evolve too, from disseminating deceitful narratives through the Telegram messaging platform to “poisoning” AI systems by littering the internet with false stories in the hope they will be regurgitated by chatbots. It is systematic and Andy Burnham has seen enough, announcing a new anti-disinformation agency, the National Centre for Information Defence. “We’re talking about an insidious campaign that reaches into people’s homes and twists what they feel about their own country and community – creating a narrative of decline, stoking division and sowing despair,” he said. Experts say picking off individual examples is the wrong approach and Burnham is right to tackle what he describes as a “poisonous tide”. Going after isolated examples of disinformation is a “losers’ game”, says Ned Mendez, head of research at Alliance4Europe, a nonprofit that analyses these destabilising threats. “You can spend all your time looking for a TikTok or a post on X but it’s not an effective use of your day. It’s the infrastructure that is the problem, so this is a step in the right direction, going after the networks,” he says. Sophie Williams-Dunning, a cyber analyst at the Royal United Services Institute (Rusi) thinktank, says there is now a “sophisticated ecosystem which exists to exacerbate provokable users for one reason or another”. Although Burnham is targeting “hostile state information attacks”, this ecosystem does not just include Russia, which likes to amplify “divisive content”, says Williams-Dunning. It also includes far-right influencers who immediately jump on social flashpoints like the Southport and Belfast riots and individuals simply looking to make money by producing highly engaging content riffing on disruption. The Burnham announcement is “welcome, if overdue”, says Williams-Dunning, who adds that there will be an accompanying debate about free speech and the right level of government intervention. Inevitably, malign networks will amplify those free-speech concerns, she says. It is not just Russia deploying information attacks. China and Iran have both used deepfake newscasters to advance their goals. One recent study, conducted mostly in February by the Social Market Foundation, a British thinktank, found that more than a quarter of posts on X that relate to news were misinformation, a third of which were anti-immigration or Islamophobic. The UK government defines misinformation as the inadvertent spread of false information, while disinformation is the deliberate creation and spread of falsehoods to create harm or disruption. The two can intertwine to highly disruptive effect. Labour has become increasingly concerned about Russian disinformation affecting the UK. The Starmer government in May cited information warfare from Moscow when it warned Britain was “confronting an industrial-scale attack on the UK’s and our allies’ information environment, aimed at undermining our security and democratic systems”. Earlier this year MPs on the foreign affairs select committee called for the creation of a national counter-disinformation centre, in a similar vein to Sweden’s Psychological Defence Agency and France’s Vigilance and Protection against Foreign Digital Interference service. Experts said Burnham’s announcement at least shows the UK government catching up, although Keir Starmer’s administration showed an awareness of social media’s contribution to unrest by launching the National Internet Intelligence Investigations unit after the Southport disturbances in 2024. Operated by the police, it monitors social media to help local forces “manage public safety threats and risks”. The UK government has been taking action prior to Burnham’s announcement, however. In May it sanctioned employees of the Social Design Agency and ANO Dialog, Russian entities which it said the Kremlin uses for large-scale interference campaigns. One example is the Doppelgänger network, so-called due to its technique of imitating the appearance of established media organisations including Le Monde, the Guardian, Der Spiegel and Fox News. Other examples include the 2023 surge in reports of bedbug infestations in France, falsely blaming Ukrainian refugees. The disinformation leaked into the British press and the French government concluded the stories were being artificially amplified by Russian-linked social media accounts One of the most longstanding misinformation campaigns has centred on the idea that London is “dangerous” and “lawless”. Analysis of Reddit accounts by King’s College London found the number of such posts rose from 874 in 2008 to 258,444 in 2024. Robert Topinka, reader in digital media and rhetoric at Birkbeck, University of London, said Russia did not necessarily start such storylines, but enthusiastically amplified them. He cautioned that counter-disinformation efforts should not assume “people are just being fooled by some sort of outside actor”. Rather, he said, Russia tends to find a point of tension and then create more content around it. “What really is happening is people are feeling like Britain is run-down – that’s the real source of it,” said Topinka. AI is adding a new dimension. Mark Zuckerberg’s Meta says AI-generated content is now a “near-standard” part of disinformation campaigns. The UK thinktank Demos recently highlighted a chatbot “poisoning” campaign where falsehoods published online by a discredited Russian organisation, including the bodies of deceased Ukrainian soldiers being processed into meat products, were repeated by chatbot models. The National Centre for Information Defence will have a lot of work to do.

webTitle: OpenAI’s Altman and Anthropic’s Amodei address UN security council

fields.headline: OpenAI’s Altman and Anthropic’s Amodei address UN security council
fields.trailText: Heads of two of the world’s largest artificial intelligence companies give separate briefings on AI safety
fields.bodyText: Sam Altman of OpenAI and Dario Amodei of Anthropic, heads of two of the world’s largest artificial intelligence companies, addressed the United Nations security council on Wednesday in separate briefings on AI safety. “We have a choice in front of us,” Altman told the council. “AI can either be more like a new renaissance of creativity and discovery, or more like a new industrial revolution of upheaval and disarray.” Altman and Amodei spoke as their companies face increasing scrutiny over the safety of their products. Public alarm over AI has grown in response to warnings from Anthropic researchers earlier this month that the technology could destroy humanity within the decade. Leaders of AI companies, including Altman and Amodei, have since called for a slowdown on advancing AI and more international cooperation on the technology’s safety standards. Altman, who sat at the corner of the security council’s horseshoe-shaped table and spoke for about 10 minutes, touted AI’s benefits to productivity while also warning of its potential abuses. He advocated for governments to come together to build a future where AI is guided by democratic institutions, rather than one where people feel like the technology is “something being done to them”. “If AI is to be democratic, the most important decisions cannot be made by labs in San Francisco alone. They must be shaped through democratic processes and by governments accountable to the people that they serve,” Altman said. The OpenAI CEO’s speech contrasted with some of his company’s lobbying efforts and the political action committee of its president, Greg Brockman. The pro-AI Leading the Future PAC has accrued more than $100m and spent millions targeting candidates who support stronger regulation on the AI industry. Altman’s speech also nodded to some of the concerns from Anthropic researchers about AI’s existential risk, warning the council against falling into “doomerism”. Altman argued there was instead a “middle path” through the safety debate that should be based on three principles: AI systems must remain under human control; AI must benefit people, from helping doctors treat patients to boosting entrepreneurs; and the technology must “empower people individually”. Amodei, who addressed the council via video call, repeated many of the points that he made in a 12 September blog post that called for increased global cooperation and oversight of AI. He advocated for several forms of international agreements, including a ban on using AI to develop biological weapons and global standards for testing new AI models. While Altman steered his address away from engaging with the warnings of existential risk that have made headlines this month, Amodei reiterated his concerns about developers losing control of AI while also framing his company as an industry leader on safety. “If managed poorly, I even believe that AI could be a risk to humanity as a whole,” Amodei said. “At Anthropic, we believe we have the best track record in the industry for preventing these risks”. AI regulation has shot up the political agenda after researchers at OpenAI’s arch-rival Anthropic warned the technology could wipe out humanity within years. These concerns are a regular refrain within sections of the AI community, who fear the technology could trigger devastation for a variety of reasons ranging from aiding development of bioweapons to triggering a financial catastrophe. Earlier, Amodei called for a slowdown in AI development, which was supported by OpenAI, Google and Elon Musk. Both Amodei and Altman have long cast themselves as stewards of AI and sought to shape how the technology is publicly received. Their companies are also jockeying for the lead in the AI race, with both eyeing potentially record-setting initial public offerings that would value each at more than $1.5tn.

webTitle: Ukraine war briefing: Moscow hammers Kyiv as Zelenskyy urges leaders at UN to keep choking Russia’s revenues

fields.headline: Ukraine war briefing: Moscow hammers Kyiv as Zelenskyy urges leaders at UN to keep choking Russia’s revenues
fields.trailText: Two killed and 41 wounded in Kyiv as Russian drone attacks that began on Wednesday stretched into Thursday
fields.bodyText: Russia hammered Kyiv with drones in daylight attacks on Wednesday hours before Ukrainian president Volodymyr Zelenskyy met with world leaders at the UN general assembly. Two people were killed and 41 wounded in Ukraine’s capital. Palls of black smoke floated above the city following the latest in what have been daily Russian attacks that torment Ukrainian civilians. The drones set off fires and damaged buildings in Kyiv and elsewhere in Ukraine overnight, authorities said. The attacks continued early into Thursday with emergency crews dispatched to three ⁠districts, said Kyiv mayor Vitali Klitschko. “Explosions in ‌Kyiv, The ‌capital is under attack ‌from ballistic missiles. Remain in shelters!” Klitschko wrote on Telegram. Unofficial Telegram channels showed what was described as a fire lighting up the horizon. A Russian ⁠aerial bomb attack ⁠also killed five people ⁠and injured six on Wednesday ⁠in the village of Oleksandrivka ⁠in Ukraine’s eastern ‌Donetsk ‌region, the regional governor ‌said. Vadym Filashkin, writing on Telegram, said Russian forces had dropped ‌four bombs on the village, near the city of Kramatorsk. Zelenskyy urged world’s leaders Wednesday to keep choking Russia’s revenues and impede its war efforts, telling the UN general assembly that “Russia’s revenues must remain a target.” “When someone gives Russia more money through trade, they give this war more time. And that is exactly why we insist on limiting trade with the aggressor, and why we are burning Russia’s revenues ourselves,” he said. Zelenskyy also reiterated his warnings to Moscow that Ukraine would strike back and make the coming winter deeply painful for Russia, if the two sides ⁠cannot agree a truce on energy ⁠attacks before the cold sets in. Ukraine and its allies are racing to secure limited agreements on energy infrastructure and Black Sea shipping before winter, fearing renewed Russian strikes on power and heating facilities, while Moscow continues to show little interest in wider negotiations ⁠to end the war. “Ukrainians understand that this winter could be very harsh for us. But in response, we will have no choice but to make it painful for Russia too,” Zelenskyy told the UN meeting. ⁠The US has invited Russian president Vladimir Putin to a December G20 meeting in ⁠Miami, Florida, where ⁠he could hold a summit with Donald Trump, US secretary of state Marco Rubio ⁠said on Wednesday. The Kremlin said Russia would consider the invitation. Rubio, speaking after meeting Russian foreign minister Sergei ⁠Lavrov on the sidelines of the UN general assembly, said the US remained ‌open to engaging ‌with Russia on the war in Ukraine, despite stalled efforts ‌to bring an end to the conflict. “We’ve invited President Putin to the G20. We think it’s an opportunity for him to engage not just with the president but with other world leaders. We hope that’s an invitation ‌he’ll accept,” Rubio said. Zelenskyy said on Wednesday he had signed a “drone deal” with Finland’s president, ⁠another in a series of agreements offering to combine Kyiv’s technical expertise with other countries’ industrial capacity. Zelenskyy met Finnish ⁠president Alexander Stubb, ⁠along with Norwegian prime minister Jonas Gahr Stoere in New York. “And today we just signed a Drone Deal with Alex (Stubb) – an important step for jointly protecting our ⁠people and an even stronger partnership between our countries,” Zelenskyy wrote on Telegram. Ukraine has transferred two North Korean prisoners of war to ⁠South Korea, Zelenskyy said on Thursday in his address to the UN. “Recently, we sent two ⁠North Korean prisoners ⁠of war to the Republic of Korea,” Zelenskyy said in his speech. “These guys are not easy to capture alive. One of them, ⁠when he realised he was going to be taken prisoner, tried to kill himself. And he was shocked that fate did not let him ⁠die.” Zelenskyy did not provide more details about the return. According to some estimates, North Korea has sent up to 15,000 soldiers since 2024 to support Russia’s war against Ukraine. Australian prime minister Anthony Albanese has announced that Australia will provide $60m more in support for Ukraine’s fight against Russia’s invasion during an emotional meeting with ⁠Zelenskyy in New York. Albanese became emotional as he paid tribute to his “friend” Zelenskyy in his fight against Russian aggression. “[His] leadership has been, I think, quite extraordinary, leading people in circumstances which are extraordinarily difficult,” he said.
