webTitle: Defiance, threats and a ‘rebirth’: five key points from day two of the UN’s big gathering

fields.headline: Defiance, threats and a ‘rebirth’: five key points from day two of the UN’s big gathering
fields.trailText: Iran took a combative tone, a new Venezuela is announced, and Ukraine’s president aims at the Kremlin’s coffers
fields.bodyText: The rubber hit the road this week at the UN general assembly at a time of global urgency, with the Middle East crisis reverberating through markets around the world, AI sparking existential concerns, and few signs of cooperation between the US and China in their great power rivalry. World leaders have gathered in New York to make their feelings known, both at the podium and at crucial meetings on the sidelines. Amid the chaos of the politicking and background briefings, here is a selection of key points we saw on day two. No bending the knee for Iran Iran’s president, Masoud Pezeshkian, balanced defiance against the US with an openness to dialogue, in an address that had been in doubt as it was unclear he would be issued a visa to enter the country. “We have only defended ourselves. We are not terrorists,” he said. “Our innocent people have been the targets of cowardly attacks and aggressions imposed upon our country.” Referring to the United States, Pezeshkian added: “Yes, they did hit us, but we did not bend the knee.” The US delegation walked out of the room. At the podium, Pezeshkian held up images of children killed in the strike on a school in Minab, which a UN fact-finding mission had found “reasonable grounds” to say was carried out by the US. Despite Donald Trump’s earlier public musings on whether to “annihilate the Islamic Republic”, the US president said there had been a “very good” meeting on the fate of the strait of Hormuz between Tehran’s foreign minister, Abbas Araghchi, and US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner. Xi Jinping gives it a miss The biggest thing not happening at the UN general assembly could well be any involvement by Xi Jinping. Amid crises in Ukraine and the Middle East that have seen Beijing accused of being at best unhelpful, Donald Trump rolled out a 100ft red carpet to personally meet his counterpart at Joint Base Andrews instead of the White House, a move not seen for decades. The two will talk about AI, trade and Taiwan during a state dinner and tea, but China will be represented at the UNGA by vice-president Han Zheng. On his arrival, Xi said “our two countries should be partners rather than rivals”, according to state news agency Xinhua, and a modest extension of their trade truce was announced, but expectations of a big breakthrough are low. ‘Today, Venezuela is being reborn’ Venezuela’s interim president described the “rebirth” of her country, as she addressed for the UN for the first time since the abduction of her old boss on the orders of Trump. Delcy Rodríguez, speaking as Nicolás Maduro languished in a prison nearly in Brooklyn, promised elections at an undisclosed point in the future and said her government had started a “political dialogue with opposition sectors”. Earlier, she had watched as Trump defended the US intervention in her country, saying: “It was a war … [and] to the victor belong the spoils”, an allusion to the controversial 65bn-barrel oil deal she agreed, which the president called “the largest oil deal in history”. ‘Russia’s revenues must remain a target’ As the war grinds towards its fifth winter, Ukraine’s president was clear-eyed about how to hurt Russia: hit the Kremlin’s coffers. “Russia’s revenues must remain a target,” Volodymyr Zelenskyy told the assembly. “When someone gives Russia more money through trade, they give this war more time. And that is exactly why we insist on limiting trade with the aggressor, and why we are burning Russia’s revenues ourselves,” he said. The president flagged that the upcoming winter could be “very harsh for us”, given the annual onslaught against its energy infrastructure, but warned that Kyiv could “make it painful for Russia too”. Ukraine has used long-range drones to strike Russian warehouses, ‌port infrastructure and oil refineries, but Trump has pressed Zelenskyy to “stop knocking out diesel fuel in Russia” because it was causing a global shortage. Although Russian president Vladimir Putin is not at the UN, Trump has invited him to December’s G20 in Miami, which would mark a significant step in welcoming Putin back on to the world stage. Coming up ... Netanyahu New York is bracing for protests, both in the assembly hall and on the streets, when Israeli prime minister Benjamin Netanyahu speaks on Thursday against a background of growing international condemnation, most recently over violence by Israeli settlers in the West Bank. New York mayor Zohran Mamdani told demonstrators this week he would protect their “right to [protest] in this city” but tempered his earlier promises to arrest Netanyahu as a war criminal. Palestinian representatives are calling for diplomatic missions to bring staff for a planned walkout of Netanyahu’s speech. Netanyahu is expected to deliver a hardline message aimed not just at world leaders, but also to his own electorate in Israel ahead of elections next month. Trump and top US officials are not expected to meet Netanyahu, but will be listening carefully to his words – 60% of American Jews in a poll released this week hope Netanyahu is voted out in October.

webTitle: The long-range drone war: Ukraine and Russia scramble for supremacy in the skies

fields.headline: The long-range drone war: Ukraine and Russia scramble for supremacy in the skies
fields.trailText: A conflict that began with tanks and then artillery is now pivoting around a new generation of drones focused on military, industrial, economic and civilian targets
fields.bodyText: Finally, in the dead of night, the threat above has passed. The rain has eased and the Ukrainian drones are ready, prepared by a ground crew shrouded in hard-to-detect green and red lights. A small succession of Ukrainian Fire Point FP-2 craft, miniature monoplanes with a 6-metre wingspan and more than 100kg of explosive, line up for an attack mission into occupied Luhansk, over 200 miles away. The drone’s main piston engine is a familiar scooter’s buzz, but its launch booster is something else. The jet sound reverberates, almost painfully. A burst of fire lurches into the distance, the last of which signifies it is time for Ukraine’s 413 Raid drone regiment to pack and go. The launch of an FP-2 drone during the mission into occupied Luhansk It is a scene that is now played out nightly by dozens of Ukrainian crews, reflecting a fast-changing conflict that began with tanks, then artillery, but is now pivoting beyond a first generation of drones. Death and destruction are delivered by new weapons in growing volumes, hundreds of miles beyond the frontline, and at targets that are military, industrial and economic but that affect civilians too. But just as Ukraine has developed its drone and missile capability to almost match Russia’s – after its cities were subject at times to hundreds of drone strikes a day – Moscow has transformed its drone arsenal with a jet-powered revolution. The balance of power remains uncertain. Pilots of the 413 Raid drone regiment preparing an FP-2 for launch Raid is a specialist drone unit, created two years ago, and has been operating Ukrainian-designed and -built FP-2 attack drones since last autumn, according to Skipper, a former corporate IT worker with a master’s in computer science who is now one of its commanders. If, he says, there was only one crew that could run two missions a week when they started, today he says “we can do 10 times more, or even more”. Speaking in a car as the rain pelts down, Skipper cautions there is “a flipside” when asked if long-distance wars are easier to fight because nobody has to be killed visibly. “They can do it as well,” he says – Raid’s crew are targets too. “Maybe you don’t see the enemy with your own eyes, but still it’s a very dangerous game,” he adds. The FP-2 was only first publicly acknowledged by Ukraine last September. It is designed to attack hardened targets at a mid-range, to disrupt Russian logistics to the frontline. The success of Raid and others engaged in mid-strike bombing has helped grind the pace of the invaders’ advance to a near halt. Russia gained a modest 90 square kilometres of Ukraine in August, compared with 505 sq km a year earlier, and western officials estimate it is losing 6,000 more soldiers a month than it can recruit. In Ukraine’s sprawling military, the specialist drone units of the Unmanned System Forces, including Raid regiment, work and overlap with army units working closer to the frontline and special forces. A major attack, such as the attack that disabled the Moscow refinery about 300 miles from the border on 20 September, involves several working at once. A long-range attack could involve launching up to 300 drones, though the target is to be able to launch 1,000 a night, in what soldiers describe as an “orchestra”, where cheap drones identify an air corridor towards the final target. An employee walks past a plume of smoke rising from a fire at the Russian e-commerce firm Wildberries’ logistics complex near the town of Podolsk, outside Moscow, on 16 August. Photograph: Tatyana Makeyeva/AFP/Getty Images The long-range, $75,000 FP-1, sister to the FP-2, has been used to repeatedly attack warehouses, refineries and other military-economic sites at a depth of 1,800 miles inside Russia, causing the country’s crude oil production to fall by 7.7% in a year, according to figures from the International Energy Agency, and interest rates to remain at 14%. “Both sides are getting better at translating deep strikes into economic effects,” says Sidharth Kaushal, of the Royal United Services Institute. A refinery burning in Moscow after Ukrainian drones strikes, 21 September. Photograph: EyePress News/Shutterstock Mission planning is rarely shown, but a short-range drone unit operating in the eastern Donetsk front – Unit 17, Special Operations Centre – is happy to show their war work from their dacha. Znakhar, 33, a software coder before the full Russian invasion, is one of a squad of English-speaking men in their early 30s. During the day, he clicks on fresh, static targets – artillery, electronic jamming systems – that have been added to a common system from western satellites or Ukrainian reconnaissance drones, studying their pictures for extra information. Pilots of Unit 17, Special Operations Centre, posing for a portrait next to a Sych mid-strike drone The temporary base of pilots of Unit 17, Special Operations Centre. Right: the ‘drop bombs’ Unit 17 used for middle strikes At night, the crew use a $25,000 Sych drone, which looks like a large model aeroplane. If the rain holds off, they can fly two to six bombing runs, dozens of miles behind enemy lines. Znakhar, whose call sign means healer or herbalist, draws up an initial flight path in seconds with a few clicks on a map, then adjusts the route to avoid population centres, high ground and known interceptor drone launch sites. What’s changed recently? “More drones,” he says. “Russian drones.” Colleagues such as Ananas, 30, head out at night, taking more precautions than they did when the unit started drone work two years ago, preparing launches underground where once they could work in a field. He studied architecture, then worked as a 3D artist in a video game studio. “I play a lot of video games,” he says, “so I’m good with a gamepad. It’s a big plus because now I’m a pilot.” It’s a narrowing of the gap between fiction and reality. *** On the other side, Moscow always has ballistic and cruise missiles available, allowing it to bomb anywhere inside Ukraine since February 2022. It imported delta-winged Shahed drones from Iran in the war’s first year to boost its long-range attack numbers, and developed a family of cheap battlefield drones plus its own version of the Shahed. But since May there has been a notable set of upgrades, allowing Russian forces to strike Ukraine more effectively with fast, jet-engined drones, allied with a new ruthlessness of targeting. Firefighters working at the site of a Russian drone strike on Kyiv business centre on 23 September “Russia never stops,” Serhii Beskrestnov, Volodymyr Zelenskyy’s defence technology adviser, said during an interview in Kyiv punctuated by an air raid and explosions in the distance. The original Iranian delta wing Shahed (known by Russia as the Geran-2) has been redesigned and a jet engine added. The new Geran-4, with more aerodynamic wings, flies at anywhere from 300km/h (186mph) to 550km/h, while the cigar-shaped Geran-5 is even faster, at closer to 600km/h. It is similar in speed to a new light cruise missile, the Banderol. The prediction is that Russia will make 36,000 jet Shaheds in 2027, a further 10,000 Banderols, plus a similar number of cheap cruise missiles, the Dan-T. All could be used to bomb Ukraine’s strained electricity, heating and water systems this winter. The new weapons, whose Telefly engines are made in China, are faster than the Ukrainian interceptors, designed to stop the old piston-engined Shahed Geran-2s. Shahed interception rates, once over 90%, are down to 60% against Russia’s newer models, with predictable results. The aftermath of a Russian attack on ammunition storage in Myla village, Kyiv region, in August A mix of jet- and traditional-engined drones made a rare morning attack into the centre of Kyiv on Wednesday, bombing a market near the central railway station and business centre, killing two people and injuring 41. At the end of August, a Geran-4 hit an ammunition dump at Myla, outside Kyiv, killing 38 and destroying homes nearby. Another struck Ukraine’s SBU domestic intelligence agency in the centre of Kyiv, though it may have been controlled in its final phase by a Russian agent on the ground. Food supplies in Kyiv supermarkets are uneven after sustained attacks on warehouses in August; petrol stations in the capital were targeted in early September. The aftermath of a Russian Geran-5-type jet-powered drone strike on an Ukrnafta petrol station in the Holosiivskyi district of Kyiv, 15 September. Photograph: Libkos/Getty Images *** Ukrainian military propaganda is excellent at highlighting successful missions on social media, but the wider picture of the impact of its drone strikes on Russia is harder to discern. “This spring we had a really nice time and almost every night we could see one, two, three, four systems destroyed,” Skipper says. “Since June, July, they are just hiding.” Other Ukrainian military sources emphasise that Russia has improved its jamming capabilities, and cheap strike drones are simply not as accurate now. In this long-distance war, civilian casualties are climbing. New UN figures show 2,222 killed in Ukraine during the first eight months of 2026, more than in all of 2025. In August, 368 were killed in Ukraine and a further 113 reported dead in Russia. Warehouses owned by Ukrainian supermarkets, its Nova Poshta postal service and e-commerce groups were hit at least 32 times. Wildberries and Ozon warehouses in Russia were bombed 17 times by Ukraine. Firefighters at a warehouse in the Kyiv region after a Russian attack The impact could be harder for Ukraine. “Russia has advantages that Ukraine does not,” says Kaushal. “A more diversified range of long-range weapons, more of an air defence network and more slack as a society, because its people have not faced so much pressure for so long.” Ukraine, meanwhile, faces economic pressure at a time when its war budget is overspent and needs to find £40bn more next year. Yet, though war is escalating as the technology changes, neither side is close to defeat or a crisis. Tests will come if Russia tries to mobilise up to 300,000 men after parliamentary elections – and as Ukraine tries again to refinance and, most urgently, get through the winter. Back in their soldiers’ dacha, Ananas and Znakhar wonder if the war will ever end. “Sometimes I catch this feeling,” Ananas admits, then Znakhar comes in: “We just need to hang on one more day than them.”

webTitle: Elif Eralp: ‘Germany’s Zohran Mamdani’ who vows to be a mayor for all Berliners

fields.headline: Elif Eralp: ‘Germany’s Zohran Mamdani’ who vows to be a mayor for all Berliners
fields.trailText: Die Linke candidate, a lawyer affected by her experiences as the child of political migrants from Turkey, poised to head Berlin coalition government
fields.bodyText: Elif Eralp launched her election bid last autumn with the blunt statement: “People like me are actually not supposed to become mayor in this country.” So the fact that the 45-year-old lawyer and daughter of political migrants from Turkey is on the verge of becoming Berlin’s next mayor and the capital’s first leader of Turkish origin is quite the moment in German politics. After last weekend’s city state election, in which her far-left party, Die Linke, came first with more than a quarter of the votes, Eralp has become a household name. The mood at Die Linke’s election celebrations on Sunday night was electric. Eralp, whose candidacy has helped propel the party from the doldrums to the brink of heading a coalition government in Berlin for the first time, was feted as a star. Some commentators suggested Germany was “having a [Zohran] Mamdani moment”, in reference to the democratic socialist mayor of New York. (One of his advisers was summoned to Berlin to help Eralp weeks before the poll. Her campaign was modelled on that of the veteran US senator Bernie Sanders.) “In our city, love and justice won over hate … this signal goes out into the world,” Eralp said at her victory party, the “hate” a pointed reference to the far-right Alternative für Deutschland, which was celebrating coming first in another regional election. Even in liberal Berlin, the populist party made considerable gains. It was Die Linke, however, that came out on top. With about 26% of the vote, the party not only outperformed the centre-left Social Democrats, whose presence has dominated Berlin politics for decades, and the Greens. It was also well ahead of the Christian Democratic Union (CDU), the conservative party of the German chancellor, Friedrich Merz, which had previously held the mayoral position. A lot is now at stake for Eralp, who has promised to be “a mayor for all Berliners”. Eralp, who was chosen in particular by the young (47% of whom voted for her) and who mobilised thousands of otherwise non-voters thanks in part to intensive door-to-door campaigning and social media, generated most interest with her ambitious promise to take on corporate giants over unaffordable housing in the German capital. Once described as “poor but sexy” by a former mayor for its low cost of living, Berlin’s rents have soared in recent years. In her nomination speech, the lawyer said: “I’m running so that our city becomes affordable again, so that real estate speculators don’t decide what happens to our city, but rather we do together.” She called sky-high rents a defining social issue, saying: “This city belongs to all of us, not to the speculators.” Merz has led the charge against Eralp’s plans to expropriate more than 200,000 Berlin flats from their corporate landlords, saying her policy – decried by some as “socialism on speed” – would have “calamitous effects” on the economy. The chancellor has said he will push for laws to prevent her plans. Eralp has pledged to plough on. It is not a given that Die Linke will take control of Berlin’s towering Rotes Rathaus, or red city hall, named after its red brick and not its association with leftwing politics. Eralp’s victory has been overshadowed by accusations that Die Linke has failed to tackle antisemitism within its own ranks as well as charges that the party has tolerated – and at worst courted – the support of criminal gangs. The Social Democrats and the Greens, potential coalition partners, have said they need urgent clarification on these alleged affiliations before they agree to be associated with Die Linke. Die Linke’s leadership has repeatedly denied the accusations while vowing to clampdown on any antisemitism in its ranks. On Tuesday it announced that one of its Berlin MPs, who is alleged to have connections both to criminal gangs and a terrorist-related, pro-Hamas organisation, would “suspend his parliamentary duties until further notice”. On Monday, Eralp sought to reassure critics. “Any form of glorification or trivialisation of violence or terror is completely out of the question,” she said. “I stand by that, and for me the promise of protection applies unequivocally to Jewish people just as it does to Muslims, Christians and all people in our city.” Eralp has been keen to stress the ordinariness of her life. She lives with her husband and two children in a rental flat in her own constituency of Kreuzberg, in south-central Berlin, one of the city’s most diverse quarters and home to one of Germany’s liveliest Turkish communities. Her children attend a state school in her kiez, or neighbourhood, and she has kept her family away from the cameras “for their own safety”, she says. Much of her campaigning in the district was carried out in Turkish. Unlike most Turkish migrants, Eralp’s parents did not come to Germany as Gastarbeiter, or guest workers, from Eastern Anatolia but were trade unionists and socialists from Istanbul who were imprisoned after a military coup for their political beliefs. Her mother, Hülya, a well-known feminist in Turkey, was only allowed out of jail because she was heavily pregnant with Eralp. She and Eralp’s father, Selçuk, a doctor, fled to Germany, where their daughter was born in Munich in 1981. The family experienced a complicated asylum process, which Eralp has said helped shape her view of the world. “I’ve experienced a lot about what it means when authorities make decisions you don’t understand. I’ve also felt racism and discrimination first-hand, so my life story has a lot to do with where I’ve ended up now,” she has said. She recalls how her parents often put up asylum seekers in their home over many years, and the 15 years of struggle that her mother, a trainer for nurses, faced before her qualifications were recognised in Germany. At the age of 10, Eralp founded a conservation club with friends in her parents’ garage, and later she went into the anti-nuclear movement. After studying law at the University of Hamburg, she moved to Berlin for two years of obligatory practical legal training, ending up working in the parliamentary group of Die Linke and later switching to the Berlin state parliament. She said she was inspired to join Die Linke in 2017 in direct response to the entry of AfD, an anti-immigration party, into the Bundestag for the first time. In 2019, with fellow members and supporters of Die Linke who had refugee and migrant backgrounds, she co-founded Links*kanax, an alliance that aimed to increase the visibility of the migrant-progressive voice within the party and beyond. When she was 12, Eralp says, she wanted to become a human rights lawyer “to fight against all these injustices I’d seen”. Now, she says, “I’m doing what I set out to do, not in a courtroom, but in the political sphere”.

webTitle: Israel facing water shortages caused by destruction of Gaza’s treatment plants

fields.headline: Israel facing water shortages caused by destruction of Gaza’s treatment plants
fields.trailText: Five desalination plants shut down for days, while Gaza remains in grip of severe water and sanitation crisis
fields.bodyText: Israel is facing weeks of water shortages after an exceptional algae bloom crippled much of its desalination capacity, in a crisis scientists say was triggered when Israeli attacks destroyed much of Gaza’s wastewater infrastructure, causing a massive discharge of untreated sewage. “Pollution does not recognise political borders,” said the Zalul Environmental Association, an Israeli NGO dedicated to protecting the country’s seas and shores. “The discharge of untreated sewage from the Gaza Strip into the sea is contributing to the worsening crisis affecting the Israeli desalination facilities. The wastewater contains nutrients such as nitrogen and phosphorus, which feed microalgae and cyanobacteria and may intensify their blooms.” Despite last year’s US-brokered ceasefire, Gaza remains gripped by a severe water and sanitation crisis. The Palestinian territory is plagued by rodents, and sewage floods its coastline after Israel destroyed its wastewater treatment plants. Just across the border, a vast bloom of microalgae stretching up to 60 miles (100km) long has clogged filters at five of Israel’s six main desalination plants, which were shut down for days and have since been operating at a reduced level. Experts say that after nearly three years of war, the environmental consequences of the destruction in Gaza are now spilling back into Israel. “The discharge of untreated sewage from Gaza into the sea increases risks to Israel’s water production infrastructure along the southern Mediterranean coast,” said Jack Gilron, a professor emeritus and desalination expert at Ben-Gurion University’s Zuckerberg Institute for Water Research. “The current incident reinforces the need to prepare against threats to one of Israel’s main sources of drinking water.” Since 7 October 2023, Israeli bombardment has destroyed 90% of Gaza’s water and sanitation infrastructure, according to a report by Médecins Sans Frontières. Direct strikes have been carried out on wells, carrier lines, reservoirs and desalination units. Gaza’s water crisis remains severe. Before the war, 80% the territory’s supply came from an aquifer under the coastal strip, but that supply is now contaminated by seawater and wastewater and unfit for human consumption. Most of Gaza’s drinking water came from desalination plants and three pipelines controlled by the Israeli water authority, but those pipelines were cut at the start of the war and have only partially reopened. Meanwhile, damaged or destroyed distribution networks have left much of the population reliant on water trucks. For many, this means a stark choice between drinking an extra cup of water or saving it to wash their hands and prevent disease, with acute diarrhoea among the leading causes of illness. “We carry water in jerry cans,” said Nas al-Barawi, 34, a mother of five from Beit Lahia. “We walk with heavy containers or wait for hours in queues. Much of the water is unsafe, and children suffer recurring stomach infections, diarrhoea and skin rashes. Damaged sewage networks and failed pumps have also left wastewater flowing between tents and through residential areas.” Omar Shatat, the deputy executive director of the Coastal Municipalities Water Utility in Gaza, said all five of the territory’s wastewater treatment plants were out of service, leaving an estimated 45,000 cubic metres of untreated sewage to flow into the Mediterranean every day. In addition, about 15,000 cubic metres of untreated waste a day seeps into the groundwater from soakaway pits, particularly in the informal camps in al-Mawasi. “This is a catastrophic situation environmentally and from a public-health perspective,” Shatat said. “The sea is heavily polluted, and the first people affected are Gaza’s residents and displaced people because they are in direct contact with the highest concentrations of sewage.” Pat Griffiths, the International Committee of the Red Cross’s spokesperson in Gaza City, said the situation was only likely to get worse with the onset of winter. “Palestinians live surrounded by wastewater. It’s all around them. It’s where they eat, where they get water, where they walk,” he said. Shaimaa al-Katari, 37, who has been displaced to al-Mawasi, said: “We have nowhere to dispose of the water from washing dishes and clothes. We have to let it run into the street, which causes pools of stagnant water to form. Algae and mosquitoes then spread around them and the streets become dirty. We suffer from foul smells, mosquitoes at night and flies during the day, as well as rodents.” Rats have infested parts of Gaza for months, thriving amid raw sewage and piles of rubbish accumulating around overcrowded camps for displaced people. Israeli communities near the Gaza border have also been grappling with an unprecedented rat infestation, with rodents swarming homes and gardens. “The consequences [of the war] do not stop at the border,” said Nada Majdalani, the Palestine director of EcoPeace Middle East, an environmental peacebuilding organisation. “We are already seeing an increase in hepatitis A in Gaza. I believe we are on the verge of a catastrophe. And a serious outbreak in Gaza would not necessarily remain within Gaza’s borders.” In Israel, authorities are urging people to use water “judiciously” until the system is fully restored. Water supplies have been reduced in the south of the country, and farmers have been instructed to halt irrigation, which economists say will cause food prices to rise. Zalul and EcoPeace urged Cogat, the Israeli agency charged with administration of Gaza, to help restore the territory’s sewage system and allow wastewater to be treated in Israeli-controlled areas. Cogat did not respond to a request for comment. Zalul said: “If the pollution continues, its impact could eventually be felt throughout the country. When the marine environment is contaminated, both people and nature suffer. Regardless of which side of the border they are on.”

webTitle: Thursday briefing: Andy Burnham wants to remake Britain from the regions up. Can it work?

fields.headline: Thursday briefing: Andy Burnham wants to remake Britain from the regions up. Can it work?
fields.trailText: In today’s newsletter: The newish prime minister wants to shift power out of Westminster, but fragile councils, patchy financial scrutiny and dwindling local journalism could put his plans at risk
fields.bodyText: Good morning. Over the summer, I interviewed more than 40 people who are trying to influence the new Labour government for the Guardian Long Read, among them thinktank researchers and politicians. The piece, published this morning, tries to work out how radical Andy Burnham intends to be. So far, his big idea is to give more power and money to England’s regions than ever before – and while “devolution” isn’t a word that sets pulses racing, this plan could be genuinely transformative. Yet, since writing the piece, one thing that has nagged at me is the wider picture. Local media has been gutted. Mechanisms for scrutinising local authority finances have disappeared. Local services and the public realm have been vaporised. Cash-strapped councils have made risky investments and gone bankrupt. All of this amounts to something bigger than a single crisis of accountability; the state’s legitimacy has been eroded, leaving people disenchanted with and distrustful of politics. Burnham is hoping that devolution will renew people’s faith in democracy. But the wider context poses huge risks to this project before it has barely even begun. Today’s newsletter discusses these risks and opportunities with Josh Halliday, the Guardian’s north of England editor, who wrote yesterday about the need for greater scrutiny of mayors. First, the headlines. Five big stories Climate crisis | The UK has warned that the climate crisis and coming El Niño threaten national security and defence around the world, presenting foreign ministries with the findings of an explosive report suppressed under Keir Starmer. US news | A federal judge has ordered the Trump administration to restore ⁠White House ⁠access to journalists from CNN, MS Now and Politico, ⁠saying his ban on the three media outlets was ⁠likely unconstitutional. Education | Teenagers are to be offered a range of new vocational GCSEs under a radical shake-up of the school system in England designed to tackle a crisis that has left nearly a million young people out of work or training. Conservatives | People claiming universal credit would have their payments cut by a third if they have not paid enough national insurance, under a Conservative plan condemned by one charity as “a fast track to increased poverty”. Football | Andy Burnham has signalled he may lift the ban on drinking alcohol in the stands at football matches, suggesting it is “unfair” for fans to be singled out when it is permitted for other sports. In depth: ‘A seminal moment … but the risks are huge’ Burnham, with his behind-the-scenes TikTok video of No 10 North, has made devolving power away from Westminster his central big idea. “If anything had brought me into parliament, it was a mission to close the North-South divide,” he wrote in his 2024 book, Head North. “Seeing how things worked from the inside, I finally understood why England has always felt like two countries.” The clearest statement of this intention since he became prime minister is a paper his cabinet published in July, which outlined plans to let mayors keep a share of income tax generated in their areas and give them greater control over skills, transport and public services. “These plans are a seminal moment in terms of how Britain is run,” Josh Halliday tells me. “But the risks are huge. It just takes one or two bad scandals – such as the bankruptcy of Birmingham council – to really damage the legitimacy of the whole project.” Here’s how those risks break down. *** The media | A shrinking local press Burnham was the mayor of a city comparatively well-served by the media. The Guardian was founded in Manchester and continues to have a newsroom of reporters there (including Josh). Despite the ongoing decline of regional journalism, flourishing media start-ups and subscription newsletters in cities like Manchester, Glasgow, and Birmingham have proven there is still demand for quality local journalism. There have also been wider initiatives to address England’s “news deserts”, such as the BBC Local Democracy Reporting Service. But the bigger picture is one of endless closures and cuts. Reach, the owner of regional titles in England, announced a further round of 220 redundancies (though plans to create 60 new roles) two weeks ago. Even Burnham, who started his career writing for publications such as Tank World, moved to London to find work in journalism. Josh, who graduated from Sunderland university in 2010, used to dream of working for a local newspaper, but found it difficult to even get a work experience placement. “There are fewer and fewer local journalists, which means fewer people keeping an eye on council meetings or scrutinising budget reports,” he tells me. “And that’s really worrying.” *** Local democracy | Participation has been ‘squeezed’ Journalism isn’t the only institution that holds politicians’ feet to the fire. Civil society plays a crucial role, but the cost of living crisis and the gradual erosion of the institutions that bind people together have diminished people’s involvement in politics. “We often talk about the cost of living crisis as a financial squeeze,” Sarah Longlands, the chief executive of the Centre for Local Economic Strategies in Manchester, tells me. “But it’s also squeezed people’s ability to turn up at local campaign groups, to attend town council meetings, to run as councillors themselves, because they’re just focused on the day-to-day of getting by.” For most people, politics isn’t about nuclear deterrents or Westminster white papers, but about how often the bins get emptied or whether the library stays open. In recent years, local authorities have sold off local assets and outsourced public services to faceless providers. This, Sarah says, has robbed people of institutions that give them a stake in their communities. “Take away publicly funded local services, and you take away the frontline engagement and relationship between councils and communities that form part of democracy,” she says. She is particularly concerned that Burnham may decide to go ahead with a plan to reorganise local government that he inherited from his predecessor. Those plans are now on pause, but two professors recently described in the Guardian’s letter pages how the scheme could result in the disappearance of as many as 75% of England’s existing councils, eliminating institutions that have close ties to communities, and making services even more anonymous and detached. *** Scrutiny | Who will keep an eye on the money Over the last decade there’s been a vacuum of information about the financial decisions taken by councils. In 2015, David Cameron abolished the Audit Commission, a body that scoured local governments’ accounts every year. Since then, some struggling councils have gone on reckless spending sprees, buying office blocks and shopping centres while cutting back on local services. Some have since declared bankruptcy. “The National Audit Office will get called in to investigate, but only once there’s already been an emergency,” Josh tells me. “They’re not a safeguard against financial crises.” The Starmer government introduced plans for a new Local Audit Office, which should help address some of these problems, and Burnham’s government is expected to publish further details of its plans for accountability in a few weeks’ time alongside its first budget. Amid all this is a wider question about how to make the devolution of power genuinely democratic. Sarah suggests that any new authority or mayoralty should commit to an ongoing citizens’ assembly, where residents can collectively decide how new resources are allocated, and scrutinise government spending. “The government mainly talks about devolution as a way to drive growth,” she says. “But this could be a cutting edge way to redesign British democracy, so it really works for people.” What else we’ve been enjoying Nesrine Malik examines why enslavement remains absent from mainstream British history in our sister newsletter, The Long Wave, after the Guardian revealed new detail of domestic slave traders and the institutions they funded. Libby Ammar Kalia’s ranking of 100 unusual crisp flavours is both useful and an absolute hoot. It also seems to have been a brave undertaking, considering some of Ammar’s verdicts: “they leave a luminescent blue powder on your fingers and smell of urinal cakes”. Lucinda Everett, newsletters team Not only are adults failing to act effectively on the climate crisis, we’re also rubbish at explaining its realities to kids. So I was pleased to read that New York Climate Week is getting some help from Sesame Street. Libby I enjoyed Matthew Pearce’s interview with author Russell Warfield, who argues that Zack Polanski’s “eco-populist” package is “not a departure from Green tradition, but the culmination of a 50-year evolution which has turned the party into the main electoral force on the British left.” Lucinda Dani Garavelli’s diary of her visit to Mussolini’s birthplace in this week’s London Review of Books is a timely reminder of the echoes of Il Duce in Italy’s current politics. Libby Sport Football | Manchester United have reported an annual loss for the seventh successive year, taking the club’s combined losses to £444m since 2019. Rugby | Steve Borthwick has secured a boost for his preparations for next year’s World Cup thanks to an overhaul in the refereeing of Prem matches for the coming season designed to help England’s hopes in Australia. Football | Cristiano Ronaldo said he considered quitting international football after the World Cup, but confirmed he plans to play on for Portugal and hopes to reach 1,000 goals for club and country. The front pages The Guardian leads with “PM unveils new vocational GCSEs in biggest exam shake-up in decade”. The Telegraph has “Tories to ban spending benefits on alcohol”, while the Times follows the same story with “Tories to cut benefits for long-term unemployed”. The Mail characterises the announcement as “Kemi’s ruthless crackdown on benefits street”. The i has “EU Brexit chief: UK can get a Canada-style membership deal with us”. The Financial Times reports “Healey weighs smaller fiscal headroom to reduce tax rises”. The Mirror covers the crash of an RAF jet under the headline “Miracle no on was killed”. And the Sun looks at the reported axing of alcohol bans in football stadiums with “Going down going down going down.. rather nicely!” Today in Focus: The Latest Has Burnham proved he can handle Trump? Andy Burnham has navigated his way through a first high-stakes meeting with Donald Trump at the UN general assembly in New York. The prime minister’s aides were delighted with how the meeting went, as Trump praised the US-UK relationship and described Burnham as a ‘natural businessman’. The anticipated sticking points – the Chagos Islands, West Bank settlement sanctions and Ireland – appear not to have derailed the talks nor cast a shadow over the future relationship. Lucy Hough speaks to policy editor Kiran Stacey. Cartoon of the day | Ben Jennings The Upside A bit of good news to remind you that the world’s not all bad The landmark documentary 7 Up, which launched 63 years ago, followed the lives of 10 boys and four girls in England, beginning when they were seven years old, and returning every seven years. As its final season, 70 Up, concludes, seven people have shared the profound effects the show has had on them over the decades. “The series changed my life,” says Martin Forsey, 65. “I retrained and became a sociologist and anthropologist because of it.” Lyle Jackson, 72, was inspired to become a documentary photographer and producer, and went on to win 18 regional Emmys. And others found important life lessons within the show. “It seemed that the real measure of success was not academic or material achievements after all,” says Sheila Lambe, 63, “but familial love and finding peace.” Sign up here for a weekly roundup of The Upside, sent to you every Sunday Bored at work? And finally, the Guardian’s puzzles are here to keep you entertained throughout the day. Until tomorrow. Quick crossword Cryptic crossword Wordiply

webTitle: Benjamin Netanyahu to deliver defiant UN speech while facing protests and political isolation

fields.headline: Benjamin Netanyahu to deliver defiant UN speech while facing protests and political isolation
fields.trailText: Prime minister will ‘highlight Israel’s achievements’ as he heads towards his toughest re-election challenge
fields.bodyText: When he takes the stage at the UN on Thursday, Benjamin Netanyahu will deliver a familiar message of defiance even as protests and international condemnation leave the Israeli leader in growing isolation. Netanyahu is facing his toughest re-election challenge in a political career spanning decades with three ongoing conflicts in Gaza, Lebanon and Iran, and a growing campaign of violence by Israeli settlers in the West Bank. Internationally, Israel is facing growing condemnation. The UK, France and Canada are planning to sanction Israeli settlements in the West Bank, and the British foreign secretary, Ed Miliband, has accused Israeli settlers of committing ethnic cleansing of Palestinian communities. And the US is in the midst of a historic shift in public opinion against Israel, with 62% of respondents telling Pew in July they had a negative opinion of Netanyahu’s government, and 60% of American Jews in a poll released this week hoping he is voted out in October. Protests are expected both in the UN’s general assembly hall and on the streets of New York City, where mayor Zohran Mamdani has tempered his earlier promises to arrest Netanyahu as a war criminal to assure demonstrators this week that he would protect their “right to [protest] in this city”. Danny Danon, Israel’s ambassador to the UN, defended Netanyahu’s government in a telephone interview before this week’s speech seeking to cast criticism of Israel’s actions as the product of misinformation and bias. “We are aware of the fact that we had a very challenging three years since October 7,” said Danon. “We accomplished a lot, but we were criticised. We were under the spotlight, and for us, I think, we are proud of our achievements.” “At the same time, we will work harder to improve the image of Israel, and we know there’s a campaign against us,” he added. Anger at Netanyahu will be on full display in New York City on Thursday, where several protests have been scheduled, including one from Bryant Park in midtown Manhattan to the UN headquarters in Turtle Bay to “reject war criminal Benjamin Netanyahu and the genocidal Zionist project”. “Netanyahu is coming to New York amid a political environment that has made it crystal clear that he is not welcome here,” said Beth Miller, the political director of Jewish Voice for Peace Action. She described a “mainstreaming” of public opinion that “Americans do not want to be supporting Israel’s genocide. We do not want to be supporting Israel’s apartheid. We do not want to be arming Israel or supporting Israel.” And Palestinian representatives are calling for diplomatic missions to bring staff for a planned walkout of Netanyahu’s speech to “send a clear message to Netanyahu and his government that no one is willing to aid, abet, or be complicit in its genocide and war crimes and illegal occupation, which all peace-loving states and peoples demand must come to an end”. But in Danon’s telling, Israel’s problem was largely one of public relations rather than of policy, and he cited a “wave of misinformation” as the reason for the precipitous shift in polling. Netanyahu would use his speech to “highlight Israel’s achievements”, he said, and to lay out “what still should be done, and how should we verify that we actually achieve the goals of the war?” He did not elaborate on those specific measures before the speech, but the White House and US policymakers will be listening as they calibrate their message to voters – as well as the backlash of public anger – ahead of the upcoming midterm elections. Netanyahu is expected to deliver a hardline message aimed not just at world leaders, but also to his own electorate in Israel ahead of the October elections. “I think that he is trying to demonstrate to the Israeli populace that he still maintains some level of control over the situation,” said Miller. “And I think that he is trying to speak to a rightwing audience and a Trump-Maga audience in this country to try to rile up the hatred and Islamophobia.” Donald Trump and top US officials are not expected to meet with Netanyahu, however, during a visit expected to last less than 24 hours. Trump will be in Washington DC to host the Chinese leader, Xi Jinping, and Netanyahu has cited Israel’s electoral campaign and the holiday of Sukkot as his reason to head home quickly after the speech. A Trump administration official said Netanyahu’s delegation had sought a high-level meeting during the visit but none was organised. There are also no plans to meet congressional leaders, Danon said. With criticism from top Republicans, including the vice-president, JD Vance, and leading democratic presidential contenders, Israel could face a 2028 campaign with two candidates who no longer support arms sales to Israel or the broad diplomatic support that it has enjoyed in the past. Even within the Maga base there are fractures, Miller noted, with “more and more people who don’t really want to be sending our tax dollars to support the Israeli government”. Danon said of a potential shift in the US-Israeli security relationship: “I think that we are still sharing the same values, and that’s why I’m sure that we will continue to have the support from the US.” But there are multiple flashpoints now for anger from both US political parties, as well as the international community, including dire humanitarian concerns and the lack of reconstruction in Gaza, the expansion of settlements in the West Bank, and continued conflicts in Lebanon and Iran, where the US has found itself mired in a conflict that has driven up global energy prices. Asked if a controversial $2.8bn (£2.1bn) arms sale indicated that Israel is preparing to resume its offensive in Gaza, Danon said Israel “hopes that we will see [Hamas’s] disarmament without our involvement”, nodding to efforts by the Trump-backed Board of Peace. But he said Israel “will do it ourselves” if that does not change, adding: “We can not leave it forever like that.” He was equally resolute on the West Bank, saying that Israel would not be swayed by recent criticism led by the UK over plans to expand settlements including E1, the planned construction which would sever East Jerusalem from the rest of the West Bank. Senate Democrats are also introducing a bill on Wednesday to sanction facilitators of the new settlement, and Senator Chris Coons, a co-sponsor, said in a statement that “as Palestinian civilians face a campaign of devastation and fear from violent extremist settlers, the United States must send a strong message that this behaviour is unacceptable”. The protests began even before Netanyahu arrived in New York. Already on Wednesday, several members of the Democratic Socialists of America’s New York City chapter rallied at the city’s John F Kennedy international airport in protest at weapons and explosive materials destined for the Israeli military being flown out of the airport on commercial aircraft. Aber Kawas, who in November is slated to become the first Palestinian-American elected official in New York state, spoke at the event and later told the Guardian she plans to join many other New Yorkers protesting Nethanyahu’s UN speech on Thursday. “Thousands of people are against his presence in our city,” she said. Even though some had hailed Netanyahu’s decision to cut his visit short as a victory, she added, “the fact that he is coming shows he continues to have a sense of entitlement to be centred on the world stage while being the head architect of a genocide”.

webTitle: Racist abuse of French judo star Teddy Riner investigated after he spoke about rise of far right

fields.headline: Racist abuse of French judo star Teddy Riner investigated after he spoke about rise of far right
fields.trailText: Paris’s public prosecutor opens investigation into online harassment of Riner, one of France’s most popular sportspeople
fields.bodyText: Paris’s public prosecutor has opened an investigation into the racist abuse and online harassment of the French judo star Teddy Riner after he expressed concern about the rise of the far right. Riner, who has often been voted France’s most popular sportsperson and is one of the most successful judo competitors of all time, told a TV sports show this month that he felt “anxiety” about the rise of the far right in France. Numerous racist insults and hate messages were subsequently directed at him online, the prosecutor’s office said. The far-right, anti-immigration National Rally (RN) party politician Marine Le Pen is polling high ahead of next spring’s presidential election. The French football team captain and Real Madrid player, Kylian Mbappé, was at the centre of a row in May when he expressed concerns that Le Pen’s party could win the presidential election. Riner, 37, who was born on the French Caribbean island of Guadeloupe and grew up in Paris, has a massive following in France, where his ability to swiftly throw and pin his judo opponents to the ground made him a star the Paris 2024 Olympics. He is a French gold medal hope for the 2028 Los Angeles Olympics. Riner wrote on social media on Thursday: “Debate and contradiction are legitimate. Hatred and racism are not.” Earlier, he told the state broadcaster France 2 he would continue to speak out. “I grew up in a France where people in difficulty were close-knit and united. Today’s attempts to divide France, to create an mood of instability are unfamiliar to me. What will we leave for our kids tomorrow? The France I want is the France I grew up in where everyone knew how to live together.” In May, Mbappé, 27, who grew up in Paris’s northern suburbs in a family with Algerian and Cameroonian heritage, was criticised by RN party figures after he told Vanity Fair: “I know what it means and what consequences it can have for my country when people like them come to power.” Le Pen told RTL radio at the time that she found it reassuring that Mbappé did not want her party to win, because his own strategy of leaving Paris Saint-Germain in order to win at Real Madrid had not worked. “Frankly I think football fans are free enough to know who to vote for without being influenced by Mbappé,” she said. Julien Odoul, an RN MP and party spokesperson, said that Mbappé, as the captain of the French men’s team, must represent all of France including the millions of RN voters, and should not become a “political activist”. Riner wrote on social media: “Being a high level sportsperson does not stop you keeping your feet on the ground and having an attentive eye on your country.” He said he shared many French people’s concerns about the “current situation” in France – describing what he called rising anger, people struggling to make ends meet, plummeting respect for institutions, the fragility of the French education system and lack of perspective for young people. Riner wrote: “I love France deeply – I’m defending its history, its talent, its heritage, its republican values and its diversity.”

webTitle: After so long in Trump’s sights, hopeful Greenlanders breathe a collective sigh of relief

fields.headline: After so long in Trump’s sights, hopeful Greenlanders breathe a collective sigh of relief
fields.trailText: Locals hope agreement signed this week is step towards independence and end to US threats to annex island
fields.bodyText: Greenland’s prime minister, Jens-Frederik Nielsen, and Múte B Egede, the foreign minister, received a hero’s welcome when they landed back in Nuuk from New York on Wednesday night – and a nation took a collective sigh of relief. Colleagues, friends and members of the public turned out to greet them at an airport where, just 20 months ago, the landing of a Trump-branded plane containing Donald Trump Jr had kickstarted a geopolitical crisis that the people of Greenland now hope is over. To cheers and applause, and waving red and white Erfalasorput flags, the politicians were credited with saving the nation thanks to a new defence agreement between Greenland, Denmark and the US signed this week at the UN in New York. It comes after an unprecedented period of turbulence in which Donald Trump repeatedly threatened to invade the Arctic island and almost tore apart Nato in the process. “Welcome home,” the speaker of Inatsisartut, the Greenlandic parliament, Kim Kielsen, said. “Welcome to a country that we were about to lose. You have ensured that we have a future here.” Like many Greenlanders, for the last year-and-a-half he said he had been holding his breath. Nielsen, who became prime minister last year in the middle of the crisis, told the crowd: “We can be calm. Our land will not be taken. Our land will not be bought. The road has been long, and it has been very difficult and dangerous.” Hundreds then attended a celebratory coffee party at Katuaq, the Greenlandic capital’s cultural centre. Aqqalukkuluk Fontain, 38, who was there with his girlfriend, Stella, and their youngest daughter, Aura, who is three, said the collective release of tension was palpable. “It was a joyous moment. It’s going to linger for a while,” said the IT manager, who earlier this year organised a protest outside the new US embassy in Nuuk. He cautioned he could not entirely relax – concerned that, after the midterms, Trump could change his mind and relations could “take a turn for the worse” – but hailed the deal with the US as a moment of pride for Greenland and a stroke of “strategy genius” from Greenlandic and Danish negotiators. “Trump is trying to angle it that he made a great deal. But he wanted total control, ownership of Greenland. He didn’t get that,” he said. Its full text contains some key differences from the 1951 defence agreement it is intended to update – for example, the US gets underwater access to Greenland and specific permission to construct a missile defence system – but is a far cry from Donald Trump’s original threat to annex the Arctic island. And in terms of tangible outcomes, the biggest winner is arguably Greenland, where it is seen as a potential stepping stone to future independence. When the 1951 agreement was signed, Greenland was still a colony of Denmark. Now, it is a largely autonomous territory that has signed an agreement alongside Denmark with the US that it played a central role in negotiating. A big question hanging over Greenland independence was what would happen to its status within Nato and relationship with the US. The new agreement answers that question. It stipulates that if it did become independent, the governments of Greenland and Denmark would “together ensure that the independent Greenlandic state will agree to remain in Nato, including by applying to become a member if necessary”. The centrality of Nato to the agreement is also seen as a boost for an alliance that was creaking under US claims against one of its fellow members’ territory. Greenlandic politician Qarsoq Høegh-Dam, who earlier this year became the first member of the pro-independence party Naleraq to be elected to the Danish parliament, said there was still considerable work to do in terms of gaining independence but that “a lot of what ifs” have now gone. “It’s a point of relief for Greenlanders,” he said. “They can lower their shoulders a bit, so we can talk about domestic issues, the road to independence more freely, instead of the search of what if?” Much of the agreement already existed in practice, he said, but now “it is written in ink” with Greenland’s explicit involvement. “It’s a continuation of an agreement since the 1950s. The difference is now that Greenland has some say in it. They want to agree for themselves instead of a country overseas agreeing on behalf of them,” he said. “That’s the difference first and foremost and it is significant.” He said, however, there were still questions about what the words will equate to in practice, for example on investment. “It’s a good foundation, but the details are missing,” he said. Given that just a few months ago Trump was threatening to invade Greenland, and a few weeks since he posted a map of Greenland covered with the US flag to social media, in many ways the very fact that a diplomatic agreement has been reached is a victory in itself. Ulrik Pram Gad, a senior researcher at the Danish Institute for International Studies (DIIS), said: “For Danes and Greenlanders, it’s a win to be able to force Trump into doing something diplomatically. And if this actually puts the Greenland crisis to rest, it will be felt as a win for Greenland, Denmark and Europe because then we can concentrate on real problems and trying to find ways to work with the US on that.” Aviaja Fontain, 41, a student from Nuuk, said the agreement puts to rest months of anxiety. At one point, amid government warnings about preparedness, she thought Nuuk was being attacked by the US during what turned out to be a power cut caused by a storm. “Many of us have been afraid that Trump will use force, but now I can feel relief,” she said. Now she feels she can finally relax. “We don’t have to think about getting attacked and just live our peaceful life again.”

webTitle: Leaders join push to create UN body to tackle ‘awful reality’ of inequality

fields.headline: Leaders join push to create UN body to tackle ‘awful reality’ of inequality
fields.trailText: Body would be modelled on climate panel and recognise inequality as a global challenge threatening world security
fields.bodyText: Plans to set up a global UN body on inequality modelled on the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC) are likely to be proposed to a meeting of the UN general assembly in the coming months. Speaking at an event on the sidelines of the general assembly in New York, left-leaning leaders from Brazil, Norway and Spain claimed momentum was building behind calls for a standing international panel on inequality that would recognise the issue as a global challenge threatening world security. Two G7 countries – Germany and Japan – have given public backing. Joseph Stiglitz, the Nobel prize-winning economist, recommended the establishment of the new body in a report commissioned by South Africa for its G20 chairing last November. The dislocation caused by inequality was also the focus of the 2024 G20 meeting, chaired by Brazil. But the proposal is likely to make little political headway during this year’s G20, to be led by Donald Trump, and some countries are wary of talk about new globally imposed taxes, or assertions that economic analysis can be compared to climate science. The UK foreign secretary, Ed Miliband, has said he wants inequality to be part of the agenda of the UK-chaired 2027 G20, but no British diplomat spoke at this week’s high-level event on the issue. Cyril Ramaphosa, the South African president, told this week’s meeting that inequality was “the new multilateral frontier”. “Inequality is not inevitable but a problem that can be solved with evidence, analysis and political action,” he said. The panel would not just track trends but propose solutions, though many would be likely to face opposition from multinationals and billionaires. The Spanish prime minister, Pedro Sánchez, argued: “Inequality is not an abstract concept but an awful reality. It is about disaffection and whether the people feel the system is working against them.” He added: “Think what the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change has done for climate change – bringing together the best available knowledge, independently assessing the evidence and giving governments around the world a scientific basis on which to act. We need something similar for inequality, and we need to do it now. Not ideology but knowledge. Not another layer of bureaucracy but instead a tool for better policymaking.” Spain’s foreign affairs minister, José Manuel Albares, said progressive tax systems and better tax cooperation were necessary to prevent tax evasion. The UN deputy secretary general, Amina Mohammed, told the meeting: “We see breathtaking levels of income and wealth inequality; the richest 10% earning 75% of all wealth. This emergency could get worse – and fast. The breakneck emergence of frontier technology, and the concentration of this technology in a tiny number of hands, could unleash global inequality on a scale far beyond what we have ever seen. A world in which only a few powerful countries are wealthy is a ticking timebomb.” Stiglitz, an advocate of a billionaire’s wealth tax in California, said: “Inequality within and between nations is a collective threat to the functioning of our economies, and our ability to support human dignity. This kind of global stress akin to the crisis of climate change needs to be very much better understood and studied in the same way.” Mia Mottley, the prime minister of Barbados, said the need for a groundbreaking general assembly resolution to establish the panel was urgent. She asked: “Who is really participating in growth, who owns the assets and who shapes the rules?” Referring to a UN resolution in March condemning the transatlantic chattel slave trade as the “gravest crime against humanity” and calling for reparative justice, she added: “If we condemn slavery, we condemn the notion of people exploiting other human beings in order to make profit, but slavery is just the extreme condition, and as I have come to reflect more and more, the mens rea [criminal intent] that informs slavery, regrettably, is still existent in the modern world.” Drawing on the Stiglitz report to last year’s G20, she said that between 2000 and 2024 the richest 1% captured 41% of all new global wealth, while 50% of the world’s population received just 1%. “Equal effort therefore does not guarantee equal opportunity,” she said. Sarah Colenbrander, the director of the climate and sustainability programme at the London-based thinktank ODI Global, said: “The IPCC has consistently demonstrated the overwhelming scientific consensus on the importance of cutting emissions and the consequences of failing to do so. A panel on inequality could likewise cut through the noise and make the case for poverty reduction and wealth redistribution. But she warned: “We have seen that the IPCC’s summaries for policymakers have consistently been watered down by countries with fossil fuel interests. In the same vein, it is hard to imagine that billionaires – and the world leaders among them or in their pockets – would engage constructively.”

webTitle: Germany investigates 105-year-old suspected former Nazi prison camp guard

fields.headline: Germany investigates 105-year-old suspected former Nazi prison camp guard
fields.trailText: Man accused of being accessory to murders at Stalag 326 VI K amid race to prosecute suspects before they die
fields.bodyText: A 105-year-old man is under investigation on suspicion of being an accessory to multiple murders at a Nazi prisoner of war camp, German prosecutors have said. The case, which is being handled by the public prosecutor’s office in Dortmund, centres on the Stalag 326 VI K camp in western Germany, in what is now the state of North Rhine-Westphalia. “The 105-year-old suspect is thought to have been a guard at the prisoner of war camp Stalag 326 VI K in the Senne region of western Germany,” prosecutors said in a statement. The man is “accused of being an accessory to multiple murders owing to his activities there”, they said. The Senne camp housed between 180,000 and 200,000 Soviet prisoners of war between 1941 and April 1945, when it was liberated by American troops. The investigation is the result of an urgent last-minute scramble by the judiciary to prosecute alleged participants in the Nazi killing machine before they die. The judicial efforts stem in part from a recognition that many of the suspects who have escaped prosecution in the eight decades since the end of the second world war on the grounds that they were considered to have played an insignificant role were in fact integral to the implementation of the Hitler regime’s murderous aims. A judicial precedent was set by the court case of John Demjanjuk, a former guard at the Nazi Sobibór death camp in occupied Poland, who was convicted in 2011 of being an accomplice to the murders of more than 28,000 Jews that took place in the time he worked there. Prosecutors had sought Ukraine-born Demjanjuk’s extradition from his Ohio home to Germany for years, arguing that he was complicit in the crimes committed at Sobibór despite a lack of evidence that he had directly killed anyone. Demjanjuk died aged 91 in March 2012 awaiting an appeal due to his age and frailty, which meant he did not go to prison. The Demjanjuk case lowered the bar for proof of complicity, paving the way for other nonagenarians and more recently centenarians to stand trial. The most prominent trial of recent years, and representative of what Hannah Arendt, a political theorist, described as a Schreibtischtäter (desk perpetrator, or bureaucratic mediator), was that of Irmgard Furchner, who worked at the Stutthof concentration camp between 1943 and 1945 as a secretary to the camp commandant. She was given a two-year suspended sentence for her role as an accessory to murder. Her trial was, contrary to normal rules, filmed for historical purposes. Furchner made headlines after running away from her retirement home on the scheduled opening day of her trial. Josef Schütz, a former guard at the Sachsenhausen concentration camp north of Berlin, was sentenced for being an accomplice to murder to five years in prison in June 2022. He died the following year, aged 102. In April last year an alleged former guard at Sachsenhausen died before he was able to face trial over charges of complicity in the murder of more than 3,300 people. A separate investigation was opened last year by Dortmund prosecutors into a 100-year-old former guard at a PoW camp in Hemer, North Rhine-Westphalia, which also held mainly Soviet prisoners. He is suspected of participating in executions of prisoners between December 1943 and September 1944. The new investigation was initiated by the Central Office for the Investigation of National Socialist Crimes in Ludwigsburg, in the southern state of Baden-Württemberg, which passed its preliminary investigation into the man to public prosecutors along with that of another former guard. The other suspect has since died, according to German media. If the trial goes ahead, like other recent cases it is expected to throw light on the Stalag system in general and on Senne in particular, drawing survivors and historians to give evidence. Up to 5.7 million Soviet prisoners were held captivity in Germany. More than half did not survive.

webTitle: Australia’s newest chicken factory looks like a modern art gallery – but will it improve animal welfare?

fields.headline: Australia’s newest chicken factory looks like a modern art gallery – but will it improve animal welfare?
fields.trailText: Three million chickens a week will be processed at the state-of-the-art facility in Tamworth – a fifth of all those eaten nationwide
fields.bodyText: Is it for birds? Is it for planes? The sleek, rust-coloured saucer settles into the earth, mirroring the surrounding hills. It looks like an art gallery or a high-end conference centre – an architectural masterpiece designed to sit lightly on the land. Until you see the shed behind it. The sweeping lines are the gateway to a $600m poultry processing plant that will, at full capacity, process 3 million chickens a week. Located in Tamworth, 300km north of Sydney, the new facility is owned by Baiada, one of Australia’s two largest chicken producers and the owner of household brand names Steggles and Lilydale Free Range. At its height, two lines will process 15,000 birds an hour as chickens fly through state-of-the-art chilling systems and automated packing machines en route to supermarkets across the state. The new plant will support more than 1,000 jobs, with workers able to spend their lunch breaks at an on-site cafeteria, at a gym or in landscaped gardens. Jeff Budd, the deputy mayor of Tamworth regional council, has toured the facility, which opened last week. He says the unusual design creates a gem for the city and will attract the skilled workers and technicians needed to run kilometres’ worth of conveyor belts and systems. “I think it’s massive for the entire region,” he says. “The Baiada company … certainly made it look that way. Once you’re inside that main building at the front, it’s like a five-star hotel.” Australians are voracious chicken eaters, consuming an average of 55kg of chicken meat per person per year. Almost half of all meat eaten in Australia is chicken, and consumption has doubled in the past 30 years. More than 800 million chickens will be slaughtered this financial year to meet the demand. Once fully operational, the Oakburn facility will account for almost 20% of that. “We’re happy to see a commitment from a Sydney-based company to one of their regional hubs, to put in such a sophisticated [facility],” says Prof Stephen Walkden-Brown, the interim director of Poultry Hub Australia at the University of New England. “It’s a pretty big development, one of the most modern plants in the world.” Sign up for the Breaking News Australia email In a media release, Baiada said the company had “grown alongside” the Tamworth community for six decades, and the facility reflected the company’s commitment to the city. “This is a long-term investment in Tamworth and the people who have supported Baiada for generations,” the managing director, Simon Camilleri, says. “Our history in this region stretches back to the 1960s, when Charlie Baiada first established operations here, and this facility reflects our confidence in the future of Tamworth.” But it did not answer questions about whether the new facility would also deliver improved animal welfare outcomes. Jed Goodfellow, the director of policy and government relations at the Australian Alliance for Animals, says while the Baiada building may be state of the art, he believes “the welfare model behind it is anything but”. Slowing the growth A leading welfare issue, Goodfellow says, is the speed at which meat chickens grow. “Chickens are still being selectively bred to grow at extraordinary speeds, with their bodies paying the price for ever greater efficiency,” he says. “Healthier, slower-growing breeds are now being used in many parts of the world, particularly Europe, with Norway, the Netherlands and France producing higher welfare breeds at scale. “It may cost slightly more but, as their experience shows, the increase is not prohibitive, as European consumers increasingly opt for the healthier option.” Melina Tensen, the senior scientific officer for farm animals at the RSPCA, says about 97% of chicken meat sold in Australia abides by the organisation’s welfare standards. “It’s a pretty big deal to have most of industry achieving standards to go well above the legal minimum,” Tensen says. “Wherever animals are farmed for food – and they’re going to be farmed for food for a long time to come – we want to be in there making sure that animals are raised and handled and transported and slaughtered in ways we find acceptable.” Welfare standards were updated this month to promote lower stocking density, variable light intensity in sheds – to allow chickens to choose between brighter and darker areas – and the phasing out of a slaughtering method called electrical water bath stunning. Those changes must be enacted by 1 January 2031 for businesses to keep their RSPCA certification. At the same time, the RSPCA has released a new category of “enhanced” welfare standards, which are primarily focused on encouraging producers to rear slower-growing breeds. Most of Australia’s commercial chickens are two fast-growing breeds, the Ross 308 and the Cobb 500, which reach slaughter weight at between four and six weeks of age. Tensen says the RSPCA would ultimately like to see chicken meat producers replace fast-growing breeds with slower-growing breeds but consumers would have to help achieve that transition. “The longer it takes to grow, the greater cost,” she says. “We definitely encourage consumers to be vocal about supporting this transition … because every dollar you spend is a message to the retailer.”

webTitle: Rebel offensive against Ethiopian army stokes fears of return to civil war

fields.headline: Rebel offensive against Ethiopian army stokes fears of return to civil war
fields.trailText: Fighting escalates after Tigrayan rebels form new coalition aimed at overthrowing Abiy Ahmed government
fields.bodyText: There are growing fears of a return to civil war in Ethiopia after an offensive by fighters from Tigray into the neighbouring states of Afar and Amhara and the formation of a new rebel alliance aimed at overthrowing the government of the prime minister, Abiy Ahmed. About 600,000 people died between 2020 and 2022 during a devastating war between the Ethiopian army and the political party and paramilitary group the Tigray People’s Liberation Front (TPLF). Both sides are now accusing the other of triggering a return to open conflict. On Sunday, seven armed groups from around the country, including the TPLF, announced the formation of the Ethiopian Peoples’ Forces Alliance for Survival, aimed at deposing the government in Addis Ababa. Then, on Wednesday, the TPLF seized control of three airports from federal police. The state-owned carrier, Ethiopian Airlines, said it had suspended flights to the region “due to the current situation”. The TPLF also launched attacks into Afar and Amhara. A humanitarian source in Afar told Agence France-Presse there were heavy artillery attacks by the group on Thursday as they attempted to take control of the town of Yallo, near the Tigrayan border. Flights to the historic Ethiopian town of Lalibela were also suspended on Thursday because of nearby fighting, while people in Tigray stocked up ⁠on food and cash, with one resident telling Reuters that people there feared they could face siege conditions similar to those during the previous war. A resident of Adigrat, a city close to the Eritrean border, ‌described panic-buying and shops emptying. “Food shortages are worsening as market shelves sit empty … Essential medicines remain scarce and astronomically expensive,” he told Reuters. “Daily survival has become a constant calculation.” The TPLF’s vice-president, Amanuel Assefa, told AFP: “We are in the situation of full-blown war now.” He confirmed Tigrayan forces were fighting alongside local armed groups in Afar and Amhara. The group took control of Abala, also on the Tigray-Afar border, on Wednesday, a foreign security source based in Ethiopia told AFP, while a TPLF source said they had seized several other towns in Afar. The foreign security source also said there was fighting around the Amhara town of Weldiya – one of the few routes to the capital. In its first public comments on the fighting, Ethiopia’s army said on ⁠Thursday it had foiled the attacks and killed, wounded or captured more than 500 enemy fighters. Analysts say the TPLF has support from Ethiopia’s neighbour and historic adversary Eritrea, which fears landlocked Ethiopia is planning to invade its territory to gain access to the Red Sea. The TPLF’s Assefa told AFP “we have no information about Eritrea’s plan”. Asked if they would request Eritrean intervention, he said: “Not yet.” The current fighting reflects shifting dynamics from the civil war, when Eritrea and Fano, an insurgent group that is now part of the new alliance, both fought with the government against the Tigrayans. Speaking at the UN general assembly on Wednesday, the Ethiopian president, Taye Atske-Selassie Amde, decried “the forces of destruction and mayhem” and “interference in our internal affairs by adversarial elements”. He said Ethiopia had exercised “immense restraint” and made progress with its neighbours. Abiy’s spokesperson, Billene Seyoum, said members of the alliance had been collaborating for a while with the financial backing of Eritrea. Eritrea has repeatedly denied similar accusations. The TPLF ruled Ethiopia from 1991 to 2018 before being sidelined by the rise of Abiy, eventually triggering the civil war. The renewed fighting marks the most serious challenge yet to the 2022 Pretoria agreement, which ended the civil war and maintained an uneasy calm until late last year, when clashes resumed. It raises fears of a broader regional conflict that could draw in armed groups from across and further destabilise a region already strained by war in neighbouring Sudan and tensions along the Red Sea. On Wednesday, the African Union chair, Mahmoud Ali Youssouf, urged “utmost restraint” from the warring parties and resumption of direct talks. An EU spokesperson called for “immediate de-escalation” and a recommitment to the Pretoria agreement. In the 2020-22 war, Tigray was largely cut off from the outside world as communications were severed, and access to food, cash and medicines was severely restricted, pushing hundreds of thousands of people into famine-like conditions. AFP and Reuters contributed reporting

webTitle: Rick Wakeman performs piano concert to 150 rescued moon bears in Vietnam
